English Translation (the source's own, p. 513) — "Through his power the rivers sport, since he has, by his thunderbolt, determined their limits ; establishing his supremacy (by killing Vritra) and granting recompense to the giver (of the oblation), he, the swift-moving, provided a resting place for Turviti."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), pp. 513–514 — tveṣasā — dīptena balena: "by shining splendour and by strength." sindhavaḥ: "here the word sindhu is explained as 'ocean', or as the seven rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā." rante — ramu krīḍāyām: "each shines (sports) in its own place: this is the sense." sīm — enān sindhūn: "this word has the sense of parigraha [taking in, i.e. 'all']; it also fills out the line, i.e. it signals an object fit to be accepted, and completes the sense of the Vedic sentence. 'sīm iti parigrahārthīyo vā padapūraṇo vā' (Ni. 1-[?] [?]) — in the Nirukta the same sense as above is stated of the word sīm." īśānakṛt: "points to Indra's greatness by his slaying of Vṛtra and the others." turvaṇiḥ — tūrṇasaṃbhajanaḥ: "one who vigilantly destroys enemies. turvaṇiḥ stūrṇavaniḥ (Ni. 6-14 [?]); or turvitā śatrūṇāṃ hiṃsitā — one who especially destroys foes (Indra)." turvītaye: "a certain great sage, Turvīta, who was sinking in the water." gādham — āvasthānayogyaṃ dhiṣṇyapradeśam: "a part of the house fit for dwelling in."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā p. 514 — noted briefly — Grammar page, noted briefly. rante: ramu krīḍāyām; chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ: laṅ in the present sense; third plural: jho 'ntaḥ: ant; bahulaṃ chandasi: loss of śap; Vedic loss of the root's final; no aṭ (bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi); nighāta, after a non-verb. āyacchat: yama uparame; laṅ, third singular tip; itaś ca: loss of i; iṣugamiyamāṃ chaḥ (Pā. 7-3-77 as read [?]): cha before śap; the augment aṭ; because of the yad word no nighāta (yadvṛttānnityam); initial acute from aṭ. īśānakṛt: īśānaṃ karoti; kṛñ + kvip; hrasvasya piti kṛti tuk: tuk; gatikārakopapadāt kṛt: accent of the first member. kaḥ: ḍukṛñ karaṇe; luṅ, third singular tip; itaś ca; cli luṅi: cli, whose loss is by mantre ghasahvaraṇaśavṛdahādyāṅ… (Pā. 2-4-80 as read [?]); sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ: guṇa of the root vowel; hal-ṅyābbhyo…: loss of ti; no aṭ by bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi; rutva, visarga; nighāta.

original pp. 515–518

Rik 12

Saṃhitā-pāṭha

अस्मा इदु प्र भरा तूतुजानो वृत्राय वज्रमीशानः कियेधाः । गोर्न पर्व वि रदा तिरश्चेष्यन्नर्णांस्यपां चरध्यै ॥ १२ ॥

asmā id u pra bharā tūtujāno vṛtrāya vajram īśānaḥ kiyedhāḥ | gor na parva vi radā tiraścēṣyann arṇāṃsy apāṃ caradhyai || 12 || Reading note: The Saṃhitā's tiraścēṣyan is read as tiraśceṣyan — tiraścā followed by iṣyan — as the Pada has tiraścā | iṣyan; the long ā of bharā and radā is the Saṃhitā lengthening of bhara, rada before a vowel/iti-less particle, noted in the grammar page.

Pada-pāṭha

अस्मै । इत् । ऊं इति । प्र । भर । तूतुजानः । वृत्राय । वज्रम् । ईशानः । कियेधाः । गोः । न । पर्व । वि । रद । तिरश्चा । इष्यन् । अर्णांसि । अपाम् । चरध्यै ॥ १२ ॥

asmai | it | ūṃ iti | pra | bhara | tūtujānaḥ | vṛtrāya | vajram | īśānaḥ | kiyedhāḥ | goḥ | na | parva | vi | rada | tiraścā | iṣyan | arṇāṃsi | apām | caradhyai || 12 ||

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

तूतुजान इति क्षिप्रनाम । तूतुजानस्त्वरमाणः । यद्वा । शत्रून्हिंसन् । ईशान ईश्वरः सर्वेषां कियेधाः कियतोऽनवधृतपरिमाणस्य बलस्य धाता । यद्वा । क्रमुमाणं शत्रुबलं दधात्यवस्थापयतीति कियेधाः । हे इन्द्र एवंभूतस्त्वमस्मै वृत्राय वज्रं प्र भर । इमं वृत्रं वज्रेण प्रहरेत्यर्थः । प्रहृत्य च अर्णांसि वृष्टिजलानीष्यन् तस्माद्वृत्रात्प्रेरयंस्त्वमपां चरध्यै तासामपां चरणाय भूप्रदेशं प्रति गमनाय तस्य वृत्रस्य मेघरूपस्य पर्व पर्वाण्यवयवसन्धीन् तिरश्चा तिर्यग्वस्थितेन वज्रेण वि रद । विलिख । छिन्धीत्यर्थः । तत्र दृष्टान्तः । गोर्न । यथा मांसस्य विकर्तारो लौकिकाः पुरुषाः पशोरवयवानितस्ततो विभजन्ति तद्वत् । अत्र निरुक्तं । अस्मै प्रहर तूर्णं त्वरमाणो वृत्राय वज्रमीशानः कियेधाः कियद्धा इति वा क्रमुमाणधा इति वा गोरिव पर्वाणि विरद मेघस्येष्यन्नर्णांस्यपां चरणाय । नि. ६-१० [?] ॥

tūtujāna iti kṣipra-nāma | tūtujānas tvaramāṇaḥ | yadvā | śatrūn hiṃsan | īśāna īśvaraḥ sarveṣāṃ kiyedhāḥ kiyato 'navadhṛtaparimāṇasya balasya dhātā | yadvā | kramumāṇaṃ śatrubalaṃ dadhāty avasthāpayatīti kiyedhāḥ | he indra evaṃbhūtas tvam asmai vṛtrāya vajraṃ pra bhara | imaṃ vṛtraṃ vajreṇa praharety arthaḥ | prahṛtya ca arṇāṃsi vṛṣṭijalāny iṣyan tasmād vṛtrāt prerayaṃs tvam apāṃ caradhyai tāsām apāṃ caraṇāya bhūpradeśaṃ prati gamanāya tasya vṛtrasya megharūpasya parva parvāṇy avayavasandhīn tiraścā tiryagavasthitena vajreṇa vi rada | vilikha | chindhīty arthaḥ | tatra dṛṣṭāntaḥ | gor na | yathā māṃsasya vikartāro laukikāḥ puruṣāḥ paśor avayavān itas tato vibhajanti tadvat | atra niruktaṃ | asmai prahara tūrṇaṃ tvaramāṇo vṛtrāya vajram īśānaḥ kiyedhāḥ kiyaddhā iti vā kramumāṇadhā iti vā gor iva parvāṇi virada meghasyeṣyann arṇāṃsy apāṃ caraṇāya | ni. 6-10 [?] || The grammatical tail, p. 516 — characterized, not transcribed: bhara (the bha for ha, the Saṃhitā lengthening); tūtujānaḥ (tuja hiṃsāyām, kānac, the reduplicative vowel lengthened, the initial acute); kiyedhāḥ (explained under the sixth Rik); rada; tiraścā (tiryañc, kvin, the n lost, the elision of a in the instrumental, ścutva, the ending acute); iṣyan (iṣa gatau, śyan, nit); caradhyai (cara gatibhakṣaṇayoḥ, the infinitive adhyai).

Translation of the bhāṣya: "Tūtujāna is a name for 'quick'; tūtujānaḥ: hastening; or: harming enemies. Īśānaḥ: the lord of all; kiyedhāḥ: the establisher of strength of boundless measure; or, he who stops the strength of enemies who advance. O Indra, such as you are, pra bhara, hurl the vajra at this Vṛtra; strike him with the vajra. And having struck, iṣyan, sending forth arṇāṃsi, the rain-waters from that Vṛtra, apām caradhyai, so that these waters may move, may go to the region of the earth, vi rada, tear off, cut up, with the vajra standing crosswise (tiraścā), the parva, the joints, the members, of that Vṛtra in the form of a cloud. Illustration: gor na, as men who cut up meat divide the limbs of an animal this way and that. On this the Nirukta says: 'strike him, hastening swiftly, with the vajra, at Vṛtra, the lord, the kiyedhāḥ — kiyaddhāḥ or kramamāṇadhāḥ — cut the joints like a cow's, sending forth the waters of the cloud that they may flow' (Ni. 6-10 [?])."

Pratipadārtha — "(he indra — O Indra;) tūtujānaḥ — swift-moving, or the destroyer of enemies; īśānaḥ — the lord of all; kiyedhāḥ — very strong, or one who lessens the strength of enemies; you; asmā idu vṛtrāya — upon this very Vṛtra; vajram — the vajra weapon; pra bhara — apply and strike; arṇāṃsi — the rain-waters; iṣyan — you who send forth from Vṛtra or from the cloud; apām — of the waters; caradhyai — for their flowing; goḥ parva na — as butchers cut the limbs of a cow's body into pieces; tiraścā — with your sharp vajra; vi rada — cut up."

Bhāvārtha — "O Indra, swift-moving, or destroyer of enemies, lord of all, very strong: strike this Vṛtra with your vajra and make the cloud fall as rain. So that the water may fall from the cloud, cut the body of Vṛtra, in cloud form, with your sharp vajra, as butchers cut the dead body of a cow into pieces."

English Translation (the source's own, p. 516) — "Indra, quick-moving and strength-endowed lord of all, hurl your thunderbolt at this Vritra and cut off his joints as (butchers cut up) a cow, that the rains may issue from him, and the waters flow (over the earth)."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), pp. 516–517 — tūtujānaḥ: "a word that gives the sense kṣipra ('quick'). In the Nirukta (Ni. 3-9 [?]) six words signifying kṣipra are read together — nu, muṃkṣu, dravat and so on [list as read, [?]]. Here the word is explained in two ways: one who hastens, or one who harms enemies." kiyedhāḥ — kiyato 'navadhṛtaparimāṇasya balasya dhātā: "the maker of strength of unmeasured measure; or kramumāṇaṃ śatrubalaṃ dadhāty avasthāpayatīti kiyedhāḥ — one who stands against the strength of enemies that advance and checks it, i.e. Indra. The word kiyaddhā is used in the Nirukta statement 'asmai prahara tūrṇam…' (Ni. 6-[?] [?]) in the sense of one who confronts the attackers." tasmāt apāṃ caradhyai: "cause the water to flow from that Vṛtra to the earth. This calls up the story that when Vṛtra, in the form of a cloud, stopped the very rain on the earth, Indra struck him with the vajra and brought the rain upon the earth." tiraścā — tiryagavasthitena vajreṇa — tiro 'ñcatīti: "tiryañc — that which enters sideways; seeming always transverse." gaur na — paśor iva: "this gives an illustration. As butchers who cut meat first cut the animal's body into pieces, so cut Vṛtra, in the form of a cloud, into pieces: this is the sense. The same sense is to be known from the Nirukta [Ni. 6-10 [?]]."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā pp. 517–518 — noted briefly — Grammar pages, noted briefly. bhara: hṛñ haraṇe; loṭ second singular, sip → hi; śap; guṇa; uraṇ raparaḥ; ato heḥ: loss of hi; hṛgrahor bhaś chandasi: bha for ha; dvyacotastiṅaḥ (Pā. 6-3-135 as read [?]): lengthening in the Saṃhitā; nighāta. tūtujānaḥ: tuja hiṃsāyām; liṭ → kānac; reduplication; halādiśeṣa; tujādīnāṃ dīrgho 'bhyāsasya (Pā. 6-1-7 as read [?]): lengthening of the reduplicative vowel; chandasy ubhayathā: kānac is also sārvadhātuka, so abhyastānām ādiḥ: initial acute. kiyedhāḥ: explained in Ṛg 1-61-6 [?] (i.e. 61.6 above). rada: rada vilekhane; loṭ second singular; ato heḥ: loss of hi; tiṅ atiṅaḥ: nighāta. tiraścā: tiro 'ñcatīti tiryañc; ṛtvigdadhṛk…: kvin after añc with an indeclinable in front; being kit, aniditāṃ hala upadhāyāḥ kṅiti: loss of n; in the instrumental singular, before an ending with the bha name, acaḥ: loss of the a of añc; with ś following, ścutva: s → ś; so tiraścā; the acute goes to the ending (anudāttasya ca yatrodāttalopaḥ). iṣyan: iṣa gatau; the root includes a causative sense; śatṛ; divādibhyaḥ śyan; apit, hence ṅit, so no guṇa; iṣyat; nit: initial acute; nominative singular: num; hal-ṅyābbhyo…: loss of su; saṃyogāntalopa: loss of t. caradhyai: cara gatibhakṣaṇayoḥ; tumarthe sesenase… (Pā. 3-4-9): adhyai; being ejanta: avyaya. apām: ūḍidaṃ padādi…: acute on the ending.

original pp. 518–520

Rik 13

Saṃhitā-pāṭha

अस्येदु प्र ब्रूहि पूर्व्याणि तुरस्य कर्माणि नव्य उक्थैः । युधे यदिष्णान आयुधान्यृघायमाणो निरिणाति शत्रून् ॥ १३ ॥

asyed u pra brūhi pūrvyāṇi turasya karmāṇi navya ukthaiḥ | yudhe yad iṣṇāna āyudhāny ṛghāyamāṇo nirināti śatrūn || 13 || Reading note: in the print's Saṃhitā, line 2, iṣṇānaḥ is joined to the next word as yad iṣṇāna āyudhāni; the Pada has iṣṇānaḥ | āyudhāni.

Pada-pāṭha

अस्य । इत् । ऊं इति । प्र । ब्रूहि । पूर्व्याणि । तुरस्य । कर्माणि । नव्यः । उक्थैः । युधे । यत् । इष्णानः । आयुधानि । ऋघायमाणः । निरिणाति । शत्रून् ॥ १३ ॥

asya | it | ūṃ iti | pra | brūhi | pūrvyāṇi | turasya | karmāṇi | navyaḥ | ukthaiḥ | yudhe | yat | iṣṇānaḥ | āyudhāni | ṛghāyamāṇaḥ | nirināti | śatrūn || 13 ||

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

उक्थैः शस्त्रैर्नव्यः स्तुत्यो य इन्द्र अस्येदु अस्यैव तुरस्य युद्धार्थं त्वरमाणस्येन्द्रस्य पूर्व्याणि पुराणानि कर्माण्येतत्कृतानि बलकर्माणि हे स्तोतः प्र ब्रूहि । प्रशंस । यद्यदा युधे योधनायायुधानि वज्रादीनीष्णान अभीक्ष्णेन प्रेरयन् शत्रूनृघायमाणो हिंसंश्चेन्द्रो निरिणाति अभिमुखं गच्छति । तदानीं प्र ब्रूहीति पूर्वेण संबन्धः । पूर्व्यमिति पुराणनामसु पाठात् ॥

ukthaiḥ śastrair navyaḥ stutyo ya indra asyed u asyaiva turasya yuddhārthaṃ tvaramāṇasyendrasya pūrvyāṇi purāṇāni karmāṇy etatkṛtāni balakarmāṇi he stotaḥ pra brūhi | praśaṃsa | yad yadā yudhe yodhanāyāyudhāni vajrādīny iṣṇāna abhīkṣṇena prerayan śatrūn ṛghāyamāṇo hiṃsaṃś cendro nirināti abhimukhaṃ gacchati | tadānīṃ pra brūhīti pūrveṇa saṃbandhaḥ | pūrvyam iti purāṇanāmasu pāṭhāt || The grammatical tail, p. 519, characterized, not transcribed: turasya — tura tvaraṇe, the suffix ka; navyaḥ — ṇu stutau, yat, āv for o; iṣṇānaḥ — iṣa ābhīkṣṇye, kryādi, the middle voice by vyatyaya, śānac; ṛghāyamāṇaḥ — explained in the passage Ṛg 1-101-4 [?]; nirināti — rī gatireṣaṇayoḥ, śnā, shortening; the absence of nighāta because of the relative yat (yadvṛttayogāt).

Translation of the bhāṣya: "Navyaḥ: praiseworthy by ukthaiḥ, the śastras, i.e. the Indra who is to be praised; of this same Indra, turasya, who hastens to battle, O singer, pra brūhi, proclaim, praise, the pūrvyāṇi, ancient, deeds — the strength-deeds done by him. Yad, when, yudhe, for fighting, iṣṇānaḥ, constantly sending forth the weapons, the vajra and the rest, ṛghāyamāṇaḥ, harming, and nirināti, going out against, the enemies [i.e. goes towards them]: then, pra brūhi is connected with the preceding. Pūrvya ['old'] is read among the names for 'old'."

Pratipadārtha — "(O singer;) yat — when; yudhe — in battle; āyudhāni — the weapons such as the vajra; iṣṇānaḥ — constantly employing; śatrūn — enemies; ṛghāyamāṇaḥ — harming and destroying; nirināti — falls on them [then]; ukthaiḥ — with hymns in the form of śastra; navyaḥ — which Indra is worthy of praise; asyedu turasya — of this very Indra, who hastens [to battle]; pūrvyāṇi — the former; karmāṇi — the deeds of valour; pra brūhi — praise well."

Bhāvārtha — "O singer, praise well the former heroic deeds of that Indra, worthy of praise through the hymns that are śastras and quick to go to battle, when he, wielding weapons such as the vajra, falls on the enemies in battle, harming and destroying them."

English Translation (the source's own, p. 519) — "Describe, with new hymns, the former exploits of that quick-moving Indra, when holding his weapons in battle, he encounters and destroys his enemies."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), pp. 519–520 — navyaḥ: "praiseworthy." asyedu — asya + it + u: "the it and the u here give the sense eva ('indeed')." turasya: "of that Indra who hastens for battle." pūrvyāṇi — purāṇāni: "'pūrvyam ahnāya' (Ni. 3-2 [?]): the Nirukta writers read this word among the words for 'old' (purāṇa)." ṛghāyamāṇaḥ: "one who harms enemies (Indra): nahi tvā rodasī ubhe ṛghāyamāṇam invataḥ (Ṛg 1-101-4 [?]) — in this mantra the sense of the word is specially explained."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā p. 520 — noted briefly — Grammar page, noted briefly. brūhi: brūñ vyaktāyāṃ vāci; loṭ second singular; the ending hi is apit, hence ṅit, so no guṇa (as the print says); nighāta. turasya: tura tvaraṇe; igupadhajñāprīkirakaḥ kaḥ (Pā. 3-1-135 as read [?]): ka; being kit, no laghūpadha-guṇa; end-acute by the suffix; genitive singular. navyaḥ: ṇu stutau; since it ends in a vowel, aco yat (Pā. 3-1-97 as read [?]): yat; sārvadhātukārdhadhātukayoḥ: guṇa; since the o arises from the yat suffix, dhātos tannimittasyaiva (Pā. 6-1-80 as read [?]): āv; yato 'nāvaḥ: initial acute. yudhe: yudha saṃprahāre; kvip; dative; sāvekācas tṛtīyādiḥ: acute on the ending. iṣṇānaḥ: iṣa ābhīkṣṇye; kryādi; vyatyayo bahulam: middle voice; śānac; kryādibhyaḥ śnā: śnā; sārvadhātukam apit is ṅit, so no laghūpadha-guṇa; ṇatva for the n by the ṣ; citaḥ: end-acute. ṛghāyamāṇaḥ: explained at Ṛg 1-101-4 [?]. nirināti: rī gatireṣaṇayoḥ; kryādi; laṭ third singular tip; kryādibhyaḥ śnā; pvādīnāṃ hrasvaḥ (Pā. 7-3-80 as read [?]): shortening; ṇatva of the n of the vikaraṇa (raṣābhyāṃ…); tip is pit and unaccented, so the accent of the vikaraṇa remains; because of the yad word, no nighāta; since a verb with the acute follows, the preposition nir is accented by tiṅ codāttavati (Pā. 8-1-71 as read [?]).

original pp. 521–523

Rik 14

Saṃhitā-pāṭha

अस्येदु भिया गिरयश्च दृळ्हा द्यावा च भूमा जनुषस्तुजेते । उपो वेनस्य जोगुवान ओणिं सद्यो भुवद्वीर्याय नोधाः ॥ १४ ॥

asyed u bhiyā girayaś ca dṛḷhā dyāvā ca bhūmā januṣas tujete | upo venasya joguvāna oṇiṃ sadyo bhuvad vīryāya nodhāḥ || 14 ||

Pada-pāṭha

अस्य । इत् । ऊं इति । भिया । गिरयः । च । दृळ्हाः । द्यावा । च । भूम । जनुषः । तुजेते इति । उपो इति । वेनस्य । जोगुवानः । ओणिम् । सद्यः । भुवत् । वीर्याय । नोधाः ॥ १४ ॥

asya | it | ūṃ iti | bhiyā | girayaḥ | ca | dṛḷhāḥ | dyāvā | ca | bhūma | januṣaḥ | tujete iti | upo iti | venasya | joguvānaḥ | oṇim | sadyaḥ | bhuvat | vīryāya | nodhāḥ || 14 || Reading note: the Saṃhitā has bhūmā, the Pada bhūma; the grammar page explains the Saṃhitā form with ā and the position of ca between dyāvā and bhūmā.

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

अस्यैवेन्द्रस्य भियो भयेनेत्यर्थः । गिरयः पर्वता अपि दृळ्हाः । निश्चलाः स्वस्वदेशेऽवतिष्ठन्ते । जनुषः प्रादुर्भूतादस्मादेवेन्द्राद्भीत्या द्यावा च भूमा च द्यावापृथिव्यावपि तुजेते । तुजिर्हिंसार्थोऽस्यत्र कंपने द्रष्टव्यः । कंपेते इत्यर्थः । किंच वेनस्य कान्तस्यास्येन्द्रस्योणिं दुःखस्यापनयनकं रक्षणमुपो जोगुवानोऽनेकैः सूक्तैः पुनः पुनरुपशब्दयन् । उपश्लोकयन्नित्यर्थः । एवंभूतो नोधा ऋषिः सद्यस्तदानीमेव वीर्याय भुवत् । वीर्यवानभवत् ॥

asyaivendrasya bhiyo bhayenety arthaḥ | girayaḥ parvatā api dṛḷhāḥ | niścalāḥ svasvadeśe 'vatiṣṭhante | januṣaḥ prādurbhūtād asmād evendrād bhītyā dyāvā ca bhūmā ca dyāvāpṛthivyāv api tujete | tujir hiṃsārtho 'syatra kaṃpane draṣṭavyaḥ | kaṃpete ity arthaḥ | kiṃca venasya kāntasyāsyendrasyoṇiṃ duḥkhasyāpanayanakaṃ rakṣaṇam upo joguvāno 'nekaiḥ sūktaiḥ punaḥ punar upaśabdayan | upaślokayann ity arthaḥ | evaṃbhūto nodhā ṛṣiḥ sadyas tadānīm eva vīryāya bhuvat | vīryavān abhavat || The grammatical tail, p. 521 foot, characterized, not transcribed: dyāvā ca bhūmā (divo dyāvā, ḍā for the dual, both members keeping their accents); januṣaḥ (janer usiḥ, an Uṇādi suffix); joguvānaḥ (guja avyakte śabde, yaṅluk, śānac, uvaṅ); oṇim (oṇṛ apanayane, the Uṇādi i); bhuvat (leṭ, aṭ, no guṇa); nodhāḥ (Yāska: "nodhā ṛṣir bhavati navanaṃ dadhātīti", Ni. 4-16 [?]; dhāñ, asun, nava → no).

Translation of the bhāṣya: "Asyed u bhiyā: through fear of this very Indra, girayaḥ, even the mountains, dṛḷhāḥ, stand firm, motionless, each in its own place. Januṣaḥ: from this very Indra who has appeared (been born), out of fear, dyāvā ca bhūmā ca, heaven and earth too, tujete. The root tuj, which means 'to harm', is to be taken here in the sense of 'trembling': the two tremble. Further, oṇim, the protection that removes the sorrow of this venasya, beloved Indra, upo joguvānaḥ, sounding it again and again with many hymns — praising it — such is the sense. Such a one, the seer Nodhas, sadyaḥ, at once, vīryāya bhuvat, became strong."

Pratipadārtha — "asyedu — of this very Indra; bhiyā — from fear (of him who cuts the wings [of the mountains]); girayaś ca — the mountains too; dṛḷhāḥ — stand firm without moving; januṣaḥ — [from fear] of this Indra who has appeared; dyāvā bhūmā ca — both heaven and earth; tujete — tremble; venasya — of the beloved Indra; oṇim — the protection that removes sorrow; upo joguvānaḥ — [with hymns] praising at every step; nodhāḥ — the seer Nodhas; sadyaḥ — at once; vīryāya bhuvat — became capable of valour."

Bhāvārtha — "From fear of Indra the mountains stand firm, without moving; from fear of him heaven and earth too tremble. The seer Nodhas, praising step by step, with excellent hymns, the sorrow-removing protection of the beloved Indra, at once became exceedingly strong."

English Translation (the source's own, p. 522) — "Though fear of him, the mountains remain still ; and through fear of his appearance, heaven and earth tremble ; praising repeatedly with hymns the preserving power of that beloved Indra, Nodhas speedily acquired vigour."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), p. 522 — januṣaḥ — janī prādurbhāve: "from the state of Indra who has manifested himself." tujete: "though the root tuj has the sense of harming, here the sense 'trembling' must be said: heaven and earth shake from fear of Indra's appearance." venasya — kāntasya: "of the charming (Indra)." joguvānaḥ — guja avyakte śabde: "one who makes an indistinct sound at every step." nodhāḥ: "the meaning of this word is 'seer'. In the Ṛg-saṃhitā: 'ūvū adarśi śundhyavo navakṣo nodhā ivāvir akṛta priyāṇi' (as read, the Ṛg numeral illegible [?]) — here too the word nodhas is explained as 'seer' (the gloss, tentative: 'as [a seer like] Nodhas makes his dear things manifest' — the reading of the verse is uncertain). The Nirukta explanations — 'nodhā iva āvir akṛta priyāṇi', 'nodhā ṛṣir bhavati navanaṃ dadhāti' and the like — also give 'seer' as its meaning."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā pp. 522–523 — noted briefly — Grammar pages, noted briefly. bhiyā: instrumental singular; sāvekācas tṛtīyādiḥ: acute on the ending. dyāvā ca bhūmā: the word dyāvābhūmī; the ca is read between the two words as a Vedic arrangement; divo dyāvā (Pā. 6-3-29 as read [?]): dyāvā in place of div; supāṃ suluk: ḍā for the dual ending; ḍit: loss of the ṭi; devatādvandve ca (Pā. 6-2-141 as read [?]): both members keep their own accent; both forms are traditional. januṣaḥ: janī prādurbhāve; janer usiḥ (Uṇ. 2-[?] as read [?]): the Aunādika suffix usi; janus; ablative singular; acute on u by the suffix. joguvānaḥ: guja avyakte śabde; yaṅ in the intensive sense; yañoś ca: its loss (luk); though a parasmaipada root, vyatyayo bahulam: śānac; as yaṅluganta roots are read in the adādi class (carkarītaṃ ca), adiprabhṛtibhyaḥ śapaḥ: loss of śap; because of yaṅ, doubling; guṇo yaṅluṅkoḥ (Pā. 7-4-82 as read [?]): guṇa of the reduplicative vowel; joguv + āna: aci śnudhātubhruvāṃ…: uvaṅ; abhyastānām ādiḥ: initial acute. oṇim: oṇṛ apanayane; the Aunādika i; end-acute by the suffix. bhuvat: bhū sattāyām; leṭ, third singular tip; itaś ca lopaḥ parasmaipadeṣu: loss of i; leṭo 'ṭāṭau: aṭ; bahulaṃ chandasi: loss of śap; bhūsuvos tiṅi (Pā. 7-3-88 as read [?]): no guṇa of the root; uvaṅ; tiṅ atiṅaḥ: nighāta. nodhāḥ: Yāska as above; ḍudhāñ dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ; asun, which arises on every root; "he holds newness" so nava → no; nodhas; gatikārakopapadāt kṛt: the first member's accent; nominative: atvasantasya cādhātoḥ: lengthening of the penultimate; hal-ṅyābbhyo…: loss of su; rutva, visarga.

original pp. 523–526

Rik 15

Saṃhitā-pāṭha

अस्मा इदु त्यदनु दायि एषामेको यद्वव्ने भूरेरीशानः । प्रैतशं सूर्ये पस्पृधानं सौवश्व्ये सुष्विमावदिन्द्रः ॥ १५ ॥

asmā id u tyad anu dāyy eṣām eko yad vavne bhūrer īśānaḥ | praitaśaṃ sūrye paspṛdhānaṃ sauvaśvye suṣvim āvad indraḥ || 15 || Reading note: the Saṃhitā prints dāyy eṣām as dāyyeṣām, i.e. dāyi eṣām with y before e; It is given as the Pada does.

Pada-pāṭha

अस्मै । इत् । ऊं इति । त्यत् । अनु । दायि । एषाम् । एकः । यत् । वव्ने । भूरेः । ईशानः । प्र । एतशम् । सूर्ये । पस्पृधानम् । सौवश्व्ये । सुस्विम् [?] । आवत् । इन्द्रः ॥ १५ ॥

asmai | it | ūṃ iti | tyat | anu | dāyi | eṣām | ekaḥ | yat | vavne | bhūreḥ | īśānaḥ | pra | etaśam | sūrye | paspṛdhānam | sauvaśvye | susvim [?] | āvat | indraḥ || 15 || Reading note: the Pada's word before āvat is printed susvim, with a plain s, while the Saṃhitā has suṣvim and the grammar page treats it as from ṣuñ abhiṣave: The Pada is given as printed with [?], not adjusted.

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

एक एक एव शत्रून्जेतुं समर्थो भूरेर्बहुविधस्य धनस्येशानः स्वामी यत्स्तोत्रं वव्ने ययाचे एषां स्तोतॄणां संबन्धि । यद्वा । विभक्तिव्यत्ययः । एभिः स्तोतृभिः तत्प्रसिद्धं स्तोत्रमस्मा इन्द्रायानु दायि । अकारीत्यर्थः [?] । उत्तरार्धस्येयमाख्यायिका । स्वश्वो नाम कश्चिद्राजा । स च पुत्रकामः सूर्यमुपासां चक्रे । तस्य च सूर्य एव पुत्रो बभूव । तेन सहैतशनाम्नो महर्षेर्युद्धं जातमिति तदेतदिहोच्यते ॥ अयमिन्द्रः सौवश्व्ये स्वश्वपुत्रे सूर्ये पस्पृधानं स्पर्धमानं सुष्विं सोमानामभिषोतारमेतशमेतशसंज्ञकमृषिं प्रावत् । प्ररक्षत् ॥

eka eka eva śatrūn jetuṃ samartho bhūrer bahuvidhasya dhanasyeśānaḥ svāmī yat stotraṃ vavne yayāce eṣāṃ stotṝṇāṃ saṃbandhi | yadvā | vibhaktivyatyayaḥ | ebhiḥ stotṛbhiḥ tatprasiddhaṃ stotram asmā indrāyānu dāyi | akārīty arthaḥ [?] | uttarārdhasyeyam ākhyāyikā | svaśvo nāma kaścid rājā | sa ca putrakāmaḥ sūryam upāsāṃ cakre | tasya ca sūrya eva putro babhūva | tena sahaitaśanāmno maharṣer yuddhaṃ jātam iti tad etad ihocyate || ayam indraḥ sauvaśvye svaśvaputre sūrye paspṛdhānaṃ spardhamānaṃ suṣviṃ somānām abhiṣotāram etaśam etaśasaṃjñakam ṛṣiṃ prāvat | prarakṣat || The grammatical tail, p. 524 foot, characterized, not transcribed: dāyi (the a-augment absent by bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi); vavne (vanu yācane, the perfect, the penultimate lost by vyatyaya); paspṛdhānam (spardha saṃgharṣe, kānac, reduplication, the p remaining by śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ, citaḥ); sauvaśvye (svaśva as a country-name that is also used of a kṣatriya, vā nāmadheyasya vṛddhasaṃjñā vaktavyā, ñyaṅ, no vṛddhi after v, initial acute by ñit); suṣvim (ṣuñ abhiṣave, kin, doubling by the perfect-like rule, yaṇ).

Translation of the bhāṣya: "Ekaḥ: he alone, capable of conquering enemies, bhūreḥ īśānaḥ, lord, master, of manifold wealth, yad vavne, whatever hymn he asked for [belonging to these eṣām praisers]; or, with a change of case, by these praisers that well-known hymn has been offered (anu dāyi) to this Indra — meaning 'was made' [reading doubtful [?]]. This is the story for the second half: there was a king named Svaśva. He, wishing for a son, worshipped Sūrya, and Sūrya himself became his son. A battle arose between him and the great seer named Etaśa; this is what is told here. This Indra, sauvaśvye, in [the war with] the son of Svaśva, sūrye, Sūrya, [protected] etaśam, the seer named Etaśa, who paspṛdhānam, was contending [with Sūrya], suṣvim, the presser of the Soma-juices: prāvat, protected him well."

Pratipadārtha — "ekaḥ — the sole one, in conquering enemies; bhūreḥ — of manifold wealth; īśānaḥ — the lord; Indra; yat — whatever hymn; vavne — he desired; eṣām — of those praisers, or by them; tyat — that famous hymn; asmā idu — to that Indra; anu dāyi — has been offered; indraḥ — Indra; sauvaśvye — [in the matter of] his own son; sūrye — with Sūrya; paspṛdhānam — who was contending; etaśam — the seer named Etaśa; pra āvat — protected well."

Bhāvārtha — "Indra, alone in conquering enemies and lord of manifold wealth: that famous hymn which he desired has been offered to him by the praisers. Indra protected well the seer Etaśa, who was contending with Sūrya, the son of Svaśva."

English Translation (the source's own, p. 525) — "He alone (is capable of subduing his enemies) and is the powerful lord of manifold riches ; give unto him the hymns which he has desired for. Indra defended the pious sacrificer Etasa, when fighting Surya, the son of Swaswa."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), p. 525 — ekaḥ: "here the word eka means 'without a helper'. Indra, without anyone's help, alone, is able to conquer enemies." eṣām: "though it should mean 'of these hymns', here, by the exchange of case (vibhaktivyatyaya), they have explained it in the sense of the third case — 'by these hymns'." sauvaśvye: "in the son of the king named Svaśva: in former times King Svaśva, desiring a son, performed penance addressed to Sūrya; pleased with his penance, Sūrya himself was born as the king's son. A terrible battle arose between him and the great seer Etaśa." suṣviṃ — ṣuñ abhiṣave: "the one who offers (presses) the Soma-juice. The great seer Etaśa, named above, satisfied Indra by the Soma sacrifice. Indra, pleased with his penance, protected him from Sūrya."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā pp. 525–526 — noted briefly — Grammar pages, noted briefly. dāyi: ḍudāñ dāne; passive luṅ, third singular ta; ciṇ bhāvakarmaṇoḥ: ciṇ for ta; ciṇo luk (Pā. 6-4-104 as read [?]): loss of the following ta; āto yuk ciṇkṛtoḥ (Pā. 7-3-33 as read [?]): yuk; no aṭ (bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi); nighāta, after a non-verb. vavne: vanu yācane; liṭ, third singular; eś; doubling; halādiśeṣa; by vyatyaya the penultimate is lost though there is no cause for it; because of the yad word, no nighāta; end-acute by the suffix. paspṛdhānam: spardha saṃgharṣe; kānac in place of liṭ; doubling; in the reduplicative syllable śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ (Pā. 7-4-61 as read [?]): the p remains; by pṛṣodarādi, the loss of the a of the root and the saṃprasāraṇa of r, as taught by "as stated" rules; citaḥ: end-acute. sauvaśvye: svaśva is the name of a country and also a kṣatriya name; vā nāmadheyasya vṛddhasaṃjñā vaktavyā (a vārttika on Pā. 1-1-73 [?]): it receives the vṛddha name; vṛddhāt kosalājādāñ ñyaṅ (Pā. 4-1-171 as read [?]): ñyaṅ in the sense of "descendant"; vṛddhi would be expected at the beginning, but na yvābhyāṃ padāntābhyāṃ pūrvau tu tābhyām aic (Pā. 7-3-3 as read [?]) prevents the vṛddhi and gives the aic augment after the v; being ñit, initial acute. suṣvim: ṣuñ abhiṣave; utsargaś chandasi (Pā. 3-2-171 as read [?]): kin; doubling by the perfect-like rule (liḍvadbhāva); being kit, no guṇa; su + i: in the Veda uvaṅ does not apply; yaṇ: suṣvi. āvat: ava rakṣaṇe; laṅ, third singular; nighāta, after a non-verb.

original pp. 526–529

Rik 16

Saṃhitā-pāṭha

एवा ते हारियोजना सुवृक्तीन्द्र ब्रह्माणि गोतमासो अक्रन् । ऐषु विश्वपेशसं धियं धाः प्रातर्मक्षू धियावसुर्जगम्यात् ॥ १६ ॥

evā te hāriyojanā suvṛktīndra brahmāṇi gotamāso akran | aiṣu viśvapeśasaṃ dhiyaṃ dhāḥ prātar makṣū dhiyāvasur jagamyāt || 16 ||

Pada-pāṭha

एव । ते । हारिऽयोजन । सुऽवृक्ति । इन्द्र । ब्रह्माणि । गोतमासः । अक्रन् । आ । एषु । विश्वऽपेशसम् । धियम् । धाः । प्रातः । मक्षु । धियाऽवसुः । जगम्यात् ॥ १६ ॥

eva | te | hāri-yojana | su-vṛkti | indra | brahmāṇi | gotamāsaḥ | akran | ā | eṣu | viśva-peśasam | dhiyam | dhāḥ | prātaḥ | makṣu | dhiyā-vasuḥ | jagamyāt || 16 ||

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

हर्योरश्वयोर्योजनं यस्मिन्रथे स तथोक्तः । तस्य स्वामित्वेन संबन्धी हारियोजनः । हे हारियोजनेन्द्र गोतमासो गोतमगोत्रोत्पन्ना ऋषयः सुवृक्ति सुष्ठ्वावर्जकान्यभिमुखीकरणकुशलानि ब्रह्माणि स्तुतिरूपाणि मन्त्रजातानि ते तवैवाक्रन् । अकृषत । एषु स्तोतृषु विश्वपेशसं बहुविधरूपयुक्तं धियं धाः । धियो लभ्यत्वाद्धीर्धनमुच्यते । यद्वा । धीशब्दः कर्मवचनः । पश्वादिबहुविधरूपं धनमग्निष्टोमादिकं बहुविधरूपं कर्म वा धाः । धेहि । स्थापय । प्रातरिदानीमिव परेद्युरपि प्रातःकाले धियावसुर्बुद्ध्या कर्मणा वा प्राप्तधन इन्द्रो मक्षु शीघ्रं जगम्यात् । अस्मद्रक्षणार्थमागच्छतु ॥

haryor aśvayor yojanaṃ yasmin rathe sa tathoktaḥ | tasya svāmitvena saṃbandhī hāriyojanaḥ | he hāriyojanendra gotamāso gotamagotrotpannā ṛṣayaḥ suvṛkti suṣṭhv āvarjakāny abhimukhīkaraṇakuśalāni brahmāṇi stutirūpāṇi mantrajātāni te tavaivākran | akṛṣata | eṣu stotṛṣu viśvapeśasaṃ bahuvidharūpayuktaṃ dhiyaṃ dhāḥ | dhiyo labhyatvād dhīr dhanam ucyate | yadvā | dhīśabdaḥ karmavacanaḥ | paśvādibahuvidharūpaṃ dhanam agniṣṭomādikaṃ bahuvidharūpaṃ karma vā dhāḥ | dhehi | sthāpaya | prātar idānīm iva paredyur api prātaḥkāle dhiyāvasur buddhyā karmaṇā vā prāptadhana indro makṣu śīghraṃ jagamyāt | asmadrakṣaṇārtham āgacchatu || The grammatical tail, p. 527 foot, characterized, not transcribed: eva — the Saṃhitā lengthening of the particle (evā); suvṛkti — loss of the accusative-plural ending; akran — kṛ, luṅ, the loss of cli (mantre ghasahvara…), ant, yaṇ, the aṭ augment; dhāḥ — dhā, luṅ in the sense of loṭ, loss of sic, no aṭ.

Translation of the bhāṣya: "Hāriyojana: he in whose chariot there is a yoking of two bay horses, thus called; one who is related to it as its owner. O Indra, owner of the yoked bays, the seers gotamāsaḥ, born in the Gotama line, akran, have made for you alone brahmāṇi, groups of mantras in the form of praise, suvṛkti, well drawing you toward them, clever in turning [you] to face [them]. Eṣu, on these singers, dhāḥ, bestow dhiyam, viśvapeśasam, wealth of manifold forms (dhī is called wealth because it is to be won); or the word dhī means 'rite': bestow wealth of many forms such as cattle, or manifold rites such as the Agniṣṭoma. [May he], as now, so on the morrow, in the morning-time too, dhiyāvasuḥ, Indra who has gained wealth by understanding or by rite, makṣu, quickly, jagamyāt, come — let him come for our protection."

Pratipadārtha — "hāriyojana — [O Indra,] who have bay horses yoked to your chariot; indra — O Indra; gotamāsaḥ — the seers born in the Gotama line; suvṛkti — good, effective; brahmāṇi — mantras in the form of praise; te eva — for you alone; akran — have made; eṣu — on these praisers; viśvapeśasam — of manifold kinds; dhiyam — wealth such as cattle, or rites such as the Agniṣṭoma; ā dhāḥ — bestow with favour; prātaḥ — (as now) also in the coming mornings; dhiyāvasuḥ — Indra who has obtained wealth by understanding or rite; makṣu — vigilantly; jagamyāt — may he come [for our protection]."

Bhāvārtha — "O Indra, who yoke bays to your chariot: the seers born in the Gotama line have composed for you alone mantras in the form of praise, good and effective. Bestow on these seers wealth of manifold kinds such as cattle. And as now, so in the mornings that come, may Indra, who has gained wealth by his own pure rites, come here vigilantly for our protection."

English Translation (the source's own, p. 527) — "O Indra, harnesser of horses, the descendants of Gotama, have offered to you well-worded hymns to secure your presence ; confer upon them manifold riches ; may he (Indra) who has acquired wealth by pious deeds, come hither quickly in the morning."

Special Topics (viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu), p. 528 — hāriyojana — haryor aśvayor yojanaṃ yasmin saḥ hariyojanaḥ: "he who is related to it as its owner is hāriyojanaḥ: one who has a chariot with horses; or one seated as master in a horse-chariot." gotamāsaḥ: "the seers born in the Gotama line." suvṛkti — suṣṭhv āvarjakāny abhimukhīkaraṇakuśalāni: "mantras that have the capacity to turn the deities, in an excellent manner, to face the singer: an epithet of the mantras." brahmāṇi: "the collections of mantras in the form of praise." viśvapeśasam — bahuvidharūpayuktam: "endowed with many forms: an epithet of the word dhiyam." dhiyaṃ dhāḥ: "give wealth. Dhiyo labhyatvāt dhīḥ dhanam ucyate: or the word dhī is [read as] expressing rite — 'wealth of manifold forms such as cattle, or manifold rites such as the Agniṣṭoma': thus they explain dhiyam in two ways, either as wealth to be won by the understanding, or as rites such as the Agniṣṭoma through the word dhī meaning 'rite'." dhiyāvasuḥ: "one who has gained complete lordship by understanding or by the fruit of rite." makṣu jagamyāt — śīghraṃ asmadrakṣaṇārtham āgacchatu: "may he come vigilantly to protect us."

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā pp. 528–529 — noted briefly — Grammar pages, noted briefly. eva: nipātasya ca (Pā. 6-3-136 as read [?]): lengthening in the Saṃhitā. hāriyojana: āmantritasya ca (Pā. 8-1-19 as read [?]): the vocative nighāta. suvṛkti: in the neuter accusative plural, loss of the ending by supāṃ suluk. gotamāsaḥ: nominative plural jas: ājjaser asuk (Pā. 7-1-50 as read [?]): asuk. akran: ḍukṛñ karaṇe; luṅ, third plural: jho 'ntaḥ: ant; itaś ca: loss of i; cli luṅi: cli with its loss by mantre ghasahvara… (Pā. 2-4-80 as read [?]); sārvadhātukam apit is ṅit, so no guṇa; iko yaṇaci: yaṇ; saṃyogāntasya lopaḥ: loss of the final t; the aṭ augment because of luṅ; nighāta, after a non-verb. viśvapeśasam: viśvāni peśāṃsi yasya; bahuvrīhau prakṛtyā pūrvapadam: accent of the first member. dhāḥ: ḍudhāñ dhāraṇapoṣaṇayoḥ; chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ: luṅ in the sense of loṭ; second singular sip; itaś ca: loss of i; cli luṅi sic: sic for cli; gātisthāghupā… (Pā. 2-4-77 as read [?]): since it is called ghu, loss of sic; no aṭ by bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi; nighāta. makṣū: ṛcitunughamakṣu… (Pā. 6-3-133 as read [?]): lengthening in the Saṃhitā.

Close of Sūkta 61 and of the Fourth Adhyāya (p. 529, PDF 545)

The print closes the sūkta with the line "ಅರವತ್ತೊಂದನೆಯ ಸೂಕ್ತವು ಸಮಾಪ್ತವು" — aravattondaneya sūktavu samāptavu — "The sixty-first sūkta is complete."

Then the Sanskrit colophon of the Adhyāya (Devanagari, IAST, translation):

वेदार्थस्य प्रकाशेन तमो हार्दं निवारयन् । पुमर्थांश्चतुरो देयाद्विद्यातीर्थमहेश्वरः ॥ इति श्रीमद्राजाधिराजपरमेश्वरवैदिकमार्गप्रवर्तकश्रीवीरबुक्कभूपालसाम्राज्यधुरंधरेण सायणाचार्येण विरचिते माधवीये वेदार्थप्रकाशे ऋक्संहिताभाष्ये प्रथमाष्टके चतुर्थोऽध्यायः समाप्तः ॥ ॐ तत्सत् ॥

vedārthasya prakāśena tamo hārdaṃ nivārayan | pumarthāṃś caturo deyād vidyātīrthamaheśvaraḥ || iti śrīmad-rājādhirāja-parameśvara-vaidikamārga-pravartaka-śrīvīra-bukka-bhūpāla-sāmrājya-dhurandhareṇa sāyaṇācāryeṇa viracite mādhavīye vedārthaprakāśe ṛksaṃhitābhāṣye prathamāṣṭake caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ samāptaḥ || oṃ tat sat ||

Translation: "May Vidyātīrtha-Maheśvara, dispelling by the light of the Veda's meaning the darkness of the heart, grant the four aims of human life. Thus ends the fourth Adhyāya in the First Aṣṭaka of the Ṛksaṃhitā-bhāṣya, the Vedārtha-prakāśa of the Mādhava school, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the bearer of the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Vīra-Bukka, the promoter of the Vedic path, the supreme lord of kings. Oṃ tat sat."

Kannada closing line: "ಇಲ್ಲಿಗೆ ಶ್ರೀ ಸಾಯಣಭಾಷ್ಯಸಹಿತವೂ ಕರ್ನಾಟಕಭಾಷಾನುವಾದಯುತವೂ ಆದ ಋಗ್ವೇದಸಂಹಿತೆಯ ಪ್ರಥಮಾಷ್ಟಕದಲ್ಲಿ ನಾಲ್ಕನೆಯ ಅಧ್ಯಾಯವು ಸಮಾಪ್ತಮಾದುದು" — "Here ends the fourth Adhyāya in the first Aṣṭaka of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, accompanied by Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya and a Kannada translation."

यदक्षरपदभ्रष्टं मात्राहीनं तु यद्भवेत् । तत्सर्वं क्षम्यतां देव वागीश्वर नमोऽस्तु ते ॥ शुभं भूयात् ॥ मङ्गळम् ॥

yad akṣarapadabhraṣṭaṃ mātrāhīnaṃ tu yad bhavet | tat sarvaṃ kṣamyatāṃ deva vāgīśvara namo 'stu te || śubhaṃ bhūyāt || maṅgaḷam ||

Translation: "Whatever syllable or word has fallen out, or whatever may be lacking in measure — may all that be forgiven, O God, Lord of Speech; salutation to you. May there be well-being. Auspiciousness." PDF 546 = printed p. 530 is blank apart from a small printer's ornament (a rose); the Pariśiṣṭa begins at printed p. 531 = PDF 547 and is not translated.

Sūkta 61 (Maṇḍala 1, Eleventh Anuvāka, 16 Riks; ṛṣi Nodhas Gautama; deity Indra; Triṣṭubh) — printed pp. 478–529, PDF 494–545. The sūkta, an ahīna-sūkta recited at the midday pressing, is a single sustained praise of Indra as warrior and creator of waters: the poet offers hymn and oblation as food to a hungry man (1–2); the hymn is a voice joined to the offering as a horse to a chariot or as a carpenter's chariot sent to its owner (3–5); Tvaṣṭṛ sharpens Indra's vajra and he pierces the vital part of Vṛtra (6); Indra drinks Soma and eats oblations at the three pressings, and the Viṣṇu-sacrifice is stolen back and its ripened wealth won (7); the goddesses, wives of the gods, offer him hymns at Ahi's slaying and his greatness exceeds heaven, earth and atmosphere (8–9); he splits Vṛtra, frees the waters like stolen cows (10), and makes the rivers flow, giving a standing-place to Turvīti (11); he is urged to cleave the cloud-Vṛtra limb by limb as a butcher cuts a cow, that the rains may flow (12); the poet is bidden to praise his old deeds (13); mountains stand firm and heaven and earth tremble for fear of him, and Nodhas gains strength (14); Indra defends Etaśa against Sūrya, the son of Svaśva (15); and the Gotamas offer these hymns, asking him to come quickly in the morning (16).

Pariśiṣṭa — Appendix on the Deities and Persons of the Ṛgveda

Added at the user's request (2026-10-06) after Volume 5's Sūktas 47–61 were complete. The Pariśiṣṭa is a Kannada prose essay with no Sāyaṇa bhāṣya; it has no Saṃhitā/Pada layers, so the Rik conventions do not apply. Conventions here: a faithful English rendering of the Kannada, page by page, with the printed page marked; Sanskrit words and quoted Ṛgveda phrases (where the print gives any) in Devanagari + IAST + English; the bracketed numerals in the print (Kannada digits) are reproduced as maṇḍala-sūkta-ṛk references exactly as read at 150 dpi, unverified — individual digits that are doubtful are marked [?]; the print's own English words (if any) keep [sic] for misprints.

original p. 531

Pariśiṣṭa.

Note (Sūcane): "[In this part we have written the summary of the investigations that Western scholars have carried out on the various deities seen in the Ṛgveda, and, in the places where we saw it to be necessary, have added some parts of our own research. For those who study the Veda with a critical eye, and for others too who are interested in the subject of the Veda, there is no need to say that this part will be of special use. The numbers placed at the ends of sentences indicate, in order, the maṇḍala, sūkta and ṛk.]"

Deities of the Heavenly Region (svargasthānada devategaḷu)

Dyauḥ

Dyauḥ Dyāḥ: "The name of the sky that we see with our eyes. It is used mostly in this sense: it occurs in the sense of 'sky' more than five hundred times [as read]; and as 'day' about fifty times. When it is personified as a deity of the sky, it generally occurs together with Pṛthivī, in the dual, as Dyāvāpṛthivī (द्यावापृथिवी, dyāvāpṛthivī, 'heaven and earth'). These two are conceived as the father and mother of the world. There is not even one hymn that praises the sky as a deity [by itself]. If at some places it is used on its own, the only idea intended there is that of fatherhood. It is found chiefly in the genitive, in about fifty places [as read]; in every such genitive some deity is said to be the son or daughter of this one. For the most part the goddess Uṣas is his daughter; the Aśvins are his offspring; Agni is his son or child; Parjanya, Sūrya, the Ādityas, the Maruts and the Aṅgirases are his sons. In the thirty places where it occurs in the nominative, in eight it is used alone; in the remaining places it is accompanied by Pṛthivī or by another deity. Three times he is 'father' (1-90-2; 1-164-33; 4-1-10); once he is Indra's father (4-17-3); once he is one of great seed (retas); and Agni is his begetter (4-12-4); a bull (5-36-5), the red bull that roars downward (5-58-6), and one who approved the slaying of Vṛtra (6-72-3) — thus three places each [as read]. In the dative case there are eight places, of which three are special: the famed father (1-27-5 [?]), the most excellent (1-54-3), and the lofty house (5-42-2). In the four places in the accusative only two are different: one in which he is given the epithet [...] (1-164-3 [?]), and one in which Agni is said to make him roar for the sake of men (1-?-4)."

"In this way, 'Dyauḥ' is used specially in the sense of father of the deities. Only in fifteen or sixteen places [as read] is his fatherhood stated; it is not stated clearly, either independently or together with Pṛthivī. This deity's chief characteristic is fatherhood. In a few passages he is compared to a bull: here it is the animal that thunders and drips towards the earth. Elsewhere (10-68-11) he is a black horse adorned with pearls; this must be the sky studded with stars. In 'in the hand of the sky-deity (an arrow), there is a thunderbolt' there is an attribution of human form, as in 'he laughs among the clouds' (3-?-?) — this too must be the sky lit by lightning. Such mantras are found here and there. Apart from these there is no mention of Dyauḥ as an animal or as a man. Fatherhood (the idea 'father') is the main intent. Pṛthivī is the mother. The use in the dual is the most frequent; the praise that applies to Dyauḥ together with Pṛthivī does not apply to Dyauḥ alone. There are six sūktas addressed to Dyāvāpṛthivī as deity. Like the other great deities he too is called an Asura (असुर, asura, here 'lord, powerful one'): (1-131-1; 1-?-?; 8-20-?) [as read]; at one place there is the vocative 'Dyauḥ pitaḥ, pṛthivi mātaḥ' (6-51-5) [द्यौः पितः पृथिवि मातः, dyauḥ pitaḥ pṛthivi mātaḥ, 'O father Heaven, O mother Earth']. In a few places this word is used also in the feminine. If it is said that 'pitṛ' means the father of everything, and that he holds all things within him, a meaning is being forced on it. Nor can it be said that there is no deity greater than he; but in this same Ṛgveda, superlatives are attributed to other deities beyond Dyauḥ."

"This word is derived from the root div (दिव्, div, 'to shine'); like deva, it means a shining, bright thing."

Varuṇa

Varuṇa. "A most excellent deity, equal to Indra. The number of mantras addressed to Varuṇa is very small: the sūktas that praise him alone are twelve. Judged by the count of mantras he would be the third great deity — or, if Mitra, who is the other deity with him, and the twenty-four sūktas praising the two together are taken, he would come to the fifth place in the list; he is in number far below even the Aśvins, and equal to the place of the Maruts. The number of mantras addressed to Varuṇa shows neither his true position nor his excellence."

"Varuṇa has a human body and human activities; but his moral activities seem to receive more attention than his physical body and activities. The description of his body and ornaments is very scanty; the description of his deeds is much fuller. He has a face, eyes, arms, hands and feet. He moves his hands; he stands on the chariot [path?] [the print's words unclear: [?]]; he sits; he eats and drinks. Varuṇa's face (anīka) is conceived as the face of Agni (7-88-2 [?]; compare 7-?-?); the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa is Sūrya (1-115-1; 6-51-1; 7-61-1; 7-63-1; 10-37-1). Since the idea that Sūrya is their eye is in the very first mantra of the sūktas addressed to Mitrāvaruṇa, it seems that this is the point that comes into view first whenever Mitra and Varuṇa are mentioned. In a sūkta addressed to Sūrya (1-50-6), when it says that Varuṇa looks at men with his eye, that eye must be Sūrya himself. Aryaman, Mitra and Varuṇa are 'sun-eyed' (7-66-10). This epithet is applied to all deities. Varuṇa is far-seeing (1-25-5; 8-90-3) and thousand-eyed (7-34-10)."

original p. 533

"Mitra and Varuṇa stretch out their arms (5-64-2; 6-67-1) and, making the very rays of Sūrya their arms, drive the chariot. Like Savitṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ they are of beautiful hands (suprāṇī, सुपाणी, supāṇī). Mitra and Varuṇa go swiftly with their feet (5-64-2), and Varuṇa treads with feet that trample evil deeds (8-41-8). He sits on the darbha grass spread in the sacrificial hall (1-25-?; 5-62-?). Like other deities he drinks Soma with Mitra (4-41-2 and following). Varuṇa wears a golden mantle, or armour (drāpi, द्रापि, drāpi, 'mantle'), and bears a shining garment (1-25-13). In some places (5-62-?; 2-41-?) it is said that he has a shining garment made of ghee: this must be connected with the ghee oblation (ājya) made in sacrifice; the 'shining garments' that they put on (1-?-?) must be in the same sense. In one place in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (the numeral read as [?]) Varuṇa is depicted as handsome, with a bald head and yellow eyes, an old man. Among his ornaments the chief is his chariot. It is radiant like Sūrya (1-122-15 [?]), has a seat and whips (5-62-?), and well-yoked horses draw it easily (5-62-4). Mitra and Varuṇa mount the chariot in a very lofty region of the sky (5-63-1). The poet has the wish that this chariot should be seen upon the earth (5-62-2)."

"The dwelling of Mitra and Varuṇa is of gold, and is in the world above (5-62-8; 1-122-2). Varuṇa, seated in his palace, looks at all that happens in the world (1-25-10 and 11). The hall (sadas) of Varuṇa and Mitra is large, very high, supported on a thousand pillars, and firm (5-62-6; 2-41-5); and their house has a thousand doors (2-41-5). The all-seeing Sūrya sets forth from his own dwelling and goes to the house of Mitra and Varuṇa to report the doings of men (7-60-1 and 2), and enters their beloved house (1-152-4). The fathers see Varuṇa in the highest heaven (10-14-7). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa there is the statement that Varuṇa, in order to see the world, sits in the middle of the sky and from there visits the regions around him that inflict punishment (11-6-1)."

"In some places it is said that Varuṇa has secret agents (cāra). They sit around him (7-34-?). They behold both heaven and earth; knowing well the matter of the sacrifices, they become inspirers of praise (2-?-?). The secret agents of Mitra and Varuṇa enter the houses one by one (6-67-5), they are not deceived, they are intelligent (6-67-?). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 4-16-4) Varuṇa's agents come down from heaven and [the sentence continues on the next page: 'the whole world …']."

original p. 534

continuing Varuṇa "…they [the agents] see with a thousand eyes, [Av.] says. Here the 'agents' must be the stars. But there is no basis in the Ṛgveda for saying that the stars, as agents of Varuṇa and the other deities, inform them of what is going on in the world. Probably, like worldly kings, these too are described as having agents. Or: agents are not for Mitra and Varuṇa alone; the Rākṣasas who fought with Agni (4-4-3), with Soma (9-?-? and 8) and with Indra (1-33-?), and other deities — all these have agents (10-10-8). The Ādityas, like secret agents, look from a lofty place (8-?-?) [as read]. Varuṇa's 'messenger with golden wings' (10-123-6) must be Sūrya himself."

"Varuṇa, alone or together with Mitra, is called 'king' in many places, like Yama and other deities (1-24-7, 8 etc.). He is king of gods and men, of all (10-132-4; 2-27-10), of the whole world (5-85-3), and of all moving and unmoving things (2-27-6). In general it is only Indra who is described as a self-dependent king; but Varuṇa too is self-dependent (3-?-?). In more passages than those that call him 'king' (rājan), Varuṇa or Mitrāvaruṇa are called saṃrāṭ (सम्राट्, samrāṭ, 'sovereign'). This epithet is seen for Agni too; but for the most part it fits Indra. The use of 'saṃrāṭ' for Varuṇa or Mitrāvaruṇa is found twice as often as for Indra. Since for every eight or ten sūktas addressed to Indra there is only one addressed to Varuṇa, it may be said that this epithet belongs, if to any, to Varuṇa."

"The epithet 'kṣatra' (क्षत्र, kṣatra, 'rule, dominion') is generally applied to Varuṇa together with Mitra, and twice with Aryaman. Besides this it is seen to be used only once each of Agni, Bṛhaspati and the Aśvins. Of the five passages in which (kṣatriya) 'ruler' occurs, in four it is said of Varuṇa or the Ādityas and in only one of the other deities. 'Asura' (असुर, asura) is used more often of Varuṇa, or of Mitra and Varuṇa, than of Indra or Agni. If the small number of sūktas addressed to Varuṇa is taken into account, the epithet asura must be said to apply most of all to Varuṇa. Among the deities these are called those of mysterious nature, worthy of worship (asurāḥ āryāḥ) (7-65-2)."

"The divine power of Mitra and Varuṇa is described by the word 'māyā' (माया, māyā, 'hidden power'). When applied to these deities it means the secret power they have to do good; in contexts where it is applied to Rākṣasas, the same word means the secret power they have to do harm. In the good sense it suits Mitra and Varuṇa; in the bad sense it applies to Rākṣasas. In the same way the word asura too, in the sense 'one who is hard for ordinary people to know', belongs to the excellent deities, and in the sense 'not a sura' ('not a god') to Rākṣasas."

original p. 535

"By this hidden power of māyā, Varuṇa, standing in the sphere of the wind, measures out the earth with Sūrya as with a measuring-rod (5-85-5); Mitra and Varuṇa send down Uṣas (7-63-2); they make Sūrya cross the atmosphere and again cover him with clouds. Then drops mixed with honey (sweet) fall (5-63-4); they make the sky rain; and with the strength that the Asura (the sky-deity, or Parjanya) has given them, they carry on all the works named above. For this reason the word 'māyā' is said chiefly of Varuṇa among the deities (5-63-3; 7-28-?; 10-99-10; 10-?-?)."

"There are many legends of Indra. But about Varuṇa there are none; it is quite the contrary. He is much praised as the controller of physical and moral laws. The one who ordains the laws of nature is Varuṇa: he established earth and heaven, and dwells in all the worlds (8-41-1). The three upper worlds and the three earthly worlds are in him (7-87-5). Varuṇa and Mitra rule the whole world (5-62-?), or rule over two worlds (?); they are the protectors of the whole world (3-?-?). By Varuṇa's command heaven and earth are placed apart (6-70-1; 7-?-?; 8-?-?). With Mitra's help, Varuṇa is the support of heaven and earth (5-69-1) or of heaven, earth and atmosphere (7-?). He has made the golden disc (Sūrya) shine in the sky (7-87-5). He has placed Agni in the water, Sūrya in the sky and Soma on the rock (5-85-2). He has made a wide path for Sūrya (1-24-8; 7-87-1). Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman release a path for Sūrya (7-60-4). In all places where Sūrya's horses run the authority of Mitra and Varuṇa is established (5-69-1). The wind that blows with a sound in the sky is Varuṇa's breath (7-87-2)."

"By Varuṇa's laws (vratāni, व्रतानि, vratāni, 'ordinances') the moon shines at night, and the many stars in the atmosphere are seen at night only, and by day become hidden (1-24-10). Varuṇa puts on the nights as a garment (paraspṛje [?]); by his hidden power he makes the morning or the day (8-41-3). From this it is not suggested that Varuṇa's relation to night is closer than to day. In truth, the one who is always with Varuṇa is Sūrya, not the night or the moon. On the whole, Varuṇa is the controller of the light of the day and also of the light of the night; but Sūrya (Mitra) is the controller of the light of the day only."

"In the Brāhmaṇas a special connection of Varuṇa with the night, or with the sky of night, is stated. Mitra created the day and Varuṇa the night (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6-4-8-?); the day belongs to Mitra and the night to Varuṇa (Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?-?)."

original p. 536

"…in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa the earth world is said plainly to be Mitra and the heaven world to be Varuṇa."

"In some places it is said that Varuṇa divided the seasons. The twelve months too are known to him (1-25-8); Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman divided the autumn, the months, the day and the nights (?-?-?)."

"In many places it is said that he is the one who regulates the waters. He made the rivers flow; by his command they flow ceaselessly (2-28-4 [?]). Though rivers run swiftly into the ocean, it is by his hidden power that it does not fill (5-85-6). Varuṇa and Mitra are breakers of the rivers (?). That Varuṇa breaks open (releases) the oceans is a settled point, yet it is very rare in the Ṛgveda; probably the reason is that it is very unimportant. Varuṇa, who joins the waters of the sea, is compared with the Maruts in the atmosphere, Agni on the earth and Vāyu in the airy region (1-161-14). 'The seven rivers flow into Varuṇa's mouth like a pit-[dwelling]…' [as read, [?]] (8-?-?) must refer to the ocean. Varuṇa descends into the ocean like the sky (7-?-?). In general whatever relates to Varuṇa is with the water that is in the sphere of the air. Like the encircling ocean, Varuṇa rises to the sky (8-41-?). Watching the truth and falsehood of men, Varuṇa moves in the midst of the water that falls gently drop by drop (7-49-3). Varuṇa bears the form [?] of water (9-90-2?; 8-69-11; compare 1-?). Among the deities who are prayed to for rain, Varuṇa and Mitra are the chief. When all the mountains are covered with clouds, Varuṇa is he who, with rain falling from above (from the cloud), makes the water descend to heaven, earth and sky, and makes the whole earth fertile (5-63-3 and 4). Near Mitra and Varuṇa are milk-giving cows and rivers giving honey (5-69-2). Here are the sky full of rain and the flowing rivers (5-68-5). They moisten pastures with ghee (rain) and other regions with honey (3-62-16). They send down rain and hail-like things from the sky (7-64-2). The rain of the heavenly water comes from them (8-35-6). One whole sūkta (5-63) praises their power to make rain. The fact that Varuṇa's name occurs among both the deities of the atmosphere and those of heaven must be because of his close relation with water and rain. In the Brāhmaṇas too Mitra and Varuṇa are deities of rain. In the Atharvaveda sovereignty is not stated of Varuṇa; only the lordship over the waters remains. As Soma has a kinship with the mountain, Varuṇa has kinship with water (Av. 4-?-?). His golden house is in the water (Av. …"

original p. 537

"…(Av. 2-?-1). He is the lord of all waters; he and Mitra are the lords of rain (Av. 5-?-? and 5). In the Yajurveda it is said that he is the child of rain, and that he has made his home in the waters, which are like mothers (Vāj. Saṃ. 10-2). The waters are Varuṇa's wives (Tai. Saṃ. 5-5-?-1); Mitra and Varuṇa are the leaders of the waters (Tai. Saṃ. 6-4-?-?)."

"At every step it is said that Varuṇa's ordinances are well established. For this reason he is called dhṛtavrata (धृतव्रत, dhṛtavrata, 'one whose ordinances are firm'). This epithet applies to both, Mitra and Varuṇa. The deities themselves follow the ordinances of Varuṇa (8-41-2), or of Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman; even the immortal deities cannot transgress his vows (5-69-4; 5-63-?; compare …). Mitra and Varuṇa are the controllers of law (ṛta) and of light. By the strength of these commands it is possible for them to make [creatures] bend to the laws (1-23-?). This quality is seen especially in these two; sometimes in the Ādityas or in other common deities. They increase truth and justice (ṛta) (1-2-8). Varuṇa or the Ādityas are called protectors of laws (ṛtasya gopāḥ, ऋतस्य गोपाः, ṛtasya gopāḥ, 'guardians of the law'). This applies also to Agni and Soma. The epithet ṛtāvan ('one who keeps the laws') is generally used of Agni; it is seen to be used of Mitra and Varuṇa also many times."

"Varuṇa's power is unfathomable. Neither the flying birds nor the flowing rivers can reach the boundary of his kingdom; they cannot exceed his power; they cannot restrain his anger (1-24-6). Neither sky nor rivers can reach the limit of Mitra and Varuṇa (1-152-?). Everything is contained in Varuṇa; the dwellings of all beings are in him (8-41-? and 7); the three heavens and three earths are placed in him (7-87-5). Varuṇa is all-knowing. The flight of birds in the sky, the passing of ships on the sea, the course of the far-going wind — all of this is known to him; he sees all things that are past or to come (1-25-7, 9, 11); he is the witness of men's truth and falsehood (7-49-3). Creatures cannot even wink without him (2-?-?); the number of men's winkings is known to him; the deeds, plans and devices of every man are known to Varuṇa (Av. 4-16-2 and 5). He can grasp everything in heaven and earth and whatever lies beyond them; however far one may run beyond the sky, no one can escape Varuṇa's sight (Av. 4-16-4 and 5). That this omniscience is a personal quality of Varuṇa is shown by the fact that Agni is compared to him in this matter."

"As the controller of moral law, Varuṇa stands in a far higher rank than all the other deities. To sin is to bring great anger upon oneself from him; transgression of his laws also brings his wrath."

original p. 538

"For both of these [sin and transgression] he lays down very severe punishment (2-28-? and 7). The noose (pāśa) that binds sinners is mentioned in many places (1-24-15; 1-25-11; 6-74-4; 10-85-24 [as read]); it is cast sevenfold or threefold, and that noose binds the speaker of untruth; it lets go the speaker of truth (Av. 4-16-6). Wearing many chains, Mitra and Varuṇa are the restrainers of untruth (7-65-3). 'Varuṇa, accompanied by Indra, binds with fetters that are not of straw' (2-28-? [?]) is said in one place. In the whole Veda it is only in one passage — in a mantra addressed to Agni, in the context of a prayer 'release the noose that binds his devotees' — that the word 'pāśa' occurs. Hence these acts of binding with the noose and of release belong to Varuṇa. Some think that this noose and the binding by it relate to the damming of water, and others that they are bonds connected with night. But it may be said that the figure is used by way of suggestion: fetters that bind those who have fallen morally. Varuṇa, together with Mitra, drives out untruth, hates it, and punishes (1-?-?; 2-?-?; 7-66-?). They punish those who are careless in the matter of their worship (1-?-?). But Varuṇa forgives those who repent: he looses them as a thief [unclear] and removes the noose (2-28-5; 5-85-7 and 8): he frees the man not only from the noose made by himself, but also from the noose made by his forefathers (7-86-5). Having transgressed every day the very laws laid down by him, he then spares even those who repent (1-25-1); and he shows mercy to those who have transgressed his commands through forgetfulness (7-89-5). It may be said that there is no other hymn to a deity that is free of prayer for worldly objects; in the same way there is no mantra addressed to Varuṇa without a prayer for forgiveness of offences."

"Varuṇa has hundreds and thousands of herbs; he drives death away and removes sin (1-24-9). He can take away life, and can also give life (1-24-11; 1-25-?; 2-?-?; 2-28-1). He is very skilled in protecting immortality (8-42-2). Worthy men look, as they reign in joy, upon the two kings — Varuṇa and Yama — in the world beyond (10-14-7)."

"His worshippers associate with him in his dwelling in the heavenly world. They see him with the eye of the mind (7-?-?; 2-?-?). With such persons Varuṇa behaves like a friend (2-?-?)."

"[Of Varuṇa's true position and nature:] Let us know what the true position of Varuṇa is, what his nature is. As far as we have known, this much is certain: Varuṇa and Mitra are related to Sūrya. Varuṇa is more closely related than Mitra. Compared with Varuṇa, Mitra seems to have no personality at all. Mitra belongs to the class of deities of the Saura (solar) group. Varuṇa reflects another part of Nature [the print breaks at the page foot]…"

original p. 539

"…he must reflect [another aspect]. The root from which the word varuṇa arises is vṛ (वृ, vṛ), 'to cover'; hence Varuṇa means 'one who covers', or 'covering'. Hence by 'varuṇa' one may take the covering of the sky that is visible all around. If this word is so taken, there is room for all the works done by Varuṇa. A great substance much more extensive than Sūrya. Between Sūrya and Varuṇa there is a close relationship; there is no thinking of the orb of the sun apart from the sky; Sūrya is Varuṇa's eye; that eye (Sūrya) makes known to Varuṇa everything that goes on in the world; Varuṇa is far-sighted; by day and by night the world is within Varuṇa's view — all these agree. Moreover, whatever other idea is held, it is not possible to find sovereignty as natural as the sky; for the sky — far away, above the earth, the resting place of Sūrya and the other masses of light, ever looking, day and night, at all moving and unmoving things — can hardly be thought of as other than a deity who is the author of inviolable commands."

Mitra

Mitra. "Since the companionship of Mitra and Varuṇa is very great, there is in the Ṛgveda only one sūkta (3-59) that has Mitra alone as deity. Even there the part that praises the deity is very meagre; but in the first mantra alone some distinctive quality of Mitra is stated: speaking (brūvāṇaḥ), he joins all men together (yātayati) and looks at the people with unwinking eyes. This 'unwinking' is said of both Mitra and Varuṇa (7-60-6)."

"In another place the same words (he joins men together, speaking) are said of Mitra (7-36-2 [?]); there Varuṇa is called the strongest, the faultless guide. In another (3-62-9) Savitṛ, the solar deity, makes all beings listen to his word and brings them together; from this it can be conjectured that Mitra belongs to the group of the solar deities. In the fifth mantra of the sūkta addressed to Mitra he is called an Āditya worthy of praise, who joins all men together. This 'yātayajjana' ('joining men together') occurs in only three more places in the Ṛgveda: at (3-?-?) it is said of Mitra and Varuṇa, at (1-?-?) of Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman, and at (8-?-?) of Agni. In the last, Agni is compared to Mitra as 'one who joins men together like Mitra'. Hence this epithet belongs to Mitra alone. According to the same sūkta, Mitra supports heaven and earth; the five peoples of men are obedient to him; he is the life-support of all other deities. In one place (3-59-4), from the point of view of the rules laid down by him, Savitṛ and Mitra are one; in another (Vāj. Saṃ. 4-?) it is said that, following Mitra's laws…" (continues next page).

original p. 540

"…Viṣṇu strode three steps. From these two it may be said that Mitra indicates the path of Sūrya. Agni, established before the time of dawn, himself causes the birth of Mitra for his own sake (1-?-?); the kindled Agni is Mitra (3-5-4); when Agni is born he is Varuṇa; when kindled he is Mitra (3-5-1). The difference between Mitra at sunrise and Varuṇa at evening is stated (Av. 13-3-13); in the night Mitra prays that what has been covered by Varuṇa may be uncovered (Av. 9-3-18 [?]). These sentences support what is said in the Brāhmaṇas, that Varuṇa is the deity of night and Mitra the deity of day. The same idea is clear in the description of sacrifices: it is laid down there that a white-coloured animal be offered to Mitra and a black-coloured animal to Varuṇa (Tai. Saṃ. 2-1-2-?; 2-1-8-1; Maitr. Saṃ. 2-5-2). Therefore Mitra may be said to be a solar deity."

"The derivation of this word [mitra] is also not clear. In many places the word is used in the sense 'friend'. Probably the 'doing of good (upakāra) in many ways by the sun to men' is expressed in this Mitra."

Sūrya

Sūrya. "In the Ṛgveda ten sūktas praise Sūrya. It cannot be said definitely how many times this word is used, nor whether it denotes the deity or the orb of the sun. There is no deity so within the range of the senses as Sūrya. The light of Sūrya in the sky is Agni's face (10-?-?). Sūrya's eye is mentioned in many places (7-?-? etc.), but he is called the eye of himself, of Mitra and Varuṇa (7-66-10), and of Agni (1-115-1); once, [it is said that] the goddess Uṣas brings the eye of all the deities (7-77-3). There is a close relation between Sūrya and the organ of sight. It is said that the organ of sight of a dead man goes to Sūrya (10-16-3; 10-?-?; and compare 10-?-?, 4). Sūrya is the lord of the organs of sight (Av. 5-?-?); he looks at all beings, sky, earth and waters (Av. 13-?-?). He is far-seeing (7-35-? ; 10-37-1), all-seeing (1-50-2), the spy of the whole world (4-13-3); he looks at the moving world and at the good and bad deeds that men do (1-50-2; 6-51-?; 7-60-2; 7-63-1; 7-?-?). Awakened by Sūrya, men do their work (7-63-4). He who belongs to all men rises, waking them (7-63-?, ?); he is the self of all moving and unmoving things, their protector (1-115-1; 7-60-2). His chariot has one horse (7-63-2), or countless horses (1-115-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-2), or female horses (as read; 5-?-?), or seven horses (5-?-?), or seven mares (called haritaḥ) (1-50-8 and 9; 7-60-3), or seven swift mares (4-13-3)."

original p. 541

"Varuṇa prepares his path for Sūrya (1-24-8; 2-?-?), or Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman, the Ādityas, prepare it (7-60-4). Pūṣan is his messenger (6-58-3). Uṣas, or the dawns, uncover or give birth to Sūrya, Agni and the sacrifices (7-?-?). Resplendent in the lap of the goddess Uṣas he comes forth (7-?-?). From another point of view Uṣas is Sūrya's wife (7-75-5)."

"From the side of his mother Sūrya has the name Āditya (आदित्य, āditya, 'son of Aditi') or Āditeya (10-88-11); but he and the Ādityas are different (8-?-?). The sky is his begetter (10-?-?). He is born of the deities. When he was hidden in the ocean, the deities lifted him up (10-72-?). Agni, taking a different form, was placed by the gods in the sky (10-88-11). A view holds that he was born from the eye of Puruṣa who is the form of the Virāṭ (10-90-13). It is said that Sūrya, the maker of day, was released from Vṛtra (Av. 9-10-?)."

"It is said that various deities are, each by himself, the cause of Sūrya's birth. Indra made him be born, raised him to the sky and made him shine there (3-44-?; 8-?-?). Indra and Viṣṇu are his begetters (7-99-4). Indra and Soma made Sūrya, who was with light, shine (6-72-2); Mitra and Varuṇa established him in the sky (5-69-?; 5-63-4 and 7). Indra and Varuṇa made him mount the sky (7-82-3). The light in Sūrya was placed by Soma (6-44-23; 9-?-?); it is by Soma that Sūrya was born (9-96-5; 9-110-5); the deity Soma made Sūrya shine (9-63-7), or made him stay high in the sky (9-?-?). It is Agni that has placed the splendour of Sūrya very high (10-?-?) and made him ascend to the sky (10-156-4). The very Creator (Dhātṛ) gave form to the sun and the moon (10-190-3). By the sacrificial acts of the Aṅgirases, Sūrya was able to ascend to the sky (10-?-?). In all these texts on the birth of Sūrya it is the radiant orb of the sun that seems to be indicated."

"In many texts Sūrya is conceived as a bird flying in the space between. He is a bird (10-177-1 and 2), a beautiful bird (5-47-3); Sūrya flies (1-191-9 [?]); he is likened to a flying bird [as read] (2-?-5); he is called a bird of fine feathers [or 'a fine-feathered one'] (5-?-?). In one place he is called a bull or a bird (5-47-3); in another a bull with variegated plumage [print: 'a bird with a coloured bill'?] (10-?-?; compare 5-47-3 [?]). In one place (2-?-?) he is a white, shining horse brought forth by the goddess Uṣas; the seven horses of Sūrya are his rays (8-61-? [?]), for these rays carry (vahanti) him. His seven mares are the daughters of his chariot (1-50-9)."

original p. 542

Sūrya, continued "In some places Sūrya is counted as a lifeless thing. He is a stone in the sky (4-?-?; compare 6-?-?); a many-coloured rock raised in the middle of the sky (5-?-?; compare Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 6-1-?-?); he is a weapon thrown as a missile, which Mitra and Varuṇa cover with rain-clouds (5-63-4). He is the pavi (the rim or bolt) weapon of Mitra and Varuṇa (5-63-3), or the shining chariot that the two have placed in the sky (5-63-?); Sūrya himself is a wheel (1-175-?; 4-30-?). Sūrya's wheel is mentioned in many places (4-28-2; 5-29-10)."

"Sūrya shines for the sake of the world (7-63-1); for men and the gods (1-50-?) he runs with his splendour, he rolls up the darkness like a skin (7-63-1). As one throws a skin, his light throws the darkness into the water (4-13-4); he conquers persons belonging to darkness and sorcerers (1-191-? and 9; 2-104-?). Statements about the fierce heat of Sūrya are only two or three (2-33-?; 8-102-?). In the Ṛgveda Sūrya is not a cruel deity; this aspect of Sūrya becomes clear in the Atharvaveda and the Brāhmaṇas."

"Sūrya measures the length of the day (1-50-7) and increases the span of life (8-?-?); he removes diseases and bad dreams (10-37-4). The sight of the rising sun is the sign of life (4-25-? ; 6-?-?). All beings depend on Sūrya (1-164-14); and the sky also depends on him (10-?-?). He is called the All-maker (Viśvakarman) (10-170-4). By his greatness he is the priest (purohita) of the deities (8-90-?). At sunrise men pray to Sūrya to tell the other deities that they are sinless (7-60-1; 7-63-?). After rising he goes near Indra who kills Vṛtra, and it is also said that when he is praised together with Indra, Sūrya himself kills Vṛtra (8-?-?, ? and 4)."

"The legend relating to Sūrya is only one: Indra defeated him (10-43-5 [?]) and stole his chariot-wheel (1-174-5; 4-30-4). Probably this applies to the disappearance of the solar orb caused by a violent storm."

Savitṛ

Savitṛ. "Eleven complete sūktas, and also parts of some more, praise Savitṛ; his name occurs about 170 times. Of the eleven, only three are in the first and tenth maṇḍalas; the rest are in the remaining maṇḍalas. Savitṛ is a deity exceedingly golden; those belonging to him, and his ornaments, are all described as golden. His eyes are golden (1-35-8); his hands are golden (1-35-9 and 10);"

original p. 543

"he has a golden tongue (6-71-3). This kind of description is a peculiarity of Savitṛ. His hands are golden (6-71-1 and 5; 2-38-2), broad (3-33-?), or beautiful (3-33-6). He is of beautiful hands (supāṇi) (6-71-4), of beautiful tongue (3-54-11); and in one place he is said to be dark-lipped [?] (6-71-4). His hair is of yellow colour (10-139-1); the hair of Agni and Indra is also of this colour. [His] garment is tawny (4-53-2). His chariot is golden, with a golden pole (1-35-2 and 5). This chariot, like himself (5-81-2), has many forms (1-35-?). His chariot has two horses of special brilliance; or two or more horses, white-footed, of the colour of the mōsalu [unclear: 'a pale colour'?] draw the chariot (1-35-5 and 3; 2-38-1)."

"Savitṛ's is boundless brilliance. His golden light is without limit; it is unequalled by other deities (3-?-?; 2-38-1). He throws out this light, or shakes it. By this the sphere of the air, heaven and earth, the world, the cavities of the earth and the sky — all are lit up (1-35-2 and 9; 4-14-2; 4-53-4; 5-81-3). Raising his golden arms, which reach to the ends of the regions, he wakes all beings and blesses them (2-38-2; 4-53-3 and 4; 6-71-1 and 5; 2-38-2). Since other deities are compared to Savitṛ raising his arms, this too may be called a personal quality of his. Agni raises his arms like Savitṛ (1-95-?); Uṣas stretches out her light as Savitṛ stretches out his arms (6-?-?). Likewise Bṛhaspati prays that praise-words be firmly uttered (1-190-?). On the path that leads downward and upward, Savitṛ, seated in his golden chariot, goes looking at all beings (1-35-2 and 3). Before the time of dawn he sets out the chariot of the Aśvins (1-34-10). Following the path of the goddess Uṣas, he himself too shines (5-81-?). He rules the regions of the earth; he goes to the three regions of heaven; he joins the rays of Sūrya (5-81-? and 4). The word 'Sūryaraśmi' occurs once in the Ṛgveda; it belongs to Savitṛ. Shining with Sūrya's rays, Savitṛ, of golden hair, ceaselessly throws his light from the eastern quarter (10-139-1). He goes three times around the sphere of the air, the three skies, and the three luminous regions of the upper world (4-53-5). The ancient paths that he follows in the sky are pure and easy to walk. Here his worshippers pray to him: 'Protect us' (1-35-11). They pray: 'For the dead, join the living to a place where living beings are' (10-?-?). It is he who gives the gods immortality and men long life (4-54-2). It is he who gave immortality to the Ṛbhus who came to his house by the strength of their works (1-110-3 and 4). Savitṛ is prayed to as one prays to Sūrya, and also for the warding off of evil dreams (5-82-4)"

original p. 544

"and for release from sin (4-54-3). He drives away evil deities and sorcerers (1-35-10; 2-38-?)."

"Like some other deities he too is an Asura (4-53-1). He follows certain well-known laws (4-53-4; 10-34-8; 10-139-3). Waters and winds are subject to his law (2-38-2). He is the one who shows the way to the waters; propelled by him, they flow widely (3-33-6; compare Nirukta 2-26). Other deities follow his leadership (5-82-3). No one can resist his determination and his independence; Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Rudra and the rest cannot resist (2-38-2 and 9; 5-82-2). The Vasus, Aditi, Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman praise his glory (2-38-3 and 4). Like Pūṣan and Sūrya, Savitṛ rules over all moving and unmoving things (4-53-6). All objects that are desired are under his control; he alone gives well-being to heaven, earth and sky (1-22-? ; 2-38-11) twice. Like Agni he is called a householder (gṛhya), 'one who has come to the house' (damūnaḥ) (1-123-?; 6-50-?). Like other deities he too is the support of the sky (4-53-3; 10-149-4). He is the support of the world (4-?-?). He has bound the earth with chains and set it firm, and has made the sky stand in space that has no support (10-149-1)."

"The epithet 'apāṃ napāt' ('born of the waters'), which suits only Agni, is said of Savitṛ once (1-22-6; 10-149-2). It seems to be said of Savitṛ in the second [passage] as well. Yāska (Nirukta 10-31), commenting on the mantra (10-149-2) mentioned above, has said that since Savitṛ is the cause of rain, and since both the middle-region deity and the Sun in the sky (the Āditya) have the name Savitṛ, Savitṛ must be a deity of this middle world. Also because he is the cause of rain, and because Savitṛ's path lies in the sphere of the air or in the middle world (1-22-10), and since in the Naighaṇṭuka section the name of this deity stands in the list of deities of the heaven and middle worlds. Once Savitṛ is called also Prajāpati (4-53-2). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa the idea is expressed that Savitṛ and Prajāpati are one deity (Śat. Brā. 12-3-5-1). In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa (1-6-?-1) it is said that Prajāpati himself, as Savitṛ, created beings. He alone is the lord of the power to give life; by his movements (yāmabhiḥ) he becomes Pūṣan (5-81-5). Pūṣan, endowed with life-giving power, goes about like a nourisher looking at all beings (10-139-1). In two mantras (6-71-6 and 10) Savitṛ is said to be connected with Pūṣan. In the first, the favour of Pūṣan who looks at all beings is asked; in the second, it is prayed that he should direct towards himself all the mental activities of those who desire to know Savitṛ's vigour and greatness, of the worshippers. This second one is the famous Sāvitrī or"

original p. 545

"Gāyatrī. At the beginning of Vedic study the way of reciting it has come about. Since Savitṛ is a controller of rules, he is called Mitra (5-82-?). Savitṛ is sometimes called 'Bhaga' (5-82-1 and 3; 2-38-1 and 6). Or this too may be an epithet belonging to him. The word bhaga (the deity who gives men good fruits) is frequently connected with Savitṛ and used as 'savitā bhagaḥ' or 'bhagaḥ savitā'. In other places a distinction of Savitṛ from Mitra, Pūṣan and Bhaga is made. In many texts the two words Savitṛ and Sūrya are used for one deity. Raising up his splendour, Savitṛ gives light to the world; and Sūrya, shining the more, fills heaven, earth and sky with his rays (4-14-2). In the Ṛks 2-?-? and 4 the epithet 'prasavitṛ', which belongs to Savitṛ, is used for Sūrya. In the third mantra of the same sūkta it is said that Savitṛ himself is Sūrya. In several other places (10-158-1 to 4; 1-35-1 to 11; 1-124-1), too, it is very difficult to separate the two. Savitṛ moves between heaven and earth; drives away disease; sends Sūrya forth (1-35-9): in this text the distinction between Sūrya and Savitṛ is plainly stated. Savitṛ tells Sūrya that men are sinless (1-123-3). He moves along with the rays of Sūrya (5-81-4), or shines together with them (10-139-1; 10-158-3; compare 1-35-?; 2-38-8 and 10). At sunrise, Savitṛ, accompanied by Mitra, Aryaman and Bhaga, is prayed to restore the worshipper to life again (2-38-4)."

"In Yāska's view Savitṛ appears after the darkness of night is removed (Nir. 12-12). Sāyaṇa (5-81-4) understood that Sūrya is called Savitṛ in the period before sunrise, and Sūrya from the time of sunrise to the time of sunset. But since it is said that Savitṛ puts creatures to sleep (4-53-6; 2-38-1), he must be connected with both the evening and the morning. In one sūkta (2-38) he is praised as the setting sun; and all the later sūktas of Savitṛ seem to be subject to a rule that they are to be used in the evening rites or at the morning oblations. It is he who, after making all two-footed and four-footed creatures take rest, rouses them again (6-?-?; 4-53-3; 2-38-1). He unyokes his horses; he makes the travellers rest; his command has come when night falls; the weaver rolls up his cloth, and the workman stops his unfinished work at his command (2-38-3 and 4). As it is said that 'Agni is in the east and Soma in the south', it is customary to say that Savitṛ is in the west (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?)."

original p. 546

"This word savitṛ is derived from the root sū (सू, sū, 'to impel, bring forth'). Only when the deity Savitṛ is praised is this root used in many forms; even in contexts where the same sense had to be expressed in mantras addressed to other deities, different roots are seen to be used. Encouragement, awakening and restoring to life — these are the meanings specially intended for this root.
