Savitṛ has set every moving thing to its task (prāsāvīt, प्रासावीत्, prāsāvīt) (1-157-1); you alone are able to give impulse (prasavasya) (5-81-2 [?]); Savitṛ has bestowed immortality (asuvat) on you (1-110-3); Savitṛ is ready to awaken us (savāya) (2-38-1); from the sky he sends down three times the objects that are desired (sosavīti) (5-82-6 [?]); 'O Savitṛ, make us sinless' (suvatāt) (4-54-3); 'by the strength of Savitṛ (save), may all boons be gained by us, who are sinless in regard to Aditi' (5-82-6); 'drive away bad dreams (parāsuva), ward off calamities, bestow what is good (asuva)' (5-82-4 and 5); 'may Savitṛ ward off disease (asāviśat [as read, ?])' (10-100-8 [?]); and in many places (2-38-6 etc.) Savitṛ is prayed to for prosperity by the very same root. In this way it may be said that this root belongs wholly to Savitṛ. But it is used two or three times of Sūrya (7-63-2 and 4; 10-37-4), with Uṣas in 7-?-1, of Varuṇa in 2-28-[?], of the Ādityas in 8-?-1, and of Mitra, Aryaman and Savitṛ together in 7-66-4. Because this root is used so often of Savitṛ, Yāska calls Savitṛ 'sarvasya prasavitā' (सर्वस्य प्रसविता, sarvasya prasavitā, 'the impeller of all'; Nir. 10-31), 'one who gives life to everything'."

"In about half of the contexts where the word savitṛ occurs it is joined with the word deva (देव, deva). In all of these places the word deva has no special meaning and simply seems to mean 'deity'. Whatever the case, in two mantras it is an epithet of Tvaṣṭṛ (devaḥ tvaṣṭā savitā viśvarūpaḥ, देवः त्वष्टा सविता विश्वरूपः, devaḥ tvaṣṭā savitā viśvarūpaḥ, 'the god Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ, of all forms', 3-55-19 [?]; 10-10-5 [?]). Seeing these words joined thus, the sense comes out that Savitṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ are one."

"This name Savitṛ may be for that one power of Sūrya that quickens the world and gives it the power to move. But compared with Sūrya (the solar orb we see), it may be said that Savitṛ is not a deity within the range of the outer senses. From the Ṛgveda it is understood that Sūrya is the orb of a mass of light, visible in this gross sky, and that Savitṛ is the embodied divine power of that Sūrya."

"According to some, Savitṛ is the quickening power; Sūrya and his regular movement, and so on, are matters of secondary importance."

original p. 547

Pūṣan

Pūṣan Pūṣaṇa. "This name occurs in the Ṛgveda in about 120 places [as read]; eight sūktas. Of these, five are in the sixth maṇḍala, two in the first, and one in the tenth. In one sūkta he is praised together with Indra (6-57), and in another with Soma (2-40). Taking the parts and portions, more mantras are in his praise than in Viṣṇu's. In the Brāhmaṇas and so on this name occurs rarely and is less frequent. There is no definite personality and few human actions such as the bearing of a body. There is a statement about his foot, in the prayer that it should trample evil-doers; and his strength too is spoken of (6-56-10). Like Rudra, he has a braided lock (6-55-2) and a beard (10-26-7). He uses a golden razor (1-42-6); he holds a goad (6-53-5, 6 and 9) or a whip (6-53-9); wheel, wheel-rim or seat (6-56-3) are all mentioned, and he is called the best of charioteers (6-56-2 and 3); his chariot is drawn by he-goats (ajāśva, अजाश्व, ajāśva, 1-38-4 [?]; 6-55-3 and 4). Gruel (karambha) is his food (6-56-1; compare 3-52-7). For this very reason one may say that he has no teeth (Śat. Brā. 1-2-4-2)."

"Pūṣan sees all creatures clearly at one time (3-62-9); these very words are said of Agni too (10-187-4 [?]); like Sūrya he breaks open [i.e. divides] all things, moving and unmoving (1-115-1; 2-40-2). He tries to win a mother's love (6-55-5) or loves his sister (6-55-4 and 5). These very words are used of Sūrya (1-115-2) and of Agni (10-3-3). The deities gave him Sūryā, the daughter of Sūrya, in marriage (6-58-4); in the marriage hymn (10-85) it is Pūṣan who, taking the bride's hand and leading her away, is prayed to grant her the boon connected with worldly life: he is the husband of Sūryā. In another place (9-67-10) he is prayed to give, to those who worship him, a maiden as their share. Moist with affection, he moves on his boats that sail in the sky, as Sūryā's messenger (6-58-3). In the same way, looking at the world, he goes forward ahead (2-40-5; 6-58-2); and he builds his house in the sky (2-40-6). Acting on Savitṛ's impulse, he too is a protector; he is known to all creatures, and looks at all of them. It is said that Pūṣan, the best of charioteers, made the golden chariot-wheel of Sūrya run downward (6-54-3). But the context is a little unclear (compare Nir. 3-?). The epithet that belongs to him alone, aghṛṇi (अघृणि, aghṛṇi, 'unwearying'), means 'shining'. Anaśrus (?) [as read: 'anagohya'], which one might say belonged to Savitṛ, is 'one who can be hidden', is used once of him also."

original p. 548

"Pūṣan, who was born, is on all the paths, on the most distant path; on the path of far-off heaven and earth; knowing those two worlds that are dear to him, he goes there and returns (6-58-2). As Agni and Savitṛ take the dead [i.e. the souls of the dead] to the place where the living are with the deities, so Pūṣan too, calling the dead from his worshippers by a very distant path, takes them safely and leaves them in the place where the living are (10-17-3 to 5). Pūṣan leads to the world of those who follow the good path, to the world of the lovely deities (Av. 18-2-?; 9-?-?). Pūṣan's he-goats lead on the sacrificial horse (1-162-2 and 3). It may be that his familiarity with these difficult paths arises from the very fact that his chariot has unfailing, sure-footed he-goats."

"Because he knows the paths, he is called the guardian of the highways. They pray to him to drive away with his reins the obstructing crooks, thieves, robbers and bandits (1-42-1 to 3). In this very context he is called the son of release (vimuco napāt, 'descendant of deliverance'); another place has the same epithet (6-55-1), and it is said that he is the one who sets free twice (vimocana) (8-4-15 and 18). Hence the prayer: 'make us free from sin' (Av. 6-112-3). 'Scatter the enemies, may our road lead to the desired things (6-53-4); strike down the enemies, make the road good, let it reach the place that is above (1-42-? and 7); avoid the crooks that may come on the road' (6-54-9). 'Make the road auspicious' (10-59-2). He is the protector of every road (6-49-8). He alone is the guide (6-53-1). He shows the road on the highway (Prapathya; Vāj. Saṃ. 22-20 [?]). For this very reason, every traveller setting out must recite the sūkta 6-53 and offer worship to Pūṣan, the craftsman of roads, and those who have lost the way must return to Pūṣan alone (Āśv. Gṛ. Sū. 3-6-? and 9; Sāṃ. Śrau. Sū. 3-4-9), it is said. And besides, at the times of the morning and evening pressing, when oblations and the like are offered to all deities, Pūṣan stands at the door of the house and receives his portion (Sāṃ. Gṛ. Sū. 3-14-9)."

"Because he knows all the paths, he can bring out hidden things, and discovery is made easy (6-48-13). Pūṣan, prayed to as 'find as one finds a stray animal', is said to have found the king who was lost and hidden (1-23-14 and 13; compare Tai. Saṃ. 2-6-?-?). For this very reason, whatever has been lost, one should worship Pūṣan (Āśv. Gṛ. Sū. 3-?-?). In the same way, driving back the robbers and protecting [cattle] is also a special mark of Pūṣan (6-54-5, 6 and 10; 6-56-3; compare 10-26-3). Like one who, seeing a person fallen into a pit, calls out and saves him, so that the cattle may not be lost, he brings them back to the house…"

original p. 549

"…and he saves again those that have strayed (6-54-2 and 10). His goad drives the robbers straight (6-53-9). That he strikes them straight is to be the sense; it is implied that he sets right the flanks of the cattle (4-?-?). He protects horses also (6-54-5) and makes smooth and sets right the hoofs of cows (10-26-6). For this reason, creatures are pure in Pūṣan's sight (1-?-1 and 2), and he is the creator of robbers [?] (Vai. Saṃ. 4-?-?; Tai. Brā. 1-2-?-?). The Sūtras teach the praise-sentences of Pūṣan that are to be used when robbers have gone to graze [cattle] and the cattle are lost (Sāṃ. Gṛ. Sū. 3-?)."

"Many characteristics common to other deities are found in Pūṣan. He too has the title Asura (5-51-11 [?]); he is mighty (5-?-?); full of truth (8-4-15); he gives much in plenty (6-54-?); he is able (1-138-1); unobstructed (8-?-?); he is lord of men [?] and is equal to other deities in fame (6-48-15). He is the leader of heroes (1-106-5); an unconquerable protector, and gives help in wars (6-48-15). He protects the world itself (10-?-?; compare 3-40-1). He is a seer; a friend who protects the priest; the ever-faithful friend of the poor (10-26-5 and 7). He is wise (1-42-5) and generous (3-?-?). His generosity is stated many times. He has all kinds of wealth (1-89-6); has immeasurable wealth (8-4-15); makes wealth grow (1-89-5); is a helper (1-138-2); generous (6-54-? ; 8-?-?); bestows all kinds of good (1-42-6). He is a firm friend of wealth, and increases nourishment (10-26-2 and 7). Dasra (दस्र, dasra, 'wonder-worker'), the 'maker of wonders', ordinarily belongs to the Aśvins, but it is said of Pūṣan too in some places (1-42-5; 6-55-?); likewise 'dasma' (दस्म, dasma, 'wondrous') (1-42-10; 1-138-4) and a brilliance of marvellous kind that belongs only to Agni and Indra (dasmavarcas) (6-58-4) are said. 'Narāśaṃsa' (praised by men), which belongs only to Agni, occurs twice of Pūṣan too (1-106-4; 10-64-3). In one place he is all-pervading (2-40-6), and a swift bringer of food (8-4-3 [?]); there is a prayer to quicken devotion (2-40-6); his goad impels praise (6-53-8)."

"The epithets used only for him are: 'āghṛṇī' ['unwearying'], 'ajāśva' ['with goats for horses'], 'vimocana', 'vimuco napāt', and once 'puṣṭimbhara' (bringer of prosperity), 'anaśvapaśu' (one who does not lose cattle), 'anaṣṭavedāḥ' (one who does not lose things) and 'karambhād' (one who eats gruel). The last may be a cause of contempt in Pūṣan's case (compare 6-56-1; 1-138-4). As Soma is Indra's food, so karambha is Pūṣan's food; but Indra takes a portion of the karambha (3-52-?). In both the places where the word karambha (gruel mixed with barley [?]) occurs, it is connected with Indra's food [the page ends and continues]…"

original p. 550

Pūṣan, end "…it is connected with Indra's food (3-52-1; 8-80-?). That he is clearly called paśupā (पशुपा, paśupā, 'protector of cattle') is said of Pūṣan alone."

"Pūṣan is used in the dual together with Soma (2-40) and with Indra (6-57) only. In one place (6-55-5) he is called Indra's brother. Other than these two, he is most often addressed together with Bhaga (6-50-?; 6-?-?; 5-?-?; 10-?-?; Śat. Brā. 11-?; Kāt. Śrau. Sū. 5-?-?). And together with Viṣṇu (1-90-?; 5-?-?; 6-21-?; 2-?-?; 10-66-5): in all these mantras Pūṣan and another deity are said to be of one mind. With other deities, here and there, it is used."

"From the passages cited so far, Pūṣan does not appear to be a deity of one natural phenomenon. But many passages show that he is connected with Sūrya. Yāska too (Nir. 12-?) calls him an Āditya who protects all things. His chief works — setting the roads right, and joining the dead with good people — by the first quality he is a guide and a protector of cattle; that is, one who improves the circumstances of the people."

"This word Pūṣan has come from the root puṣ (पुष्, puṣ, 'to nourish'). This quality is clear from his epithets (viśvavedāḥ, anaṣṭavedāḥ, puruvasu, puṣṭimbhara) and from the prayers for wealth (6-48-13; etc.). He is a breaker of immeasurable wealth and of the flow of wealth, and of heaps (6-53-2 and 3). But the wealth obtained from Pūṣan is not rain-connected wealth like that obtained from Indra, Parjanya, the Maruts and others; it is connected with light [with brightness]. In this world to men, to the cattle-keepers, his fearless protection; in the other world, the showing of the road to joyful regions. By these the condition of the people is improved; people become happy. That is, Pūṣan may be called that portion of Sūrya which is beneficial to the people."

Viṣṇu

Viṣṇu. "Though he is a most important deity in the Brāhmaṇas and the rest, Viṣṇu has not so much prominence in the Ṛgveda. His influence is much greater than the number would show. Five sūktas and some portions of one sūkta are for the deity Viṣṇu. His name has not occurred more than a hundred times. Taking these alone, he is a deity of the fourth rank. Nor is there much detail about his body: he is described as a young man with a boundless body (1-155-6). The most important point in his case is the three steps (vikrama) that he takes; this is stated about twelve times. His epithets are 'urugāya' (उरुगाय, urugāya, 'of wide movement') and"

original p. 551

"'urukrama' (उरुक्रम, urukrama, 'of wide stride'); these also say the same thing. With three steps he has covered the entire earth. Of these, two steps are seen; the third is beyond the reach of birds and men (1-155-5; 7-99-1). The highest place of Viṣṇu is Agni's own place; for Viṣṇu is exceedingly lofty, and protects Agni's third place (10-1-3), and Agni guards the cattle from that lofty place of Viṣṇu (5-3-3). The wise look at the third step of Viṣṇu in the sky with the eye fixed (1-22-20). The devoted are plunged in bliss, there is the spring of honey (1-154-5), and the deities rejoice (8-29-7) in that beloved house of his. The step in that height, shining well downward, is the very dwelling of Indra and Viṣṇu. There are many-horned, swiftly moving cows there. The wish of the one who praises is for those (1-154-6). In these three steps all creatures dwell (1-154-2); they are filled with honey (1-154-4); Viṣṇu protects his own beloved dwelling (3-55-10; 1-154-5). He dwells very far from this world (7-100-5). He has three dwelling-places (tripasthā, 1-155-? [?]). This epithet commonly belongs to Agni; here only it is used of Viṣṇu."

"There is no difference of opinion on this matter, that these three steps of Viṣṇu mean the path of Sūrya. Yāska's predecessor Aurṇavābha (Nir. 12-19), and many Western scholars as well, hold that these three steps indicate the rising of Sūrya, his being at the zenith, and his setting. The three Vedas such as the Yajus, the Brāhmaṇas, Yāska's other predecessor Śākapūṇi, and some other Western scholars hold that the three steps indicate the movement of Sūrya in the three divisions of the world [earth, atmosphere, sky]."

"Movement is the distinguishing feature of Viṣṇu: the roots urugāya, urukrama and vikrama are applied to him. This root is used of Sūrya also. He is said to have gone, taking a many-coloured stone in the middle of the sky and great strides (5-?-?). Viṣṇu is swift (viṣa, 'fast') or hastening (evayā, evayāvan). In Viṣṇu's rapid and far-reaching movements there is regularity. His taking the three steps is also in accordance with some rules (1-22-18). Like the other deities that go in a regular course (Agni, Soma, Sūrya and Uṣas), Viṣṇu is always devoted to the rules, the establisher of rules, and — like Agni, Sūrya and Uṣas — ancient and also modern (1-156-2 onwards). Like Savitṛ, Viṣṇu too fixes the limits of the portions of the earth (1-154-1; 6-49-13). In one place (1-155-6; compare 1-156-5) Viṣṇu, like a wheel, made four of his own names (seasons) of 90 days move: it cannot be other than the year of 360 days. There is a prayer, 'bestow the branch needed for the sacrifice' (Av. 7-26-?). The Brāhmaṇas say that when Viṣṇu's head is cut off it becomes Sūrya. The whirling wheel…"

original p. 552

"…is one of his weapons; his vehicle is Garuḍa, the king of birds. This vehicle, like Agni, is of especially radiant brilliance. It has names such as Garutmān (गरुत्मान्, garutmān) and Suparṇa (सुपर्ण, suparṇa). These names are said of the bird of Sūrya. A jewel called Kaustubha shines on his breast; to say that this is Sūrya is a view. Viṣṇu does not clearly resemble any one portion of Nature. But it may be said that Viṣṇu is a swiftly moving light, which moves far and wide taking steps and encircles the world. It is also a part of Sūrya. The root viś (विश्, viś) too gives the same meaning. In this sense Viṣṇu must be called Sūrya. But some do not accept this view: they hold that Viṣṇu is a distinct deity."

"The third step of Viṣṇu, the one raised upward, is his abode (dhāman). The highest position of Sūrya's course is called viṣṇupada by Yāska, and must be in this very sense, and in this sense he is called one who dwells on the mountain (girikṣit, गिरिक्षित्, girikṣit); [giriṣṭhāḥ], 'one who stays on a mountain', must be said of Viṣṇu [1-154-2 and 3]. In the 155th sūkta [1-155-1] it is said of Viṣṇu and Indra together: 'the two who are not to be deceived have stood on the peak of the mountain [the slope].' The previous sentence applies to Sūrya who stands on cloud-masses of mountain form and looks at the earth [compare 5-?-?]. From such statements Viṣṇu has the name 'one with mountains' (Tai. Saṃ. 3-4-?-1)."

"That Viṣṇu takes steps in this way for such a reason is a matter of secondary importance. For the sake of man who is afflicted, Viṣṇu strode over the regions of the earth three times [6-49-13]; to give man a house to live in, he took steps [7-100-4]; with Indra he took steps far and wide and spread out the world so that we may live [6-69-5 and 6]. In connection with this, the stories of the Vāmana incarnation, etc., arise later in the Purāṇas. On the basis of this story, it is said in the Brāhmaṇas (Śat. Brā. 1-2-5-?; Tai. Saṃ. 2-1-3-1; Tai. Brā. 1-?-?-?) that Viṣṇu became a dwarf (vāmana) in order to give back to the gods the earth covered by the Asuras."

"Among the secondary characteristics of Viṣṇu the most important is his friendship with Indra, and Viṣṇu's help to Indra when he fights with Vṛtra. There is a sūkta praising both Indra and Viṣṇu [6-69] and their names occur together very often. And even in the sūktas addressed to Viṣṇu, whether clearly [6-69-? and 6; 1-154-3] or indistinctly [2-?-?; 1-154-6; 1-155-?], the deity suggested is Indra alone. By Indra's might Viṣṇu took the three steps [8-?-12]. In the matter of killing Vṛtra, Indra says: 'O Viṣṇu, my friend, stride out widely' [4-18-11]."

original p. 553

"Keeping Viṣṇu with him, Indra killed Vṛtra (6-20-2). Indra and Viṣṇu conquered the servitude of Dāsa and destroyed Śambara's ninety-nine forts (7-99-5 and 6). Viṣṇu is Indra's dear friend (1-22-19). Together with his friend, Viṣṇu opens the doors of the cowpen (1-156-4). When Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, Viṣṇu stands just behind him (Śat. Brā. 5-?-?-1). In many mantras Viṣṇu is invoked together with Indra (4-?-?; 4-55-?; 8-100-?; 10-66-?). Where the dual Indrāviṣṇū is used, it is seen that Viṣṇu also has some qualities of Indra: the power of drinking Soma (6-69-?) and Indra's victories (6-?-?). In the same way Indra too shares in the power of Viṣṇu to take great steps (6-69-5; 6-69-?). Both together: the task of creating the vast sphere of the air and of spreading out the regions (6-69-5), and the work of the birth of Sūrya, Uṣas and Agni (6-69-?): these are stated as their characteristics. For the sake of this friendship Indra drinks Soma with Viṣṇu (8-3-?; 8-?-?), and thereby increases his strength (8-?-?; 10-113-?). The Soma pressed by Viṣṇu Indra drank in three bowls (2-22-1); this brings the three steps of Viṣṇu, filled with honey, to the level of knowledge (1-154-4). Viṣṇu cooks a hundred buffaloes for Indra (6-17-11 [?]) or cooks a hundred buffaloes and a drink made of milk (8-66-10). Together with Mitra, Varuṇa and the Maruts, Viṣṇu praises Indra (8-?-?)."

"In the war with Vṛtra the Maruts, who are always with Indra, are Viṣṇu's companions. When Viṣṇu desired the intoxicating Soma, the Maruts sat on their altar like birds (1-85-?). When oblation is made for the swift-moving Viṣṇu, the Maruts are invited (5-?-?). These Maruts are the very fruit of the generosity of the swift Viṣṇu (8-20-3). When Pūṣan and Viṣṇu were cooking a hundred buffaloes for Indra, the Maruts were Indra's helpers (6-17-11). Varuṇa and the Aśvins follow the very intentions of the Maruts; it is with such Maruts as companions that Viṣṇu lays down rules (1-156-4). In one whole sūkta (5-87) Viṣṇu and the Maruts are together. And he goes quickly, calling the Maruts along when he sets forth (5-87-4 and 3)."

"Apart from these, here and there Viṣṇu is described with many qualities and many forms: 'Though you take another form in the time of war, let this form of yours not be forgotten by us' (7-100-6). He is the protector of the embryo (7-36-9); with some other deities he is prayed to as a helper in conception (10-184-1). In the khila (supplementary) mantra that follows 10-184-2, he is prayed to place in the womb a male child, in the form of ... [the print: 'who is as handsome as Viṣṇu'] or 'to place a male child in the form of Viṣṇu who is exceedingly beautiful'."

original p. 554

Viṣṇu, continued "The other qualities of Viṣṇu are common ones, such as are seen in other deities. He is generous, and a benefactor of those who do him service (8-52-? [?]; 1-156-3); liberal (2-40-5); a protector (3-55-10); he cannot be deceived (1-22-18 [?]); he is the releaser who is without harm and generous (1-155-4). He alone is the cause of the existence of the three worlds and of all beings (1-154-4). He has bound the earth round with mountains [or 'with pegs'] (7-99-3). He is the ordainer of rules (1-154-4)."

"In the Brāhmaṇas it is said that Viṣṇu placed three steps in heaven, sky and earth (Śat. Brā. 1-9-3-9; Tai. Brā. 3-1-2-2). The performer of the sacrifice imitates these three steps in the sacrifice (Śat. Brā. 1-9-3, 10 and 13)."

"Two stories connected with Viṣṇu have a basis in the Ṛgveda. Carrying Indra's anger, he did the destruction of the Rākṣasas. In the Brāhmaṇas the deities and Asuras are ever enemies; they fight at every step. The deities are not always victorious; often they are wholly defeated. Hence the deities have to find means to win (Ait. Brā. 6-15): there, Indra and Viṣṇu, having fought with the Asuras, come to an agreement that the two deities (Indra and Viṣṇu) should take as much of the earth as Viṣṇu could cover in three steps. Accordingly Viṣṇu finished the world, the Vedas, speech — everything — in three steps. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (1-2-5) it is said thus: the Asuras, having defeated the gods, began to divide the earth among themselves; then the gods came forward with Viṣṇu and asked for their own share. The Asuras agreed to give as much space as Viṣṇu, in the form of a dwarf, could cover. Then the gods performed a sacrifice and obtained, through Viṣṇu, all the earth. Here it is not said 'three steps'; it is in another place (Śat. Brā. 1-2-5-5 to 9): having pervaded the three worlds, Viṣṇu procured for the gods all-pervasiveness. Viṣṇu, as a dwarf, conquered the three worlds (Tai. Saṃ. 2-1-3-1). The assumption of the dwarf form was a device to go beyond the Daityas' hopes. This is the basis of the story of Viṣṇu's Vāmana incarnation in later Purāṇas."

"The basis of the second story is two mantras of the Ṛgveda (1-61-7; 8-66-10). Viṣṇu, having drunk Soma and, urged by Indra, took away a hundred buffaloes belonging to the boar Varāha Vṛtra and a vessel of milk; then Indra struck, by means of clouds of mountain form, an arrow, and killed that boar. This is formed thus in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (6-2-4): Taking the wealth of the Asuras, a boar placed that wealth beyond the seven mountains; then Indra, taking a blade of darbha grass and splitting the seven mountains with it, killed the boar; Viṣṇu (the sacrifice) lifted it up forcibly for the gods, and the gods obtained the Rākṣasas' wealth. The same story, slightly altered, is said in the Caraka Brāhmaṇa, as Sāyaṇa says in explaining the mantra 8-66-10 [?]. In"

original p. 555

"the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (14-1-2-11) it is said that a boar named Emūṣa lifted up the earth sunk in water, and in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (7-1-5-1) that the boar that raised the earth from the waters of dissolution is a form of Prajāpati. Later, in the Purāṇas, this boar became famous as an incarnation of Viṣṇu."

"The fish that released Manu from the flood (Śat. Brā. 1-8-1-1) was later counted an incarnation of Viṣṇu. In the same way, in the desire to create, Prajāpati moves in the water of the dissolution in the form of a tortoise (Śat. Brā. 7-5-1-5; Tai. Ā. 1-23-3); later this too becomes known as an incarnation of Viṣṇu."

"Viṣṇu was the first to know the matter of sacrifice and attained great pre-eminence: the bow-string, snapping, cut off the head of Viṣṇu (of the sacrifice), and that very head became Sūrya (Āditya) (Śat. Brā. 14-1-1). Afterwards the Aśvins put the head of the sacrifice in its former place (Tai. Ā. 5-1-1 to 6); then, when it was complete, there is a story that the gods won the world of heaven."

"Viṣṇu is the greatest of the gods; Agni is the smallest; the other deities are between them (Ait. Brā. 1-1). There is also the statement that Viṣṇu is the guardian of the gods' door (Ait. Brā. 1-30); in this context the mantra 1-154-? is quoted, saying that with his friend, Viṣṇu opened the door of the cowpens."

Vivasvān

Vivasvān. "There is no separate sūkta praising Vivasvat; but his name occurs about thirty times. He is the father of the Aśvins (10-17-2) and of Yama (10-14-5; 10-17-1), and the father of Manu, the first man of mankind. This Manu has the name Vaivasvata ('son of Vivasvat') (Vāl. 4-1 [?]). In the Atharvaveda and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa Manu has the title Vaivasvata. Manu is a descendant of the Āditya Vivasvān (Tai. Saṃ. 6-5-6-2; Śat. Brā. 3-1-3-4). Sometimes it is said that the deities too were born of Vivasvat (10-63-1). Saraṇyū, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, is Vivasvat's wife (10-17-1 and 2)."

"Agni was first seen by Vivasvat and Mātariśvan (1-60-1). In only one place Mātariśvan is Vivasvat's messenger (6-8-4); in all other places Agni is his messenger (1-58-1; 4-7-4; 8-39-3; 10-21-5). Agni was churned out by his mother and father (the two fire-sticks) when Vivasvat became a seer (5-11-3)."

"The seat or place of Vivasvat is mentioned in five places. The deities (10-12-2) and Indra (3-51-3) rejoice at that place; there singers sing the praise of Indra (1-53-1; 6-?-2), or sing the glory of the water (10-?-1). The statement that a sūkta was composed on Vivasvat (1-139-1 [?]) must be with this same idea."

original p. 556

"The connection between Indra and Vivasvat is stated in many mantras. Indra's joy comes from the praise of Vivasvat; he places his treasure near Vivasvat (3-34-? ). With the fingers of Vivasvat, Indra pours down the vessel from the sky (8-?-?; compare 8-?-?). Since there is so much nearness between Vivasvat and Indra, Soma must be there. In the ninth maṇḍala a close relation of Soma with Vivasvat is imagined. Soma dwells with Vivasvat (9-?-?), and Soma is purified by the daughters (fingers) of Vivasvat (9-14-5). At Vivasvat's prayer the flowing Soma, the seven brothers (waters), wise Soma, make [the waters] follow Vivasvat's path (9-66-?; 9-99-?). Receiving the favour of Vivasvat, the streams of Soma fall from the sky and bless Uṣas (9-10-5)."

"The Aśvins who live with Vivasvat are invited to the oblation (1-46-13). When the chariot of the Aśvins is yoked, the daughter of the sky (Uṣas) and the two days of Vivasvat (probably day and night) are born (10-39-12; compare Śat. Brā. 10-5-2-?)."

"Vivasvat is worshipped together with Varuṇa and other deities (10-65-6). In Vivasvat there is one bad quality: those who worship the Ādityas pray that Vivasvat's sharp arrow may not strike them before old age (8-?-?; compare Av. 8-?-?). Contrary to this, it is said in Av. 18-3-6 that Vivasvat protects from Yama."

"Vivasvat means 'one who shines'. In this sense it is used with Agni and Uṣas in some places. Agni created men's children, and the sky and the waters, by his boundless brilliance (1-96-2). Agni, the wise, the boundless one, the brilliant seer, shines at the beginning of dawn (2-?-?). Agni is prayed to favour the radiant Uṣas (1-44-1), and men are eager to see the shining face of the radiant goddess Uṣas (3-30-?). From the root vivās (विवास्, vivās, 'to shine well') the words vivasvān and uṣaḥ arise. The derivation of these words is clear in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa: Āditya Vivasvat lights up night and days (Śat. Brā. 10-5-?-?)."

"In the Yajurveda (Vāj. Saṃ. 8-5; Vai. Saṃ. 1-6-?) and the Brāhmaṇas, Vivasvat has the name Āditya. In later books this too is a name of Sūrya."

"Vivasvat is not very well known as the hero of a Purāṇic story. Taking together the derivation of the word, his connection with Agni, Soma and the Aśvins, and his seat being the sacrificial hall, it may be said that Vivasvat is the rising Sūrya. Many scholars hold that Vivasvat is meant to be Sūrya. Some say he is a deity presiding over the sky; one holds that Agni is Vivasvat."

original p. 557

"Bergaigne and another, Oldenberg, say that Vivasvat is a deity presiding over light, and that the grounds are sufficient to hold that he was the first to perform a sacrifice, and the original progenitor of mankind."

The Ādityas

Ādityas Ādityaru. "This is a group of deities. Six sūktas and two portions of sūktas praise this group. It cannot be said definitely how many deities are included in it, or what their names are. It is not counted as more than six, and even that is in only one place: Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Varuṇa, Dakṣa, Aṃśa (2-27-1). In other maṇḍalas the number is said to be seven (9-114-3), once eight (10-72-8), and it is said that Aditi, having first presented seven to the deities, afterwards brought the eighth, Mārtāṇḍa. In neither of these two mantras are they called Ādityas. Aditi has eight sons (Av. 8-9-21): Mitra, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Aṃśa, Bhaga, Dhātṛ, Indra and Vivasvat (Tai. Brā. 1-1-9-1); the first five of these names are in the Ṛgveda (2-27-1). Including Mārtāṇḍa, the Ādityas are eight persons (Tai. Brā.); in two places (Śat. Brā. 6-1-2-8; 11-6-3-8) it is said that the Ādityas are twelve persons, one for each month. In the Purāṇas the Ādityas are twelve persons, one for each month; among them Viṣṇu is one, and he is the greatest of them all. Along with the six persons of the Ṛgveda (2-27-1), Sūrya too is counted as an Āditya. In the Purāṇas the name Āditya is commonly applied to Sūrya. Sūrya, counted as Agni, was established in the sky by the deities under the name Āditya (10-88-11). In one place four persons (Bhaga, Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman) are with the Ādityas, and Savitṛ is added (8-18-3). In the Ṛgveda the Ādityas are 'seven'. Sūrya is the seventh; Aditi, having once cast off [the eighth], brought him [back], the Mārtāṇḍa (the setting sun), who must be the eighth (10-72-8 and 9). Sūrya is the son of Aditi (Av. 13-2-?; 17-?-?), Sūrya and Candra are Ādityas (8-?-?), and Viṣṇu is one among Mitra, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Bhaga, Aṃśa and Vivasvat (11-6-3) — an Āditya. In one place alone (8-1-?) it is said that the mother of the Ādityas is not Aditi, but a golden-coloured Madhukaśā, daughter of the Vasus."

"Along with Varuṇa, the greatest of the Ādityas, Indra too is once counted as an Āditya (2-?-?; and Vāl. 4-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (2-?-?) Indra is one of Aditi's sons, but in Śat. Brā. 11-6-3 he is said to be different from the twelve Ādityas. When one deity is said to be an Āditya, it is Varuṇa; but in the sūkta of the deity Mitra (3-59) the deity Mitra is called an Āditya and Sūrya. When only two are mentioned, Mitra and Varuṇa are the Ādityas; once only Indra and Varuṇa are. If three, Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman are Ādityas. If five (said once)… With the previous three, Savitṛ and Bhaga are joined. As for Dakṣa, which was mentioned before [the page ends]…"

original p. 558

Ādityas, continued "…[Dakṣa] occurs only together with these names. Many hymns praise the group of the Ādityas. In every hymn, together with them, the names of Mitra and Varuṇa are stated. Their names occur also together with those of the Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, Aṅgirases, Ṛbhus and Viśve-devas. 'Ādityas' seems to be used not only for the solar group but also for ordinary deities. Their nature is no different from that of other deities. In general it may be said that they are the deities of heavenly light; they show no special distinction like Mitra and Varuṇa. Or, in the way of Sūrya, Candra and the stars, like Uṣas, they perform no particular function of light that has been set down for them."

"In the sūktas addressed to the Ādityas, generally (2-27), above all Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman are the ones specially indicated by 'Ādityas'. Being far away they are [yet] near: all moving and unmoving things they protect, as the deities protect the world (2-27-3 and 4). They can see the good and the bad in the minds of men and know the distinction between true and false statement (2-27-3; 8-47-13). They punish with hatred and punishment him who is crooked and sinful (2-27-4; 2-29-2; 2-?-?; 2-66-13). They are prayed to forgive sin (2-27-4; 2-29-5), to avoid its evil result, or to remove it from [the sage] Trita Āptya (5-?-?; 8-47-?). They bind enemies with a covenant (2-27-16); they protect those who worship them, as birds protect their young under the shelter of their wings (8-47-9). Like armour, they protect their servants, and as one arrow does not strike (8-47-8 and 9). They ward off disease and sorrow (8-47-10), and bestow wealth, light, long life, progeny and the leading of a good path (2-27; 8-47-12; 8-18-12 and 10)."

"The epithets used of them are these: pure, golden-coloured, many-eyed (bhūryakṣa), unwinking (animiṣa), sleepless (asvapnaja), far-seeing, long-lived [?], and so on. They are kings, of great strength, very great, deep, unassailable, firm in ordinance, faultless, free from sin, pure and holy."

"The name Ādityas is derived from the name of the mother. This is one of the three derivations of the word āditya (Nir. 2-13 [?]; compare Tai. Ā. 1-14-1)."

"The great deities among the Ādityas have been described separately. Let us know a little of the other deities who have no personal distinction."

Aryaman. "Though the name occurs in about a hundred places in the Ṛgveda, since it is not completely personal it has been omitted from the list of deities in the Nighaṇṭu. Except in two mantras, in all the other places it is spoken of only together with other deities; and that most often together with Mitra and Varuṇa. In ten or twelve sentences this word is used in a conventional sense — 'companion', 'bridegroom' —"

original p. 559

"in places; sometimes this sense may apply to the deity too. Addressing Agni, 'you are Aryaman when you woo maidens' (5-3-2) is said. Aryamya ('relating to Aryaman') is used in the sense mitrya ('belonging to a friend') (1-?-?). Mitra and Aryaman — these two conceptions show no difference."

Bhaga. "One sūkta (7-41) is devoted to this deity; other deities too are praised in it. The name occurs about sixty times. The word means 'giver, distributor'; in about fifty places it is used in this sense, most often as an epithet of Savitṛ. In the sūktas the idea is that he is one who distributes wealth; when the generosity of Indra and Agni is praised, they are compared with Bhaga. In the senses 'generosity, wealth, fortune' the word is used about twenty times, and this pun is also seen to be used in a figurative way. In (7-41-2) he is named 'the one who distributes', and men hope that they too may become sharers in this. In another place (10-64-16) he is the distributor; the prayer is made that he may be a bhagavān — one who gives the worshippers abundant wealth."

"The goddess Uṣas is the sister of Bhaga (1-123-5). Bhaga's eye is adorned with rays (3-?-?). Yāska (Nir. 12-13) says that Bhaga is the lord of the day's brightness (or: before the light). One must say that Bhaga is a generous giver; or, more clearly stated, a deity of immeasurable wealth."

Aṃśa. "It occurs fewer than twelve times. Another name for Bhaga is Aṃśa: 'one who gives a share or shares'. It is the name of a deity only three times; and in these three, in only one is it a name of the deity [proper]. Know the other matter [as secondary]. Here, Agni is described as Aṃśa and as the generous deity (2-1-?)."

Dakṣa. "As the name of a deity it occurs about six times. This word is used mostly as an epithet of Agni and Soma (3-14-2; 6-?-?; etc.) in the sense 'quick, strong, clever, intelligent'. Wherever there is no personification, the sense is 'a clever or skilful deity'. The word Dakṣa occurs as the name of one of the six Ādityas only in the mantra 2-27-1, and once in each of the first and tenth maṇḍalas. In (1-?-?) it is indicated together with the other Ādityas, and in (10-64-5) with Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman. In the second of these contexts Aditi is called his mother. In one sūkta on creation (10-72-4 and 5) it is said that Dakṣa was born of Aditi, and in the later mantras it is said that Aditi was born of him, that she is his daughter, and that afterwards the deities were born. In the womb of Aditi, the birthplace of Dakṣa, all created and uncreated things were set (10-5-7). From these last"

original p. 560

"two sentences it is understood that Dakṣa and Aditi are the parents of the world. The apparent contradiction that the children are the cause of the birth of the father and mother is not new in the Ṛgveda. The Ādityas have the name 'dakṣapitaraḥ' (दक्षपितरः, dakṣapitaraḥ), that is, those who have Dakṣa (skill) as father (6-50-2). Mitra and Varuṇa too have this same name (2-27-?; dakṣapitarau), and they are also sudakṣa ('very skilful'). In another place (8-25-5) this same idea is still more clear (sūnū dakṣasya). In these contexts the word dakṣa applies to no person. Even ordinary sacrificers have the name dakṣapitaraḥ, which confirms this sense. Such arrangements of words themselves leave room for the attribution of personality to Dakṣa and for his connection with Aditi. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā the name dakṣapitaraḥ is generally given to all the deities. Dakṣa and Prajāpati the creator are one deity (Śat. Brā. 2-4-4-2)."

Uṣas

Uṣas Uṣāḥ. "The sūktas that praise the goddess Uṣas number about twenty, and the word uṣas occurs more than 300 times. The word uṣas denotes both the deity and the times of dawn; and whenever the deity is discussed, the red dawn (aruṇodaya) is always in the background. No deity of the Veda is so lovely in form as Uṣas. In no other place in the poetry connected with religion is there so charming a description. Sacrifices or the explanations connected with them have not made use of her beauty. Like a dancer she puts on beautiful clothes and shows her bosom (1-92-4; compare 6-64-2). Like a maiden adorned by her mother she shows her form (1-123-11). Possessed of splendour, appearing in the eastern quarter, she displays her beauty (1-124-3 and 4). Shining with incomparable beauty, she gives light to all, small and great (1-124-6). Like one who has finished bathing and comes forth pure, she rises, drives away the darkness and gives the light (5-80-5 and 6). Though ancient, being born again and again, she is a young woman; shining on the same footing for all, she wears away the lives of mortals (1-92-10). As she shone in the past, so she shines now and will shine in the future; she is immortal and never grows old (1-113-1 and 13). That young woman comes again and, in the world, wakes everyone before all else (1-123-2). Last of the Uṣases that have gone and first of those to come, always lessening mortals' life, she shines (1-124-2). Always new, she revolves like a wheel (3-61-3). She wakes the creatures that have feet and makes the birds fly; to everyone her breath is life (1-48-5 and 10; 1-?-3). She rouses and sends forth every creature to go about (1-92-9; 7-?-?). The Uṣases wake the two-footed and four-footed creatures,"

original p. 561

"rouse them from sleep, and make them go about their tasks (7-?-?). When the dawn comes, birds fly from the nest; men go seeking food (1-?-?). She wakes the five kinds of people and shows men the paths that they must follow (7-79-1). She makes all creatures visible; she gives new life to all of them (7-80-1 and 2). She makes evil dreams run to Trita Āptya's house (8-47-14 and 18); she removes the black cloth of night (1-113-14). She removes darkness, the evil deities and the ill-omened darkness (7-?-?). She brings out the treasures hidden in darkness and distributes them liberally (1-123-4 and 6). When she rises she lights up the ends of the regions (1-?-11). She opens the doors of heaven (the sky) (1-48-15; 1-113-4). As cows open the door of the cow-pen, Uṣas, as soon as she comes, opens the doors of darkness (1-92-4). Like the udders of cows, her rays are seen (4-52-2 onward). She is seen from far, like a woman moving the wealth-bringing cows [?] (1-92-12). Rays of red colour issue forth; the tawny cows themselves set about their work; the red Uṣases cast their net of light as before (1-92-2). Therefore the goddess Uṣas has the name 'mother of cattle-keepers' [or 'speech of the wealth-givers'] (4-52-2 and 3; 7-77-2)."

"Without transgressing the order of the deities and of Nature, Uṣas appears day after day in the same place (1-92-12; 1-123-8; 1-124-3; 2-28-5); she moves in a regulated path; since she knows the path she is to follow she is never lost (5-80-4). She wakes all the performers of the sacrifice from sleep and makes them kindle the household fire; thus she does good to all the deities (1-113-9). She is prayed to wake only the faithful and generous worshipper, and to leave the faithless and the poor so (1-124-10; 4-51-3). In some places it is said that, leaving the work of awakening the worshippers, they wake her (4-51-4; etc.); and Vasiṣṭha claims that we were the first to do this work (7-80-1). In one place (5-?-?) she is warned that she is the one who acts as an enemy or a thief, and that Sūrya must hurry. She is prayed to call the deities to drink Soma (1-48-12). Perhaps for that reason it is said that all the deities rise together with Uṣas (1-14-9 etc.)."

"Uṣas moves in a shining chariot (2-28-1); the chariot is gleaming (1-92-?); shining (3-61-2); well adorned (1-49-?); an ornament to all and to all things (2-?-?); very firm (1-48-10 etc.); and by her own free…"

original p. 562

Uṣas, continued "…wins herself freely (2-28-1). She comes on a hundred chariots (1-48-7). To her chariot she yokes horses of a red-gold colour (2-?-?), easy to drive (3-61-2), and brought without fail (4-?-?). Yoked with horses, she shines (5-?-?). Her chariot is drawn by red cows (1-92-2; 1-123-11; 5-80-3). By 'horses and cows' the rays of the morning are meant; but the word 'cow' in general means 'cloud'. In one day the goddess Uṣas goes thirty yojanas (1-123-8)."

"It is natural that there is close kinship between Sūrya and Uṣas. She opens a path for Sūrya to travel (1-113-16). She crosses the eyes of the gods (Sūrya) and shows the way to the best bay horses (7-77-3). She shines with the splendour of Sūrya, her beloved (1-92-11). Savitṛ shines in the path of Uṣas (5-81-2). Sūrya follows Uṣas as a young man follows a young woman (1-115-2). He meets the deity who looks towards her (1-123-10). She is Sūrya's wife (7-75-5); the Uṣases are Sūrya's wives (4-5-13). Followed by him in the sky, she is thought of as his wife or beloved. From the point of view of time, she who comes before Sūrya is sometimes counted as his mother. She gave birth to Sūrya, the sacrifice and Agni (7-78-3). She was born only for the birth of Savitṛ, and comes and joins the child who is a mass of splendour (1-113-1 and 2). She is the sister of Bhaga (an Āditya) (1-123-5) and the kinswoman of Varuṇa (1-123-5). She is the sister of Night (1-113-2 and 3; 10-127-3) or her own sister (6-?-?); and the names of Night and the Uṣases are used in the dual: 'naktoṣāsā', 'uṣāsānaktā'. Uṣas is born in the sky (3-61-1); hence she is called a daughter of the sky (1-30-22 etc.), and once she is called the beloved of the sky (1-46-1)."

"Between the household fire (homāgni) that is kindled at the dawn and Uṣas there is a connection. In such contexts Sūrya also is generally suggested: Sūrya is seen at the time of kindling Agni (1-134-1 and 11; etc.). Agni is seen before the time of dawn or together with Uṣas. The goddess Uṣas makes the kindling of Agni happen (1-113-9). Hence, at times, like Sūrya, Agni too is her beloved (1-69-1; 2-10-1; compare 10-3-3). Agni goes to meet the shining Uṣas and expects of her superior wealth and so forth (3-61-6). With the morning deities, the Aśvins, too, she has kinship (1-46-3 etc.). They come with her (1-183-2) and she is their friend (4-52-2 and 3). She is prayed to wake them (8-9-17), and her praise rouses them…"

original p. 563

"(3-58-1). When the chariot of the Aśvins is ready, the goddess Uṣas is born (10-39-12). In one place it is said that Uṣas is related to Indra. Because the moon is born anew each time and so announces the coming of day, he shines before the dawn (10-85-19)."

"Many deities were the cause of Uṣas or found her. Indra, famed as a conqueror of light, created Uṣas or gave light to her (2-12-7 etc.). In some places he is her enemy; he smashed her chariot into bits. When the Uṣases were born, they were made radiant by Soma (6-44-23). Like Agni (2-1-?), Soma too made the Uṣases wives of the best man (6-44-22). Bṛhaspati, sporting with the light and splitting the cows, found Uṣas, the sky and Agni (10-68-9). The Fathers (pitṛs), companions of the deities, saw by their praises the hidden light, and by it created Uṣas (7-76-4)."

"Uṣas has been asked many times to protect her worshippers, to grant them progeny and wealth, and to give long life (1-30-22; 1-48-1; etc.). There is a prayer that she should bring fame to all who praise her (5-79-6; compare 1-48-?). All her devotees expect wealth from her, and desire to be her children (7-81-4). The soul of the dead goes to the company of Sūrya and Uṣas (10-58-?), and when it is said that the Fathers sit in the lap of golden things, the golden things must be Uṣas herself."

"Besides the eighteen mentioned in the Nirukta (1-8), Uṣas has still many epithets. She is shining, brilliant, pure. She is of bright colour, red-hued, golden, generous, born of law (ṛta), like Indra, divine in form, immortal. Generosity (maghoni) is a natural quality of hers."

The Aśvins (Aśvinīdevategaḷu)

The Aśvins. "Apart from Indra, Agni and Soma, the twin deities called Aśvins are the chief. They are praised in more than fifty sūktas and also in portions of some sūktas. The name of the Aśvins occurs more than four hundred times. Though they are determined to be deities of light (splendour), it is hard to say which aspect of it they reflect. They are deities of the dawn (3-58-1; 10-?-?) and cannot be separately distinguished. In one whole sūkta they are likened to the many pairs of things in the universe (eyes, hands, feet, wings"

original p. 564

"of birds, or pairs of animals, etc.) (5-78-1 to 3; 8-?-2 onward; 10-106-2 to 10). But some sentences seem to suggest that they were originally distinct individuals. They were born separately (nānā; 5-73-4); they were born in different places (iheha); one was a victorious royal prince, and the other a son of the sky (1-181-4). Yāska too (Nir. 12-2) mentions a statement that one is the son of Night and the other the son of Dawn. In the Ṛgveda itself, in one place (4-3-6), only one is addressed: 'Nāsatya, who guards'. This word (Nāsatya) applies generally to both."

"The Aśvins are young (2-39-?). They are the youngest of the deities (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?). They are also ancient (3-?-?). They are bright (2-?-?); they are limited by light [i.e. bounded by brightness] (3-?-?; 10-?-?); they shine like gold (8-5-?), and are of the colour of the honey-bee (8-?-?). They have many forms (1-112-?). They are of shining form (6-63-?; 6-?-?); they wear garlands of lotus flowers (10-184-2; Av. 3-?-?; Śat. Brā. 4-1-?). They are quick (6-63-5), swift like the mind (8-?-?), or like the falcon (5-?-?). They are very strong (10-?-?), and have many strong limbs (6-63-?), and are many times called 'red' [with the sense of Raudra-form] (5-?-?). They are good knowers (8-?-?) and have the power of māyā (6-63-?; 10-?-?). The epithets used again and again and peculiar to them are dasra (दस्र, dasra, 'wonder-working') and nāsatya (नासत्य, nāsatya, 'not untrue'); the meanings 'protectors' etc. are also suggested for these two. These two epithets themselves became their names. Rudravartanī ('of red path') and hiraṇyavartanī ('of golden path') are their two epithets; the latter is used elsewhere also of rivers."

"The Aśvins have a greater connection with honey (madhu) than other deities. In many mantras both are used together. They have a leather bag filled with honey; in it there are many bees that drink honey (8-?-?). They poured out a hundred jars of honey (1-117-6). The honey-whip is peculiar to them (1-22-3; 1-157-4); by it they sprinkle the sacrifice and the sacrificer. Their chariot alone is described as 'of the colour of honey' (madhuvarṇa) or 'bearing honey' (madhuvāhana). They love honey much, and are drinkers of it (madhupā). The priest near whom the Aśvins are called to come is also 'honey-handed' (10-41-3). They themselves give honey to the bee (1-112-?;"

original p. 565

"compare 10-40-6); they are likened to bees (10-106-10). Like other deities they too love the Soma juice (3-58-? and 9; etc.), and are invited to drink Soma with Uṣas and Sūrya (8-35-1). Some scholars hold that they do not belong to the class of deities worthy to drink Soma."

"Their chariot is like Sūrya (8-8-2), or is golden (4-44-4 and 5), and all its parts, wheels and so on, are made of gold (1-180-1; 5-77-3; 8-22-?). It has a thousand rays (1-118-1) or ornaments (8-8-11 and 14). It is a most remarkable chariot: it has three kinds; three wheels, three seats, and some other parts, also three each (1-118-1 and 2; etc.). It travels with great speed (8-?-?), quicker than the mind (1-117-2 etc.) or quicker than the blink of an eye (6-62-?). It was made by the Ṛbhus (4-36-?). 'The chariot with three wheels' is theirs alone. When Sūryā went to the wedding, one wheel of the chariot was left lost (10-85-16)."

"Their name means 'owners of horses', but nowhere does it mean that they are horsemen and hence got that name. The horses that draw their chariot (1-117-2; etc.); and more often birds (6-63-6; etc.) or winged ones (10-143-5); swans (8-?-?); eagles (1-118-4); birds in the form of horses (3-?-?); falcon-formed horses (8-5-2) are the draught animals. Sometimes it is said that one buffalo, or buffaloes (5-73-?; 1-?-?), or an ass (1-?-?; 8-?-?) drew it. In the wedding of Sūryā the Aśvins won the race with their ass-chariot (Ait. Brā. 4-?-?; Av. 1-?-? and Sāyaṇa's commentary on it). Their chariot reaches the ends of the regions and is worshipped by the five peoples (2-?-? and 3). It goes round the sky (1-180-10), crosses the earth and sky in one day like the chariots of Sūrya [1-118-?] and Uṣas [4-?-?] (3-58-8). It goes round Sūrya at a great distance [1-118-?]. The epithet 'puruṣṭhā' ['one who goes in a ring'] is used of them in many places; it is used also of Vāta, Agni and Sūrya."

"Their dwelling is not definitely fixed, and is described in many ways. They come from very far (8-5-?), from heaven (8-8-?), from heaven and earth (1-?-?), from heaven and the sphere of the air (8-8-4; 6-?-?), from the sphere of the air (8-?-?), from earth, heaven and sky (8-10-?), and from the air, from afar, from near (5-?-?). They dwell in the ocean of the sky (8-?-?), in the streams of heaven, in trees, in houses, on mountain-peaks (2-?-?). They come from behind, before, below and above, from all directions (2-?-?). Their dwelling has been asked about without being known for certain…"

original p. 566

Aśvins, continued "…[They have three places (8-8-?), perhaps because they are invoked three times a day]."

"While it is still dark, at the time of the red dawn, they generally come to the sacrificial hall (10-40-?); they come to earth to receive oblations from their worshippers, and yoke horses to the chariot (1-?-?; etc.). Uṣas wakes them from sleep (5-?-?). Sitting in their chariot they court Uṣas herself (8-?-?). As they yoke the chariot, Uṣas rises (10-?-?). Their time is generally between the red dawn and sunrise; yet in one place (1-34-10) it is said that Savitṛ makes their chariot move even before the red dawn. Somewhere, in one place and another, it is said that the coming of the Aśvins, the kindling of the sacrificial fire, the red dawn and sunrise — all these take place at one time (1-?-1; 2-?-?). The request that they come to the sacrificial hall is not only for the dawn that is natural to them; they are asked to come also at the evening time (8-?-?), at morning, at midday and at sunset (5-?-?). The suggestion is that the Aśvins should be present at all three pressings, morning and the rest; and it seems to be the basis of praising them with three-fold sets in one whole sūkta (1-34). As deities of the morning they make the darkness run away (3-?-?), and sometimes they drive away Piśācas and the like (2-?-?; 8-?-?). The Aśvins, Uṣas and Agni are the deities of dawn (Ait. Brā. 3-?); in Vedic sacrifices they are the deities relating to the morning. The Aśvins are of white-and-red colour (Śat. Brā. 5-?-?); therefore a goat of that kind must be offered to them."

"Both of them are sons of the sky (1-182-1; 1-184-1; 10-61-4); once it is said that one of the two is the son of the sky (1-181-4). In one place alone the ocean is their mother (Sindhumātarau, 1-46-2). In one mantra (10-17-2) the Aśvins are the children of Viśvavat [Vivasvat] and of the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, Saraṇyū, these two; the rising Sūrya and the time of dawn must, in turn, be Vivasvat and Saraṇyū. Pūṣan calls the Aśvins his progenitors (10-?-?). Their sister (1-?-?) is most likely Uṣas. As deities of the light, they are connected with Sūryā, or the daughter of Sūrya, many times: Sūryā chose them (2-?-?); both are her husbands (8-?-?; compare 1-?-?). Sūryā [or the maiden] mounted their chariot (8-?-?). Sūrya's daughter mounts their chariot (1-34-5; 1-116-17; 1-119-5; 6-63-5) or chose it (1-116-17; 4-43-2). They consider Sūryā their own (2-?-?), and one of the distinctions is that she goes with them in their chariot (8-?-?)."

original p. 567

"The deity called 'Aśvinī' (अश्विनी) mentioned along with other goddesses (5-46-8) must be herself. When Savitṛ gave Sūryā to her husband, it is said that the deity Soma did not charm her, and that the Aśvins were the suitors (10-85-9). In another place (6-58-4) it is said that the deities gave Pūṣan to Sūryā. Because of this connection with Sūryā, the prayer is made that they take the bride in the chariot to her home (10-85-?). They are prayed together with the other deities to bless the bride with sons. They show compassion even to the wife of a eunuch and cause a barren cow to give milk (1-116-13). To a maiden who had grown old they gave a husband, and to a lover a wife (1-117-?). They unite lovers (Av. 2-30-2; etc.)."

"They are foremost in helping those in distress and in releasing them from sorrow. No others are so quick in giving help (1-112-?; 1-119-?). They are always praised for such acts. In particular they protect in the sea by means of a boat. They are prayed to bring wealth from the sea or from heaven (1-?-?) and their chariot approaches from the shore of the sea (8-?-?); here 'sea' must be the sky. The help they give to the afflicted is by peaceful means; they do not protect from enemies in battle, as Indra and others do (but it is said once that they fought enemies together with Indra, and elsewhere that they killed Vṛtra). For this reason they are specially the physicians of the gods (8-?-?; etc.). They cure diseases with their herbs (8-22-10; etc.); they make the blind see (1-116-16); the lame, the sick and those with defective limbs they set right (10-39-3). They are physicians of the deities, immortal protectors; they ward off death from those who worship them (Av. 2-?-1; Tai. Brā. 1-?-?). They are helpers; their healing and their wonder-working deeds are praised for just these qualities. To their devotee they grant youth and keen sight, and bestow wealth, progeny and so on (1-116-?; 8-?-?)."

"There are many stories showing that they are quick to help in distress. They freed Cyavana, who had grown old and been forsaken by wife, children and others, from his weak affection [for them]; gave him long life, made him young again, made his wife look at him with desire, and caused the other maidens to choose him (1-116-10; etc.). The story of Cyavana's rejuvenation is told in detail in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (4-1-5). They gave youth again to an old man named Kali (10-39-8), and he became a friend of theirs (1-112-?). They gave to Vimada's wife, a young woman, a chariot (1-?-?), or gave him a wife (1-112-?). She was seen as the wife of Purumitra"

original p. 568

"(1-116-?; 10-39-7) and her name is Kamadyū (10-65-12 [?]). They made Viṣṇāpu, the son of Kṛṣṇa, who had been lost to his worshipper Viśvaka, appear again (1-116-23; 1-117-7; 10-65-12). But the story most often told is that of the protection of Bhujyu."

"Bhujyu was the son of Tugra. As he was sinking in the sea, the Aśvins came to his help. They took him in a boat of a hundred oars on the unfathomable ocean and carried him to their house. Flying, as it seemed, through the sky — in a hundred-footed boat, in a ship without support or hold, with four [ropes], with wings, in a chariot of three wheels drawn by horses [the print: 'with a hundred feet and six horses'] flying quickly — with the help of their swift horses, or in their chariot swift as thought, they landed Bhujyu safely at home. In the midst of the waves Bhujyu was clinging to the end of a log of wood and floating. He was bound hand and foot and attacked by enemies [the print: 'by the waves']; ten nights and nine days he lay in the water. Like Rebha, who was counted as dead [and lifted], like one who lifts Soma juice from the vessel with a ladle, the Aśvins lifted him and gave him life. They rescued Vandana from a pit and brought him to the light (1-116-3; 1-118-6; 1-112-5; 1-119-6), and [him] who lay in a pit, bound and fallen as if dead, they lifted up (10-39-8), or restored one bent double to life (1-?-?). The sage Atri, thrown into a fire-pit by the māyā of a Rākṣasa, and his companions they saved. They gave cooling water and revival, and saved him from the heat; and at last they gave him youth, strength and so on. It is also said that they made him see with his eyes. When it is said that Agni spared Atri from the heat of a hot bath [the print: 'a fire-chamber'] (10-80-3), it was probably done through the mediation of the Aśvins. It is also said that the bird Vartikā, who asked for their help, was saved by them from the wolf's mouth."

"Rjrāśva had killed a hundred and one sheep and given them as food to a she-wolf. His father, enraged, made him blind. Then the she-wolf praised the Aśvins, and they, pleased, gave Rjrāśva his sight (1-116-16; 1-112-16 and 8). They cured the crookedness and lameness of Parāvṛja (1-112-8). In a battle Viśpalā's foot was cut off; the Aśvins gave her an iron foot. They gave a husband to Ghoṣā, who was growing old in her father's house, unmarried, and helped her (1-117-7; 10-39-3 and 6; 10-40-5). To the wife of a eunuch they gave a son called Hiraṇyahasta (1-116-13; 1-117-24; 6-62-7; 10-39-7), who was also named Śyāva (10-65-12 [?]). Śayu's cow gave no milk; the Aśvins made such a cow give milk (1-116-22; etc.). To Pedu they gave a swift, very strong, white, matchless horse, destroyer of Rākṣasas and urged by Indra; by it he gained boundless profit"

original p. 569

"(1-116-6; etc.). To Kakṣīvat of the Pajra family they gave boons as he wished; and, as one pours a hundred jars of liquor or honey in one stream, they made it flow from the hoof of a horse (1-116-7; 1-117-6). Besides those mentioned above, many more are said to have been helped by the Aśvins (the sūktas 1-112 and 1-116 to 1-119). There may be many who were protected or cured in extraordinary ways. Since the Aśvins are physicians of the gods, it may be said that they all obtained these helps from them. As some modern scholars say, it does not seem right to hold that, for the many natural acts connected with the sun, a deity has given only a form by his deeds, but that there are no truly divine deeds."

"What portion of Nature is reflected in the Aśvins is an uncertain matter. No definite and clear function is stated for them, as for Agni, Uṣas, Sūrya and others connected with light. Even for authorities like Yāska the nature of the Aśvins is doubtful; they too (Nir. 12-1) give various views — some say the Aśvins are heaven and earth (the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4-1-5-16 has the same sense), some day and night, some Sūrya and Candra, and others two kings who perform holy acts: they only give diverse opinions and do not give their own. Modern scholars have each taken a different view. Some say that the Aśvins correspond to the morning star Śukra (the star of dawn); it is seen at that time, gives light, and goes round the sky: in every way the Aśvins agree with Śukra (the Morning Star). But the point 'twins' alone does not fit."

"It may be that the morning star (Śukra) and the evening star (Budha or Guru) form a pair; but those two are always separate. The Aśvins, on the other hand, are always together. But in the Ṛgveda they are also said to be separate (two deities). Though the early morning is favoured for Vedic rites and not the evening (5-?-?), the Aśvins are called at two times (8-?-1; 10-?-?; 10-40-4). The view that these two are twilight and the Morning Star seems to be correct to a great extent; for, in all other respects, along with the characteristics of the Aśvins, it also fits that they are goddesses of light [this sentence is as read: 'they are also deities relating to the evening']."

Deities of the Atmosphere (Antarikṣada devategaḷu)

Indra

Indra Indraḥ. "A very important deity. Some 250 sūktas and portions of sūktas praise him. Indra is also praised together with some other deities. Taking all of these together, about 300 sūktas are for him: that is, about one fourth of the Ṛgveda is for him. It cannot be said definitely that he reflects any one portion of Nature…"

original p. 570

Indra, continued "…it cannot be said [of any one portion of Nature]. For this reason Indra displays human characteristics the most, and historical descriptions have wrapped him round in great number. Chiefly he is the deity of lightning. His chief work is to conquer the evil deities of darkness or of drought, or the Rākṣasas, and to win the water or the light."

"He is the foremost of the deities of the middle world. He has pervaded the sphere of the air (1-52-12 [?]). In the Nirukta (Nir. 7-4) he is spoken of separately in the list of the deities of the atmosphere, and in the three-fold arrangement of deities — Agni, Indra (Vāyu), Sūrya — he is the representative of Vāyu."

"Various parts of Indra's body are mentioned in the Veda. He has a body, a head, shoulders and hands (3-?-?; 8-?-?). Whenever his drinking of Soma comes up, his belly is mentioned (2-16-?, etc.); filled with Soma his belly is compared to a lake (3-?-?). His jaws are described as beautiful jaws. After drinking Soma he moves his jaws (8-?-?). When he is greatly pleased, or when he moves, his beard shakes strongly (3-?-?; 10-?-?). His hair (10-96-5 and 8) and his beard are tawny, and his very form is tawny (10-96-?). In some places he is golden-coloured (1-?-?; 8-?-?). This golden colour is Savitṛ's special mark; like Savitṛ Indra is golden-armed (2-?-?); and, like him, he has firm, black-hued arms (1-?-?; 10-?-?). His arms, which especially wield the vajra, are described as growing steadily larger. They are broad, much praised, reaching far (6-?-?; 8-?-?), strong and well formed (Sām. Ve. 2-?-?). Like Sūrya, Indra takes forms with a red glow and splendid shapes (10-?-?); he becomes of many forms as he desires (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?)."

"The vajra (वज्र, vajra, 'thunderbolt') is a weapon suited to Indra alone. In the Itihāsa this name occurs frequently. In general it is said that Tvaṣṭṛ made it (1-?-?, etc.); but there is also a statement that Kāvya Uśanā made it and gave it to Indra (1-121-?; 5-34-2). The deities delivered the vajra to Indra (Ait. Brā. 4-1). In the sea, surrounded by water, the vajra lies (8-?-?); its place is beneath the sun (10-?-?). In general it is said to be made of iron or of metals (1-?-?). Sometimes it is of the colour of gold (1-?-?, etc.); of tawny colour (3-?-?; 10-?-?); or of pure white colour (3-?-?). It has four edges (8-?-?), a hundred edges (4-?-?), a hundred points (8-?-?, etc.), and a thousand points (10-?-?; etc.). It is green (2-?-?, etc.). Indra whets it like a knife, or raising it makes his horns straight (1-?-?; 1-?-?). It has the names 'stone' or 'mountain' (2-?-?)"

original p. 571

"[also]. The vajra in Indra's hand is compared to Sūrya in the sky (8-?-?). Words formed from the word vajra, or compounded with it, are generally used of Indra alone. Vajrabhṛt, vajravat and vajradakṣiṇa belong to him only; but vajrabāhu, vajrahasta and vajrī are each once used also of Rudra, the Maruts and Manyu."

"Indra comes sitting in a golden chariot (6-?-?; etc.), swifter than the mind (10-112-?). To it two tawny horses are yoked: the name of these two is Hari ('bay'). In some mantras the number of horses is more than two — a hundred; a thousand, or a thousand and hundreds (3-?-?; 8-?-?; 6-?-?; 7-?-?). Sūrya himself is the eye of these horses (1-?-?). They neigh and whinny (1-?-?). They have flying manes (1-?-?; etc.), or golden-coloured locks (8-?-?; 8-?-?), and their locks are like the fruits of the ripe bilva (3-?-?; 8-?-?). However far away the place they must reach, they go very swiftly and arrive. As one flies with the help of wings, so Indra moves with the help of these horses (3-?-?; 8-?-?). It is the praises that yoke the horses to the chariot (3-?-?, etc.): that is, the praises call Indra to the sacrificial hall. In some places it is said that the horses of Sūrya (10-?-?), or those of Vāyu (10-?-? to 6), draw Indra. Indra is the charioteer of Vāyu (8-?-?) or his fellow-rider (4-?-?). The Ṛbhus built Indra's chariot and horses (1-?-?; 3-?-?). Indra uses a golden whip (8-?-?)."

"All the deities love Soma-drinking greatly (8-?-?; 8-?-?); and of them Indra loves it the most (1-?-?, etc.). He has cried out for it in order to drink it (3-?-?; 4-?-?). Among the deities he alone is the Soma-drinker (7-?-?); his companion Vāyu is somewhat on a par with him. Soma juice is nourishing for Indra (8-?-?); the epithets somapā and somapāvan belong to him alone. Though Agni, Bṛhaspati and Vāyu are with Indra, only for Vāyu alone is it used, once, separately."

"To make the works of the world, such as supporting earth and sky, or spreading the earth and so on, Soma is a help (2-?-?). In particular, for doing the war-works, such as killing Rākṣasas and Vṛtra, he is a help (2-?-?; 2-?-?; 6-?-?), or for the work of conquering enemies (6-?-?; 7-?-?; 8-?-?). His own mother gave it to him to drink, or, from the very day he was born he drank Soma — from this it may be imagined how necessary it is to him (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; …"

original p. 572

"…6-?-?). When he was making ready to kill Vṛtra he drank as much as three lakes of Soma (5-?-?); he drank thirty lakes at one gulp (8-?-?). The after-effects of Soma-drinking Indra describes in a whole sūkta (10-119). As with men who take too much intoxicating matter, disease comes; the stupor that came upon Indra from too much Soma-drinking the deities had to cure by the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice. Milk mixed with honey also is his drink (8-?-?)."

"He eats the flesh of bulls (10-28-3): one (10-?-?), twenty (10-86-14), a hundred (6-17-11; 8-66-10), or three hundred (5-29-8) buffaloes, roasted in fire. He accepts bread offered in sacrifice (3-?-?) and grain (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 1-16-2). This grain his horses also eat (3-?-?; 3-?-?)."

"Many times it is said that Indra was born. Two sūktas (3-?; 4-18) treat of his birth. Contrary to nature, he wished to be born from his mother's side (4-18-1 and 2). Probably, since the lightning comes from the side of the cloud, this matter must have come up. Having been born, he lights up the sky (3-?-?). At the moment of birth he made Sūrya's wheel move (1-?-?). He was a warrior as soon as he was born (3-?-?; 8-?-?; etc.) and unassailable from the beginning of his birth. At his birth the unshaken mountains, heaven and earth trembled at his fear (1-?-?). In the time of his birth, from fear of his wrath, heaven and earth shook (8-?-?), and all the deities were afraid of him (3-?-?). His mother's name is mentioned many times (3-?-?; etc.). Once (4-18-10) she is a cow, and he is her calf; and he is also called a bull born of a cow (Gārbhīya?); at another place (10-101-?) he is the son of Niṣṭigrī; it is Sāyaṇa's view that Niṣṭigrī is Aditi. The mother of Indra (and Agni) is a daughter of the Prajāpati named 'Ekāṣṭakā' (Av. 3-10-?). Heaven and earth are father and mother to Agni (6-?-?); for Indra also they are the same. In the mantra (4-?-?) too, in one way of explaining, the sky itself is Indra's father (10-?-?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?; 1-?-?): the same idea comes in these. Tvaṣṭṛ, who made the vajra, is also called his father (3-?-?). Indra drank the Soma given by his mother, in his father's house (3-?-?); he drank Soma in Tvaṣṭṛ's house (4-?-?). As soon as he was born he conquered Tvaṣṭṛ, seized the Soma and drank it in the cups (3-?-?). Indra, taking his father by the foot, struck him to the ground. In the same verse the question is also asked, who made his mother a widow (4-18-12). From these statements it is understood that, in order to get the Soma, Indra killed his father Tvaṣṭṛ"

original p. 573

"(1-?-?). All the deities fought him — this must be in this very context of taking Soma by force (4-?-?)."

"There are certain different statements about Indra's birth. The deities created him to destroy the evil-doers (3-?-?); but here the root jan seems to be used in the sense of 'to bend' (compare 2-?-?; 3-?-?). Soma created Indra and some other deities (9-?-?). In the Puruṣa-sūkta it is said that Indra and Agni were born from the mouth of the Virāṭ-Puruṣa (10-90-13); that Indra, Agni, Soma and Parameṣṭhin were created by Prajāpati (Śat. Brā. 11-1-6-14); that Prajāpati created Indra last of all the deities (Tai. Brā. 2-2-10-1)."

"Agni is Indra's twin brother (6-59-2), and Pūṣan is also his brother. In one place (10-?-?) there are sons of Indra's brother; but who they are is not clear."

"Indra's wife's name occurs many times (1-82-5 and 6; 3-53-4 and 6; 10-86-9 and 10); she is called Indrāṇī (10-86-11 and 12); in some more mantras this name occurs together with other goddesses (1-22-12; 2-32-8; 5-46-8). Indrāṇī is Indra's wife (Śat. Brā. 14-2-1-8). Prabhā and Senā are his wives (Ait. Brā. 3-22-2); both are names of Indrāṇī (Tai. Brā. 3-?-?; Mai. Saṃ. 4-?-?; 4-13-1). Śacī is her proper name (Vāj. Saṃ. 8-?-?). A demon's wife lifted Indra from among the deities, down (Av. 3-?-?); having charmed a demon-woman named Vilistengā, Indra lived in the world of the Asuras, appearing like a female in a group of females and like a male in the midst of males. (Kāṭhaka)"

"Indra is seen to fight with many deities. He has many chief friends: the Maruts and the deities. They help him in many wars. The epithet marutvān is applied to Indra especially, though it is applied to other deities; so also being followed by the group of Maruts (5-?-?; 8-?-?). The double deity Indrāgnī occurs especially with Agni; since lightning too is one form of fire, the close connection of Indra and Agni is natural. Indra generated Agni between two stones (2-?-?), or discovered Agni hidden in the water (10-?-?). With Varuṇa and Vāyu, and sometimes Soma, Bṛhaspati, Pūṣan and Viṣṇu, he is united. Viṣṇu is Indra's supreme friend; in wars with Rākṣasas he is Indra's helper."

original p. 574

"…Indra is said, a little more or less clearly, three or four times to be equal to Sūrya. Indra himself states that in a former time he was Manu and Sūrya (4-26-1). Once he is addressed as 'Sūrya' (10-89-2); Indra and Sūrya are invoked as if they were a single deity (8-?-?). The word 'Savitṛ' is used of Indra in one place (3-30-1). 'Indra is Sūrya, Vṛtra is the moon' (Śat. Brā. 1-6-4-18)."

"Indra has a huge form. When he took the two boundless worlds in his hands, they were only a fistful (3-30-5). In his form he surpasses heaven, earth and sky (3-46-3). The two worlds together are only half of him (3-32-11; 10-89-?). Heaven, earth and sky cannot match the girdle of his waist (1-?-?). If the earth were ten times as large, it would be equal to Indra (1-52-11). Even a hundred heavens and a hundred earths together, or a thousand Sūryas, could not equal him (8-?-?)."

"His greatness and powers are praised in unreserved terms. Among those born before there is none equal to him (4-?-?); neither in heaven nor on earth has anyone like him been born (7-32-23). Among deities and men there is no equal or greater (6-30-4); none, past, future or present, dares so much (8-?-?). Neither gods nor men nor waters have seen even a part of his power (1-100-15). Among the deities there is none like him; those born, whether before or now, cannot compete with him (1-165-9). He surpasses all the deities (3-46-2). In strength and might all the deities bow before him (8-?-?). Even the great deities put their authority under his fame and weight (2-?-?). Though all assembled together, they cannot render his deeds fruitless (3-?-?). Even Varuṇa and Sūrya are subject to his command (1-101-3; compare 2-?-?). Mitra, Varuṇa and Aryaman pray to Indra to destroy their enemies (10-?-?), and it is said that, fighting, he provided room for the deities (2-?-?). Indra alone is ruler of the whole world (3-46-2), of all that moves and breathes (1-100-?); king of moving things and of men (3-?-?); the eye of all that moves and sees (10-?-?). He is the leader of human and divine races. Often he is called saṃrāṭ (सम्राट्, samrāṭ, 'supreme sovereign') (8-?-?, etc.), and still more often self-dependent and wholly independent (3-46-1, etc.). An ancient seer, he alone rules by his own strength the whole world (8-?-?). Sometimes he is called an Asura (1-174-1; 8-?-?). There are some special epithets showing his might. 'Śakra' (शक्र, śakra, 'mighty') is used of him some forty times and of others about five; 'śacīvat' (शचीवत्, śacīvat) is used some thirteen times for Indra and twice for another; 'śacīpati' (शचीपति, śacīpati) ten times of Indra and only once of the Aśvins."

original p. 575

"'Śacīpate śacīnām' ('lord of powers') (10-?-?) is an epithet of Indra at one place; in the Purāṇas the same epithet has become fixed in the sense 'husband of the goddess Śacī'. 'Śatakratu' (शतक्रतु, śatakratu, 'of a hundred powers') is used some sixty times, of which only twice is it applied to other deities. Likewise 'satpati' (सत्पति, satpati, 'lord of the able') is generally an epithet of Indra. Many more words express his might and ability: strong (tavaḥ), quick (nṛtu), victorious (turaḥ), heroic (śūra), of boundless power (1-?-?; 1-?-?), of unobstructed ability (1-?-?). He has his own power as armour and uses weapons with the courage of a lion (4-?-?). He is a youth (1-?-?, etc.), never old (ajara), and ancient (pūrva)."

"Let us now examine the history connected with him. Intoxicated by Soma-drinking, and accompanied by the Maruts, he who is the cause of the end of drought makes himself ready for war with Rākṣasas called Vṛtra, Ahi and so on. When he strikes Vṛtra with his vajra, heaven and earth tremble (1-80-11; 2-?-?; 6-?-?); even Tvaṣṭṛ, who made the vajra, trembles at the sight of Indra's wrath (10-?-?). With the vajra-weapon Indra smashes Vṛtra to bits (1-32-5; 1-61-10; 10-?-?); he strikes Vṛtra on the back with the vajra (1-32-?; 10-?-?), strikes him on the face with his own weapon (1-52-?). He finds and seizes the places without a guard (3-?-?; 3-?-?). He struck Vṛtra, who was lying with the water spread around him, or the serpent that lay encircled by the water (4-?-?), he struck him (6-?-?); he defeated the serpent lying on the water (3-?-?); he killed the serpent who, enclosing the waters, shut out the sky (2-11-5) and split Vṛtra, who was covering the waters, as one splits a tree (2-14-2). In this context the epithet apsujit ('conqueror in the waters') is used of no other deity. 'Indra killed Vṛtra', 'he kills Vṛtra', 'kill Vṛtra' — such praises: taken all together, it is clear that this is an event taking place constantly. After the killing of Vṛtra Indra releases the waters in many dawns and autumn seasons (4-19-8), or is prayed to do so in the future (8-?-?). He splits the mountains so that waters flow, or so that cows come out (1-?-?; 10-?-?), and by the mere sound of the vajra this work is done (6-?-?). When the mountains were split, the streams burst out; the Rākṣasa was killed; like the broken ridges of mountains, the waters shut in all around came out (5-?-?). Having killed the Rākṣasa, broken the mountain into bits, burst open the well, he released the waters that had been shut up (1-?-?; 5-?-?). He sets free the streams that were like cows tied up, or they flow to the ocean like the earnings of one who has toiled (1-61-10; 2-?-?). Having won the cows and the Soma, he made the seven rivers flow (1-?-?; 2-12-12). The waters that had been bound, the waters that had been seized by the serpent (1-?-?), he set free, he made channels for the streams with the vajra (2-?-?), made the water's stream flow to the ocean (2-?-?); he made flow the waters that had been blocked by Vṛtra (3-?-?; 4-?-?). Having killed Vṛtra, he opened the door of the shut-up water"

original p. 576

"(1-32-11). His weapons have burst in sixty rivers (1-80-?). The story of killing Vṛtra and releasing the waters comes up at every step. One whole sūkta (1-80) is wholly devoted to this in various ways. One (1-32) sūkta describes the war with Vṛtra. In all these descriptions, apart from the words vajra, mountain, stream, it may be said that there is no use of the natural words lightning, thunder, cloud and rain (1-32-5, 6 and 13; etc.). Though the streams here intended are the rivers of the earth, in the Veda the water of the sphere of the air and of the sky is also spoken of (1-100-?; 2-30-?; 2-?-?). The cows released by Indra must be the waters; in many places water is likened to cows. After killing the serpent, Indra found the cows for man (3-?-?; compare 1-?-?). When it is said that Indra brought out light and cows from the darkness with the help of his vajra (1-33-10), 'cows' means waters. In general, where it is said that light was obtained, the cows are also to be taken as cattle. The red rays first seen in the morning are compared to cows coming out of the cow-pen. Though clouds are not seen clearly, the words gṛṣṭi, bugga, bāne, maḍike and so on must mean clouds. Likewise: when Indra was born, the cows roared (8-?-?) must mean clouds."

"But in all the stories connected with Indra, the words are mountain, giri; these are the mountains where the Rākṣasas live (1-32-2; 1-33-?; 2-?-11); by them he smashes down the Rākṣasas (1-131-2; 4-30-?; 6-?-?). Taking good aim, Indra strikes with arrows from these very mountains (8-66-6).
