In order to release the cows he pressed this mountain greatly (8-?-?); or the mountain that was covering the cows was shifted by Indra from its place (6-?-?). Shaking the rocks, he made the cows easy to find (10-?-?); he released the cows that had been well hidden in the rock (6-?-?; compare 5-?-?). The cloud-masses that are like mountains may also be the clouds, cows, rain and moving, thundering rain-clouds."

"The clouds are sometimes forts of the Rākṣasas living in the sky. Such forts are ninety, ninety-nine or a hundred (2-14-6; 2-?-?; 8-?-?). They move (8-1-?); are seen in autumn (1-130-?; 1-131-4; 1-174-?; 6-20-10); are made of iron (2-20-8) or of stone (4-30-20). Indra smashes them into bits (1-53-?, etc.): for this he is called Purbhid (पुर्भिद्, purbhid, 'breaker of forts'). In a Ṛk the one who breaks forts and loves water is mentioned (10-?-10). In another, various parts of this history are pictured: he killed Vṛtra, broke the forts, made channels for the rivers, split the mountain, and gave cows to his friend (10-?-?)."

"How important this story of the killing of Vṛtra is, is known from the epithet Vṛtrahā (वृत्रहा, vṛtrahā, 'slayer of Vṛtra') that has become fixed for Indra. This name is used about 70 times. Since Agni is Indra's companion, the name is used of him also. It is also used of Soma, once or twice,"

original p. 577

"but it is clear that it is not so important there. It is plainly said that Indra killed Vṛtra by his own power (1-?-?; 2-?-?; 10-?-?); yet, other deities are helpers to Indra in this work. The deities yoked Indra to the chariot for the sake of battle (1-?-?; 6-?-?) or for the killing of Vṛtra (8-?-?). To fight Vṛtra the deities increased his heroism (10-?-?), or gave him strength and ability (10-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?), or placed the vajra in his hand (2-?-?). Most of all it is the Maruts who urge him on and are friends to him (3-?-?; 10-?-?; etc.). When all the other deities fled in fear of Vṛtra (8-?-?; compare Ait. Brā. 6-?), the Maruts stood by Indra; but in one place (8-?-?) it is said that the Maruts themselves once abandoned him. While he fought with Vṛtra, Agni, Soma and Viṣṇu too were helpers to him. The seers too stood by him in this war (3-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?). The worshipper (stotṛ) placed the vajra in his hands (1-?-?), and the sacrifice was a help to the vajra in the killing of the Rākṣasa (3-?-?). Sūktas, praises, worship and Soma — all these increase Indra's power."

"Besides Vṛtra, Indra has fought with minor Rākṣasas too. Uraṇa has ninety-nine arms (2-14-4); Viśvarūpa has three heads and six eyes (10-99-6). Indra does not kill them with the vajra alone: he crushes one Arbuda with his foot, or throws him down with a bamboo [staff?] (1-51-6; 8-32-26). He destroys ordinary Rākṣasas; with a chariot-wheel he crushes Rākṣasas (8-?-?). Agni burns the Śuṣṇa-forest [Śuṣṇa's wood?], and Indra uproots Rākṣasas with the vajra (6-?-10) and drives away evil deities (8-?-?; 8-?-?)."

"With the release of the waters there is also the gain of light, Sūrya and Uṣas. Indra won the heavenly splendour and the water (3-34-4); it was prayed to Indra, 'kill Vṛtra and obtain splendour' (6-?-?). When Indra, with his iron vajra, killed Vṛtra and let flow the water for the use of men, he set Sūrya in the sky so that all could see (1-?-?; 1-?-?). Indra, the destroyer of Vṛtra, made the water flow to the ocean, created Sūrya and found the cows (2-19-3). After the killing of Rākṣasas, he won Sūrya and the water (3-34-8 and 9). Indra, having killed the leader of the Rākṣasas and set the water free, made Sūrya, the sky and the Uṣases be born (1-?-?; 6-30-5). After Indra made the Rākṣasa be carried off into the air, Sūrya shone (8-?-?). Though Sūrya is the result of this overcoming of the Rākṣasas, once the solar orb has also been Indra's weapon. With the rays of the sun, Indra burns the Rākṣasas (8-?-?). Just as with the killing of Vṛtra, Indra found light in the darkness (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?). Indra himself is the cause of Sūrya's birth (3-49-?). He placed Sūrya, a blazing light, in the sky (8-?-?). He makes Sūrya shine (8-?-?; 8-?-?) and goes upward in the sky (1-?-?)…"

original p. 578

"…[he raises] him upward. He himself obtained Sūrya (1-100-6 and 8; 3-34-8), or found him in the darkness (3-49-?), and made a path for him (10-111-?)."

"Indra brings forth Sūrya and the Uṣases (2-12-7; 2-?-4; 3-31-15; 3-?-?; 3-?-?). He himself made the Uṣases and Sūrya shine (3-44-?). He has removed the darkness from Sūrya and the Uṣases (1-?-?). He drives Uṣas along with Sūrya (2-?-?). Together with Sūrya and the Uṣases (1-?-?; 2-?-?; 6-?-?) or with Sūrya alone (1-?-?; 3-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?) — it is so said. The cows said to be obtained, given or won by Indra cannot be waters or clouds; they must be rays of light. The cows that are delicate and made of water (8-?-?) are to be understood as clouds. In the passages that follow, the rays of light or the clouds are to be understood. Uṣas at once went forward to receive Indra, who was possessed of the cows (3-31-?). Having defeated Vṛtra, Night makes the cows visible (3-34-?). In the matter of Uṣas too the gaining of cows is suggested. Like a cow-pen, Uṣas opens the doors of darkness (6-?-?); like the door of a firm rock, the goddess Uṣas opens (2-?-?). The cows low in the direction of Uṣas (2-?-?). The Aṅgirases break and open the doors of the cow-pens of the high regions of the goddess Uṣas (6-?-?). In the mantras where the subject is water, Uṣas is introduced together with Sūrya (1-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?). Thus, in these matters — Sūrya's release from the darkness of the storm-cloud, and his release from the darkness of night — there seems to be some connection. Though the second quality is not in Indra, expanding the first a little, it is said that he released Sūrya from the darkness of night as well."

"In the matter of rain and thunder the part played by Indra is stated more clearly in some places. Indra is the cause of lightning in the sky (3-?-?), and he is also the one who makes the water flow downward (2-?-?)."

"Soma is also connected with the war with Vṛtra and the gain of Sūrya and the cows. When Indra drove off the Rākṣasa by the nearness of Vāyu, Agni and Sūrya, Soma became manifest (8-?-?). After conquering the Rākṣasa, he chose the Soma juice as his drink (3-?-?); after the Rākṣasas were conquered, Soma became his own wealth (2-?-?); he became king of the Soma plant (6-?-?). Indra made the Soma juice pressed with stones famous in the world and brought out the cows (3-?-?). Together with the cows he made the Soma juice flow (1-?-?). He found the hidden aprutva (?) in heaven (6-?-?); he found the honey kept in the tawny cow (3-?-?). Ordinary cows have milk, which is of the best nourishing kind; but the tawny cow has all sweetness within her — Indra himself placed it there, for the experience of delight (3-?-?). Dark or"

original p. 579

"red (1-62-9) [the cow] (and the one who opens the door and goes out) (6-72-?) makes the best ripened milk (utkṛṣṭa) in the cows (8-?-?). All these contexts, in general, suggest the connection between Indra and the rain-clouds."

"Indra brought the quaking mountains and the plains to a standstill (2-12-2; 10-44-8). It is said that, when they desired, they flew about, and he cut the wings of the mountains that were harming the stability of the earth. These wings must be the clouds that thundered forward (Vai. Saṃ. 1-10-?). The basis of this story is as stated in the Ṛk (5-?-?). It was Indra who set the shining regions in the sky (8-?-?). He is the support of earth and sky (3-?-?; etc.). He alone separates earth and sky, as the two wheels of a chariot are separated by the axle (10-?-?). He spreads out heaven and earth as one spreads a skin (8-?-?). He alone is the maker of earth and sky (8-?-?; compare 6-?-?). By his secret name he created all that is and all that will be (10-?-?), and in a moment made the non-existent into the existent (6-?-?). That earth and sky stand each by itself, and are held apart as in a grip — this is the result of Indra's conquest of a Rākṣasa who held these two regions together (5-?-?). When Indra was born for the killing of Vṛtra, he spread out the earth and made the sky firm (8-?-?). Having killed the Rākṣasa, Indra made a way for the rivers and made the earth visible to heaven (2-?-?). He found earth and sky that were hidden (8-?-?), or released both of them, along with light and waters (3-?-?). What is seen as sky and earth seeming to be joined in the dark — that, when light comes, they are seen separately — may be the basis for the above-mentioned ideas."

"Warriors constantly praise Indra, the wielder of the vajra, who destroys the Rākṣasas of the sphere of the air in battle (8-?-?, etc.). As the god of war he is prayed to above the other deities, that he be the helper in destroying the enemies of the earth, the Āryas' foes. He protects the Āryan colour and subdues the Dasyus (3-?-?; 1-130-8). He destroyed 30,000 Dasyus of black colour and ruined all their cities (4-?-?). Subduing the Dasyus, he gave the earth to the Āryas (4-?-?). In the region of the seven rivers, when the weapons of the Dasyus fall on the Āryas, he turns them elsewhere (8-?-?); sometimes the Aśvins (1-112-?), Agni (8-?-?) or other deities (6-20-11) alone are protectors of the Ārya."

"Indra alone is a helper who feels the troubles [of others] (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?); he is one who sets his worshippers free and speaks for them (8-?-?); he gives strength to worshippers"

original p. 580

"and is also their fortress (8-?-?). There is none that kills his friends or defeats them (10-?-?). To those who worship Indra, is he a friend? Sometimes he is the brother (3-?-?), father (4-?-?; 10-?-?), or both mother and father (8-?-?). To the Fathers (pitṛs) he is a friend (6-?-?; compare 6-?-?), and to the Kauśika family he is the highest friend; that is why the name Kauśika (1-10-11) has come to him. He does not need the friendship of him who does not offer oblations (10-?-?), but he gives wealth to him who is without a yoke [i.e. to the one who is devoted] (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 2-?-?). A prayer that he may not go to other worshippers (3-?-?, etc.). All men receive help from him (8-?-?). His two hands are full of wealth (2-?-?). He is a treasury filled with wealth (10-?-?): as a man shakes a tree to make the fruits fall. Indra is able to shower wealth upon his worshippers (3-?-?). To hold back a ball dipped in sandalwood-like mud [the print: 'a ball smeared with red earth'] may be easy, but to stop him once he has decided to give is impossible (8-?-?). He is like the ocean in wealth (1-?-?); as rivers all run to the ocean, all wealth gathers in him (6-?-?). One whole sūkta (10-42) describes the many kinds of wealth received from Indra. Like the other deities, cows and horses are prayed for from Indra (1-?-?; 1-?-?; etc.). 'The lord of cows' (gopati) is chiefly Indra. All the wars that he makes — generally called gaviṣṭi ('desire for cows', 8-?-?, etc.) — the fruit of his victory goes entirely to him (4-?-?, etc.). That Indra gives wives and sons and the like (4-?-?; 1-?-?) — his generosity is a special quality of his; hence the epithets maghavan ('bountiful'), vasupati ('lord of wealth') and so on."

"Among the stories connected with Indra, though the killing of Vṛtra is the main one, he is known to have performed many heroic deeds. In some sentences it is said that there was a quarrel with Uṣas. Indra destroyed the cart of Uṣas (10-73-6); having broken her cart with the vajra, he destroyed her slow-footed mules [?] with his swift horses (2-?-?). Afraid of Indra's vajra, Uṣas abandoned her chariot's cart (10-138-5). Having struck and destroyed Uṣas, the inwardly moving evil deity, Indra performed a great deed: her broken chariot lay in the river Vipāś, and she fled in fear (4-30-8 to 11). The disappearance of Uṣas by the heat of the sun is the basis of this story. Some think that the surpassing of Uṣas by Indra, who stays beyond the usual time and makes Sūrya rise, is the basis."

"There is a somewhat unclear story: a fight between Etaśa (a horse) and the horses of Sūrya called Harita; Sūrya himself stays ahead. Indra stops Sūrya. At that"

original p. 581

"time one wheel of Sūrya's chariot gets detached. 'Indra stopped the horses of Sūrya' (10-?-?) must be in this context. It is also said that Indra took Soma by force. Another story: Indra obtained the cows seized by an Asura named Paṇi (10-?-?). These Paṇis are very greedy; they do not release the cows even when they are needed for sacrifices and the like. Indra's messenger, the bitch Saramā, finds the place where the cows are and tells them to give them back. The Paṇis make fun of her. Elsewhere (6-?-?) it is said that Indra, wishing to gain the cows, split Vala's fort, conquered the Paṇis and set the cows free. In another place Vala held the cows captive, and Indra brought them out (2-?-?; 2-?-?). Here the Paṇi is not named. In many passages the Aṅgirases are said to have been Indra's helpers in this defeat of Vala and in the release of the cows."

"In some places it is said that Indra conquered the Dāsas or Dasyus. These Dāsas or Dasyus belong to the human race; their colour is black (compare 1-130-8; 2-20-?); they have no noses (5-?-?), no devotion to the gods and no performance of sacrifices. They must generally be said to be dwellers on earth; for, since the killing of Vṛtra and so on is said to be for the benefit of ordinary men, the destruction of these Dasyus is for the sake of some one person, or by the help of a person. Those who got help from Indra in this way are generally not seers and the like, but kings or warriors. Divodāsa Atithigva is the son of King Sudāsa; his enemy was Śambara, the son of Kulitara. But for the word 'dāsa' the meaning 'Rākṣasa' applies to the contexts where it is used of: Ahi, killed by Indra to release the waters (2-11-2); the three-headed and six-eyed Piśāca (10-99-6), or the Vyaṃsa who struck Indra's... [the print: 'who beat Indra's moustaches'] (4-?-?). The battles of Indra with such Dasyus as Namuci and the others are rightly discussed as matters concerning Rākṣasas."

"There are still many less important stories concerning Indra. One is the story about Indra, Indrāṇī and Vṛṣākapi (10-86): Indra's anger over Vṛṣākapi, the punishment given to Vṛṣākapi, his running away, and then Indra's reconciliation with Vṛṣākapi, and Vṛṣākapi's return. Indra safely took Turvaśa and Yadu across a river (1-174-9, etc.). In another, there are many wars waged by Sudās, in which he had Indra's help; this too is one. Last of all, there is the story that a woman named Apālā, seeing a Soma plant on the bank of a river, crushed it with her teeth, offered the juice that came to Indra, and obtained from him the boons she wanted."

original p. 582

Indra, end "To sum up: superhuman power and authority over the material world are the chief qualities of Indra. Action full of passion is his distinction. His is a kind of rule that Varuṇa lacks: his is not an authority that works by fixed laws. Like Varuṇa, Indra too is a sovereign; but his sovereignty is not that of one who follows fixed ordinances; he is a very powerful warrior; there is none to oppose him; by his own power he can conquer the whole world. Moreover there is no limit to his generosity; pleased by the Soma-drinking, he bestows boundless wealth on those who worship him. He does not have the moral eminence and weight that Varuṇa has. In one place it is said that he too, like Varuṇa, obtained moral eminence, and, being bound by the rule, thereby gained heaven (10-167-1; compare 10-159-?)."

Trita Āptya

Trita Āptya. "There is no sūkta addressed to this deity. But in about 40 mantras scattered through 26 sūktas the name occurs as Trita Āptya, Trita or Āptya. Of these, Trita Āptya or Āptya occurs in four sūktas (1-105; 5-41; 8-47; 10-8) and in only seven sentences; everywhere else the word is used simply as Trita. He is mostly together with Indra; seven times with Agni (or in the sense of Agni), often with the Maruts; and ten times with Soma, or the Soma juice. It is said that by the power of the Soma juice Trita alone split Vṛtra (1-187-1)."

"The Maruts helped Trita and Indra to conquer the Asura Vṛtra (8-7-24). Such acts must be a distinction of Trita. In other places this same is used as the example. Trita split the forts of Vala, as, when Vṛtra, who was blocking the rain, fought, Indra split Vṛtra (1-52-4 and 5). By Indra and Agni, even a man who has obtained their help splits strong fortresses as Trita did (3-?-1). Trita Āptya, with the weapon given by his father, urged by Indra, fought the three-headed Rākṣasa, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, killed him and released the cows (10-8-8). Indra does the same thing: splitting the three heads of Viśvarūpa, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, he makes the cows his own. Indra (or Agni) subdued the three-headed and six-eyed Rākṣasa; Trita, by his strength, using the iron-tipped vajra-weapon, killed that boar (Rākṣasa) (10-99-6). Both deities did the same bold deed: Indra released the cows from the grip of a serpent, for Trita (10-48-2). Indra gave Viśvarūpa, son of Tvaṣṭṛ, to Trita (2-11-19), being joined by Trita who was pressing Soma. Indra, rolling Arbuda, with the Aṅgirases split Vala (2-11-20). The wind"

original p. 583

"blows and the lightning flashes; Trita roars and the water roars (5-?-?). In the sūkta (2-34) addressed to the Maruts, when Trita saw, the path of the Maruts shines, and the Maruts were called by Trita in his chariot. In one sūkta the winds saw Trita and asked him for help (10-115-?). When Trita blew [the wind], as the blacksmith blows the bellows, the flames rise from the sky (6-?-?)."

"Trita, much distressed, searched for Agni and found him on the head of the cow. When that Agni was born in houses, he stays firmly in those houses, resting on splendour like a young man. Surrounded by flames, Trita sat in his own place (10-46-3 and 6). Trita's dwelling must be in heaven (5-?-?). His dwelling is hidden (9-?-?). It is very far away; for this reason the Ādityas and the Uṣases are asked to put bad deeds and evil dreams in Trita Āptya's house (very far from us) (8-47-13 and 14 [?]). His dwelling must be in the neighbourhood of Sūrya; for Trita is said to be in connection with it (1-105-9 [?]). In the same sūkta it is said that Trita fell into a well and prayed to the deities, and that Bṛhaspati, hearing it, delivered him from the trouble. In another place (10-8-7), Trita, who had fallen into a pit, remembered his father, received his weapons from him and set out to fight with Viśvarūpa. Indra, Viṣṇu, Trita Āptya or the Maruts, sitting by their sides, drink Soma (8-12-16); Trita, hearing the praise sung by him from his side, is pleased (Vāl. 4-1). Trita himself prepares the Soma (9-?-?); Trita alone purifies the Soma juice (9-34-4). Trita's maidens (the fingers) drive the juice of the Soma plant down from the stone for Indra's drinking (9-32-2; 9-38-2). Soma passes over the hidden place near Trita's two stones (9-102-2); Soma is prayed to carry wealth over Trita's hairs like a stream (9-102-3). In the bend of Trita's ridge Soma has made Sūrya and his sisters shine (9-?-?). Trita gives Varuṇa in the ocean the stirring-power (9-95-4). When Soma ferments the honey, he calls 'Trita!' (9-86-20)."

"About the real nature of the deity Trita there are no clear grounds. His name is in many lists (2-31-6; 5-41-4; 10-64-3), but nothing can be known from them. In two other passages (5-41-9 and 10) the sense is not settled. In a Varuṇa sūkta it is said that all knowledge is centred in Trita, like the spokes in the hub of a wheel (8-41-6). In another place it is said that Trita harnessed to the chariot a horse given by Yama and the transformed form of Sūrya, and that in the next mantra this horse, by a secret rite, becomes Yama, Sūrya"

original p. 584

"and Trita (1-163-2 and 3). Though the word trita is used at five places in the Atharvaveda, nothing can be known there either. Everywhere all that is known is this much: Trita is a deity dwelling very far away, in whom sin and bad dreams are cast off. The Taittirīya Saṃhitā says he is able to give long life (Tai. Saṃ. 1-5-10-3). Because he prepares the Soma that gives immortality, this may be a quality arising from that. In the Brāhmaṇas, Trita is one of the three deities Ekata, Dvita and Trita; these three are sons of Agni; Trita arose from water (Śat. Brā. 1-2-1-1 and 3; Tai. Brā. 3-2-8-10 and 11). In his explanation of Ṛgveda 1-105, Sāyaṇa mentions a story of Sātyāyani in which Ekata, Dvita and Trita are three seers, and the first two throw Trita into a well. In these contexts these words must be numerals. Dvita occurs in the Ṛgveda once together with Trita (8-47-15), and once in the Agni sūkta as indicating Agni (5-18-2). The name Trita is not in the Nighaṇṭu. Yāska (Nir. 4-6) explains this word as 'great knower' (mahājñānī); in another place (Nir. 9-2) he calls it a numeral word out of Ekata and so on, and in another place also said he is Indra residing in the three worlds (heaven, earth and sky)."

"Taking the Ṛgveda sentences, in 8–10 contexts Indra and Trita do the same work — killing Rākṣasas. Once Indra is the inspirer of Trita; in one place Trita is the inspirer of Indra; twice Indra has done work for Trita. The Maruts and Trita join together in the storm. Moreover Trita searches for Agni, and kindles Agni in heaven, and Agni dwells in the houses of men in his place. His dwelling is far away and hidden; Soma is there too. This is also a difference between Indra and Trita: Indra only drinks Soma, but Trita prepares Soma."

"The epithet Āptya applied to Trita comes from ap (water); hence it may be said to be equal to 'apāṃ napāt'. Once only the epithet 'vaibhūvasa' is used of Trita (10-46-3); it may be connected with Soma."

"From the above, it may be said that Trita is the deity of lightning — that is, a third form of Agni, or the form of the sphere of the air. He is the middle deity among the three deities Agni, Vāyu or Indra, and Sūrya. But since all the works of this deity are done by Indra alone, he is a deity of secondary importance in the Ṛgveda. He is in the form of lightning, and since he brought Soma from heaven to the earth, the connection of Trita with Soma may have been mentioned. Because the grounds are few,"

original p. 585

"each scholar has held some opinion. To mention a few only: Roth says he is the deity of water and wind; Hillebrandt that he is the deity of the blazing sky; Perry that he is a deity of the storm. Another, Pischel, said that he was first a deity of the sea and water, afterwards a physician among men, and then obtained divinity. Hardy has said that he is a deity of the moon."

Apāṃ napāt

Apāṃ napāt Apāṃnapāt. "One sūkta (2-35) is addressed to this deity, and two mantras (10-30-3 and 4) in a sūkta addressed to the deity of waters praise him. The name occurs some thirty-three times. Around the resplendent Apāṃ napāt (child of waters) the water stood still. The young man is surrounded by the waters. The three women-deities, who are best of all, wait to give him food; he drinks the milk of the first mothers (2-35-3 and 5). He, a bull in form, placed in them the embryo; as an infant he drinks their milk; they kiss him. He appears, growing in the water itself, to the light. By day and night and the like he blazes in the water (10-30-4). Taking the cloud as his garment, he joins the slightly flowing water of the pestle (?). The swiftly flowing, golden-coloured water bears him and goes round in a circle (2-35-? and Śat.… compare Agni in 6-?-?). His is golden splendour and golden body colour; born from a golden womb, he gives food to those who worship him. Standing in the very high regions, he shines without growing less. The swiftly flowing waters bring ghee for their son (Apāṃ napāt) for food, wear the stars, and flow round about. His face is of golden colour; maidens make him shine; he has tuppa (ghee) as food; he grows in the way that no one's going is heavy. In his house there is a good milch cow. Horses swift as thought carry him. He has relation to the rivers too. It is he who has made all creatures be born; all of them are his parts. At the end of the sūkta addressed to this deity he is called Agni. In the same way, in some sūktas of Agni, Agni is called Apāṃ napāt (compare Vāj. Saṃ. 8-?). Agni is the son of water (3-?-?). Agni, together with Apāṃ napāt, grants victory over Vṛtra (6-?-?). The deity Apāṃ napāt seems to be the same as another person's body (2-35-?)."

"The name Apāṃ napāt occurs in the lists of many deities; but especially it is joined with Aja Ekapād (2-31-6; 2-35-13), Ahirbudhnya (1-186-5; 2-31-6; 2-35-13) and Savitṛ (2-31-6;"

original p. 586

Apāṃ napāt, end "…2-31-6 and 7 [?]) are said together with these [deities]. Since Savitṛ too has a special form that gives Agni fruit, even Savitṛ has the name 'Apāṃ napāt' at one place (1-22-6). The deity Apāṃ napāt — golden-coloured, with lightning for his garments, dwelling in the very highest region, growing secretly, shining most, son of water, descending to earth, equal to Agni — may well be Agni himself, in the form of lightning confined in the clouds. Agni is called not only Apāṃ napāt but also 'the embryo of water' (apāṃgarbhaḥ) (2-?-?; 1-?-?). In that same form he is placed in the houses of men (3-?-?); his dwelling is in the water (8-?-?); Agni, as the embryo of plants and of water, is born from the fire-sticks (3-1-13). Agni is also named 'son of the mountain' (adreḥ sūnum, 10-?-?; compare 6-?-?): the lightning born from the cloud of mountain form must be the 'son of the mountain'. As opposed to the forms of the heavenly world and the mortal world, the third form of Agni blazes in the water, in the ocean, in the breast of the sky or in the lap of the water (10-?-? onward). That the water is the dwelling of the heavenly Agni is very well known in Vedic history."

"This deity has given occasion to various opinions: the deity of water; Agni, moon, Sūrya and lightning, born of water, and so on."

Mātariśvan

Mātariśvan Mātariśvā. "There is no sūkta that praises this deity alone. The name occurs only twenty-seven times. It appears that Mātariśvan and Agni are one, or that Mātariśvan generates Agni. Mātariśvan is a name of Agni (3-5-9; 3-?-?; 1-?-?). The vocative in (8-?-?) too must be applied to Agni. In another place, 'in the atomic form of the heavenly one' he has the name 'Tanūnapāt'; after birth he is called 'Narāśaṃsa'; when born as Mātariśvan, he himself becomes the swift-moving wind (3-29-11). The wise call the One by many names: Agni, Yama, Mātariśvan, they say (1-164-46). There is a name Bṛhaspati, many times said to be equal to Agni, which also belongs to Mātariśvan: 'That Bṛhaspati himself became Mātariśvan at the time of the sacrifice' (1-190-?)."

"In some other places, Agni and Mātariśvan are said to be different. He (Agni), born in the very high heaven, appeared to Mātariśvan (1-143-2). Agni first appeared to Mātariśvan and Viśvavat (1-60-1). As Agni is the best of the planets that are full of light, he has become the support of the sky with his flames; Mātariśvan made him blaze, the carrier of oblations that had been hidden (3-5-10). From the sky Mātariśvan brought one (Agni); the bird brought another (Soma) from the mountain"

original p. 587

"(1-93-6). Mātariśvan brought the Agni who is worshipful, the priest and the dweller in heaven (3-2-13). The deities made Agni, born of Bhṛgu, the first priest for men (10-46-9). The deity Mātariśvan brought him (Agni) from very far for men (1-128-2). Mātariśvan, the messenger of Viśvavat, brought Vaiśvānara-Agni from very far; the mighty ones had seized him in the water (6-8-4). Mātariśvan brought from very far Agni, who was born of churning of the fire-sticks and hidden (3-9-5). Mātariśvan churned the hidden Agni and brought him to birth (1-148-1). Churned by Mātariśvan, Agni was placed in the dwellings of men (1-60-1; 1-148-1). Indra, having seized by the grip, released the cows for Trita, and gave the cow-pens to Dadhyañc and to Mātariśvan (10-48-2)."

"In some sūktas of the later part of the Ṛgveda, though the subject of Mātariśvan is raised, nothing is known of his nature, qualities and so on. In two places (9-86-?; 10-114-1) it is said that he purifies Soma and drinks it. In another place (Vāl. 4-2) the name occurs in the list of the Fathers; there Indra, seated at his side, drinks Soma. Once Indra is compared with him as with an excellent craftsman (10-105-6 [?]). In the marriage sūkta, even though there is a prayer that Mātariśvan, with the other deities, should enter the hearts of lovers, this too is a feat of skill. Last of all, in one place Mātariśvan is said to be a swift-moving one and one who whirls around (10-109-1). Both these qualities support the view that Mātariśvan is Vāyu (wind)."

"Thus Mātariśvan is heavenly Agni embodied; moreover, it is he who brought Agni from heaven to the earth. Lightning may be said to be the root of Mātariśvan. As Agni, being a messenger between the two worlds, so Mātariśvan, the messenger of Viśvavat, may be said to have come from heaven to earth. In the Atharvaveda too Mātariśvan is a name of Agni (Av. 10-?-?). But in the Brāhmaṇas and so on Mātariśvan means Vāyu; the basis for this opinion is stated even earlier (3-29-11). Agni, who in the sphere of air is like a snake hissing, is described elsewhere as a wind that blows with a sound (1-?-?)."

"The word Mātariśvan may mean 'one who grows in the mother' or 'one formed' [as read]. The root śvi means 'to grow, to increase in the body'. From it come words like śiśu ('infant'). Like Mātariśvan, Agni too grows in the mothers (the fire-sticks) (1-140-?). When applied to Mātariśvan, the lower fire-stick or the cloud only can be meant; since he comes from the sky, the cloud may be called his mother. In Yāska's view Mātariśvan is Vāyu; 'mātari' means in the sky, 'śvan' one who breathes, or 'āśu an', one who breathes swiftly — that is, wind."

original p. 588

Ahirbudhnya

Ahirbudhnya. "Ahi budhnya means a serpent of the sea or of the nether world. This name occurs chiefly in the sūktas addressed to the Viśve-devas. In all it is used only twelve times in the Ṛgveda. Five times it is said with Aja Ekapād, three times with Apāṃ napāt, three times with the sea, and twice with Savitṛ. In only three Ṛks (5-41-16; 2-31-6 and 7 [?]) this name stands alone. Whenever another deity is mentioned with him, that deity is generally Aja Ekapād (10-64-4) or Apāṃ napāt (1-186-5). Aja Ekapād and Ahirbudhnya are generally joined side by side; only in (10-66-11) is it somewhat contrary. The lists in which this name occurs are as follows: Aja Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, Sāgara, Apāṃ napāt and Pṛśni (2-31-6); Ahirbudhnya, Aja Ekapād, Trita, Ṛbhukṣan, Savitṛ, Apāṃ napāt (2-31-6); Sāgara, Sindhu, Ākāśa, Gāḷi [wind], Aja Ekapād, the roaring stream, Ahirbudhnya, and the Viśve-devas (10-66-11). On examining these lists, Ahirbudhnya must be said to be one of the deities of the atmosphere. In the Nirukta (Nir. 9-4) he is counted as a deity of the middle world or sphere of the air. In the mantra that alone treats of this deity, something definite is known of him. 'We praise with song the serpent born in the water, seated at the bottom of the stream of the atmosphere' (2-?-?; compare 10-?-?) — from this it is indicated that this deity lives in the mass of water in the sky. Yāska (Nir. 10-44) has explained the word budhna as 'wind'. In the Ṛk that follows (2-?-?) it is prayed that he should not injure his worshippers. Elsewhere the same words are used (5-41-?). From these sentences it is evident that his nature is not wicked. The word ahi is generally used of Vṛtra. Vṛtra too is described in this way: enclosing the water, he lay with the water flowing over him, or fallen in the water or in the bottom of the sky (1-32-?). The fire of the atmosphere too is called ahi (1-?-?); he is said to have been born in the depths of the atmosphere (4-?-?). Ahi Budhnya and Ahivṛtra were one; but, because the idea came that Ahirbudhnya too is a deity, his evil nature is only subtly indicated. In the other Vedas a connection of Ahirbudhnya with the Gārhapatya fire is shown (Vāj. Saṃ. 5-?; Ait. Brā. 3-?; Tai. Brā. 1-1-10-3). In the Purāṇas, Ahirbudhnya is one of the names of Rudra."

Aja Ekapād

Aja Ekapād. "Ahirbudhnya and Aja Ekapād have a very close kinship. Both together occur five times, and Aja Ekapād alone only once (10-65-14). The roaring Sāvīrī,"

original p. 589

"Ekapāt Aja, the one who holds up the sky (divodharmā), Sindhu, the water of the ocean, the Viśve-devas, Sarasvatī (10-65-13) and Sāgara, Sindhu, Antarikṣa, Aja Ekapād, the roaring stream, Ahirbudhnya and the Viśve-devas (10-66-11) — in both these lists the sense is about the same. From these it is known that Aja Ekapād too is one of the deities of the sphere of the air. In the Nirukta, however, he is counted as a deity of heaven. In the Atharvaveda it is said that Aja Ekapād has made the two worlds firm (Av. 13-1-6). 'Aja Ekapād rose in the eastern quarter' (Tai. Brā. 3-1-2-8). The commentator says that Aja Ekapād is a form of Agni, and the commentator Durga (on Nir. 12-29) takes him as Sūrya. Yāska himself has said nothing clear about it. In his view aja means 'one who makes go' and ekapād 'one with one leg', or 'one who protects with one foot', or 'one who drinks'. Though he has no fixed place as an independent deity, offerings are made to him and to Ahirbudhnya in the domestic sacrifices (Pāraskara 2-?-?). In the Purāṇas Aja Ekapād is one of the names of the eleven Rudras."

"Among the modern scholars each has taken a different view. A form of storm-wind, one of the deities of the Saurya group; this Aja that moves alone is the moon — 'one-footed, unborn', the deity who lives in some unknown world: these and other opinions are seen."

Rudra

Rudra Rudra. "In the Ṛgveda the place of Rudra is not of great importance: only three sūktas and one portion of a sūkta, one together with the deity Soma, praise this deity. The name occurs only seventy-five times."

"The description of his limbs is as follows. He has an arm (2-33-2; etc.), arms (2-33-3; Vāj. Saṃ. 16-1) and firm limbs (2-33-11). His jaws are beautiful (2-33-5) and he wears his hair braided like Pūṣan (1-114-1 and 5). He is tawny in colour (2-33-8; etc.). His form is bright enough to dazzle the eyes (1-114-5), and he has many forms (2-33-?). Like the blazing Sūrya he shines as gold (1-43-5). He wears gold ornaments (2-33-?) and a shining necklace of many colours (2-33-10). He sits on the seat of a chariot (2-33-4). In other Saṃhitās, especially in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, many more characteristics are stated. He is thousand-eyed (Av. 11-2-? and 2; Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?). He has belly, mouth, nose and teeth (Av. 11-2-?). His belly is black and his back red (Av. 15-1-? and 7). His neck (Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?) is blue and his hair blue…"

original p. 590

Rudra, continued "…(Av. 2-?-?). His colour is copper-red, tawny (Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?). He wears a skin (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-?; 16-?) and dwells in the mountains (Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?)."

"He has many weapons of attack. He holds the vajra weapon (2-33-3). His arrow, loosed from the sky, goes over the earth (7-46-3). Generally he carries bow and arrows (2-33-10 and 11; 5-?-?; 10-?-?); those arrows are strong and swift (2-?-?). He is praised together with Kṛśānu and other archers (10-?-?). Where it is said that Indra sits in the chariot with the archer (6-?-?; compare 2-33-11), the archer must be Rudra himself. In the Atharvaveda too the name 'archer' is given to him (Av. 1-?-?; 6-?-?; 15-?-?). In the Atharvaveda and other portions of the Vedas his bow, arrow, weapon, vajra-weapon or club are mentioned at every step (Av. 1-?-?, etc.; Śat. Brā. 9-1-1-?)."

"The matter that comes up at every step in connection with Rudra is his relation to the Maruts. Rudra is the father of the Maruts (1-114-?; 2-33-1); or the Maruts are said to be Rudra's sons; and they have the name Rudras, or sometimes Rudriyas (1-?-?; 2-34-10; etc.), children of Pṛśni (2-34-2; 5-?-?; 5-60-5; 6-66-3); many times they are called Pṛśnimātaraḥ (those who have Pṛśni as their mother) (1-23-10; etc.; Av. 5-?-?). Pṛśni, the cow (5-?-?), or in general the cow (8-?-?), is their mother; they are also called Gomātaraḥ (compare 8-?-?; 8-20-?). This cow is probably the cloud tinted with many colours in the storm. Rudra created the Maruts out of the udder of Pṛśni, who was shining (2-34-2). But just as Indra and the Maruts join in battles and the like, Rudra and the Maruts do not join together everywhere; for Rudra is never found at war with the Rākṣasas. The name Tryambaka (त्र्यम्बक, tryambaka), which is often applied to Rudra in the Purāṇas and elsewhere, is seen in the Vedas too (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-?; Śat. Brā. 2-6-2-?); in the Ṛgveda also it is applied to him in one place (7-59-12). The word means 'one who has three fathers and mothers' [or 'three mothers'] (compare 3-56-?). Here the three persons known as mothers may be the three parts of the world. In the Purāṇas, Ambikā is Rudra's wife; but in the Vedas she is his sister (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-57). Umā and Pārvatī, names of Śiva's wife, occur in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka and the Kena Upaniṣad."

"Among the many deities said to be equal to Agni, Rudra is also one (2-1-6). Elsewhere also he and Agni are one (Av. 7-?-?; Tai. Saṃ. 5-4-3-1; 5-5-2-4; and compare Śat. Brā. 6-1-3-10; 9-1-1-?). The word rudra is often used as an epithet; many times of Agni, and still more of the Aśvins, this epithet is said. Rudra has two new names, Śarva and Bhava (Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?). These two names and his destroying arrows are mentioned in the Atharvaveda also (Av. 2-?-?; 6-93-1; 10-1-23; 11-2-1 and 13); but here Śarva, Bhava and Rudra seem to be thought of as separate deities. Śarva and Bhava are sons of Rudra, and in the Brāhmaṇas…"

original p. 591

"…they are many (Sāṃ. Śrau. Sū. 4-?-?). Agni, Aśani, Paśupati, Bhava, Śarva, Īśāna, Mahādeva, Ugradeva and others are one deity in various forms (Vāj. Saṃ. 39-?). Rudra, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Aśani, Bhava and Mahān Deva — these are eight forms of Agni (compare Śat. Brā. 6-1-3-?; Śāṅ. Brā. 6-1, etc.); and Śarva, Bhava, Paśupati and Rudra — all are names of Agni (Śat. Brā. 1-7-3-8). Of the above names Aśani is the name of the child of Agni (lightning) (6-?-?); but in another place (Śāṅ. Brā.) it is a name of Indra. The cows driven from the house are more apt to fall under Rudra's stroke; for that reason such are all put under his protection. Hence the name Paśupati ('lord of cattle') for him."

"Rudra is of terrible form (2-33-9 and 11; 10-?-?) and is a destroyer like a fierce beast (2-33-11). He is a red-hued boar of the sky (1-114-5). A bull (2-33-?, and others). Exalted (2-?-?); rich in strength (1-?-?; 1-114-?); the strongest among the strong (2-33-3); unobstructed (2-?-?); not surpassed in prowess (2-33-10); swift (10-?-?); quick (1-114-4). He is young (5-60-5) and never grows old (6-49-10). He bears the name Asura (5-42-11) or is a great Asura of heaven (2-1-6). Self-renowned (1-?-?; 10-?-?); he rules over heroes (1-114-1 and 3; etc.), and is the lord and father of this world (2-33-9; 6-49-10). He ordains the rules (6-?-?), and by his ordinances and his sovereignty over the world he takes hold of all the works of the deities (2-?-?). That the rivers run and make the whole earth moist is by his command (10-?-?). He is wise (1-43-1), knowing (1-114-4) and generous (2-33-2; 6-49-10). Many times he is mīḍhvān ('bountiful'; 'generous') (the usage is at 1-114-3, and in other Vedas this usage applies to Rudra alone). He is easily praised (2-33-6) and beneficent (Śiva; 10-92-9)."

"Doing harm is a special quality of his. In all the sūktas praising him, the fear of his arrow and the ill results of his anger are the matters spoken of. Those who praise him pray that he not kill or injure their parents, children, followers, cattle or horses in anger (1-114-7 and 8), but protect the horses (2-33-1) and turn his arrows elsewhere to destroy others with them (2-33-11 and 14); that when angry he should turn his vajra-weapon away, and not trouble his worshippers (6-28-?; 6-?-? onward), and that he should put at a distance from them the weapon that kills their cows, their children, cattle and men (2-33-1). They pray that he not make them suffer his anger (2-33-? onward and 15), and they beseech him to be gracious in the matter of 'the food that moves' (10-?-?). He has the epithet 'killer of men' (nṛghnī; 4-3-6); he looks out for chances to kill men (Āś. Gṛ. 4-8-?)."

original p. 592

"His anger has become still more prominent in the other Vedas. At every step he is prayed to (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-?; etc.; Av. 1-?-?; etc.). They pray him not to use the heavenly fire on them, but to make the thunderbolt fall in some other place (Av. 11-2-26; 10-1-23). Through fever, cough and poison he acts against them, against men (Av. 11-2-22 and 26). Dogs with wide mouths, red and yellow-coloured and always barking are with him (compare Av. 10-1-30; Vāj. Saṃ. 16-?). When they see his stretched bow and arrows even the deities are afraid, 'whom will he destroy?' (Śat. Brā. 9-1-1-? and 6); he is known as Mahādeva. He kills the cows (Tāṇḍya Mahā Brā. 6-9-2). He is formed of all things that are terrible (Ait. Brā. 3-33-1). That in the Brāhmaṇas and Sūtras he is said to stay apart from the other deities must be because of these terrible qualities. When all the deities went to the heaven-world, Rudra stayed behind (Śat. Brā. 1-2-3-1). In Vedic rites, generally, after oblations are given to the other deities, what remains is offered to Rudra (Āp. Dh. Sū. 2-4-?). In sacrifices, blood is given as the share of the Piśācas (Ait. Brā. 2-?-1); his soldiers attack men with diseases and death, and eat the remains of the oblation, the blood-stained food of those who have been sacrificed (Sāṃ. Śrau. Sū. 4-?-?). The dwelling-places of other deities are in the eastern quarter, but Rudra dwells in the northern quarter. Because of his terrible nature he does not particularly join the other deities, and is a deity without a pair; he has only one short sūkta together with Soma, and no praise otherwise."

"Besides these, the terrible and sometimes insufferable qualities of Rudra, as drawn in the Purāṇas and elsewhere, are stated in some of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā."

"But Rudra is not wholly a causer of evil like Piśācas and others. He is prayed to ward off the afflictions caused by other deities (1-114-4; 2-33-2). He gives protection from accidents, and grants boons (1-114-1 and 2; 2-33-6), and makes human beings and animals prosper (1-43-6). That he has the power to cure diseases is said at every step. He bestows herbs (2-33-2); all herbs are under him (5-42-11); and he has a thousand herbs (2-?-?). In his hand are the best herbs (1-114-5); his hand itself has healing power (2-33-7). By his healing he makes the heroes prosper; for he is the best physician among physicians (2-33-4), and, with the help of the best herbs, he wishes his worshipper to live a hundred years (2-33-2). He is prayed to be auspicious to the offspring of those who worship (2-?-?), and that there be no one in the village who is sick or ill, but that cattle and men be well (1-114-1). In this context he has two epithets, 'one who has the water-healer' (jalāśa) and 'water-healer' (jalāśabheṣaja) (1-43-4; Av. 2-27-6). 'Herbs' here must mean rain-water (compare 7-?-?; 10-?-?). Rudra's lightning and his healing powers are spoken of together (2-?-?). The physician Rudra is prayed to be gracious together with the other Rudras (2-33-?), and the Maruts too are said to have healing power along with Rudra (2-33-13). This power of Rudra is mentioned in the other Vedas also (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-59; 16-?; Av. 2-27-6); but his destructive power"

original p. 593

"is not mentioned so much as this. For driving away disease or for warding it off, sacrifices are prescribed in the name of Rudra (Āś. Gṛ. 4-8-10; Kau. Sū. 32-?; etc.)."

"What portion of Nature Rudra reflects is not determined. He too is a deity of the storm. But, like Indra, his wrath is only against those who do harm, and not above; there is harm to all from it. So he is a part of the storm. He is both a destroyer and a gale. If this view is accepted, the arrows are deadly. The ideas of Maruts, as father or chief of the storm-deities, are made meaningful. The benefit from him, healing and so on, may be the good results of rain brought by the storm. The pleasant (saumya) name 'Śiva' ('auspicious'), which has been given to him in order to avert the evil results of his anger, became fixed for him. Through this too the close relation between him and Agni is understood."

The Maruts (Marud-devategaḷu)

The Maruts. "Very important deities. 33 sūktas wholly, and, with Indra, 6, and with Agni and Pūṣan one each, so in all 43 sūktas praise them. They are always together in a group or crowd (1-37-1; etc.), and used in the plural. They are in number sixty times three [i.e. 180] (8-96-8) or seven times three [i.e. 21] (1-133-6; Av. 13-1-18). It has been said many times that they were born (5-52-?; etc.). They are the sons of Rudra, hence the name Rudras (1-64-2 and 5, etc.); sometimes also Rudriyas (1-?-?; 2-34-10; etc.), the children of Pṛśni (2-34-2; 5-?-?; 5-60-5; 6-66-3); Pṛśnimātaraḥ ('those who have Pṛśni as mother') is said many times (1-23-10; etc.; Av. 5-?-?). Pṛśni the cow (5-?-?), or ordinarily the cow (8-?-?), is their mother; they are also called Gomātaraḥ (compare 8-?-?; 8-20-?). This cow is perhaps the cloud coloured with many colours in the storm. Big, rough-bellied cows come roaring (2-34-5): these are only the clouds in the storm season, with lightning and thunder. When born of Pṛśni, the Maruts are likened to Agni (6-66-1 onward). From the laughter of the lightning the Maruts were born (1-23-12; compare 1-?-?). Agni gave them form, or obtained them (6-3-?; 1-?-?). Vāyu placed them in the womb of the sky (1-134-?) and they are children of the sky (11-?-?), and heroes of the sky (vīrāḥ; 1-64-?; 1-133-1; 5-54-10) or males of the sky (3-54-13; 5-?-6). In one place it is said that the ocean is their mother (samudramātaraḥ; 10-78-6). In some other places they are said to be self-born (born of themselves; 1-168-3; 5-?-?)."

original p. 594

Maruts, continued "They are brothers; but there is no distinction of elder and younger (5-59-6; 5-60-5), for they are all of the same age (1-165-1). All of them grew up together (5-58-?; 2-?-?) and are of one mind (8-20-1 and 20). They all have one birthplace (5-53-?) and one dwelling-place (1-165-1; 2-?-1). They grew in the sky, on earth, in heaven (5-55-2) or in the three heavens (5-60-6). In one place (8-?-1 and 3) they are called mountain-dwellers."

"Indrāṇī is their friend. She quarrels with Indrāṇī (10-?-?) and Sarasvatī (2-?-3). That they have such kinship is more with the goddess named Rodasī; she gives them the means of comfort and stands with them in their chariot (5-56-8), or stands at their side (6-66-6). In all five places where her name occurs she is with the Maruts (compare 1-167-4 and 5). Therefore she is counted as the wife of the Aśvins, like Sūryā. For this reason they have the epithet 'bhadrajānayaḥ' ('having excellent wives') (5-61-4), and they are likened to bridegrooms (5-60-4) or to young lovers (10-?-6)."

"Their brilliance comes up often. They are of golden colour, of bright lustre like Sūrya, of a slightly red colour like a blazing fire (6-66-3; 2-34-11; 8-?-2). They shine like flames of fire (10-?-3). They have the form of Agni or the splendour of Agni (10-?-1; 3-?-5); they are compared with Agni in splendour (10-?-3). They are like Agni (2-34-1) or like blazing Agni (6-66-2); the name Agni is given to them (3-?-4). They have the lustre of serpents (ahibhānavaḥ, 1-172-1). They shine on the mountains (8-?-1). They are 'svabhānu' ('self-shining', 1-37-2; etc.). This epithet is not said of any other deity. 'Bright' and 'blazing' come at every step (1-165-13; etc.)."

"In particular they have a connection with lightning (5-54-2, 3 and 11; 1-64-5). When the Maruts churn the milk, the lightnings look at the earth and laugh (1-168-8; compare 5-52-6). When the Maruts call the rain, the thunder makes a noise like a lowing cow (2-34-13). The lightning is related to them to such a degree that in the five places where vidyut is used as a compound word, in four of them it is with marut alone. The thunder they hold in their hand (2-?-3; 5-54-11); thunder is their inner delight (5-54-3). In their hands are bhārjis (spears). Here too bharji (a fist) must be thunder only; for they are specially described as those who use thunder itself as the bhārji [the print: 'fist-lightning'] (1-168-5; 5-52-13). In a few places less often they have a hammer of gold (8-?-13)"

original p. 595

"[and] a golden-made axe as a weapon (1-37-2, 1-88-3; 5-53-4; 5-52-2; 8-20-4). Once it is said that they hold the vajra-weapon. In some places they are said to be bow-and-arrow bearers (5-53-4; 5-52-2; 8-20-4 and 11) and once archers loosing arrows. But this quality is not natural to them. They are adorned with ornaments such as garlands of flowers (5-53-4); they wear golden belts (5-53-6); like a prosperous man for a wedding, they adorn their bodies with golden ornaments (5-60-4). The armlet or anklet is their personal ornament. Adorned with these ornaments, they shine like the sky studded with stars, or like the waters that fall from the cloud. On their arms are spears; on their feet anklets; on their breasts golden ornaments; in their hands whips that crack; and on their heads golden helmets (5-54-11)."

"The chariots the Maruts use shine with lightning (1-88-1; 3-54-13); they are made of gold (5-57-1); they have golden wheels or rims (1-64-11; 1-88-5). In them are weapons (5-57-6); they have arrows of water (1-37-2). The horses that draw the chariot are tawny (1-88-2; 5-57-4); golden-hoofed (8-7-32) and swift as thought (1-85-4). These horses have spots; their special name is Pṛṣadaśvāḥ ('those with spotted horses'). It is also said that the Maruts have yoked she-horses to their chariot (1-64-9). It is said that they have yoked the wind itself as a horse for their chariot (5-58-2)."

"The Maruts are huge like the sky (5-57-4); they surpass heaven and earth (10-77-3). Their greatness is boundless (5-58-3); no one can know the measure of their power (1-168-?). They are young (1-64-3; 1-165-?; 5-?-13) and have no old age (1-64-3). They are Asuras, energetic, bright, without fault (1-64-2 and 3) and without dust (6-66-3); terrible in form (1-19-4); of fierce nature (2-34-6); terrible like wild beasts (3-26-?), and so on. They are playful like children or calves (1-166-2; 5-?-1; 10-77-6). They are like geese with black backs (5-59-2); like wild boars with iron tusks (1-88-5); like lions (1-64-8)."

"They roar loudly (1-165-2; etc.). This roar is thunder (1-38-11), and the sound of the blowing wind (5-58-3). When they come, the sky seems to be trembling with fear (8-7-34). They shake the mountains, and make the earth or the two worlds tremble. They crush mountains with the wheel-rims, or the rocks (1-64-11; 5-52-9). When they come with the wind, they make the mountains shake (8-7-4). They roll trees like wild elephants…"

original p. 596

"…and devour forests (1-64-7; 1-88-2). The forests bow to the ground in fear of them (5-60-2). Like mountains they are unobstructed, and throw the creatures of heaven and earth down (1-64-4). All creatures fear them (1-85-5). Like the wind they move swiftly (10-78-3); they raise dust in whirling form (1-64-?). They produce the wind or the sound of the wind (2-34-3). They come with the wind (8-7-3, 4 and 17); they make it their horse (5-58-2)."

"Giving rain is the chief of their works. Rain is their garment (5-?-?). Rising from the sea, they send down rain (1-38-9). In both worlds they pour down rain and blow (1-64-6; 8-7-17). Rain follows them (5-53-10). They bring the waters and make the rain (5-58-3). With the rain they hide their light (5-59-1). With the rain they cover the eye of Sūrya (5-59-5). When the rain falls they make darkness with the clouds (1-38-9). Along with the wind they move swiftly, scattering frost (8-7-4). The arrows of the sky (the cloud, 5-53-6; 5-59-?) and the mountain-streams make the water flow (5-59-?). When they run, the water flows (5-58-6). By this work a river of the earth has the name 'Marudvṛdhā' ('increased by the Maruts', 10-75-5). Rudra's sons alone are the rain (5-58-2). The rain made clear by the Maruts has been compared in a figurative way to milk (1-168-?), ghee (1-85-5; 10-?-?), milk and ghee (1-64-6). They pour like the spring (madhu) (1-85-11) or drench the earth with honey (5-54-?). Raising water from the sea to the sky, they pour it from there upon the earth as rain (Av. 4-?-?). With the rain that they pour, there is always lightning and thunder. In their desire to pour water, the Maruts roar and swallow with force (5-54-3). By their power they create wind, lightning and hail; they milk the heavenly things from the cloud and fill the earth with milk (1-64-5); the thundering cloud, milked by them, roars (1-64-6). Through them the water becomes full, and the sky, the golden bull, thunders (5-58-6). They make the horse [i.e. the cloud] create water (1-64-6). They favour the rain of the sky and make the streams born of the horse flow well (5-58-6). Joining the horse, when they create the water, the Maruts become golden-coloured (2-34-13). When the clouds thunder, the streams echo the sound of the Maruts' chariot-rims (1-168-8). The water that Indra sends is called 'marutprītiḥ' ('accompanied by the Maruts', 1-100-?). In the sense of rain-makers they have the names 'purudraptsāḥ' (5-52-?) or 'dṛpsinaḥ' (1-64-?) ('having many drops of water') and 'sudānavaḥ' ('well steeped in water')."

original p. 597

"They also diminish the branches [of trees]. But they themselves make the forests wave [?] (2-34-?). They create light (1-86-10) and make a path for Sūrya (8-7-4). They have determined the limit of the wind (5-55-?); they have spread out the regions of the earth and the parts of the sky that are distinguished by splendour, and have separated the two worlds (8-7-4 and 11)."

"The sound that is heard in the wind may be the reason why they are called singers (5-52-?; 5-60-?; 2-34-?); they are the singers of the heaven-world (5-?-?). They sing a song (1-?-?; 1-?-?). By singing they made Sūrya shine (8-?-10); blowing flutes, they split the mountain (1-85-10). When Indra killed the serpent, the Maruts, singing for him, prepared the Soma juice (5-29-2; 5-?-?). By singing they gave strength to Indra (1-?-?). What they sing is mainly the sound heard in the wind (compare 8-?-?); yet that is thought of as a praise (3-?-?). When with Indra they are invited as priests (5-?-3) and are compared with priests (10-?-1). They were the first to perform sacrifice (2-?-?); they are the ones who purified Agni in the houses of the Śiṣṭas; the Bhṛgus kindled Agni (10-?-?). Like many other deities, they too are said to drink Soma (2-?-?; 8-?-? to ?; etc.)."

"Because of the idea that thunder-rain and they are one, they are by nature friends of Indra; as fellow-workers they are closely related to him. By their praise and singing they increase Indra's power and strength (3-?-?; 6-?-?). In the war with Vṛtra, generally the Maruts themselves are his helpers (8-?-?; 10-?-?). They help Trita and Indra in killing Vṛtra (8-?-?). They are prayed to sing the sūkta that kills Vṛtra (8-?-?). In the wars that Indra made with the serpent and with Śambara, they helped him (2-?-?). Together with the Maruts, Indra obtained light (8-?-?) and cows (1-?-?) and became the support of the sky (2-?-?). Truly, it is with their help that Indra has performed all his bold deeds (1-100, 101 and 165th sūktas; 10-?-?). In some contexts the Marut deities in these bold works are more independent than Indra. Together with Indra, the Maruts strike Vṛtra (1-?-?). They split the joints of Vṛtra (8-?-?) and found the cows (2-?-?). As with other deities, Indra is their leader (1-?-?; etc.). They are joined with Indra (10-?-?). They are like sons to Indra (1-100-?); they have accepted his brothers (1-?-?). Only once or twice it is said that the Maruts abandoned Indra, making a plan to fight against the serpent alone (1-?-?), and left him alone (8-?-?). In one single Ṛk, enmity between Indra and them is also stated."

original p. 598

Maruts, end "…The Maruts said to Indra, 'O Indra, why do you wish to kill us? Do not kill us in the battle' (1-170-2; compare 1-171-?). In a Brāhmaṇa too (Tai. Brā. 3-?-11-1) it is said that there was a quarrel between Indra and the Maruts."

"When they are not accompanied by Indra, destructive qualities are seen in the Maruts. In this matter they show the qualities of their father Rudra. They are prayed that they should not afflict their worshippers with hail, and that their evil design should not touch them (2-?-?). It is begged that the arrows and stones they hurl (1-172-?), the hail (2-?-?), and the vajra-weapon that kills cows and men (2-?-?) be avoided. Harm may come from them (1-?-?); it is asked that they not become angry (1-?-?; 5-?-?); anger comes upon them like serpents (1-64-? and 8). Like Rudra, remedies are sought from these also, from the herbs in the Sindhu, Asikni, the oceans and the mountains (8-?-? to ?). Pure, favourable and pleasing methods of cure are with Rudra, the friend of the Maruts (2-33-13). The Maruts give it in the form of rain (5-53-14); hence 'herb' must mean water. Like Agni, they too have the name 'pāvaka' ('purifiers') (5-?-?; etc.)."

"From the qualities above it is clear that the Maruts are deities of the storm. To take 'marut' as meaning wind is mostly correct, but all the qualities above are not included in it."

Vāyu–Vāta

Vāyu and Vāta. "The two words Vāyu and Vāta are used for the deity Vāyu and for wind, in the sense of both. But Vāyu is a deity; Vāta is gross wind. One whole sūkta, and parts of some sūktas, are addressed to Vāyu as deity; with Indra there are about twelve sūktas. For Vāta there are only two small sūktas at the end of the tenth maṇḍala; both sometimes come in the same Ṛk (6-?-?; 10-?-?). In both of these, Vāyu alone is praised together with Indra. In the Nirukta (Nir. 7-5) Vāyu or Vāta is counted as one among the three deities (Agni, Indra, Vāyu, Sūrya). Vāta is related to Parjanya. The epithets used for these two are also generally different; the epithets of Vāta mainly indicate speed and violence."

"There is not much basis for the origin of Vāyu. The two worlds created him for lordship (2-?-?). Though his wife's name is not given, Vāyu is said to be the son-in-law of Tvaṣṭṛ (8-?-? and ?). In the Puruṣa-sūkta Vāyu is said to have been born from the breath of the Virāṭ-Puruṣa"

original p. 599

"(10-90-13). It may be said that no relation is stated between Vāyu and the Maruts. Only in one place (1-134-4) is it said that Vāyu made the Marut group be born from the womb of the sphere of the air, and that they (1-?-?) and the Viśve-devas urged Vāyu. His (qualities and) marks are unclear. Of beautiful form (1-2-1), thousand-eyed, he touched the sky together with Indra with the speed of thought (1-?-? and ?). Vāyu's chariot is yoked; to it a team or a pair of horses, of the colour of red or of tawny. In that team there are ninety-nine (4-?-?) or a hundred, or a thousand (4-?-?) horses, and they are harnessed by his mere wish. The epithet niyutvat ('possessing a team') of this sense is, apart from once or twice for Indra, Agni, Pūṣan or the Maruts, generally used of Vāyu alone. Seated in the chariot, Indra is his companion (4-?-?; 4-?-?; 2-?-?); it has a golden seat; it touches the sky (4-?-?). As with the other deities, Soma-juice is dear to him too; he is called, with his horses and with Indra, to drink Soma first (1-?-?); of all the deities he is the one of swift motion (Śat. Brā. 14-?-?; etc.). In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2-?) there is a story that, among the deities, Vāyu was first, and Indra second, to drink the first drink of Soma juice. He is a guardian of the Soma juice (10-?-?). He alone has the epithet śucipā ('drinker of the pure Soma'); once this epithet is used of Indra and Vāyu together. Vāyu grants fame, offspring, horses, cows, gold and so on (2-?-? and ?). He destroys enemies (4-?-?); he is prayed to protect the weak (1-?-?)."

"Vāta, another name of the wind, is derived from the root vā; in the sūkta (10-168) this description is given: scattering everything, making a loud noise and raising dust, he moves in the sphere of the air; he does not rest even for a day; he, born at the beginning, is the friend of the water; his birthplace is not known. This deity goes wherever he likes; his sound is heard by all, but no one has seen him (compare 1-164-?). He is the breath of the deities (compare 7-?-?; 10-?-?); oblations are made to him in sacrifices."

"Like Rudra, Vāta also gives herbs to people and increases life; for in his house there is the treasure of immortality (10-186-?). By his power of healing, the purifying power of Vāyu must be meant. All the works of the wind are related to the storm (4-?-?; 5-?-?; 10-?-?). Since the wind generally blows strongly before the rain falls and before sunrise, Vāta is said to produce red-coloured light (10-168-1) and to make Uṣas shine (1-134-3)."

original p. 600

"The speed of the wind is the basis for comparison with the speed of deities (4-?-?; 5-?-?; 6-?-?) and of imagined horses (1-?-?; 10-?-?). Its sound too is mentioned in many places (4-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?)."

Parjanya

Parjanya. "In the Ṛgveda the position of this deity is very minor. Only three sūktas praise him; the name occurs only thirty times. In the Atharvaveda too (4-15) there is one sūkta addressed to Parjanya as deity; but the Ṛks in that sūkta are for the most part taken from the Ṛgveda. In the sentences that follow, Parjanya generally means only the familiar cloud. Rain-clouds (Parjanya) enliven the earth (1-164-51). The Maruts, even in the daytime, make darkness with water-bearing clouds (Parjanya) (1-38-9). They milk the clouds in both worlds (5-53-6). Bṛhaspati has been prayed to make the rain fall and to send the rain-cloud away (10-98-1 and 8). Soma flows like a rain-cloud (9-2-9), and the drops of Soma fall like rain from the cloud (9-22-2). In the Atharvaveda, in praising the cow called 'vaśā' which rains, it is said, 'your udder is Parjanya' (Av. 10-10-?). But in (Vāj. Saṃ. 13-?), Parjanya is used in the sense of 'thundering' (stanayitnu, hail), and in (Śat. Brā. 14-?-?-10) in the sense 'sky' (dyauḥ, Vāj. Saṃ. 12-?). It is hard to say in some contexts whether it is of the meaning 'excited' or of the meaning 'deity'. Like Parjanya, Agni's power gives an echo (8-?-?). Cows that have been awakened by Parjanya bow down (2-103-1). That Parjanya means a deity is clearly seen in many sentences. In such contexts he is called by the name cloud, hailstone, arrow, a skin of water and so on (5-83-? and 7; 2-?-?). To some extent the deity Parjanya is described as an animal such as a bull. He is a pot with fast-flowing quick drops, firmly pressed down (5-83-1; compare 5-83-2 and 7; Av. 4-15-1). The water that comes from the thundering water-bull and flows with a sound delights the earth (Av. 4-15-1). Sometimes Parjanya is a big cow; sometimes a cow giving milk; Parjanya uses his body as he likes (2-?-?)."

"Giving rain is the chief work of Parjanya. Moving about in a chariot made of water (5-83-?), he casts a skin of water and holds it face downward. As a charioteer drives horses, Parjanya shows the messengers of rain; when the rain falls, a lion's roar is heard from afar. Pouring rain, the thundering Parjanya comes like our heavenly father (Asura)…"

original p. 601

"(5-83-5 and 6). He is prayed to pour rain (2-?-?), and after pouring to stop (5-83-10). Parjanya and the Maruts pour rain. While subject to Mitra and Varuṇa (5-63-3 to 6), he many times, it is said, makes the arbhaṭi ('stir') (5-83). Making that stir, he uproots trees, Piśācas, evil-doers, everyone. The whole world fears this weapon of his (5-83-2). He and Vāta, the two, are the ones who use that weapon (10-66-10). Hail too is a little connected with him. When Parjanya enlivens the earth with seeds, the wind blows and hail strikes (5-83-4). Parjanya, together with hail, thunders in the ocean (Av. 19-?-?)."

"Because he gives rain, Parjanya is the cause of the growth of crops. When he casts seed on the earth, plants rise up. All kinds of plants are under his sphere of action; for the sake of nourishment he generates plants (5-83-1, 4 and 10; compare 6-?-?; Av. 4-15-3, 5 and 13; 7-?-?). He is the one who makes plants thrive and bear fruit; protected by that deity, crops give good fruit (7-101-1 and 3). By his action, tubers and grass grow (7-?-?; 5-?-?; compare Av. 1-?-?; 1-?-?; 19-?-?). Parjanya places the embryo not only in plants but also in cows, mares and women (7-102-2) and is prayed to for fruitfulness (5-83-2; compare 6-?-?). He is a bull that makes everything fruitful; the soul of all moving and unmoving things in the universe is in him (7-101-6; compare 1-?-?). The king who rules the whole world and is wholly independent; in him all creatures and the three worlds are placed. In him the threefold water flows (7-101-2, 4 and 5). Because of this generative power the epithet janitā ('father') is used of him many times (7-101-?; 9-?-?; Av. 4-?-?). He is our heavenly father (asuraḥ pitā) (5-83-6)."

"The earth is hinted to be his wife (5-83-?; 7-101-?). In the Atharvaveda (12-1-12) the earth is the mother and Parjanya the father; elsewhere (10-10-?) it is plainly said that vaśā is his wife. In being called a bull, and in relation to thunder, hail and rain, Parjanya is like Dyaus (10-?-?; 2-?-?; 2-?-?). In one place Parjanya is the son of Dyaus (7-102-1). Parjanya himself generates a calf (a young one); this is the sprout of plants (7-101-1; compare 5-83-1). This calf may be hail or Soma. In one place Parjanya is said to be the father of Soma (9-82-3), and that it grew by Parjanya (9-113-3)."

"Parjanya has a connection with many other deities, but the connection is greater with Vāta. Apart from being once named with Agni, Vāta is mentioned as a paired deity chiefly with Parjanya. The Maruts too are praised along with Parjanya (5-?-?; 5-?-?); they praise Parjanya (Av. 4-?-?). In two mantras Agni is praised with him (6-?-?"

original p. 602

Parjanya, end "…and 6-?-?). Parjanya, the giver of rain, and Indra have many common qualities (8-6-1). The same part of Nature is the basis of both deities; in the case of Parjanya this is more clear."

"The derivation of this word is not clear. In the Ṛgveda, in this form, both a cloud (a word of conventional meaning) and the deity who presides over the cloud are intended. In the Brāhmaṇas too both these senses seem to be in use. In the Mahābhārata, Indra and Parjanya are conceived as one."

The Waters (Āpaḥ)

Āpaḥ. "Four sūktas (7-49 and 6-52; 10-9 and 30) and some more Ṛks praise the water. In this way, along with other deities, in every other mantra its praise is also seen. Personification is mostly at the beginning: ideas are found of the Waters as mothers, as women who, in the form of young wives, come to the sacrifices and grant boons and favours, as female deities. The goddesses follow the path of the deities (2-?-?). Holding the vajra-weapon, he made a way for the water to flow for Indra (2-?-?; 2-?-?), and they never transgress his commands (2-?-?). Even the commands of Savitṛ are within the sway of water (2-?-?). They came from the heaven-world; they flow in channels; the ocean is their place of going (7-49-2). It is held (10-?-?) that waters are in the place where Mitra and Varuṇa and the other deities are. They are at the side of Sūrya, and Sūrya is with them (1-23-17). Varuṇa moves among them, looking at the truth and falsehood of men (7-49-3). In the Nighaṇṭu the water is counted among the deities of the earth (Nir. 5-1)."

"It is said many times that Agni made his home in the water. Agni entered the water (2-?-?); one form of Agni has the name 'Apāṃ napāt' ('son of water'). The waters, themselves mothers, give birth to Agni (10-?-?; 10-?-?; compare Av. 1-?-?). The water-goddesses are mothers (10-?-?; 10-?-?); wives to the world; equal in age and birth (10-?-?). They are prayed, as loving mothers, to give auspicious things (10-?-?). They create things moving and unmoving; their motherliness is shown in them most (6-?-?)."

"Water purifies [men] and makes them clean; those deities remove impurity. The worshipper comes out of the water pure and holy [10-?-?]. They are prayed to purify from sins connected with bad conduct, violence, defilement and untruth [1-?-?; 10-?-?]. They are removers of disease [6-?-?]; they grant long life, herbs and the like. Among the herbs is immortality too [10-?-? onward; 1-?-? onward]. In the house it guards the health of man [Hi. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?]. They grant the best things, wealth, and half of the body and immortality [10-?-?]. Their help and favour is prayed for at every step"

original p. 603

"[2-?-?; 7-49-? onward; 10-9 (the Neṣa-sūkta) and 10-30-11]; seated on the sacred grass together with Apāṃ napāt, they are invited to receive the Soma offering [10-30-? and 13]."

"A connection of honey with water is stated. These mothers make honey flow along with their milk [1-?-?]. In the waves of water there is much honey. This water mixed with ghee became Indra's drink and produced intoxication in him [2-?-? and ?]. Apāṃ napāt is prayed to give Indra boundless strength and to favour him with honey-mixed water [10-30-?]. They have been asked to send waves, rich in honey, which give delight to the deities, for Indra; for Indra released the water from its bondage. The wave makes intoxication, and it is Indra's drink; it is produced in the sky [10-30-? onward]. In some of these sentences the sense is that water itself is Soma or is mixed with Soma. In other contexts the water used to prepare the Soma juice may be intended. When mixed with ghee, milk and honey, favourable to the priests, they become well-prepared vessels of Soma juice for Indra [10-30-?]. As a young man is glad on seeing young women, Soma delights in the water. He approaches the water as a lover. They are the maidens standing with heads bowed before the young man [10-30-? onward]."

Deities of the Earth (Bhūmiya devategaḷu)

Rivers (Nadigaḷu)

"Like the water of heaven, the river deities too hold an important place. One whole sūkta [10-75] praises the river Sindhu. In it, the fifth Ṛk praises the tributaries of the Sindhu. In the sixth Ṛk many more rivers are named as its tributaries. In another sūkta [3-33] the pair of rivers Vipāś and Śutudri are praised."

"Of all the other rivers the river Sarasvatī has the greater importance. Although in this context the feeling of deity is much greater, the close kinship between the deity and the rivers is always borne in mind. Three sūktas and many solitary Ṛks praise this river. Sarasvatī, Sarayū and the Sindhus are great rivers [10-?-?]; Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudri, Paruṣṇī and some more known and unknown, 21 rivers in all, are spoken of [10-75-5]. The matter of kings and people living on the bank of the Sarasvatī is raised [2-?-?; 8-?-?]. Sarasvatī is the greatest of all rivers in glory; she has abundant water, and she is the purest of all rivers. She comes down from the sea of the sky [2-?-?, ?]"

original p. 604

"[compare 6-61-11]. With huge waves she bursts the mountain peaks and carries them off. Her deep stream moves with a roar, swallowing with force [6-61-2 and 8]. She is prayed to give her milk generously to the greatest among the great and to the quickest among the quick [6-61-14]. She is begged to flow to new places [6-61-14]. She has seven sisters and she has seven forms [6-61-10 and 12]. She is the mother of rivers, one of the seven rivers [2-?-?]. Among the rivers and the deities she is the best mother [2-41-16]. She has the name Pāvīravī [daughter of the lightning] and is the wife of a hero [6-?-?]. She strides over the regions of the earth, the vast sky and the three dwellings [6-61-11 and 12]. There is an invocation to come from the sky, from the great mountain, to the sacrificial hall [3-?-11]. From these three sentences, as is said of Gaṅgā in the Purāṇas, a birth in the heaven-world is suggested for Sarasvatī too. In one place she has the title Asūryā ('without the sun', a goddess [2-?-?]). In the chariot of the deities of the Fathers, together with them, that goddess comes and adorns the sacred grass [10-?-? and 8]; and in the two Ṛks that follow [10-?-? and 11] the river itself is intended, so the river-goddess is intended here too."

"She herself purifies [1-3-10]; she is called 'flowing, coming', because she runs with her flows [6-?-?]; she is prayed to bestow strength together with the giving of wealth, children and immortality [10-30-12]. She gives strength and children [2-?-?] and is joined with the deities who help in obtaining children [10-?-?]. She gave a son named Divodāsa to Vadhryaśva [6-61-1]. Her breasts, always unfailing, bring every kind of wealth [compare Ait. Brā. 4-?]. She is a giver of wealth, prosperity and nourishment [2-?-?; 8-?-?; 7-?-?; 10-?-? and 8], and many times is called Subhagā ('fortunate'). As a mother (Ambā) she makes the unknown famous [2-?-?]; she makes devotion to her worshippers grow and increases it [1-?-? and ?; 2-?-?; 6-?-?]. She is invoked together with the deities connected with praise [2-?-?; 10-?-?]. She destroys those who revile the deities; she is fierce and the slayer of Vṛtra [6-?-? and ?]. But she protects those who worship her and destroys their enemies [7-?-? and ?; 3-?-?; 8-?-?]."

"Sarasvatī is invoked together with many other deities. She is praised specially together with the Marut deities, apart from Pūṣan and Indra [3-?-?;"

original p. 605

"6-?-?; 6-?-?; 6-?-?]. She follows them [3-?-?] or is placed together with them as their friend. She is also joined with the Aśvins [2-?-?]. When the Aśvins helped Indra, Sarasvatī poured out his drink [10-?-?]. When the deities performed a sacrifice, the Aśvins, by their medical skill, and Sarasvatī, by her speech, gave Indra vitality [Vāj. Saṃ. 19-?]. Sarasvatī is the wife of the Aśvins [Vāj. Saṃ. 19-?]. In the Āprī-sūktas, in the eighth and ninth Ṛks, she is joined many times with Iḷā and Bhāratī; the idea is that the three together form one deity-group; at times Mahī and Hotrā too are joined. This combination may indicate the purity of Sarasvatī. On the bank of Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī, Agni was kindled [3-23-4]. The seers performed sacrifices on the bank of Sarasvatī (Ait. Brā. 2-19)."

"In the Ṛgveda, nothing is said of Sarasvatī other than that she is a river-deity. But in the Brāhmaṇas, Sarasvatī is the presiding deity of speech (Śat. Brā. 2-5-1-?; Ait. Brā. 3-1-10); in the Purāṇas and elsewhere she is the presiding goddess of knowledge and eloquence, and the wife of Brahmā."

"Which river the Sarasvatī river is, is not said clearly. Some Western scholars think that Sarasvatī must be a great river (probably the Indus). Others say that it must be the small river in the Madhyadeśa which, now sunk in the sand and no longer reaching the sea, was formerly a big river that reached the ocean. Some also say that Sarasvatī is a tributary of the Śutudri."

"Apart from the praise of Sarasvatī, in the second and third Ṛks of one sūkta, one deity named Sarasvat is praised; there, wives are indicated. Progeny, protection and prosperity are prayed for [7-96]."

Pṛthivī

Pṛthivī. "Pṛthivī (Bhūmi) is generally praised as a paired deity with the sky-deity. Only a small sūkta of three Ṛks praises Pṛthivī alone [5-84]. In the Atharvaveda there is a large sūkta addressed to Pṛthivī as deity [Av. 12-1]. Personification is very small; all the characteristics of the deity are physical. There are many high places. She bears the weight of the mountains; she is the support of the trees of the forests (kṣamā). She makes the earth fruitful; she gives rain; she is great, firm and endowed with light."

"Pṛthivī means 'the broad one'. Indra lifted up and held the earth, and spread it out (Patrathak. 3-?-?). In other places too (Tai. Saṃ. 2-1-5; Tai. Brā. 1-1-3-?) the word pṛthivī is derived from the root pṛth ('to spread')."

original p. 606

Pṛthivī, end "…It is said that Pṛthivī is the mother Pṛthivī, of loving nature, and that the dead man goes to her lap (10-18-10). Whenever she is mentioned together with the sky-deity, Pṛthivī is generally called 'mother'."

Agni

Agni. "Since in the Vedas Agni is the chief object of all the mantras connected with rites, Agni is the foremost among the deities of the earth. Among the deities of the Vedas, after Indra, the one that holds the prominent place is Agni. More than two hundred sūktas, and many more portions of sūktas, praise Agni."

"Since fire is a very tangible thing, the attribution of human nature began very early. The whole description of Agni's limbs reflects the various parts of the sacrificial fire. His back is made of ghee (3-?-?; etc.), his face too (3-1-18; etc.), and he has a beautiful tongue (1-?-?). Ghee itself is his hair, flames are his hair (8-?-?; 1-?-?; etc.), or his locks are tawny (3-?-?) and his beard tawny (5-?-?). He has the cūpāda (the flaming jaws) (6-?-?; etc.) or burning jaws (1-?-?; etc.), golden (5-?-?) or shining teeth, and iron-like teeth (10-?-?). In one place (4-1-11) it is said that he has no feet and no head; but elsewhere he has a burning head (2-?-?) or three heads and seven rays (1-?-?; 3-?-?). He is 'faced on all sides' (3-?-?; etc.). His tongue is stated in many places (8-?-?; etc.). He has three (3-?-?) or seven (Vāj. Saṃ. 17-?) tongues. His horses too have seven tongues (3-?-?), and each of these seven has a name. Ghee is Agni's eye (3-?-?); his tongue (1-?-?) and his thousand eyes and thousand horns (6-?-?). He has many arms, which are always for the honour of men (1-?-?). He is an archer (4-?-?) or is compared with an archer (1-?-?). He sounds his flame like an iron axe (6-?-?)."

"In many places Agni is compared to various animals; generally, this is to indicate his various works, and not to describe his form. At every step he is called a bull (1-?-?; etc.): a bull of stout body, very strong (3-?-?). Therefore he roars (10-?-?). He is full of seed (4-?-?); he has horns (5-?-?; 6-?-?), and he whets those horns (8-?-?) and shakes them. Because he has them, he is difficult to hold (1-140-6), and so on. It is said many times that he was a calf (karu) when born"

original p. 607

"[3-?-?]. In many places Agni is compared with a horse (1-?-?; etc.) or called a horse (1-163-?; 6-?-?). The tail with which he strikes like a horse must be his flame (2-?-?). Agni, purified by the sacrificers, is compared to a well-groomed horse (1-?-?; etc.). Those who perform the sacrifice drive him like a horse (3-?-?), excite him and make him move (2-?-?). Agni is the horse that is wished to be controlled by those who bring it under their will and wish to go as they please (2-?-?; 3-?-?). He is made ready as the horse that carries the gods (3-?-?). In the sacrificial halls they have joined Agni to the sacrificial post (2-?-?) or, in the rite that is a limb of the sacrifice, to the post (1-?-?). To carry the oblation to the deities they yoke Agni (the horse) (10-?-?). He is compared to a horse that neighs (3-?-?), or he himself is called a neighing horse (1-?-?).
