He is like a victorious horse (8-?-?), or helps people to escape from distress (4-?-?). Besides these, Agni is described like a bird. He is the eagle of the sky (2-?-?) and a bird of the world of deities (1-?-?). He who dwells in the water is like a swan-bird (4-?-?). As a bird builds a nest on a tree, Agni too controls the forest (1-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?). He has wings (1-?-?; 2-?-?) and his going is flight (6-?-?; 6-?-? etc.). He swiftly flies and approaches the deities (10-?-?). Once he is described as a serpent that hisses (1-?-?)."

"In many places Agni is compared even to lifeless things. Like Sūrya, Agni too is like gold (2-?-?; 2-?-?); when asked, he is like a hand-held lamp [?] (2-?-?; 1-?-?). He himself is a chariot (4-?-?) or like a chariot (1-?-?); he brings wealth and the like (1-?-?; 3-?-?) and in battle is the one to be taken to meet the opponent (1-?-?). Like a full chariot driven by others, he is also driven to the sacrificial hall (10-?-?). He is likened to wealth (1-?-?; 1-?-?) or to wealth gained from the father (1-?-?)."

"Forest (2-?-?) or ghee (2-?-?) is his food, and the ghee mixed with butter is his drink (2-?-?; 10-?-?). He is nourished by the tuppa (ghee) poured into his mouth (3-?-?; 5-?-?; etc.) and uses oil (Av. 1-?-?). He eats the forests with his green grass and makes them black with his tongue (1-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?). He eats everything (8-?-?). He takes food that gives nourishment three times a day (4-?-?; 1-?-?; 2-?-?; compare). So that the deities may receive the oblations, Agni is the mouth and the tongue (2-?-?; 1-?-?); the ladles that give the deities food are his flames (1-?-?; 10-?-?). But especially he is the one who has been prayed to receive the oblations (3-?-? onward; 3-?-? onward) and, standing erect, with his body turned towards the deities, he comes forward to receive the ghee that has been offered (1-?-?). Though ordinarily Soma or ghee alone is his food, he is also invited to drink Soma at times. In such contexts he is invited along with the other deities (1-?-?, 10; 1-?-?, 1-?-?, 3-?-?, 3-?-?). He has the epithet Somagopa ('protector of Soma') (10-?-? and ?). He is begged to come to the sacrifice (10-?-?) and, having come, to adorn the seat of darbha grass with the deities (3-?-?; 5-?-?; 5-?-?; 2-?-?; 2-?-?; compare)."

original p. 608

"The qualities of the light of Agni have been discussed at much length, as is natural. His bright lustre (3-?-?; etc.); flames that blaze (6-?-?); shining flames (2-?-?; etc.); clear radiance (8-?-?); shining colour (1-?-?; 5-?-?). His form is of golden colour (4-?-?; 10-?-?). He shines like Sūrya (1-?-?; 2-?-?). His lustre is like the rays of Uṣas, of Sūrya or of lightning (10-?-? and ?). He shines also at night (5-?-?). Like Sūrya, he makes darkness fly by his rays (8-?-?). He is the remover of darkness, and he can see even in the darkness of night (1-?-?; 2-?-?). Blazing, he opens the doors of darkness (3-?-?). When Agni is born, the earth and the sky that were covered with darkness become visible (1-?-?). At the time of dawn men bring Agni; of Agni alone it is said that he is the 'awakened at dawn' (upabudh)."

"But the path of Agni's journey and the rims of his chariot are all black (1-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?), and his horses draw him with black ridges (1-?-?). Roused by the wind, he swallows the forests with force (1-?-?); invading the forests, he cuts even the roots of the earth (1-?-?); like a razor he shaves the earth's hair (10-?-?)."

"His flames roar like the waves of the sea (1-?-?). His sound is like the sound of the wind, or like the thunder of the sky (3-?-?; 2-?-?), like the sky (10-?-?), like Parjanya (8-?-?) or like the roar of a lion (2-?-?). When he invades forest trees he rages like a bull, and at the sound of his grass-destroying tusks the birds are all afraid (1-?-? and ?). To bring Agni under control is as easy as to bring under control the host that attacks the Maruts or the guardians of the regions, or the hail."

original p. 609

"Agni burns upward-faced (6-?-?). Stirred by the wind, his flames lick toward the sky (8-?-?). His smoke is thick and his flame cannot be held (8-?-?). The red smoke goes to the sky [2-?-?; 2-?-?]; the smoke spreads in the sky (3-?-?). Like one who sets up a pillar, Agni supports the sky with smoke (4-?-?). Striking the clouds with his upper part, he shines together with the rays of Sūrya (2-?-?). With his tongue he covers the atmosphere (8-?-?). The word dhūmaketu ('banner of smoke') is used of Agni at every step."

"Agni moves in a chariot (3-?-?) of the mass of light of hail, shining (1-?-?), glittering (5-?-?), blazing (10-?-?), golden (4-?-?) or beautiful (4-?-?). To it two or more horses are yoked. Those horses have the ghee as their back (1-?-?); they are tawny (4-?-?), beautiful (4-?-?), of all forms (10-?-?), swift (3-?-?), driven by the wind (1-?-?), and yoked by the ibhyā mantra (1-?-?). For the calling of the deities, Agni yokes them (1-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 6-?-?). He is the charioteer of the sacrifice (10-?-?; etc.; 1-?-? etc.). In a chariot yoked with horses he brings the deities (3-?-?); in that same chariot he himself comes (3-?-?; 2-?-?) or comes before them (10-?-?). To the sacrifice he brings Varuṇa, from the sky Indra, and from the sphere of the air the Maruts (10-?-?)."

"The sky-deity is the progenitor of Agni; it is he who generated Agni (10-?-?). Agni is the child of the sky (6-?-?; 6-?-?) and is said to have been born from the belly of that 'Asura' (3-?-?). Many times (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 3-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?) it is said that he is the son of Heaven and Earth. Also that he is the son of Tvaṣṭṛ and of the water-deities, and of the sky and the earth (10-?-?; 10-?-?). Or that he is the son of Tvaṣṭṛ (1-?-?) or of the water-deity (10-?-?; Av. 1-?-?). The Uṣas deities gave birth to Agni, Sūrya and the sacrifices (2-?-?); or Indra and Viṣṇu to Agni, Sūrya and the Uṣases [6-?-?]; or Indra generated Agni between the two stones (3-?-?). Agni is also called the son of Iḷā (3-?-?) or the sprout of the sacrifice (6-?-?). Sometimes Agni is made to be born by the deities (6-?-?; 8-?-?), for the sake of 'the Ārya' (1-?-?), or for the sake of men (10-?-?), and was placed among men (1-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?). Agni is the father of the deities (1-?-?). It is clear that these different notions, at first sight, have arisen from differences of viewpoint."

"The histories connected with Agni do not tell much about him; the one chief work he does as the sacrificial fire; apart from this, something is gathered about his birth, special forms and dwelling-places."

original p. 610

Agni, continued "The differing views that are known about his birth are not really contradictory. According to the places of birth they have been described in different ways. Churned from the fire-sticks (araṇi), he is born on earth every day (3-29-?; 3-?-?; 2-?-?; 10-?-?). In this context the fire-sticks themselves are his mother and father; the upper fire-stick is counted as the father and the lower alone as the mother (3-29-3); or, since it is said that he has two mothers, both fire-sticks are his mothers (1-31-2). The two pieces of wood generate him like a child that has just been born; but it is difficult to hold the child (5-9-3 and 4). From the dry piece of wood, the deity is born together with life (1-68-2). As soon as he is born, the child devours his parents (10-79-4). Agni is born of a mother who gives no milk (10-115-1). Because men exert themselves in this churning, men bring Agni to birth (1-?-?; 4-1-?; 2-1-?); the ten fingers, ten maidens, are suitable for turning the upper piece of wood (1-95-2). This upper piece of wood has the name pramantha (Karma-pradīpa 1-?)."

"Much force must be used for churning out fire. Hence Agni has the epithet 'sahasaḥ sūnuḥ', 'putraḥ' ('son of strength'). The same idea is confirmed by the next sentence: 'Churned strongly by men, Agni is born on the earth' (6-48-5). In one place (Mai. Saṃ. 1-6-10) it is said that Agni should not be churned before sunrise. Because he is born every day, the epithets 'yaviṣṭha', 'yaviṣṭhya' ('the youngest') are apt. Each of his births is opposed to the previous birth (3-1-20). The aged Agni is born again as a youth (10-?-?). In this sense he has no age (1-?-?); his new light is as if it were the old (6-?-?). Like other deities he is young; but also he is old. He was the first to perform sacrifice (3-?-?); so there is no sacrificer older than he (5-?-?). After the earliest Uṣases Agni shone (1-?-?). The part played by Agni in the sacrifices of the ancients is spoken of at every step (8-?-?; etc.). In one sentence the two quite opposed epithets 'purātana' ('ancient') and 'bahuvidha-kartā' ('doer of many kinds') are seen together (10-4-1 and ?)."

"In general it is said that Agni was born in the forest (6-?-?; 10-?-?); that he is the sprout of trees (3-1-14; 3-?-?), or that he is shared among the plants (10-1-?). He has entered all trees, or makes effort to obtain them (8-?-?), and is the sprout of trees (1-?-?) or of the trunks of the plants (3-1-?). Since Agni is born from the mutual rubbing of trees, it may be said so."

original p. 611

"There is another ground for the idea that Agni is in the earth. Agni is called 'pṛthivyā nābhiḥ' ('navel of the earth') (1-?-?). In all the places where these words are used for Agni the reference must be to the altar made for the sacrificial fire. In Vedic rites the hollow on the northern altar is called 'nābhi'. Here Agni is established. This name may also have come because all the deities have made Agni the centre of their immortality (3-?-?). Twice in the Ṛgveda the word 'vedisad' ('one seated on the altar') is used, and in both places it is applied to Agni."

"It has been said many times that Agni was born in the water of the sky. 'Apāṃ napāt' has become a separate deity. Agni is also the embryo of water (3-1-13 and ?); he blazes in the water itself (10-?-?; Av. 13-1-?); a bull raised in the lap of water (10-8-1); he is surrounded by the ocean (8-?-?). He has come down from the abode of Dhanu (the island of clouds) (1-?-?; 1-?-?), the shining lightning in the sphere of the air full of splendour (6-8-?). In such sentences Agni in the form of lightning must be intended. In some parts of the eighth maṇḍala there is a story that Agni, hidden in water and plants, was afterwards found by the deities (the sūktas 10-51, 52, 53 and 124). The same subject is handled in the Brāhmaṇas. In the Atharvaveda a distinction is made between the fire in the water, the fire of lightning and the fire of heaven (Av. 3-?-1 and 2; 6-?-?). The fires in the water settled on the earth (Av. 12-1-?). Agni has made his dwelling in all streams (6-?-?; compare Āp. Śrau. Sū. 6-?-?). In contexts of pools and ponds the Agnis who live in water are praised. As the sky is for Sūrya, water is the dwelling-place of Agni (3-?-?; Av. 14-1-?). Together with trees and plants, water is counted as Agni's dwelling (3-1-1; etc.)."

"Many times it is said that Agni was born in the atmosphere. In the loftiest part of the sky he was born (1-143-2; 6-8-2). Though in the form of Agni he is not there, he is hidden in the atmosphere (10-5-2). From that region, from very far, he was brought by Mātariśvan. Here Agni must be the Agni of lightning. The lightning-Agni is that which comes from the atmosphere and the water (Av. 3-?-? and 8; 8-1-11); in a Brāhmaṇa (Ait. Brā. 2-?-?) it is said that he exists in both the heaven and the water (divya and apsumat). The word vidyut ('lightning') occurs about 30 times together with 'Agni'. In all these contexts it is compared with Agni and understood as different from Agni. This may suggest a difference between the deity and the natural phenomenon. That Agni comes down from the atmosphere to the earth may be applied to the fire that comes from lightning. And the lightning shows the non-difference of fires. Man obtains Agni by the favour of the deities, and it was brought by Mātariśvan and so reaches the hand of man."

original p. 612

"[Having said this, it became a settled view that Agni is of the heaven-world. In the same sense Agni may be said to be the guest of men.]"

"Further, in some sentences Agni is reckoned equal to Sūrya; that Sūrya is a form of Agni is the idea of the Vedas. Chief of the whole sky, rising at the time of dawn, Agni becomes the light of the sky (3-?-?). He is born at the end of the sphere of the air, and sees all things (10-?-? and ?). He was born as the Sūrya who rises at dawn (10-?-?). When Sūrya sets he enters Agni and is born again from him (Ait. Brā. 8-?-? and ?). In all the places where it is said that Agni shines with the light or the rays of Sūrya, the likeness of Agni and Sūrya must be intended (5-?-?; 2-?-?); likewise where it is said that when man bears Agni, the deities also make him shine (6-?-?), or that Agni shines in the heaven-world (3-?-?; 8-?-?). In some contexts it is hard to say whether it applies to lightning or to Sūrya. To speak of a mildness (saumyatva) or a difference of form in Agni, Sūrya is not just a general natural event. Generally the comparison of Sūrya with Agni is seen to be prominent. When Sūrya is lost sight of, the mind runs to Agni (1-?-?). The other forms of Agni too are sometimes intended; hence in what context which form of Agni, or which kind of the blazing one, is intended cannot be said for certain."

"Because various kinds of birth are said for Agni, three kinds of characteristics are stated for Agni. This triple form of Agni is of great importance. Agni has three kinds of birth (1-?-?; 4-1-?). The deities made him threefold (10-?-?). He is a light of three forms (3-?-?); he has three heads (1-?-?), three tongues, three bodies and three places (3-20-2). The epithet 'tripastya' ('having three abodes') is generally used; 'trisadhastha' (8-?-?) is used of Agni alone. These three forms or places do not always come in the same order. Agni was born first from the sky, a second time (from men) from us, and a third time in the water (10-45-1). The places of Agni (sky, earth and water) are in the same order (8-?-?; 10-2-?; 10-?-?). But in one place (1-95-3) his three places are said to be the ocean, the sky and the water. Sometimes it is the earthly Agni who comes first. He was born first in houses, then in the lower part of the sky and in the sphere of the air (4-1-11); the immortal deities created three flames of Agni: one they placed on earth for the use of men; the remaining two went to another world (3-2-9). The Agni of the earth (Pṛthivī) is in living beings; the Agni of the sphere of the air in the water; and the Agni of the heaven-world in Sūrya (Āp. Śrau."

original p. 613

"Sū. 5-?-?). Pṛthivī, in another form, becomes the third Agni. Agni is one of three brothers; of them the middle one is the lightning, and the third one has ghee as his back (1-164-1; compare 1-?-?). Agni shines from the sky; the atmosphere is his own; men bear Agni, who gives the deities what is offered and who expects ghee (Av. 13-?-?; 13-?-?; 11-?-?)."

"In some places it is said that the third form is the best (10-?-?; 5-?-?; 1-?-?, and so on). According to Śākapūṇi, the three forms of Agni mentioned in (10-88-10) are in earth, sky and heaven; and, as one Brāhmaṇa says, the Agni in the heaven-world is Sūrya (Nir. 7-?; compare Nir. 12-?). The three divisions of Agni, and the three deity-groups Sūrya, Vāyu and Agni (8-?-?), and the group of three deities Sūrya, Indra and Agni mentioned in other Vedas, must be one and the same. Within the Agni-group the middle Agni is given the name Vaidyutāgni ('lightning-fire') in the Brāhmaṇas. In the remaining two deity-groups, instead of the lightning-fire, Vāta (or Vāyu) and Indra are included. In sacrifices, besides the ordinary fire, they perform homa and the rest keeping three other fires. The idea of the triad of fires (agnitraya) may be applied to this division. It has become the custom to pray to Agni, 'call the deities and sit in three places' (3-?-?; 5-11-?; 10-?-?)."

"Following the division of the world into heaven and the mortal world, it is also common to speak of two births for Agni. He alone is called 'dvijanmā' ('twice-born') (1-60-1; 1-140-?; 1-?-?; 3-?-?). Upper (ūrdhva) and lower (adhaḥ) births (2-?-?) and high and low dwellings (1-?-?) are also said. It is said that the Agni of the earth and the Agni of heaven are always opposed (3-?-?; 10-?-?); but in one single place (8-?-?) a difference in Agni's births in heaven and the water is mentioned. Agni, being invoked from his lofty dwelling-place, comes to the lower worlds (8-?-?). Having come from there, he enters the trees (1-?-?). Agni comes down by means of rain and enters the plants; from those plants he is again produced. Like water, Agni too comes to the earth and again rises upward (1-?-?). Relying on this two-fold nature of Agni, Agni should perform homa for himself (10-?-?) and carry Agni across (2-?-?), or he should come down to the sacrificial hall with the deities (3-?-?, and so on). Not only men bore Agni: the deities too bore him — and this too supports the idea that this Agni is two-fold (6-?-?). The Agni of the heaven-world too must have been kindled by someone."

original p. 614

"…and since 'the deities too must perform sacrifice like men' (Ait. Brā. 2-?), it must have come into usage that Agni is kindled separately by the deities and by men."

"From another point of view too Agni can be said to have various births (10-5-1). The variety of Agni is established by the fact that he is borne in many hearths on earth. In every household, in the houses and dwellings, Agni is placed (4-?-?; 4-?-?; 5-?-?; etc.). Born in many places (3-?-?), he has many bodies (10-?-?); though kindled in many places, he is but one (3-?-?). Though blazing in many places, he is but one (Vāl. 10-?). As branches depend on a tree, many fires depend on him (8-?-?). Therefore he is invoked together with other fires (2-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?) or with all fires (1-?-?; 6-?-?)."

"If one examines the various statements about Agni's birth, one has to take the places in various ways. His light is in heaven, earth, atmosphere, water and plants (3-?-?), or he is born in sky, water, stone, forest and plants (2-1-1). Still more such lists are found here and there (Av. 3-?-?; 12-1-19; Āp. Śrau. Sū. 5-?-?). Agni is in the mountain (1-?-?; compare 6-?-?): this must be the lightning hidden in the cloud. 'Agni was born of the stone' (2-?-?) or 'Indra made Agni between two stones' (2-?-?) — the saying is for this purpose; or it may refer to the making of fire from flint stone. When it is said that Agni is in men (10-5-1), or in beings, horses, birds, two-footed and four-footed creatures (Av. 3-?-?; 12-?-?; 13-?-?; Tai. Saṃ. 4-?-?), the fire of the stomach (jāṭharāgni) must be intended. It is no wonder that, as the support of life, the fire that pervades so much of Nature is called the root support of all things moving and unmoving (1-?-?; Av. 5-?-?)."

"This threefold nature of Agni has given room for the idea of three brothers (1-164-1), and the existence of Agni's elder brothers — many — rests on the countless homa fires (10-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā they are said to be three (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?). For the gods there are four priests (hotṛs), of whom the first three died (Śat. ?-?): this too confirms the same point. In one place Varuṇa is said to be Agni's brother (4-1-2). In another story, both Indra and Agni are called twins (6-59-2). More than any other deity it is Indra who joins Agni. Apart from twice, it is Indra who is the paired deity with Agni (1-?-?, 1-?-?, 2-?-?, 8-?-?, etc.)."

original p. 615

"From the close kinship of Indra and Agni arise the statements that Agni split the mountain with his heat (8-?-?) and that he destroyed the faithless Paṇis (2-?-?). One whole sūkta (1-93) praises the pair Agni and Soma."

"In form, Agni is said to be equal to some other deities, especially to Mitra and Varuṇa (3-1-?; 3-5-?; 2-?-?). When he comes to the sacrifice Agni himself is Varuṇa (10-?-?). When Agni is born he becomes Varuṇa, and when kindled, Mitra (3-5-1). In the evening Agni is Varuṇa, at dawn he rises as Mitra; as Savitṛ he moves in the atmosphere; as Indra in the middle of the sky, on the pole, he lights up everything (Av. 13-3-13). In one place (3-1-? to ?) Agni is said to be equal to twelve deities other than the five goddesses. Taking many divine forms (3-?-?), he becomes one with many names (3-20-3). All the deities are contained in him (5-3-1); as the rim of a wheel encloses the spokes, Agni encloses all the deities (5-13-6)."

"The oldest work of Agni, of all these, is the driving away of evil Piśācas and the turning back or burning of sorcerers. That Agni has done these works is seen in the Veda. By his light Agni drives away the Piśācas (3-15-1; etc.); hence the epithet 'rakṣohā' ('destroyer of Rākṣasas') has been applied to him (10-?-?). Blazing, he swallows up with his iron teeth the sorcerers and the Piśācas, and burns them with his flame (10-87-3, 5 and 14); he guards the sacrifice with great care. He knows the lineages of the Mantra-sorcerers and destroys them all (Av. 1-?-?). In the task of driving away the Piśācas of the earth, though Indra, Bṛhaspati, the Aśvins and especially Soma are helpers to Agni, this work may be said to be Agni's. Just as in the works like the killing of Asuras, which suit Indra alone, Agni has an incidental share, here too, in the sūktas and in the ritual portions addressed to Indra and others, it is plain that the work of driving away and destroying the Piśācas is Agni's."

"There is no other deity who has as much influence on a man's life as Agni. Agni's relation with human dwellings is a peculiar one. The epithet gṛhapati ('master of the house') applies to him alone. He dwells in every house (2-?-?); he never leaves the house (8-?-?). The epithet 'damūnāḥ' ('belonging to the work of the house') is used of Agni alone (1-60-4; etc.). In the triad of fires at the sacrifices the Āhavanīya and Dakṣiṇa fires are taken from the Gārhapatya fire. From place to place there is a taking and bringing of the sacrificial fire. Agni is borne around (4-?-?; 4-?-?); he makes a hundred forts round the oblation substances (4-?-?); round the place of sacrifice"

original p. 616

"he is carried three times with circumambulation (4-?-? and ?; and 4-?-?); as soon as he is freed from his parents (the fire-sticks), he is carried first to the east and then to the west (1-?-?)."

"Apart from the epithets mentioned before, Agni has the epithet 'guest of men'; he is the guest in every house (10-?-?); the first of the guests (5-?-?). Among the immortals he alone is the one who has settled among mortals (8-?-?). He is established, or has settled, in men's dwellings (3-?-?; 4-?-?). It is this Gārhapatya fire that has helped men to settle firmly each in his own house (3-1-12). He is a friend (3-?-?) and a protector (1-?-?) of those who settle in new places; in this context the name 'viśpati' ('lord of the settlements') is said of Agni alone."

"As said above, Agni is a friend to man (1-?-?), or a kinsman by marriage (1-?-?; etc.) or a relation (2-?-?; 6-?-?). He is called by his worshippers father (many times: 6-?-?; etc.), son (3-1-?), mother (6-1-?), brother (8-?-?; 10-?-?; etc.) and so on. So close a kinship shows that Agni is not only a means of sacrifice but a thing absolutely necessary for the everyday life."

"Since Agni is in human houses in this way, it is natural that the ancestors of men and Agni should have more kinship than other deities (1-?-?). The ancestors kindled him and praised him. The fires of Bharata (3-?-?; 2-?-?; etc.), Vadhryaśva (10-69-1), Devavāta (3-23-2), Divodāsa (6-?-?) and Trasadasyu (8-?-?) are mentioned. The lineages of the seers, by the authority of the mantra-seers, are said to be equal to Agni. Among them, some, Vasiṣṭha and others, may be spoken of as historical persons; the Aṅgirases, Bhṛgus and others as imagined persons."

"In sacrifices too a close kinship is formed between Agni and man's everyday life. Agni not only accepts what has been offered by man, but also works as a go-between for heaven and earth. He is the one who gives to the deities the substances offered in homa; without him there would be no delight to the deities (2-?-?). He brings the deities to the sacrificial hall (3-?-?) and, taking the oblations, goes and delivers them to them (2-?-?). To devour the oblation substances (3-1-11; etc.) he seats them on the darbha seat (1-?-?; 8-?-?). He who knows the paths well (6-?-?) goes, on the two ways to earth (8-?-?) and to the proximity of the deities (10-?-?)."

original p. 617

"[that go ?]. For that reason he is always called the messenger (dūta); he knows the paths well and takes the sacrifice to another place (1-?-?) or begs it of all dwellings (4-?-?); he runs very swiftly (10-?-?) between earth and sky (4-?-?; 4-?-?; 10-?-?) or between the two peoples, the deities and men (4-?-? and ?). The deities (5-?-?; etc.) and men (10-?-?) appointed him havyavāha or havyavāhana ('carrier of oblations'). (This name has become fixed for Agni alone.) He makes the mantra uttered by the sacrificer known to the deities (1-?-?) or calls the deities to the sacrificial hall (4-?-?). These are his works. He is the messenger of the deities (6-?-?) and of Vivasvān (1-?-?; 4-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?). One who knows the root and the root of the heavenly world, who accomplishes sacrifices, who calls the deities: such an Agni is more fitly said to be the messenger of men than of the deities. In another Veda (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?; 2-?-?), Agni is said to be the messenger of the deities, and Kāvya Uśanā or Daivya is said to be the messenger of the Asuras. In another place (Tai. Brā. 2-?-?) it is said that Agni, described as a messenger, is a path to go to the proximity of the deities, and that, going on that path, one can go to the very best places of heaven."

"Because it is said that Agni plays a very important part in accomplishing the works of sacrifice, the place that has been given to the priests among men has been given to Agni among the deities. Therefore he has the epithets ṛtvik, vipra, especially purohita, and so on. More than all these, Agni is called 'hotā' ('the praiser, the chief priest'). Agni is a hotṛ appointed by men (8-?-?; 10-?-?) and by the deities (6-?-?). Among all hotṛs he is the most beloved and the best (10-?-?; 10-?-?). He is named also Adhvaryu (3-?-?), and Brahmā, like Bṛhaspati, Soma and Indra (6-?-?). In one way it may be said that he alone does all the works of the above-mentioned priests (hotṛ, adhvaryu, brahmā) and of others (6-?-?; 3-?-?; etc.). He is always begged to worship or honour the deities (3-?-?; 2-?-?; etc.), and in return the deities too are asked to worship Agni three times a day (3-?-?). He accomplishes the sacrifice or the work (3-?-?; 3-?-?), and with his special power he completes it with all its limbs (3-?-?); he makes the homas fragrant (10-?-?); he joins to the deities the oblations protected by him (1-?-?). He is the father of the sacrifice (3-?-?), its king (4-?-?), its breaker (10-?-?), the one who looks after it (8-?-?) and is like a banner (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 10-?-?). In a sūkta (10-?-?)…"

original p. 618

"…[In a sūkta (10-51) it is said that Agni, tired of his work as] carrier, left the sacrificial works, and that, when the share due from the deities had come, he agreed to work for men as chief priest (purohita). What is most prominent in Agni's character is his priesthood. As Indra is the chief warrior, Agni is the chief priest. It may be said that this form of Agni is of the itthaṃ-[?]… nature. The work of carrying the oblation is Agni's chief work. Later, in the Brāhmaṇas, a distinction is stated even between Agni the carrier of oblations and Agni the eater of raw flesh (kravyāda, one who burns dead bodies). In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Vāj. Saṃ. 1-?; 19-?) three forms of Agni are stated: havyavāhana (one who carries the homa to the deities), kavyavāhana (one who joins to the Fathers what is given in rites for the dead) and saharakṣāḥ (one who is with Piśācas, Rākṣasas and the like)."

"Agni is a seer and a purohita (7-?-?); because he is the best of seers, he is kindled (3-?-?); a very merciful seer (6-?-?); the very first seer called Aṅgiras (1-?-?). Among the wise he is the divine wise one (asura, 3-?-?); the sacrifices are plainly known to him (10-?-?) and he knows all the rites (10-?-?). He sets right the mistakes that men make, who do not know the divine rules connected with sacrifice, being the knower of time (10-?-?). All the hidden places of the heaven-world are known to him (4-?-? and ?). By his own intellect he knows everything (10-?-?). He knows all (3-1-?; 10-?-?); as the felly encloses the spokes of a wheel, he has enclosed all (2-?-?). This omniscience is inborn in him (1-?-?). Words indicating omniscience, such as viśvavit ('knower of all'), viśvavedāḥ, kavi and kavikratu, are applied to him especially. Jātavedāḥ is explained (6-?-?) as 'one who knows all those who are born at all times.' This (jātavedas) is used about 130 times in the Ṛgveda of Agni alone. He knows the divine rules and the whole lineage (1-?-? and ?). All beings are known to him, and he can see all of them (3-?-?; 10-?-?). He hears all the praises addressed to him (8-?-?). Agni is also a giver of knowledge (6-?-?). Knowledge and praises arise from him (4-?-?). He is the giver of inspiration (10-?-?); he found the best of speech (3-?-?) and was the first to find the hymns (6-?-?). He is himself a speaker (6-?-?) and a singer."

"Agni is a great benefactor to his worshippers. He protects them by a hundred forts of iron (2-?-?; 2-?-?; 6-?-?; compare 1-?-?). He protects them from distress, or takes them across distress as one takes a ship across the ocean (3-?-?; 5-?-?; 2-?-?). To those who worship him as a guest he is a friend (4-?-?), and releases the worshippers from sorrow…"

original p. 619

"…(8-?-?). He protects him who brings oblations for him with effort (4-?-?). He looks after those who give him food and feed him with homa and the like, with thousands of eyes (10-?-?). He reduces his worshippers' enemies, like dry bladders, to ashes (4-?-?); he destroys their enemies as one fells trees (8-?-?; compare Av. 3-?-?, etc.). Therefore he is prayed to for help in battle (8-?-?) and goes at the head of the army as its leader (8-?-?). One protected and encouraged by Agni in a battle gets food as he wishes and is unconquerable (1-?-?). As branches come out of a tree, all boons come out of him (6-?-?). Agni, the master of boundless wealth, becomes the giver of lordship (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?). All treasures are gathered in him (10-?-?) and he opens the door of treasures (1-?-?). All the wealth in heaven and earth (4-?-?) or in heaven, earth and ocean (2-?-?; 10-?-?) belongs to him. He draws rain from the sky (3-?-?) and appears to establish a river in the desert (10-?-?). For this very reason Agni is prayed to to free [people] from hunger, poverty, lack of progeny, enemies, Piśācas and the like. All that is obtained from Indra concerns war and battle-fields. But what is obtained from Agni is mostly concerned with the world. He forgives the sins committed through ignorance (4-?-?; 2-?-?); he watches over [men] as one who is moved by Varuṇa's anger (4-1-4). Pleased with a son, he forgives even the fault done by the father and the mother (Av. 5-?-?; Tai. Brā. 2-?-?)."

"Agni is an Asura, a sovereign, and strong like Indra (2-?-?). His greatness is greater than the great sky (1-?-?). When he was born, he was greater than all the worlds he covered (3-3-10), or than heaven and earth (3-6-?; 10-?-?), and better than all the other deities (1-?-?). When he was hidden in the water, all the deities feared him and offered him honour (4-?-?). Varuṇa, Mitra, the Maruts and all the other deities praise and worship him (3-?-?; 3-?-?; 10-?-?). Agni accomplished ancient great deeds (2-?-?); hearing of his valorous deeds men tremble. In battle, he made room for the deities (1-?-?); he released them from the curse (2-?-?); he conquered thousands of men; he drove the Dasyu from the house and obtained light for the Ārya (2-?-?; 7-?-?). He encouraged the Āryas (8-?-?) and destroyed the Paṇis, who were wicked (2-?-?). Chiefly the epithet 'Vṛtrahā' ('slayer of Vṛtra'), which Indra alone ought to have, and 'Purandara' ('breaker of enemy forts, destroyer') are used about 2–3 times of Agni. For Agni's form of lightning such"

original p. 620

"deeds of valour are fitting; yet it is correct to say that these qualities were obtained from Indra."

"Though it is well known that Agni is the son of heaven and earth, he is also said to have created both of them (1-?-?; compare 2-?-?). His undestroyed rules are followed by both heaven and earth (3-?-?; 2-?-?). He spread out both worlds (3-?-?; 2-?-?) or spread them out like a hide (6-?-?). By his flame or smoke he supported the sky (3-?-?; 4-?-?). He has set the two worlds apart (6-?-?). By his mantras of truth he made heaven and earth firm (1-?-?). He is at the front of the world; or at night he is the master of the whole earth (10-?-?). He is master and also the chief of the sky (1-?-?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?). Knowing the limits by the wind, he touched by his greatness the ridge of the sky (6-?-?). He measured the regions of the atmosphere and of the heaven-world full of splendour (6-?-?). It is Agni who made Sūrya ascend the sky (10-?-?). That there is a peculiar kinship between the bearing of Agni on earth and the rising of the sun is clear. 'Here we kindle you (Agni); may your wonderful form be in the atmosphere' (3-?-?). In the Brāhmaṇas this idea is clearer still: before sunrise a man does homa in Agni, and so makes Sūrya rise; otherwise Sūrya would not rise at all (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?; Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?). In general it is said that sunrise and the kindling of fire take place at the same time. When Agni was born Sūrya became visible (4-?-?). Agni himself made the sky studded with stars (1-?-?). Everything that flies, walks, stands or moves he created (10-?-?). In these beings (3-?-?), in true things and in all living things, the embryo was placed by him; through him the earth and women became fruitful (10-?-?). Agni was the first to create men (8-?-?): in saying that the earth, sky, water and the like were made by him, this idea has also come in by the way; it is not said that he created men. Last of all, Agni is the giver of immortality (2-?-?), a protector (2-?-?), and grants it to mortals (1-?-?)."

"Some names of heavenly Agni, such as 'Apāṃ napāt', are counted as separate deities, and some have obtained partial personalities. The word Vaiśvānara occurs about 60 times (in five whole Ṛks and fourteen sūktas). In all contexts, according to the Anukramaṇī, Vaiśvānara-Agni is the deity. The word Vaiśvānara does not occur anywhere alone"

original p. 621

"[by itself]. Vaiśvānara means 'belonging to all men'; that is, this word may mean all forms of Agni. In the mantras addressed to Vaiśvānara-Agni there is the story of the heavenly Agni coming down to the earth (3-?-?; 6-?-?); and the usage 'Mātariśvan' is also for Vaiśvānara-Agni (3-?-?). In the Nirukta (7-?) Vaiśvānara is one of the names of Agni. In his explanation on this (Nir. 7-?) Yāska has written that the ancient ritualists thought Vaiśvānara-Agni meant Sūrya, and that Śākapūṇi thought it meant the fire that is now current. The fire in use now is named Vaiśvānara-Agni. It is he who is kindled for praise, homa and so on; only once, Yāska gives his own view, this name is used for the fires of the atmosphere and of the heaven-world. But in the books on Vedic ritual, Vaiśvānara is counted as one special form of Agni (Āś. Śrau. Sū. 1-?-?; Kā. Śrau. Sū. ?-?-?; Paṃ. Brā. ?-?-?; Śat. Brā. 1-?-?)."

"The name of Agni, Tanūnapāt, is used eight times in the Ṛgveda in the Āprī-sūktas. Of these eight, except twice (3-29-11; 10-?-?), all occur in the second Ṛk of the Āprī-sūktas. In the Nirukta this too is a separate name of Agni (8-?). Yāska has explained this word (Nir. 8-?) as 'one born as a son to himself', that is, 'one who becomes manifest of himself in the forest and in the clouds'. Of Tanūnapāt it is said: 'Asura; womb (garbha)' (3-29-11), that is, 'a divine embryo belonging to the world of the deities'. This is not said anywhere of Mātariśvan and Narāśaṃsa. The goddess Uṣas kisses the purohita Tanūnapāt [compare 10-?-?; 5-?-?]. Tanūnapāt is addressed as 'sujihva' ('having a beautiful tongue') (10-?-?). He is prayed to carry the sacrifice to the deities [1-?-?; 10-?-?]. He increases the homa that is boundless, filled with ghee and with honey (1-?-?; compare 1-?-?). The deities pay him honour three times a day, and Varuṇa, Mitra and Agni once (3-?-?)."

"The name used even more than Tanūnapāt is Narāśaṃsa. According to the Nirukta (8-?), this too is an independent name. But it is not said of Agni alone; it is used of Pūṣan in two places [1-?-?; 10-?-?]. This word occurs in the third Ṛk of the Āprī-sūktas, and also in the second Ṛk of those called 'Āprī'. Narāśaṃsa has four limbs [caturaṅgaḥ, 10-?-?] and has a wife of the heaven-world [Gnāspatiḥ, 3-?-?]. He performs sacrifice with honey on his hands and tongue [1-?-?; 5-?-?]. Three times a day he pours honey in the sacrifice [1-?-?]. He pours oil for the three heaven-worlds and for the deities [3-?-?]. He comes in front of the deities and makes the sacrifice pleasant for them [10-?-?]. The worshippers praise through his sacrifices the greatness of the deities [2-?-?]. Both Narāśaṃsa and Daivya and"

original p. 622

Agni, end "…[Narāśaṃsa and Daivya and] Soma-deity are placed in the middle [9-?-?]; that is, it may be between the heaven-world and the fires. When Agni was born he received the name Narāśaṃsa [3-29-11]. In one mantra of a sūkta addressed to Bṛhaspati [10-?-?] protection from Narāśaṃsa is prayed for; in another he is said to be the sacrificer of the world of the deities [1-?-?]. In these two he seems to be counted as Bṛhaspati himself. As the word narāśaṃsa is a compound formed from the words nara ('man') and śaṃsa ('praise'), and as it is used in the forms 'narāṃ śaṃsaḥ' and [2-?-?; 1-?-?] 'devānāṃ śaṃsam' ('praise of the gods'), the sense of this word may be 'one praised by men'."

Bṛhaspati

Bṛhaspati. "This deity holds a position of considerable importance. Eleven sūktas praise this deity. With Indra, as a paired deity, he is praised in two sūktas [4-49; 6-73]. The word Bṛhaspati occurs about 130 times; and also Brahmaṇaspati about 50 times. Bṛhaspati and Brahmaṇaspati are exchanged for each other in one and the same mantra [2-?]. The description of his limbs is very scanty. He has seven mouths and seven rays [4-50-4], a beautiful tongue [1-?-?; 4-50-1], horns not yet bent [10-?-?]. His back is dark blue [5-?-?] and he has a hundred wings [6-?-?]. He is golden-coloured and of reddish hue [5-?-?], radiant [3-?-?; 6-?-?], pure [6-?-?] and clear-voiced [6-?-?]. He has one bow, the Ṛta (sacrifice, truth) is the string and the arrow is sādhutva ('goodness') [2-?-?; Av. 5-?-?]. He holds a golden axe [6-?-?] and uses an iron-blue [black?] axe forged by Tvaṣṭṛ [10-?-?]. He moves in the chariot of sacrifice [10-?-?]; it kills Piśācas, breaks open the doors of the cow-pens and brings light [2-?-?]. His chariot is drawn by red-coloured horses."

"At the very high regions of the heaven-world, Bṛhaspati, born of a mass of lustre, roared and drove away the darkness [4-50-4; compare 10-?-?], he is the progeny of the two worlds [6-?-?]. But it is also said that Tvaṣṭṛ created him [2-?-?]. He is said to be the father of the deities [2-?-?]; as sparks fly from the bellows of a smith, the deities were born from him [10-?-?]."

"The word purohita, which is particularly used for Agni, is used for him too [2-?-?; Vāj. Saṃ. 20-?; Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?; Ait. Brā. 8-?-?]. The ancient seers placed him as their leader [4-50-1]. He is the purohita of Soma [Śat. Brā. 4-?-?]. He is also Brahmā [2-1-3; 4-50-?; 10-?-?]. In other Vedas, it is said that he worked as brahmā (the brahmā priest) at the sacrifices of the deities"

original p. 623

"[of the deities]. He is the brahma used by the deities (that is, the praise, Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?; etc.). Bṛhaspati is an inspirer of devotion, and without him a sacrifice cannot be seen to bring victory [1-?-?]. As a guide on the path, he makes the gathering of the deities easily obtained [2-?-?; ?]. By him the deities obtained their shares of homa [2-?-?]. With these homas he rouses the deities [Av. 19-?-?]. He himself pronounces the sūkta that pleases Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman and the other deities [1-?-?]; he sings songs [10-?-?]. His singing reaches heaven [1-?-?] and the metres belong to him [Mai. Saṃ. 1-?-?]. He is sometimes surrounded by singers [2-?-?; 10-?-?]. With his friends who make a sound like swans (here the swans may be the Aṅgirases who occur in the preceding Ṛk 10-?-?), he sings [10-?-?]. A group of singers is with him [4-?-?]. For this reason he may have obtained the name 'Gaṇapati' ('lord of the groups') [2-23-1]. This name is used once of Indra also [10-?-?]."

"As is clear from the word Brahmaṇaspati ('lord of the sacred word'), he is the lord of the praises. He is praised as the king of the praise-sentences, and as the best of seers among all the seers [2-23-1]. Mounting the chariot of Ṛta (the limbs of the sacrifice), he conquers those who hate praise and the enemies of the deities [2-23-3 and ?]. From him all the praise-sentences issue [1-?-?]. He himself utters the sentences of prayer [1-?-?] and makes them known to the human purohita [10-?-?]. For this reason he came later to have the name 'Vācaspati' ('lord of speech') [Mai. Saṃ. 2-?-?; compare Śat. Brā. 14-?-?]. In the Purāṇas, beyond the Vedas, 'Vācaspati' became fixed as a name of Bṛhaspati."

"There are many sentences that seem to say that Agni and Bṛhaspati are equal. Agni is prayed to as one who is lord of praise-sentences and, like Mitra, beautiful in form [1-?-?]. In another sentence, though it is said that Agni is equal to Bṛhaspati and some other deities, since Agni and Bṛhaspati alone are specially addressed, it seems that the equality with Agni is what is intended. In one mantra [3-?-?], Mātariśvan and Bṛhaspati are both names of Agni; in another [1-?-?], Mātariśvan is a name of Bṛhaspati. Bṛhaspati [5-?-?] who dwells in every house and shines well, red of face, must be Agni. Again, in two sentences it seems that Bṛhaspati and Narāśaṃsa are spoken of as one [1-?-?; 10-?-?]. Like Agni, Bṛhaspati, the son of strength [1-?-?], burns or kills Aṅgiras, Piśācas and the like [2-?-?; 10-?-?], and so on. In such characteristics he is distinguished. Bṛhaspati too goes to the heaven-world, mounting to the houses of the upper world [10-?-?]."

original p. 624

"Like Agni, he has three dwelling-places [4-50-1], is a thing beloved in houses [2-?-?], and is Sadaspati ('lord of the assembly') [1-?-?]. Of Agni too, at one place, the words 'brahmaṇaḥ kavī' are used; he is prayed to make heaven and earth easily attainable by the brahma (praise) [2-?-?]. But the name Bṛhaspati has been stated separately in the lists of Agni and the other deities [3-20-3; etc.]; so it is right to say that Agni and Bṛhaspati are different [2-?-?; 2-?-?; 10-?-?]."

"In the history of the release of the cows by Indra, Bṛhaspati too has an important part, like Agni. The mountain bowed its head before Bṛhaspati's roar and gave him room to open the cow-pens; accompanied by Indra, Bṛhaspati made the water, which had been covered by darkness, flow again [compare 2-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?]. With the singer (Aṅgiras) Ati-theya he roared, split Vala, and drove out the cows that were bellowing and shut up [4-50-5]. He obtained the treasures and big cow-pens; desiring water and light, the unobstructed Bṛhaspati destroys the enemies with his flames [6-?-?]. What was firm was shaken by him; what was strong was overcome; he drove out the cows; he split Vala by mantra; he made the darkness uncovered, and made the sky visible to the eye; Bṛhaspati broke open, by his own power, the stone door of the well filled with honey; the deities drank that honey and rained as they wished [2-?-? and ?]. When Bṛhaspati split the fortresses of Vala and so on with the red rays that shine, the herds of cows came into view; like breaking nuts, he drove out the cows; seeing the honey covered by the rock, he split it with his lion's roar and brought it out; he drove out the marrow of Vala [10-?-? onward]. Having driven out the cows, he divided them in heaven [2-?-?]. Bṛhaspati brought out the cows by means of stones; seizing Vala's cows, he brought them under his own control [10-?-?]. His conquering of Vala is his special distinction. It is a story with four feet [Av. 9-?-?]. Since he is in the clouds, he thunders the cows [10-?-?; compare 10-?-?]; the cows here, as was clearly said, may be water [2-?-?; 6-?-?] or the rays of Uṣas [10-?-?; 10-?-?]."

"In the release of the cows, trying to obtain the light hidden in darkness, he achieves it; he obtains Uṣas, light and Agni, and drives away the darkness [10-?-? and ?]. While splitting the fortress, Sūrya, Uṣas and the cows were obtained [10-?-?]. Covering and driving out the darkness, he brought out the light [2-?-?;"

original p. 625

"4-?-?]. Thus the characteristics of a warrior are seen in Bṛhaspati. He split the mountain bound with treasures, entered it, and split Śambara's fortresses [2-?-?]. Bṛhaspati, the seer born at the beginning, crushes the Aṅgiras stones. He shoots like a ball in both worlds; he kills Vṛtra; splits fortresses; and conquers enemies [6-?-? and ?]. Driving away enemies, he conquers [10-?-?]. Whether the battle is small or large, no one can defeat Bṛhaspati [1-?-?]. In war he uproots the enemy [2-?-?]. He alone is to be prayed to at times of war [2-?-?], and in such circumstances he is the purohita most often praised for his help [2-?-?]."

"Because he is a friend and companion of Indra [2-?-?; 2-?-?; 8-?-?], at every step he is praised together with that deity [4-50-10 and 11; etc.]. With Indra he too drinks Soma [4-?-?; 4-50-10] and is generous like him (maghavan) [2-?-?]. He is a paired deity with Indra alone [2-?-?; 4-49 and 6-73]. For this reason the name 'Vajrī' ('wielder of the vajra') is applied to him [1-?-?], and he is said to use the vajra weapon that kills Asuras [Av. 11-?-?]. Once [1-?-?] he is praised along with Indra and the Maruts, and is invited to come along with whichever of Mitra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan and the Maruts [10-?-?]. He released Trita from the well on hearing his prayer [1-?-?]."

"Bṛhaspati loves the praiser [2-?-?] but punishes the hater of praise [1-?-?]. He rescues the righteous from all calamities and favours them with wealth and the like [1-?-?; 2-?-? to 10]. Bṛhaspati, distinguished by all the things desirable [2-?-?; 2-?-?], is rich and a giver of prosperity [1-?-?], a remover of disease and a giver of long life [1-?-?]. Being so merciful he is addressed as father [4-50-6; 6-?-?]."

"He is distinguished by divinity (an Asura [2-?-?]), is a relation of all the deities [3-?-?; 4-50-6], and has the most divinity among the deities [2-?-?]. In the form of the deity he gathers all the deities and all things into himself [2-?-?; compare 6-?-?]. Capable of this, he has set the two ends of the earth far apart [4-50-1]. The rising of the sun and the moon one after the other is his unimitable deed [10-?-?]. He causes the growth of crops [10-?-? and ?]. A connection of Bṛhaspati with some of the stars is stated. The deity of the star Puṣya is Bṛhaspati [Tai. Saṃ. 4-?-?]; in the Purāṇas and so on he is called the planet Bṛhaspati or Guru."

original p. 626

Bṛhaspati, end "From the points stated above, it may be said that Bṛhaspati is a special form of Agni; or that Bhakti or Śraddhā is the presiding deity. The name Bṛhaspati, like Viśāṃpati ('lord of the settlements'), Gṛhapati ('master of the house') and Sadaspati ('lord of the assembly'), which remain as epithets of Agni, is counted as an independent deity. But modern scholars have held various views: a special form of Agni, Śraddhā, another form of Indra, the moon, and so on."

Soma

Soma. "Since the Soma sacrifices are very important among the rites of the Ṛgveda, it is natural that the deity Soma too is one of the principal deities. In the ninth maṇḍala, 114 sūktas, and six others besides — in all 120 sūktas — praise the deity Soma. Portions of 45 sūktas, and 5–6 sūktas together with Indra, Agni, Pūṣan or Rudra, also praise the deity Soma. The name Soma, alone or in compounds, occurs about 120 [?] times. Judged by number, the deity Soma is the third. The attribution of human form is very slight. The plant Soma and its juice are mentioned at every step, so that it is impossible to forget them completely; therefore the deity's form, limbs and the attribution of movement and the like are all imperfect. Though deeds of valour are stated, they are borrowed from other deities, and are unimportant or secondary. Like the other deities, in the name of Indu or Soma he is invited to come to the sacrifice, adorn the seat of darbha and receive the oblations. The whole of the ninth maṇḍala deals with the juice of Soma: the pressing of the juice with stones, its purification through the woollen filter, its offering to the deities through Agni as a drink (1-?-?; 5-?-?; 8-?-? etc.), or its being drunk by the priests, and so on, are the subjects stated."

"Before understanding the plant, its juice, and the history connected with them, one must know what is said about it. The part of the plant used to extract the juice has the name 'aṃśu' (9-?-?). As cows give milk through eagerness, the plant gives milk (the juice) (9-?-?). 'Andhas' means the Soma plant (9-?-?; 10-?-? etc.); it came from heaven (9-?-?); the eagle (śyena) brought it (4-?-?; 9-?-?; 10-?-?). The word andhas is used also for the juice. The word 'indu' indicates the deity (9-?-?; 10-?-?). For the juice there is also the word soma; but generally the word rasa alone is used. In one sūkta (1-?) only, in the sense of juice, 'pitu' ('drink') is used, in many places 'mada' ('intoxicant'), and sometimes 'anna' ('food')"

original p. 627

"[9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; Śat. Brā. 1-?-?]. When it is used in the sense relating to the Aśvins, the word madhu means honey or a stimulating substance. In the ordinary sense of a sweet drink, milk, ghee and especially the Soma juices are used (4-?-?; 8-?-?). In the Itihāsa, madhu means nectar or Soma. Likewise the Soma juice, when stirred, is used in the sense of the state of immortality (9-?-?; 6-?-?; etc.; Vāj. Saṃ. 6-?; Śat. Brā. 9-?-?). When the king Soma is pressed, he becomes immortal (Vāj. Saṃ. 19-?). There is a usage 'saumyaṃ madhu' ('the intoxicating substance connected with Soma') (4-?-?; 8-?-?). Figuratively Soma is called pīyūṣa (3-?-?; etc.), milk (9-?-?), a wave of sweetness, or the essence of honey (9-?-?). Among the figurative names the most used is indu (a flowing drop, a drop). In fewer cases the word drapsa, meaning a drop, is also used."

"For taking out the juice both the root su ('to press') (9-?-?; etc.) and the root duh ('to milk') (3-?-? and ?; etc.) are used. The juice produces intoxication (1-?-?; 6-?-?; etc.) and is mixed with honey (9-?-?). Though the word madhu means sweet, in relation to Soma it must be taken as 'mixed with honey' (mixed with honey-like sweet substance). In some places this mixing is plainly stated (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?). The Soma juice that flows down from the filter is compared to the waves of a stream of water (9-?-?), or plainly to waves (9-?-?; etc.), or called waves of honey (3-?-?; etc.). To Soma standing in the wooden vessel the names arṇava (10-?-?), samudra ('ocean') (9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.) and the like are given. The Soma of heaven is called a well (utsa); it is in the highest place where the cows are (9-?-?); it is placed in the cows (that is, the milk) and is driven with ten reins (the fingers) (6-?-?); this Soma is in the third step that was raised up by Viṣṇu (1-?-?)."

"The colour of the plant and the juice is said to be babhru (brown), or aruṇa ('ruddy'), or often hari (tawny-yellow). Soma is the branch of a dusky plant (10-?-?). The plant that gives the red-coloured juice (2-?-?); the tawny plant is pressed into the woollen filter (9-?-?). The colour of Soma, or of the substance used in its place, is determined to be tawny (Kā. Brā. 4-?-?; Śat. Brā. 4-?-?); the cow that is given in exchange for Soma too must be of tawny colour (Tai. Saṃ. 6-?-?; Śat. Brā. 3-?-?)."

"The Soma juice is purified by the hands (9-?-?); by the ten fingers (9-?-?; 9-?-?), or, figuratively, by ten sisters or maidens (9-?-?;"

original p. 628

"9-?-?), or by the maidens, the daughters of Vivasvān (9-?-?). To be a drink for Indra, the maidens of Trita make the red-coloured juice come out through the stones (9-?-?; 9-?-?). The Soma juice was purified by the daughters of Sūrya (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?). Sometimes it is purified also by mantra (9-?-?; 9-?-?). The priests who press the Soma are the adhvaryus (4-?-?)."

"The plant is crushed by stones (9-?-?) or ground by slabs (9-?-?); the plant is pounded and the juice is produced (10-?-?). The stones strip off its covering (Tai. Brā. 3-?-?). Those stones are placed on a skin; on the skin of a cow they grind the Soma plant (9-?-?). Soma is placed on the altar (3-?-?). Nowadays it is not placed on the altar; it is held with the hands (2-?-?; 9-?-?; Av. 11-?-?). The two arms and the ten fingers push the stone (9-?-?). For this reason it is said that the stones are driven with ten reins (10-?-?). Since they are said to be 'yoked' (yukta), the fingers are compared to horses (10-?-?). For the stones, the words adri or grāvan are used generally, in the plural or singular. To these stones the words aśman (9-?-?), bharitra (3-?-?), parvata (3-?-?) and parvaśa adrayaḥ (10-?-?) are applied. It appears that pounding Soma with stones was the general practice; yet pounding in a mortar (ulūkhala) in some places too is accepted (1-?-?)."

"After being pounded, the juice is poured over a filter made from the wool of a sheep and is thus purified (9-?-?; etc.; 9-?-?). Here all the dregs are removed, and the pure Soma juice is used for the deities to taste (9-?-?). To this filter there are many names: tvac, roma, vāra (tail-hair), pavitra (filter), sānu and so on. All these words commonly have the epithet avi ('of a sheep'), or the word avi itself indicates this filter. Because of this Soma, which flows through it, is called Pavamāna or Punāna ('purifying') (the root is pū, 'to be purified'). The root mṛj ('to purify') applies not only to purification by the filter but also to the mixing of Soma with milk and water (9-?-?; 9-?-?). The pure Soma, other than the mixed, has the names śuddha, śukra, śuci and so on (9-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?). This pure Soma is offered to Vāyu and Indra only; śucipā ('drinker of pure Soma') is a mark specially of Vāyu. In Soma sacrifices, when the grahas (cups of Soma offered to the paired deities) are offered, the pure Soma is used for Indra and Vāyu, the milk-mixed for Mitra and Varuṇa, and the honey-mixed for the Aśvins."

original p. 629

"After it has come from the filter, Soma enters the pots (kalaśa) or droṇa (wooden vessels) (9-?-?; etc.). As buffaloes plunge into the forest, Soma plunges towards the droṇas (9-?-?; 9-?-?). To take his seat in the vessel of the deity, he flies like a bird (9-?-?); as a bird sits on a tree, the red-coloured liquid sits in the wooden vessels (9-?-?). In the vessel the Soma is mixed with water. Together with the waves it flows through the kāṇḍa ('reed') (9-?-?). As a ball swallows a lump of curds, Soma, roaring loudly, swallows toward the droṇa vessel; singing, he flows swiftly round the droṇa vessel when the priests mix water (9-?-?; 9-?-?). The sages draw out the Soma juice into the water with their hands, as one milks (9-?-?). Coming over the wool, he, dancing in the droṇa vessel, is purified by ten maidens (9-?-?). There are many more sentences that establish the mixing of this Soma and water (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?, etc.). The Soma drops give the flood a stream (9-?-?). For purification (mixing with water) not only the root mṛj but also the root ā-dhāv is used (9-?-?). In preparing Soma, first savana (pressing) and then udakamiśraṇa (mixing of water) come (2-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; Av. 6-?-?). In Soma sacrifices first the pressing and then the ādhāvana (washing) come in order. In the wide vessels (troughs), to give sweetness, milk too is mixed with the Soma juice (9-?-?; etc.). It is said in many sentences that both water and milk are mixed. The deity Soma holds the clothes of water. When he desires to hold the cows (milk), streams of water run to him (9-?-?). The people, having pounded the Soma plant with stones, washed the juice in water, adorned it with garments in the form of cows [i.e. milk], and bring him out with Soma plants (compare 9-?-?; 3-?-?; 6-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?)."

"Soma juice is mixed in three ways: Trāśiraḥ? [as read: 'Traiśiraḥ'] (9-?-?): milk-mixed (gavāśir), curd-mixed (dadhyāśir) and barley-mixed (yavāśir). For this mixing, the wearing of a garment (vastra, vāsas, atka) is used as a figure; sometimes it is called 'nirṇij' ('a flowing cloth', 9-?-?). This word is applied also to the filter (9-?-?). Because of this, Soma is described as beautiful (9-?-?; etc.) and adorned with ornaments as one wishes (9-?-?). The mixing of ghee (9-?-?) or of water too is said, but for these the word āśir is not used."

"In sacrifices, there is a rite named āpyāyana ('swelling'; meaning that the Soma plants that have been pounded are made to swell again by soaking them in water) (Mai. Saṃ. 4-?-?). In the Ṛgveda this root (āpyā) for Soma…"

original p. 630

Soma, continued "…is used in relation to [the swelling]. But here the root is used to suggest that Soma is equal to the moon. Only in one place (9-31-4) may this limb of the sacrificial rite be indicated. The Soma juice swells like a river or the ocean (9-?-?; 9-102-12)."

"Soma is pressed three times a day. The Ṛbhu deities are invited to the evening pressing (4-33-11; etc.); Indra alone [1-?-?] to the midday pressing [3-?-1 and ?; 8-?-1], and Indra is invited to the morning pressing, to be the first to drink [10-?-?]."

"The seat (sadhastha) of the Soma juice or of the deity is mentioned at every step; once three seats are stated. Besides the pure one, he adorns these three seats [9-?-?]. The epithet 'tripadasthā' ('having three seats') is said of Soma [8-?-?]. These three seats must be the three droṇa vessels in which pure Soma is put [compare Tai. Saṃ. 3-?-?; Kā. Śrau. Sū. ?-?-?; Ṛk. Ve. 8-?-?]. Indra drinks from three lakes (5-?-? and ?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?). The epithet 'tripṛṣṭha' ('with three backs') is peculiar to the deity Soma. It is used once for the juice [2-?-?]. As when 'ghṛtapṛṣṭha' is said of Agni it is understood to mean ghee-homa, so here too three kinds of mixing must be understood."

"It is described in many ways that water is mixed with the Soma juice. The rivers flow towards Soma [9-?-?]. The streams observe his rules [9-?-?]. Soma runs in front of the streams [9-?-?]; the rivers are all his wives, and he is their sacrificer and king [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]; he is the sacrificer of the many wives (9-?-?) and the king of the ocean, a deity [9-?-?]. The waters are his sisters [9-?-?]. As he is the leader of the waters, he is the lord of rain [9-?-?]. He generates water and makes the earth and the sky pour rain [9-?-?]. He sends the stream of rain from the sky [9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.]. Sometimes the Soma drops themselves are called rain-drops [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]. Honey-mixed Soma flows like a rain-cloud [9-?-?]. In that way, the purifying drops (Soma-drops) fall from heaven, from the sky, upon the regions of the earth [9-?-?]. In many other places Soma, when pressed, is compared to rain-water (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 10-?-? compare)."

"The waters are prayed to make the intoxicating substance, Indra's drink, flow [10-?-?]. Soma is a drop that grows in the water [9-?-?; 9-?-?]. For this reason he is the sprout of water [9-?-?; Śat. Brā. 4-?-?] or an infant: the Gandharva in the water (apāṃ gandharvaḥ), just born as a child, is cherished by the seven brothers as by mothers [9-?-?; 10-?-?]; or the waters themselves are his mothers [9-?-?]. The water is described as being like a young man among the cows [9-?-?; 9-?-?]."

original p. 631

"The sound made when purifying in the droṇa vessels or when pouring into the pots is like the sound of rain [9-?-?]. In this context exaggerated statements are many. The sound made when the Soma drops run over the filter is like the sound of warriors fighting [9-?-?]. To indicate this sound, roots meaning 'to roar' and 'to cry' — krand, nad, mā, ru, vāś and the like — are used (9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.). The root stan ('to thunder') is also used [9-?-?]. The sages draw the juice from the thundering Soma plants [9-?-?]. In the context of purifying Soma, hail too is mentioned [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]. These must be words applying either to the way of purifying heavenly Soma or to the rain-clouds."

"When it is said that Soma roars, it is generally by comparison with a bull, or the usage is of the bull itself. Like a ball, he roars in the forest [9-?-?]; the tawny bull roars and shines together with Sūrya [9-?-?]. Because the words go ('cow') are said for the waters or milk-waters mixed with Soma, a relation of Soma and the streams with the bull and cows is stated. He is like a bull among the cows [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?], or he breaks all the cows [9-?-?]. He roars like a bull moving among cows, or like a bull hating cows he roars; and the cows hate him and cry out [9-?-?; etc.]. He is the bull of earth, sky and rivers [6-?-?]. The roaring of Soma is many times compared to a buffalo. Soma is called 'paśu' ('beast') itself [9-?-?]. As he is a bull among the go (vāra, i.e. the filter) cows, Soma makes the water (go) fruitful [10-?-?; 9-?-?], and is also the retodhā ('bearer of seed'); this epithet is said mostly of Candra in the Yajurveda [Vai. Saṃ. 1-?-?]. Hence he grants fruitfulness [9-?-?; 9-?-?]. Since Soma is called a bull at every step (ukṣā, vṛṣā, vṛṣabha), he is described as having sharp horns (tigmaśṛṅga). This word occurs six times in the Ṛgveda; of these, five times, in the sense of bull, it is used together with it. Indra's drink, 'mādha', is like a bull with keen horns [10-?-?]. The deity Soma, like Agni, sharpens his horns [9-?-?; 9-?-?]."

"Soma is swift. The speed of the flowing juice is many times compared with the speed of a horse. The ten maidens (the fingers) lead Soma, like a good horse, by the arms [?], and clean it [9-?-?]"

original p. 632

"[they wash it]. The drop of Soma that creates intoxication for Indra is a tawny horse [9-?-?]. The Soma juice flowing into the droṇa vessels is compared to a bird that flies [9-?-?; etc.]."

"Since the juice is of a yellow colour, its physical qualities are specially discussed; its brightness and its rays are described. They compare it with Sūrya, above and above. He shines like Sūrya or with Sūrya, and is covered with the rays of Sūrya [compare 9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]; mounting Sūrya's chariot, he stands over all beings like Sūrya. Like Sūrya he covers earth and sky with his rays [9-?-?]. He was born as the son of the radiant one, and made his parents brighter [9-?-?]. The daughter of Sūrya purifies him [9-?-?]. For the reasons stated above, he fights with the darkness [9-?-?]. He removes it with light [9-?-?], or drives away the darkness and gives excellent light [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.], it is said."

"The Soma juice has a certain irresistible power, which is not in ordinary food or drink. By this power it rouses men, or anyone who drinks it, and makes them accomplish deeds that are not possible to men. For this very reason it is a divine drink, equal to nectar, or the very idea that it is nectar is given room. Even to say that one who drinks it becomes immortal is not an exaggeration. It is the intoxicant liked by the deities and the cause of immortality [9-?-?; 1-?-?]. All the deities drink this juice, which has been pressed by men and mixed with milk [9-?-?]; from it they quickly get joy [8-?-?] and after drinking become youthful [8-?-?]. Soma is eternal [1-?-?; 8-?-?; 9-?-?]. The deities drank it to attain immortality [9-?-?]. He (the deity Soma) grants immortality to the deities [1-?-?; 9-?-?] and to men [1-?-?; 8-?-?]; in the world that is the abode of eternal lustre and fame, indestructible, and the dwelling-place of Vaivasvata, he makes his worshipper immortal and dwells [9-?-? and ?]."

"Therefore, naturally, Soma too must have the power of healing. For the sick, the Soma juice is a medicine [8-?-?]. Hence the deity Soma cures whatever disease there is; he gives eyes to the blind and legs to the lame [8-?-?; 10-?-?]. He is the protector of men's bodies; he pervades all their limbs [8-?-?]. He grants long life in this world [1-?-?; 8-?-? and ?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]. If one drinks Soma, the sin in the heart too is removed; untruth is destroyed and truth is increased."

original p. 633

"The Soma juice enters the body and increases the power of speech, as an Ambikā leads the ship forward [9-?-?]; [6-?-?; 8-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]. For the same reason Soma has the name Vācaspati ('lord of speech') [9-?-?; 9-?-?] or vāco agriyaḥ, the leader of speech, or 'at the front of speech' [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?]. It is said that he calls even from heaven [9-?-?]. In the Brāhmaṇas it is said that the deities gave speech as the price of Soma. Soma rouses strong emotions [6-?-?]. The worshippers declare in this way: 'We have drunk Soma; we have become immortal; we have come into the portion of light (we have become knowers); we have known the deities' [8-?-?]. Soma is the lord of emotions; he brings prayer-sentences and is called leader or father [of speech]. He is the leader of poets; among the vipras he is the seer (vipra) [9-?-?]. His mind is like the mind of seers; he is the begetter of the seers [9-?-?] and the protector of prayer-mantras [6-?-?]. He is the very soul of sacrifice [9-?-?; 9-?-?]; the sacrificial priest called Brahmā to the deities [9-?-?], and he distributes to each their shares [10-?-?]. Thus knowledge of him is attributed. He is a seer who is the one knowing [8-?-?]. All the lineages of the deities are known to him [9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; 10-?-?]. He is the wise stream that observes men [9-?-?]. The deity Soma sees all creatures minutely [9-?-?]. Hence he has many eyes [9-?-?] and a thousand eyes [9-?-?]."

"Soma made the Fathers go towards the accomplishing of work [9-?-?]; through him they gained splendour and cows [9-?-?]. Soma has kinship with the Fathers [8-?-?], or is joined by them [Av. 14-?-?; Śat. Brā. 2-?-?; etc.]. The Fathers (the deities of the Fathers) have the name Somya ('dear to Soma') [10-?-?; Av. 3-?-?]."

"By the Soma juice man's enthusiasm increases. But the Soma juice is chiefly offered to the deities; hence the joy and enthusiasm born of Soma arise in the deities. The result of the intoxication born of Soma falls chiefly upon Indra. He becomes the helper of Indra in checking the hostile powers in the sphere of the air. It is said many times that the special power and ability needed to fight with Vṛtra came to Indra from the Soma juice [8-?-?; etc.]. In the intoxication that comes from Soma, Indra defeats all his enemies [9-?-?], and no one can face Indra when he has drunk Soma in battle [6-?-?]. Soma is the soul of Indra [9-?-?]; a friend (Mitra) who does good [10-?-?]; he increases Indra's valour [9-?-?] and is a helper in the killing of Vṛtra"

original p. 634

"…[and is a helper in the killing of Vṛtra] (9-?-?). Accompanied by Soma, Indra made the water flow for men and killed the serpent (4-?-?). For this reason Soma is sometimes called Indra's vajra-weapon (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?). This Soma juice belonging to Indra becomes the vajra that obtains thousandfold victory (9-?-?). The Soma juice that can destroy a hundred and more forts (9-?-?), and the plant that kills Vṛtra and gives intoxication (6-?-?): in such ways the deity Soma himself, like Indra, becomes one who kills Vṛtra and splits forts (9-?-?). The personal epithet of Indra, 'Vṛtrahā', is used of Soma fifteen or sixteen times."

"When drunk by Indra, the Soma juice became the cause of the rising of the sun (9-?-?). This work is stated of Soma independently also. Soma made the sun (9-?-?, 9-?-?) and the other masses of light in the sky (9-?-?) shine, and produced the sun in the water (9-?-?). The cause of sunrise, the awakener: having struck, he gave the sun to the world; and made the Uṣases rise. He causes his worshippers to take part at the time of sunrise (9-?-?) and provides light for them (9-?-?). He found light (9-?-?) and provides light and sky (9-?-?). Ghee is the centre of immortality, and the whole universe is said to stand upon it (4-?-? and ?). In the same way supremacy over the whole universe is said of the Soma juice or of the deity (9-?-? and ?). He is the lord of all the regions (9-?-?); he does the work of creation of the two worlds (9-?-?); the creation and preservation of earth and sky, being the support of the sky and placing splendour in the sun — he does these works (6-?-? and ?; 6-?-?)."

"While fighting with the Asura Vṛtra, Soma, who was Indra's helper, came to be regarded as a warrior himself. He is victorious, unconquerable, and born for battle (9-?-?). The bravest of the brave, the most terrible of the terrible, Soma is always victorious (9-?-? and ?). For his worshippers, he wins for them cows, chariots, horses, gold, heaven, water and thousands of other boons (9-?-?); indeed he obtains all things in battle (9-?-?). Without praise of valour and the like, he is always said to be the giver of cows and other things and of heaven (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.). He is the treasure of the deities (9-?-?) or their wealth (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?). The deity Soma is able to protect from enemies (10-?-?). He can drive away Piśācas (9-?-?) and, like some other deities, has more often become 'rakṣohā' ('destroyer of Rākṣasas'). He alone is able to kill the wicked (9-?-?; etc.). The Brāhmaṇas who have drunk Soma cannot kill with the eye alone (Vai. Saṃ. 4-?-?)."

original p. 635

"As he is a warrior, he too has weapons (9-?-?). Like a hero he is clad in armour (9-?-?; 9-?-?). He holds firmly those weapons in his hands (9-?-?). It is said that he took the weapons from his father, Vaivasvata (6-?-?). He uses an arrow with a thousand points (9-?-?; 9-?-?) and his bow is very swift (9-?-?)."

"The deity Soma and Indra travel in one chariot (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?). Soma is the charioteer of Indra, who fights in the chariot (Ai. Ve. ?-?-?). He travels in one divine chariot (9-?-?). Light (9-?-?) or the filter is his chariot (9-?-?). He is the best of charioteers (9-?-?). Beautiful winged mares (9-?-?) or, like Vāyu, a herd of horses (9-?-?) are his."

"Sometimes he lives together with the Maruts, companions of Indra. They milk Soma, the bull of the sky (9-?-?; compare 9-?-?) and adorn the infant as soon as it is born (9-?-?). Like Indra, the Maruts (6-?-?) or the Marut group (9-?-?) wait on him too. Those winds are a delight to Soma (9-?-?), and Vāyu is the guardian of Soma (10-?-?). With Agni, Pūṣan and Rudra he is counted as a paired deity (2-?-?; 6-?-?; etc.). At times equality of Varuṇa and Soma is stated; how this is so is a matter beyond the senses (compare 9-?-?, 9-?-?, and 9-?-? and ?, 9-?-?)."

"The Soma plant is described as Mūjavata ('growing on Mūjavat mountain') (10-?-?). In the same way, many times it is described as giriṣṭhā ('being on the mountain') or parvatavṛdh ('growing on the mountain') (9-?-?). It is also said of the mountains that they have placed Soma on their back (Av. 3-?-?), and of the stones used for extracting the Soma juice (adrayaḥ, 9-?-?). Such descriptions may have arisen so. In all these contexts the mountains of the earth may be intended (compare 9-?-?). The friends who roam in the knot of the sky milked the bull who lives on the mountain (9-?-?; compare 9-?-?). Varuṇa placed Agni in the waters, Sūrya in the sky and Soma on the rock (5-?-?); or one (Agni) was brought by Mātariśvan from the sky, and another (Soma) was carried off by the eagle from the rock (1-?-?). In these contexts too the mountains of the earth must be what is meant."

original p. 636

"But since the words mountain and rock in the Itihāsas also give the sense of clouds, there is a little room for doubt."

"Though the Soma plant belongs to the earth, it is divine too (10-?-?); in truth, the idea is that its root and its seat are in heaven. That plant was born in the world above and from there came to the earth (9-?-?). Its intoxicating juice is the child of heaven (9-?-?). In one sentence it is said to be born of Sūrya (9-?-?), and in another that Parjanya is the father of that great bird (compare 9-?-?; 9-?-?). In the Atharvaveda it is said that the root of immortality is a seed that came from Parjanya (Av. 8-?-?). In many places the Soma juice is called an infant or a youth; this too must be because it is prepared again and again like Agni. The Soma juice is the pīyūṣa (milk) of heaven (9-?-?; etc.) and is purified in heaven (9-?-?; 9-?-?; etc.). It runs through its streams to the dear places of heaven (9-?-?) and settles in heaven (9-?-?); it is in heaven (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?) or is the lord of heaven (9-?-? and ?). Like a bird of heaven it looks on the earth and observes all creatures (9-?-?). Like Sūrya, it is above all the worlds (9-?-?). Pure Soma drops fall from heaven, from the sky, on the earth (9-?-?); it moves in the atmosphere (4-?-?; 8-?-?). The fingers raise him, clothed in milk (9-?-?). His dwelling is in the very high sky (3-?-?; 4-?-?; 9-?-?) or in the third heaven (Tai. Saṃ. 3-?-?, etc.). Here everywhere the words vyoman, dyauḥ and the like seem to be words that are synonyms of the filter. In the navel of heaven, in the woollen filter, there stands Soma (9-?-?); he runs over the filter in the sky with Sūrya (9-?-?). In some places (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?) it is plain that the filter is intended. All these must refer to the Soma of the earth. It is a settled point that the heavenly Soma, or the abode of nectar, is heaven."

"The Soma juice has been brought from heaven (9-?-?; 9-?-?). The history of Soma and the eagle (śyena) is the basis of this idea. Soma was carried by the eagle (10-?-?). From the lofty heaven that bird brought Soma (4-?-?). The bird brought Soma or honey for Indra (3-?-?; 4-?-?). A swift-going eagle flew off with the Soma plant (5-?-?) and cut for Indra the part of that plant's reed (4-?-?). Holding it in its foot, through the sky, it brought it for Indra (4-?-?). Flying with the speed of thought, the bird split the iron fort and, going to heaven for the sake of the wielder of the vajra, brought the Soma juice"

original p. 637

"(4-?-?). From very far, from heaven, it came carrying the plant itself (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?). This story is described in detail in the sūktas 4-26 and 4-27. In the Brāhmaṇas it is said that Gāyatrī, a special form of Agni, goes off carrying Soma. Indra and the eagle are different; the eagle always brings Soma and gives it to Indra. In a mantra connected with this history Indra himself is called the eagle (10-?-?). At one place Agni is called the eagle of heaven (2-?-?); twice the Maruts are called so. It is specially said of the lightning-Agni that it is the eagle (compare Tai. Brā. 3-?-?; ?-?-?) and Agni is many times called a bird. Some hold that this is a description of the falling of hail: the iron fort is the cloud, the hail that issues from it is the bringing of Soma by the eagle, the description of water is the description of Soma drops, and so on. Some sentences are also cited as the basis for this. It is natural that both Soma and Agni should have come down to the earth (1-?-?). That the eagle that carried Soma was struck with an arrow, and that an archer named Kṛśānu cut off a feather, belongs to the Kavi's description of the colour-divisions. This is told still more at length in the Brāhmaṇas. The feather or the barb fell to the earth and became the parṇa or śalyaka tree. That tree has a very sacred place."

"Because it is the most important plant, the Soma plant is called lord of all plants (9-?-?) and king (9-?-? and ?). It is called the lord of the forest (1-?-?; 1-?-?) and the root of all crops (1-?-?). In the Brāhmaṇas all the plants are named Saumya ('belonging to Soma') (Śat. Brā. ?-?-?-?). Besides, like other principal deities, Soma has the name 'king'. He is the king of the rivers (9-?-?), of the whole universe (9-?-?); of the deities, a king or father (9-?-?; 9-?-?; 9-?-?); of the devamānavas (9-?-?), and of the Brāhmaṇas (Vāj. Saṃ. 9-?; Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?; Vai. Saṃ. 3-?-?). What the deity is is said at many places; only in one place (9-?-? and ?) is he said to be a drink made for the deities (a substance to be pressed)."

"In later literature, 'Soma' is a name of the moon. As the deities drank him, he waned, and the sun fills him up. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5-?-?) the moon is said to be Soma, to be the food of the deities, and that they drink him. In the Brāhmaṇas the identity of the moon and Soma is a commonly accepted matter. In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (2-?) the moon is said to be the Soma of the deities; the king Soma is the food of the deities and he himself is the moon (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?); the plant used in sacrifices, or its juice, indicates the moon deity (Kau. Brā. 2-?; 4-?). The Fathers and deities eat him, who is of the form of nectar, and therefore the moon…"

original p. 638

Soma, end "…the moon wanes day by day: this is the sense of the Brāhmaṇas. In the Yajurveda it is said that the daughters of Prajāpati are the wives of the moon, and that they themselves are the cluster of stars. In the Atharvaveda (Av. 2-?-?; 11-?-? etc.), wherever 'Soma' is said, generally the moon is meant. Among the sentences that state the identity of the moon and Soma, the sūkta 10-85, which describes the marriage of Soma and Sūryā, is the chief. Here it is said that Soma is in the lap of the stars; that no one enjoys the Soma known to the priests; that there is a difference between this Soma and what they must press; and that only Brāhmaṇas know the secret of these two. Soma is described as heavenly, bright, remover of darkness and so on; and besides, it has the name 'indu' (6-?-?). Soma in the vessels is compared to the moon reflected in the water (compare 9-?-?; 1-?-?). The Soma that goes to the ocean, described as a drop (drapsa, a drop, a spark) (10-?-?), may also be the moon."

"In the opinion of some, 'Soma' means the moon alone, and no other deity. The whole ninth maṇḍala praises this very moon. Wherever this word occurs in the Ṛgveda it indicates either the Soma plant or the moon. They argue that the juice that comes from that plant is nectar, that the moon takes shelter in that nectar, that the moon is the chief deity, greater than Sūrya, and that after him comes Indra."

"Others again say that there is no basis, or very little, in the Ṛgveda for this view. However much support there is in later works for the identity of the moon and Soma, though it is hinted indistinctly in one place and another among the hundreds of sentences on the deity Soma in the Ṛgveda, it is not said plainly anywhere. Besides, none of the commentators has said that there is a basis in the Veda for this point."
