Deities in the Form of Abstract Ideas (Bhāvanārūpa devategaḷu)

"There is a usage that ideas that are formless and can be grasped only by the mind are also called deities. Of these there are chiefly two kinds. One kind: the names that indicate mental activities such as desire and hatred. The other kind: the names that indicate actions. The first class is rare. The second is found in large numbers. Such words, indicating qualities or actions, have come again and again and obtained an independent position, separate from the objects they qualify."

1. Deities who bear a function (Kāryabhārī devategaḷu)

"All the words that indicate these deities are generally formed by adding the suffix 'tṛ' to roots indicating the respective actions: Savitṛ, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ and so on. Savitṛ is a very important deity. He has been discussed separately before. The other deities appear in an imperfect way."

original p. 639

Dhātṛ (धातृ, dhātṛ, 'establisher'). "This word is generally used as an epithet in the sense of the priest who establishes the sacrifice. It has been used only some twelve times as the name of a deity. Except once (2-?-?), all the rest are in the tenth maṇḍala. Of these, once (10-?-?) it is used as a name for Indra and once (10-?-?) for Viśvakarman. The action that distributes worldly works among the various deities gradually became a separate deity. Thus Dhātṛ created Sūrya, Candra, heaven, earth and the sky (10-?-?); he is the lord of the whole world (10-?-?). In a sūkta addressed to Sūrya (10-?-?) Dhātṛ is prayed to grant clear vision. Along with Viṣṇu, Tvaṣṭṛ and Prajāpati, he is prayed to for offspring (10-?-?) and independently for long life (10-?-?). Without expecting any return, Viṣṇu is praised together with Savitṛ (10-?-?) or with Mātariśvan and Dhātṛ (10-?-?). In the Nirukta (Nir. 12-?) Dhātṛ is included in the list of the deities of the middle world; and the sense of dhātṛ is given as 'all-controller'. In the Purāṇas Dhātṛ is the cause of creation and preservation of the universe; Dhātṛ, Prajāpati and Brahmā are all one."

Vidhātṛ (विधातृ, vidhātṛ, 'arranger'). "This word, meaning 'one who carries out', is seen used as an epithet of Indra (10-?-?) and Viśvakarman (10-?-?) in two places; but in two other places it occurs as an independent deity together with certain other deities (6-?-?; 8-?-?)."

Dhartṛ (धर्तृ, dhartṛ, 'supporter'). "This word, in the sense 'support, refuge', is mostly used as an epithet of Indra and others. Only once (2-?-?) it is counted as an independent deity together with Dhātṛ and others."

Trātṛ (त्रातृ, trātṛ, 'protector'). "This too, like Dhātṛ, is used as an epithet in the sense 'protector' of Agni, the Ādityas or Indra; and independently in five contexts as a protecting deity [1-?-?; 4-?-? and ?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?]. According to some it is Savitṛ or Bhaga who is meant by this name."

Devanetṛ (देवनेतृ, devanetṛ). "A deity of the name Deva-netṛ is praised, two or three times in one sūkta, as the guide of the one who seeks welfare in life (8-?)."

Tvaṣṭṛ (त्वष्टृ, tvaṣṭṛ). "In this class of deities, apart from Savitṛ, only the name of Tvaṣṭṛ is seen so often. The name occurs about sixty times. It is used chiefly in the seventh [sic: the print's numeral reads 'seven' — ?] maṇḍalas; but there is not even one sūkta addressed to this deity."

original p. 640

"There is very little description of Tvaṣṭṛ's body. Only his arm or hand is mentioned at every step. To hold an iron axe as a weapon is a distinguishing mark of his (8-?-?). He yokes two horses to his chariot and shines (6-?-?). Tvaṣṭṛ has beautiful arms (sugabhastiḥ, 6-?-?) or beautiful hands (supāṇiḥ, 6-?-?). This second epithet is used especially of Savitṛ and Tvaṣṭṛ alone."

"He is a very skilled worker (1-?-?; 3-?-?). He makes many kinds of objects that show his skill. In truth, there is no worker so skilful as he. With great intelligence he prepares various instruments (10-?-?). He who shaped Indra's vajra-weapon is said many times to be Tvaṣṭṛ (3-?-?; etc.). He sharpens Bṛhaspati's iron axe (10-?-?). He prepared a new vessel filled with food (caṣāla?) for the deities (1-?-?; 3-?-?) or for the 'Asura' (1-?-?). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 9-?-? and ?) he is described as an old man holding a vessel full of splendour and a Soma-pressing bowl. The swift horse was made by him (Vāj. Saṃ. 29-?), and the one who grants speed to horses is he (Av. 6-?-?)."

"Tvaṣṭṛ is the one who gives form to all things (10-?-?). He is the one who makes the embryo grow in the womb, and who gives form to human beings and to the whole animal kingdom (1-?-?; 9-?-?; 10-?-?). In the other Vedas too there are sentences of this sense (Av. 2-?-?; etc.). In all contexts this quality is specially said of him (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?; Tai. Brā. 1-?-?). In the Ṛgveda, more than all the other deities, he has the name Viśvarūpa ('one with all kinds of forms'). Because he gives form to the whole animal kingdom, he is said to be the controller in the works of progeny and the like (3-?-?; etc.). He is the one who ties husband and wife together even in the state of embryo (10-?-?; Av. 6-?-?). He is the cause of the creation of life of many kinds and of the growth of the world (3-?-?). All the beasts belong to Tvaṣṭṛ (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?; 3-?-?-?). Since the whole world was made by him, he is the creator of the world (Vāj. Saṃ. 29-?)."

"His daughter, and wife of Vivasvān, is Saraṇyū. She is the mother of Yama and Yamī, the twins of the first creation; hence he too may be said to be the original man of the human race (compare 10-?-?, ? and ?; 5-?-?). Once Vāyu is said to be his son-in-law (8-?-?). Bṛhaspati was born from Tvaṣṭṛ (2-?-?). From the ten fingers (in the fire-sticks)…"

original p. 641

"…the Agni who was born is also one born of Tvaṣṭṛ (1-?-?). Earth, sky, water, the Bhṛgus and Agni — these were created by Tvaṣṭṛ (10-?-?; 10-?-?). It must be guessed that Indra too was a son of Tvaṣṭṛ (3-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?). That Tvaṣṭṛ is the guardian of the Soma juice is a settled point (1-?-?). In his house Indra, stealing the Soma juice and drinking it, killed his father in order to obtain it. This Viśvarūpa, Tvaṣṭṛ's son, had a son who was Viśvarūpa; the cows were stolen under his authority. As in the case of obtaining Soma from Tvaṣṭṛ, so, to obtain the cows, Indra fights with his son Viśvarūpa. Tvaṣṭṛ too was afraid of Indra's anger (1-?-?). Because Tvaṣṭṛ too did not do the deeds Indra performed (10-?-?), he is thought to be lesser than Indra. It is said that, because Indra had killed his son, Tvaṣṭṛ did not let Indra have a share in the Soma sacrifice he performed; then Indra drank the Soma juice by force (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?). In other Brāhmaṇas too the same story is told (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?; etc.)."

"In the works connected with the womb and the embryo, Tvaṣṭṛ has a chief part; so he has friendship with the women of the heaven-world (gnāḥ, janayaḥ); they are his attendants (1-?-?; etc.). He is joined especially with deities such as Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Dhātṛ and Prajāpati. In two contexts 'Savitā' is an epithet of his (3-?-?; 10-?-?); in both of them, his work as creator is relevant. In the Kauṣītaki Sūtra, Tvaṣṭṛ, Savitṛ and Prajāpati are said to be names of one deity, and in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, Tvaṣṭā, Viśvakarman and Prajāpati are said to be one. In the Purāṇas and elsewhere Tvaṣṭā is counted as one of the twelve Ādityas."

"Some other characteristics are also stated of him. None of these makes any definite quality clear. He is the first (1-?-?) or the first born (agraja) and the leader (9-?-?). As a companion of the Aṅgirases, all the worlds of the deities are known to him (10-?-?); he goes to the abode of the deities in the middle of the earth and sky (Vai. Saṃ. 4-?-?; 2-?-?). He grants boons; he has the best wealth (10-?-?; 10-?-?). Satisfied with the praises of his worshippers, he is prayed to bestow wealth and so on (2-?-?). Long life is attained from him (10-?-?; Av. 6-?-?)."

"The word tvaṣṭṛ is derived from the root tvakṣ. This root and the root takṣ may be one and the same in meaning. This root is used when it is said that he sharpened Indra's vajra-weapon. By it, tvaṣṭā means 'maker'."

original p. 642

Tvaṣṭṛ, end "[He is] a most unknown deity among the Vedic deities. His origin, his nature and so on are matters hard to determine. Each scholar has given a different view: Sūrya, the deity of the year, the moon and so on — there is room for various guesses."

Viśvakarman–Prajāpati

"Some more deities in the form of abstract ideas — that is, a usage of calling words that indicate actions 'deities' — are seen. These are not all actions: they belong to one supreme deity. Viśvakarman ('maker of all') is one of such names. It occurs only in one maṇḍala, the tenth, and only five times. Two sūktas praise this deity (10-81; 10-82). This same Viśvakarman is used once as an epithet of Indra (8-?-?) and once of Sūrya, who creates all (10-?-?). In the other Vedas the use as an epithet is general. It is an epithet of Prajāpati too (Vāj. Saṃ. 12-?)."

"In the two sūktas of the Ṛgveda, Viśvakarman is described thus. He is all-seeing; he has eyes on all sides, a face, arms and feet on all sides. By this description Viśvakarman resembles Brahmā, who has four faces and four arms. He has wings too. He is a seer, a purohita and a father. He is Vācaspati; swift as the mind; a benefactor; the root of all kinds of prosperity. All regions and all beings are known to him; he alone knows the names of all the deities. Wise and capable; supreme among superhuman persons; the support of everything and the controller; he it was who created the earth and brought the sky to light. Probably this word, which was at first used chiefly as an epithet of Sūrya, later came to be reckoned as a separate deity. Skill in craft is the distinguishing mark of this deity. In the Brāhmaṇas it is plainly said that Viśvakarman and Prajāpati are one (Śat. Brā. 8-?-?-?; 8-?-?-?; Ai. Brā. 4-?)). In the Purāṇas and elsewhere, Viśvakarman is the craftsman of the deities."

Prajāpati. "'Savitṛ is the support of the sky, and Prajāpati the support of the world' [4-?-?]: so in one place; and in a context that compares the deity Soma with Tvaṣṭṛ and Indra, this word is used as an epithet of Soma. As the name of a separate deity, it has come only four times, and that too in the tenth maṇḍala. 'May Prajāpati grant us progeny' (10-?-?); 'with Viṣṇu, Tvaṣṭṛ and Dhātṛ may he grant offspring' (10-?-?) and 'may he increase the wealth of cattle' (10-?-?) and so on is prayed. That he is the protector of offspring and of beings is said in the Atharvaveda too. In the one sūkta (10-121) that praises this deity, the name of the deity comes only in the last Ṛk; in this sūkta he is the creator of heaven and earth, of the waters, and of all beings, the one master of all that exists (now existing), born in the beginning, who breathes and who is the king of all that moves, the god above all deities. All beings and deities follow his commands. He is the one who established earth and sky. He can move in the atmosphere, and with his arms he embraces the whole world and all creatures. This is the first of such descriptions. Here, Prajāpati must be the Supreme Self (paramātman). In the Ṛgveda this has been used only once in the sense of Supreme Self; but in the Atharvaveda and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitās, in general, and in the Brāhmaṇas, regularly, the Prajāpati intended is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). He is the father of all the deities (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?; Tai. Brā. 2-?-?-?; etc.); he was alone at the beginning (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?-?). He created the Rākṣasas also (Tai. Brā. 2-?-?-?). He was the first to perform a sacrifice (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?-?; 6-?-?-?). In the Sūtras, Brahmā is called Prajāpati (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 3-?; etc.). In the Upaniṣads, Brahmā has become fixed in place of this Supreme Person or Supreme Self."

original p. 643

"In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (Mai. Saṃ. 4-?-?) there is a story: Prajāpati became enamoured of his own daughter Uṣas. She took the form of a doe; he too took the same form. Seeing this, Rudra became angry and raised his arrow to shoot; then Prajāpati said to Rudra, 'I will make you lord of all the wild beasts; do not shoot the arrow' (compare 10-?-?). This story comes up many times in the Brāhmaṇas (Ait. Brā. 3-?; Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?; Paṃ. Brā. 8-?-?). Four Ṛks (1-?-?; 10-?-?, ? and ?) that have the suggestion that a father (perhaps the sky-deity) took up improper relations with his daughter (perhaps the earth) seem to be the basis for this story."

"At the beginning of the sūkta 10-121, in the refrain of the nine mantras, it is said that it is not known 'to whom (kasmai)', that is, to which supreme deity [the offering is to be made]. In the tenth mantra the answer is that Prajāpati alone is all-pervading. On this basis, afterwards the meaning 'Prajāpati' came into use for the word 'ka' (Ait. Brā. 3-?-?). It is not an epithet; it is the very name of that deity (Vai. Saṃ. 3-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?-?) it is said plainly that Kaḥ and Prajāpati are one."

"In the first mantra of the sūkta 10-121, Hiraṇyagarbha ('golden womb') is used for Prajāpati. The use of the word Hiraṇyagarbha in the Ṛgveda is only one. But in the Atharvaveda and the Brāhmaṇas it is common. In one mantra of the Atharvaveda (Av. 4-?-?) it is said that the water created an embryo and that, at birth, this embryo was golden-coloured. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā this too is one name of Prajāpati (Tai. Saṃ. 5-?-?-?). In later literature, Hiraṇyagarbha is one of the names of Brahmā, the creator."

Manyu, Śraddhā and others

"Many more words indicating ideas are counted as deities. Manyu (anger) too has been conceived as a deity. There are two sūktas praising him (10-83, 84). His (Manyu's) power is unobstructed and can be checked by his own strength alone. He blazes like Agni. He is the deity who is called Indra, Varuṇa and Jātavedas. He kills Vṛtra; he is followed by the Maruts; and like Indra he can bestow victory and wealth. Possessed of tapas, he protects his worshippers and kills the haters."

"Only one small sūkta praises Śraddhā ('faith') (10-151). She is praised in the morning, at midday and in the evening. By śraddhā the fire is kindled and the ājya (ghee) homas are carried out. By śraddhā wealth is gained. In the Brāhmaṇas, Śraddhā is a daughter of Sūrya (Śat. Brā. 12-?-?-?) or of Prajāpati (Tai. Brā. 2-?-?-?). In the Purāṇas and Itihāsas many more relations of hers are told."

"Anumati ('favour of the deities') is also stated twice as a deity. She is prayed to be favourable and to give the worshippers the chance to see the sun (10-?-?); her work of protection too is stated (10-?-?). In the Atharvaveda and Vājasaneyi Saṃhitās she is the presiding deity of love and an urger of the work of increasing progeny. Later, a relation between her and the moon is imagined in rites; she is held to be the presiding deity of the day before the full moon. Aramati ('devotion' or 'dharma') too is said in an imperfect way to be a deity. Sūnṛtā ('generosity') is also a deity. There are two or three usages (1-?-?; 10-?-?). Anunīti ('guidance') is prayed to (10-?-?, ?) for long life, strength and nourishment. Nirṛti ('disease, decay') too is, in some twelve places, mentioned as the presiding deity of death."

"Some other words that indicate ideas are said to be deities in the Yajurveda and the other Vedas. Kāma ('desire') has obtained divinity in the Atharvaveda (Av. 9-?; 19-?). Here Kāma is not a deity of mere love or affection, as in later literature; all desired things may be obtained from him. His arrows that pierce hearts are mentioned (Av. 3-?-?). He is the first among those who were born (Av. 9-?-?). All these may have come from the sentence in the Ṛgveda (10-?-?) that 'the first sprout of the mind was Kāma (desire)'. Time too has been given personality in the idea of a universal power (Av. 19-?, ?). Since a power that lifts up and holds the universe created by Prajāpati was needed, a deity called Skambha ('pillar') seems to have been imagined (Av. 10-?-?). Breath (prāṇa) too is a name of Prajāpati…"

original p. 645

"…(Av. 11-?-?; etc.). In the Atharvaveda many more such deities are found. The idea of Śrī as the presiding deity of beauty or wealth is first seen in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?)."

Aditi

Aditi. "There is no complete sūkta praising this goddess; but she is praised in an incidental way in many places, about eighty times. To be praised alone is very rare (8-?-?). Generally she is praised only together with her sons, the Ādityas."

"There is no clear description of her body. She is mostly addressed as 'goddess' (devī); in some places it is said that she is anarvā ('unbroken, not crooked') (3-?-?; 2-?-?). She is much spread out (5-?-?). She is unfathomable, and the breaker of the cow-pens, the great ones (uruvraja) (8-?-?). She is bright and shining, the support of beings (1-?-?; ordinarily this is applied to Mitra and Varuṇa). She belongs to all men (2-?-?, and is said of heaven and earth). She is invoked in the morning, at midday and in the evening (5-?-?)."

"Aditi is the mother of Mitra and Varuṇa (8-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?) and of Aryaman (8-?-?). For this reason she has been called the mother of kings (2-?-?), of excellent sons (3-?-?), of sons rich in strength (8-?-?), of heroic sons (Av. 3-?-?; 11-?-?) or of eight children (10-?-?; Av. 9-?-?). In one place she is called the mother of the Rudras, the daughter of the Vasus and the sister of the Ādityas (8-?-?). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 6-?-?) her brothers and children are all stated. In another (Av. 6-?-?; Vāj. Saṃ. 20-?) she is praised as the mother of Bhakta, the beloved of Ṛta, the able, the undying, the very widely spread, the protector and the skilful leader. Such sentences, and her praise together with her sons the Ādityas, indicate that motherhood is her special mark. Another epithet of hers is pastyā ('housewife') (4-?-?; 8-?-?). This too may indicate her motherhood. In the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, Aditi is the daughter of Dakṣa, the mother of all the deities in general, chiefly of Vivasvān, Sūrya and Viṣṇu in the form of Vāmana. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Vāj. Saṃ. 29-?; Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?) she is said to be the wife of Viṣṇu."

"In many places (1-?-?; 4-?-?) it is said that she delivers from sin (aṃhas) and grants welfare and security to those who are well protected; but more often she is prayed to release from sin. In the matter of Aditi, so that no mistake may be made, and for protection…"

original p. 646

Aditi, continued "…'so that [mistakes] may not be made,' Varuṇa (1-?-?), Agni (4-?-?) and Savitṛ (5-?-?) are prayed to protect. Aditi, Mitra and Varuṇa are prayed to forgive sins (2-?-?); Aditi and Aryaman to loosen the bonds of sin (8-?-?). The worshippers beg Aditi to make them sinless (1-?-?); that they may follow her rules, and that she should favour them so that no mistakes are made in regard to Varuṇa (8-?-?), and that sinners be kept away (10-?-?). Agni (3-?-?), Savitṛ (4-?-?), Sūrya, Uṣas, the earth and the sky (10-?-?) are prayed to forgive faults; but the work of release from sin belongs to Aditi and her son Varuṇa; the noose of Varuṇa is well known; and Varuṇa, pleased, takes the noose off as one removes a rope (5-?-?)."

"The derivation of the word 'Aditi' too suggests the same meaning. The root dā means 'to bind, to tie'. From it the word diti is made, meaning 'bondage'. Therefore aditi means 'release, freedom from bondage'. In this very sense it is said that Śunaḥśepa was bound to the sacrificial post (5-?-?). It is natural that Aditi is prayed to release the worshippers, as one releases a bound thief (8-?-?). The word is also used in the sense 'independence'. In one place (1-?-?) there is: 'Who will give us back Aditi (independence), that I may see my father and mother?' The Ādityas are prayed to make the homa sinless (anāgastva) and independent (aditva) (2-?-?). When she is longed for as one seen by earth and sky, strong and boundless, Aditi must mean just this (1-?-?). The word aditi is also used many times as an epithet in the sense 'boundless'. In this sense it is used twice as an epithet of the sky-deity (5-?-?; 10-?-?) and many times of Agni (1-?-?; 4-?-?; 6-?-?; 8-?-?)."

"Since this name does not give any definite meaning in this way, it gives room for various guesses. Because deity-lineage and the creations of the universe are relevant, Aditi has become the name of various deities. The deities were born of Aditi, water and earth (10-?-?). The boundless sky (dyaur aditiḥ) provided the nectar for all those deities (10-?-?). In other places (2-?-?; Av. 7-?-?) it is said that Aditi and the earth are one; this identity is stated specially in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. In the Nirukta it is said that Aditi indicates the earth, and that the word aditi, in the dual, indicates heaven and earth. But in the Ṛgveda they are thought of as separate; in one single mantra, heaven, earth and Aditi are all spoken of (10-?-?; etc.). In another place Aditi means 'nature' (1-?-?): 'Aditi is the sky, the air, the mother, the father…"

original p. 647

"…and the son; Aditi is all the deities and the five peoples; Aditi is whatever is born or will be born' (Kaśopaniṣat 4-?)."

"As stated in the histories of the Ṛgveda, Aditi is the mother of the Āditya named Dakṣa (2-?-?). But in a sūkta that deals with the creation of the universe (10-?-?, ?), Aditi is the mother of Dakṣa and also his daughter; such a relation is new in the Ṛgveda (compare 10-?-?). In two other places (10-?-?; 10-?-?) the mutual relation of Dakṣa and Aditi is quite peculiar; to say that Aditi is the mother of Dakṣa is not what is mainly seen; she appears to be subordinate to him. Though she is the mother of some principal deities, she is only an ordinary figure. She praises Savitṛ, together with her sons Varuṇa, Mitra and Aryaman (2-?-?), and she composed a hymn for Indra (8-?-?; 5-?-?; compare)."

"Since she is the mother of the Ādityas, who are full of lustre, there is a little connection of lustre. She is prayed to give light (4-?-?; 10-?-?); her undying light is praised (2-?-?), and Uṣas is called her face (1-?-?). In an indefinite way, ordinary prayers are directed to her as to other deities: that the worshippers should be protected in their offspring and their cows, or blessed (8-?-?, ?; 1-?-?). Wealth too is obtainable from her (2-?-?). The favour of Aditi, who is pure, unbroken, divine and undying, is prayed for (1-?-?), and the favour of the Maruts is compared to the benevolent works of Aditi (1-?-?)."

"In some sentences of the Ṛgveda (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?; etc.) and in other Vedas (Vāj. Saṃ. 13-?-?) Aditi is spoken of as a cow, and in sacrifices too the cow is called Aditi. The Soma juice of the earth is compared to the udder of Aditi (9-?-?). In the Soma flowing into the droṇa vessel, subdued by the daughter of Aditi, the milk too must be intended (9-?-?). In the context where the priests purify, with their ten fingers, the Soma that lies in Aditi's lap (9-?-?; 9-?-?), too, the same sense must be meant."

"From the sentences cited above, two qualities of Aditi stand out. The first is motherhood. Among the names derived from her name, such as Āditya and Āditeya, she is the mother of the deities. The second is that which is indicated by the root of the word: the power that rescues from distress and from moral falls. To suggest her boundless prosperity she may be imagined as the cow, the earth, heaven, or the universe. From this, that Aditi…"

original p. 648

"…is the mother of the Ādityas cannot be supported. Some hold that, since it is said 'dyaur aditiḥ' ('Dyaus is Aditi'), that the boundless sky-natured mother gives milk to the deities (10-?-?), the idea of mother for the Ādityas and others has come about. If one takes this view, her power of releasing from bondage is not satisfactorily explained. It may be explained in another way. In the phrase aditeḥ putrāḥ ('sons of Aditi'), often used for the Ādityas, the sense may be 'sons of independence'. Usages such as śavasaḥ sūnum and sahasaḥ putrāḥ support this. As, from śavasaḥ sūnum ('son of strength'), the name of Indra's mother has become fixed as Śavasī, and, from śacīpati, Śacī as Indra's wife, so, from aditeḥ putrāḥ, the idea that Aditi too is a deity has probably come. By the meaning 'independence' of the word aditi, this deity is without bonds. The quality of being a cause of freedom from bonds comes by itself. Through contact with the Ādityas and the rest, lustre and the like are ascribed. Since the main deities are mothers of some or of the deities in general, the descriptions such as 'mother of the world' too, when she is joined with earth, sky, universe or the sky-deity, come naturally."

"In the Nirukta it is said that Aditi is the earth, speech, the cow, and, with the dual ending, (aditī) heaven and earth are equal to them. Yāska describes Aditi as the mother of the deities, and says that she should be placed in the atmosphere, the Ādityas in the heaven-world, and Varuṇa in both places."

Diti

Diti. "This word Diti occurs in the Ṛgveda only three times, and in two of them together with Aditi. Mitra and Varuṇa, seated in their chariot, look at Aditi and Diti (5-?-?). Here Sāyaṇācārya has explained the word aditi as the 'unbroken earth' and diti as the various classes of beings on the earth. Modern scholars like Roth explain these words as 'eternal and non-eternal, or permanent and perishable things'. In the second sentence (4-?-?) Diti's favour and Aditi's protection are prayed from Agni. According to Sāyaṇa, diti here means 'generous giver' and aditi 'a niggardly giver'. Roth takes them as 'poverty and wealth'. In the opinion of Bergaigne, the feminine deities Aditi and Diti are intended. But it may not be so here. It is clear that these words, derived from the root dā ('to give'), give the senses 'one who gives' and 'one who does not give'. This sense appears appropriate to the context and to the order in which the words are used from both viewpoints. In the third sentence (2-?-?) the word diti…"

original p. 649

"[is used] only together with Agni, Savitṛ and Bhaga, in the sense 'giver of desirable things'. In other Saṃhitās too, diti is used with aditi (Vāj. Saṃ. 13-?; Av. 13-?-?; 11-?-?). In the Atharvaveda her sons too are mentioned (Av. 2-?-?); they are the Daityas. Later they become enemies of the deities. As the word sura (deity) was formed from asura (Rākṣasa), Diti was conceived as a deity in opposition to Aditi; there does not seem to be a deity called Diti existing independently."

Female Deities (Strī devategaḷu)

"In the Vedic religion and rites the place of the female deities is very minor: in the management of the world they have, one may say, no hand. The chief among the female deities is the goddess Uṣas. Taking the number of sūktas, she is of the third rank. But as with the male deities, Soma has no share for the goddess Uṣas. After Uṣas the chief female deity is Sarasvatī; but she seems to be of a lower rank. Again, some are praised each in one sūkta: there is hardly any way of separating Pṛthivī from the sky-deity; there are only three mantras in the sūkta that praises her. The deity Night is also praised in one sūkta (10-127). She is the sister of the goddess Uṣas, and she too is a daughter of the sky (dyauḥ). By 'Night' is not meant a dark night; she is a night adorned with stars, and full of lustre. With her many eyes she shines in many forms. Adorned with all kinds of lights, she makes the darkness fly with her radiance, and covers mountain, valley, everything. As she comes near, all men, like birds going to their nests, return to their houses. She is prayed to drive away thieves, wolves and so on in the time of night, and to bring men to a safe place. She is often praised as a paired deity with Uṣas. Deity-hood may be ascribed to every night by the dawn."

"Taking speech (bhāṣā) as a person, a sūkta (10-125) praises Vāk ('Speech'). In this sūkta the goddess describes herself. She follows all the deities and is the support of Mitra-Varuṇa, Indra, Agni and the Aśvins. For the one without faith she turns Rudra's bow. She pervades the water, the ocean, all living beings. In another place (8-100-10, 11) she is called the queen of the deities and the goddess (devīṃ vācam). In the Nirukta (Nir. 11-?) Vāk is one of the deities of the atmosphere, the thunder; or, as the commentators of the Nirukta say, the middle Vāk (the sound of the middle world, Nir. 11-?) may have been the beginning of the personification. A story is told about Vāk in the Brāhmaṇas too: when Soma was being brought from the neighbourhood of the Gandharvas, they bought Vāk, one…"

original p. 650

Female deities, continued "…one of them, changing [her] into a woman, gave her as the price of the Soma juice (Ait. Brā. 1-?). Purandhi ('the fruitful, abundant'), who occurs about nine times in the Ṛgveda, is the presiding deity of prosperity. Generally she is used together with Bhaga; two or three times only with Pūṣan and Savitṛ, and once with Viṣṇu and with Agni. Another deity indicating the same prosperity, Dhiṣaṇā, is found some twelve times. Iḷā is another. It has occurred not less than twelve times. The homa of milk and butter has become the presiding deity of the increase of cows. In the Brāhmaṇas, though Iḍā is not a name of the cow, it is used at every step with cows. In the Nirukta iḍā and iḷā are among the names of the cow (Nir. 2-?-?). It must be in the form of homa that she is described as ghee-handed (ghṛtahastā, 2-?-?) and ghee-footed (ghṛtapadī, 10-?-?). This Iḷā, in deity-form, is generally found in the Āprī-sūktas; there too in a group (a triad of deities) with Sarasvatī and Mahī or Bhāratī. In the phrase 'iḷāyāḥ pade' it is doubtful whether the ordinary meaning or the deity is meant. Once Agni is called the son of Iḷā (3-?-?, ?). Purūravas too is her son (10-?-?). Once she is called the mother of the herd and related to Urvaśī (5-?-?). In relation to the morning pressing she is mentioned together with Dadhikrāvan and the Aśvins (2-?-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa she is called the daughter of Manu (1-?-?-?; 11-?-?-?) and of Mitra-Varuṇa (1-?-?-?; 14-?-?-?; Āś. Śrau. Sū. 1-?-?)."

"The name of a deity called Bṛhaddivā has come four times in the sūktas of the Viśve-devas. She is called Mātā ('mother') in one place (10-?-?). She is mentioned twice together with Iḷā (3-?-?; 5-?-?) and once with Sarasvatī and Rākā (5-?-?). Rākā (perhaps formed from the root rā, 'to give'), a deity full of prosperity and abundance, is praised in two places along with other deities (2-?-?; 5-?-?). The name Sinīvālī has occurred in two sūktas (2-?; 10-?). She is the sister of the deities; one with beautiful arms and fingers; prosperous; mistress of the household; she is prayed to grant offspring. She is praised with Sarasvatī, Rākā and Gungū (the word Gungū is used only once). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 8-?-?) Sinīvālī is the wife of Viṣṇu. In other Vedas and Brāhmaṇas, Kuhū is the presiding deity of the new-moon day; in other Vedas, Rākā is the presiding deity of the day of the full moon, and Sinīvālī of the day before the new moon. There is no basis for this in the Ṛgveda."

"As the occasion has come, some other female deities have been mentioned before. Pṛśni, the mother of the Maruts (1-?-?), must be the cloud of various colours. This word…"

original p. 651

"…is used with the sense 'spotted'; in the singular for both the bull and the cow, and, in the plural, as an epithet of the cows that are milked for Indra's Soma juice (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?). Thus pṛśni means a variegated cow, a cloud. Saraṇyū, wife of Vivasvān and daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, is mentioned once (10-?-?). This Saraṇyū may be Sūryā or Uṣas. The meaning of this word is 'swift, going quickly'. It is seen used in this sense four times. It must be a word formed by adding the suffix yu to saraṇa ('speed'; from the root sṛ, 'to run')."

"Although these female deities are wives of the great deities, they do not hold so very important a place. The great deities such as Indra must have had wives; hence these names occur. Nothing else is said of them. These names too are generally not new: from words like Indra with the suffix āṇī added, words such as Indrāṇī, Varuṇānī, Āgnāyī have been used. The word Rudrāṇī is found only in the Sūtras; but Rudrāṇī and the others, Indrāṇī etc., are not prominent in the Śrauta rites. The wife of the Aśvins is Aśvinī. The wives of the deities (devānāṃ patnīḥ), who are used in an imperfect way in the Ṛgveda, have a distinct place in the Brāhmaṇas and so on (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?)."

Paired Deities (Devatā dvandvagaḷu)

"A peculiarity of Vedic history is the praising of many deities in pairs. In these pairs both words have case-endings and accents. About twelve pairs of deities are praised in this way in about sixty sūktas. Among these it is mostly Indra who is joined with other deities. In seven pairs or more, Indra shows himself. But the greatest number of sūktas — twenty-three sūktas and some portions of sūktas — is for the pair of Mitra and Varuṇa. Eleven for Indra and Agni, nine for Indra and Varuṇa, seven for Indra and Vāyu, six for Heaven and Earth; two each for Indra and Soma and for Indra and Bṛhaspati; one each for Indra and Viṣṇu, Indra and Pūṣan, Soma and Pūṣan, Soma and Rudra, and Agni and Soma. Besides these, along with the deities mentioned above, some more pairs, joined with eight or nine other deities, are praised in whole mantras. Indrā-Nāsatyā, Indrā-Parvatā, Indrā-Marutaḥ, Agnī-Parjanyā, Parjanyā-Vātā (once Vātā-Parjanyā), Uṣāsānaktā, Naktoṣāsā, Sūryāmāsā, Sūryācandramasā and so on."

"It must have begun with Dyāvāpṛthivī, where the use of such paired words in the Vedas is more prevalent. In nature there are no objects more firmly bound together than heaven and earth…"

original p. 652

"…and in this way both came to be thought of as a married pair (dampatī). In the Ṛgveda, among the six sūktas addressed to Heaven and Earth, not one praises the sky-deity alone. Only one small sūkta of three Ṛks praises the earth (alone); even there the sky-deity is referred to (5-?-?). The names of these deities, rather than appearing singly, occur more often as a pair. Counting also the imperfect usages dyāvākṣāmā, dyāvābhūmī, there are about a hundred usages. There is no other pair stated so many times. Heaven and earth also have the name Rodasī (said to mean 'sisters', 1-?-?). It occurs about a hundred times. Earth and sky are the Fathers; for them there are epithets such as pitarā, mātarā, janitrī; and singly there is the address 'father and mother' (1-?-?, ?; 1-?-?). They are the original parents of the universe (2-?-?; 10-?-?). The Aitareya Brāhmaṇa speaks of their marriage (Ai. Brā. 4-?-?, ?). They created all beings; they are the cause of their existence (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?). Though themselves without feet, they make many creatures stand on their feet (1-?-?). They are also the parents of the deities; they alone have the name devaputre ('having the deities as children'). In particular, they are the father and mother of Bṛhaspati (2-?-?); and the waters, together with Vṛtra and Tvaṣṭṛ, generated Agni (10-?-?). It is also said that they were created by some other deities. One who created earth and sky must have been a most skilful workman (1-?-?; 4-?-?). Indra created them or gave them form (6-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?). Viśvakarman fashioned them (10-?-?; compare Av. 13-?-?). They obtained their bodies from Tvaṣṭṛ (10-?-?). They were born in order from the head and feet of the Virāṭ-Puruṣa (10-?-?). How were these two born? Which of the two was born first? — this is asked at one place (1-?-?). In the epithets of Heaven and Earth many come from their physical features. One is a great bull, and the other a cow of various colours (1-?-?). Both bear abundant seed (1-?-?; 6-?-?). Both milk milk, ghee and honey abundantly (6-?-?, ?) and produce immortality (1-?-?; 1-?-?). They never grow old (6-?-?). They are wide (1-?-?) and spread out (1-?-?). They have spacious, great dwelling-places (1-?-?). They have pleasing faces, spreading widely, of many forms (1-?-?, ?). Sometimes moral qualities are also stated: the wise ones, they encourage righteousness (1-?-?). These parents protect living beings (1-?-?), and see that they do not suffer disgrace and misfortune (1-?-?). They grant food and wealth (6-?-?; 1-?-?; or 1-?-?) or fame and authority (1-?-?). They are the leaders in the sacrifice; sitting round the sacrificial seat (4-?-?, ?), they come to the sacrifices together with the other creatures of heaven (2-?-?) or take the shares of the sacrifice to the deities and join them (3-?-?). But in sacrifices they do not hold a chief position like the other deities. These two deities have an equal place and equal honour."

original p. 653

"In other pairs of deities, one deity has more prominence. The many qualities of that deity are found also in the other deity. For example, Indra and Agni are both wielders of the vajra-weapon, and slayers of Vṛtra. In general, the qualities of the less prominent deity are stated also of the principal deity. Indra and Viṣṇu both took wide steps (6-?-?). Since it is said so at every step, the quality which is not found naturally in the deity too becomes proper for that deity. Thus it is said that Agni killed Vṛtra. In some sentences the qualities of each are stated separately."

"Except for Heaven and Earth, the principal paired deities are Mitra and Varuṇa. The number of sūktas praising this pair exceeds the number of sūktas addressed to each of them separately. Mitra's personal qualities are very few, or one may say there are none. Hence the special characteristics of Varuṇa have been said of the pair Mitrāvaruṇa. Once the subject of the deity Varuṇa has been dealt with at length, it is unnecessary to speak of this pair. Both are young (3-?-?; 6-?-?). Like many other deities, they flow (are candra), are pure (śuci) and are like Sūrya. They are of ruddy colour, and terrible. Observing that the first word in this pair is always Mitra, it may be that Mitra was the chief deity and has now, for some other reason, become secondary; or it may have been the custom to put the shorter word at the beginning of a compound."

"Indra and Varuṇa are rulers of the world (1-?-?); they broke open channels for water to flow and made the sun move in the atmosphere (6-?-?). They are the killers of Vṛtra (6-?-?); they help in battle (4-?-?); and grant victory (1-?-?). In times of difficulty they use their fierce vajra-weapon (4-?-?). They show mercy to those who are protected, increased, famed, wealthy and who have countless horses (4-?-?, ?; 6-?-?). They drink the Soma that has been pressed. Their chariot comes to the sacrifice; they are prayed to be satisfied by sitting on the kuśa seat and drinking Soma (6-?-?, ?). In some more sentences, the personal qualities of the two are stated separately. Varuṇa is prayed not to be angry with the worshipper, and Indra to give them a spacious place (2-?-?). Indra is the deity who loves war, who kills the Asura Vṛtra; Varuṇa, in contrast, gives men knowledge and peace (6-?-?; 7-?-?, ?; 7-?-?). The relation of Indra and Agni is very close…"

original p. 654

Paired deities, continued "…[The relation of Indra and Agni is very close]. There are as many sūktas praising the pair Indra–Agni as there are praising Indra and any other deity. Moreover, it is rare that Agni, apart from Indra, is counted as a pair with some other deity: one sūkta and two mantras praise Agni and Soma, and one mantra Agni and Parjanya. Indra and Agni are the foremost of all who drink Soma (1-?-?); in order to drink Soma they come in their chariot (1-?-?). Both together are to come and drink (2-?-?; 8-?-?, ?, ?); they are invited to sit on the seat of kuśa grass and drink the pressed Soma as they wish and become intoxicated (1-?-?). It is said that they kill Vṛtra together. They are wielders of the vajra-weapon (6-?-?; etc.); their grip is very sharp (5-?-?). Joining together they destroyed ninety-nine forts (3-?-?) and none can face them in battle (5-?-?). They freed the imprisoned rivers (8-?-?) and together have done many more deeds of valour (1-?-?). They are generous (5-?-?). All of this is a peculiarity of Indra. Both Indra and Agni choose sacrificial priests (8-?-?) and wise ones (8-?-?). It is they who drive away Piśācas and the householders of the house (1-?-?). That these qualities suit Agni is the very point of the sūkta. The two are children of one father and are twins (6-?-?). It must be because of this close kinship that they have been called Aśvins once (1-?-?). They grant food, wealth, strength, cows and everything (8-?-?, ?), earth and sky, rivers and mountains, and what is greater than all (1-?-?). A difference between the two is stated in one place; but there it is not said with regard to the pair-deity: 'Indra killed the Dasyus and Agni burns them' (6-?-?). Indra and Bṛhaspati are praised in only two sūktas (4-?; 6-?); there, chiefly, the invitation to drink Soma, and the favour of wealth including horses and the like, and the increase of devotion, are the subjects. In the case of Indra and Vāyu, nothing is said except the invitation to drink Soma (1-?-?, ?; etc.); they come with their horses (4-?-?, ?, ?) or in a chariot with a golden seat (4-?-?), and sit on the kuśa seat in the sacrificial hall (2-?-?). They are lords of a thousand eyes, of understanding (1-?-?) and of strength (4-?-?). They help in battle (2-?-?) and bestow wealth in the form of cows, horses and gold (2-?-?). Indra and Soma perform daring deeds with Indra's special characteristics, or the deeds of the creation of the world performed by Indra. They make water flow for men's use; they set free the seven rivers; they killed the serpent and cast the wheel of Sūrya downward (4-?-?, ?; 6-?-?). Their great service is to destroy enemies, to split rocks, and to bring out things (4-?-?, ?). They found Sūrya and the lights…"

original p. 655

"…[They] removed darkness, made Sūrya shine, held up the sky like a pillar and spread out the earth; these are the great deeds they did at the beginning of creation (6-?-?, ?). They are also the ones who made ripe milk in the cows (6-?-?), and they grant to men the powers and abilities that give victory (6-?-?). Indra and Viṣṇu are the ones to whom the Soma juice is a refuge; they are called 'intoxication-wedded' (i.e. subject to the intoxication produced by Soma). They are invited to come with their horses, drink Soma and fill their bellies. Having drunk Soma and become intoxicated, they set out, spread out the sphere of the air, and widened the regions of the earth for people to live in. These two, always victorious, grant lordship and protect from sin. They are the root of all praise; they are prayed to take pleasure in the praise-songs of the worshippers (6-?). Indra and Pūṣan are praised only in one small sūkta (6-?), and this pair Indrāpūṣaṇau occurs only twice. When Indra caused the water to flow, Pūṣan was his companion. Accompanied by Pūṣan, Indra kills Vṛtra (6-?-?). One of them drinks Soma, the horses draw his chariot, and he kills Vṛtra; the other has she-goats to draw his chariot, and what he drinks is gruel. The dwelling-place of Indra and Pūṣan is spoken of in one place (1-?-?); a she-goat goes there, taking the sacrificial horse. Welfare, lordship and the rest are asked of both."

"Soma and Pūṣan (2-?) drive away enemies and make the chariot with seven wheels and five rims go swiftly, and are prayed to measure the sky by it. They are the ones who created wealth and the sky and earth, and the protectors of the world (compare 10-?-?); the deities made them eternal or placed them in the state of immortality. Indra is prayed to produce the best milk in the cows for their sake. Both, being alone, give victory over enemies and boundless wealth and food. There is a difference between the two. One lives in the very high sphere of the air, the other on the earth or in the atmosphere. One created all beings; the other moves, looking at all beings. Soma and Rudra are praised in the sūkta 6-?. They are to drive disease out of the houses. They are prayed that all the herbs may be in the bodies of the worshippers always, that they may be sinless, and that they be released from the noose of Varuṇa. They are also begged to be merciful, being armed with sharp weapons. Agni and Soma are praised as those who set free the obstructed streams, who brought light and who stirred masses of lustre in the sky. But in the matter of the source of these two…"

original p. 656

"…there is a difference. One is said to have been brought from heaven (1-?). It is prayed that both together help and grant cows, horses, offspring, health, happiness and lordship (10-?-?; 10-?-?). This pair occurs many times in the Atharvaveda. In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (Mai. Saṃ. 3-?-?) the two have two eyes. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?) these two are brothers; Sūrya belongs to Agni and the Moon to Soma (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?); in sacrifices Agni does not get Soma's share of Soma, and they offer only the puroḍāśa cake and animals to him. The pair Agnīṣomau comes up at every step in sacrifices. But in the Veda the praise of them is one sūkta only (1-?). Apart from that, twice only is the name of the pair found in the whole Ṛgveda. It is surprising that so important a pair of deities has so insignificant a place."

"Some more pairs of deities are praised here and there in a mantra. Agni and Parjanya are praised in one mantra (6-?-?). Both are desired for food and offspring; but it is said that one produces the homa (Iḷā) and the other the embryo (garbha). There are four mantras on Parjanya and Vāta. They, as bulls on the earth (6-?-?), are prayed to bring out the cows (waters). Together with Indra, Vāyu and other deities they are called the balls filled with water (10-?-?). In another list of deities, they grant immeasurable food (6-?-?). In one place (10-?-?; compare Nir. 2-?) they are said to belong to the roaring buffalo (probably the sky-deity). Uṣas and the nights are praised many times. In the sūktas addressed to the Viśve-devas, the pair Uṣāsā-naktā is praised specially. They are female deities rich in wealth (3-?-?; 10-?-?); maidens of the deity-world (2-?-?; 10-?-?) and daughters of the sky (3-?-?; 10-?-?). Both are wives (1-?-?) and, wishing freely, give milk (2-?-?); changing their colours, the two nourish a single child with their breast and make it grow. That child shines between earth and sky (1-?-?). The two are sisters. Though their mind is one, only the colour is different. The two have one path of movement, and it has no end. Being taught by the deities, they move one after the other; they do not collide, and yet they do not stand still (1-?-?). They are the mothers of Ṛta (truth, rule, sacrifice) (1-?-?). They cause each of the works of sacrifice to shine by their rays (3-?-?) and bring the works of sacrifice to completion with all their limbs (2-?-?). Generous, great, seated on the kuśa seat (2-?-?), great, handsome and well adorned…"

original p. 657

"…(10-?-?; 10-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?). After one has gone, the other shines and makes all beings wakeful (3-?-?). Sūrya and the moon are mentioned five times as Sūryāmāsā and three times as Sūryācandramasā. In many contexts the masses of light that we see are intended. They move, one after another, for our sight (10-?-?). The sun and the moon move one after the other by the command of Bṛhaspati (10-?-?). The creator made the forms of the sun and the moon (10-?-?). 'As the sun and the moon do, so may we walk in our appointed ways' is said in one place (5-?-?). When praised together with other deities, they seem to be thought of as deities (10-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?). In some sentences the pair of sun and moon is not clearly named, but it appears to be spoken of. The two, like children, revolve round the sacrificial hall; one looks at all beings, and the other, fixing the seasons, is born again and again (10-?-?). The two beautiful eyes of Varuṇa (8-?-?) and the two eyes of the sky made by the immortals (1-?-?): in both these contexts the sun and moon must be meant."

Groups of Deities (Devatāgaṇagaḷu)

"Some groups of deities connected with some principal deity are customary. The chief of these is the Marut group. The number of deities in this group, as in the Ṛgveda itself, is from twenty-one to one hundred and eighty (8-?-?; 1-?-?), and, as said before, they are always helpers of Indra in his bold deeds. For this group, sometimes, they are called Rudras, after the name of their father Rudra (2-?-?; 2-?-?). In the Brāhmaṇas, the Rudras are a separate group. In this group there are eleven (Ait. Brā. and Śat. Brā.) or thirty-three (Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?-?) deities. The Ādityas are a smaller group than this. Of these there are seven or eight (9-?-?; 10-?-?); but in the Brāhmaṇas the number of deities in this same group is twelve. In the Ṛgveda they are always together with their mother Aditi (2-?-?) or with Varuṇa, their leader (2-?-?). Of all, even more than the Maruts, this group of the Ādityas is more clearly distinct. In the Āditya group each deity has a separate name. There is another group, mentioned many times in the Ṛgveda: the Vasus. At present this is less clear than the Marut and Āditya groups. In one sentence, as the Ādityas are praised with Aditi or Varuṇa, and the Rudras with Rudra, the Vasus are praised with Indra (2-?-?; 2-?-?). From this it may be said that Indra is the leader of the Vasus. But in other Vedas and Brāhmaṇas,…"

original p. 658

Groups of deities, continued "…Agni is the leader of the Vasu group. In the Aitareya and Śatapatha Brāhmaṇas their number is eight; but in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Tai. Saṃ. 4-?-?-?) they are 333 persons. The three groups, Ādityas, Rudras and Vasus, are in some places praised together (2-?-?; 10-?-?; compare 2-?-?; 3-?-?). A difference among these three groups is imagined in the Brāhmaṇas: the Vasus are on earth, the Rudras in the sphere of the air, and the Ādityas in the heaven-world (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?; 4-?-?-?). In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (3-?, from 6 to 10) five groups are stated: the Vasus are joined with Agni, the Rudras with Indra, the Ādityas with Varuṇa, the Maruts with Soma, and the Sādhyas with Brahmā (compare 10-?-?, ?). There is a group of the Aṅgirases, counted as slightly more or less than deities, and connected with Bṛhaspati. There is a group of three persons, the Ṛbhus, who are generally always together with Indra. Last of all there is the group called the Viśve-devāḥ ('all the deities'). It has a very prominent place in sacrifices. Fifty sūktas are devoted to their praise. Probably this group was formed with the intention that, when all the deities are invoked, none should be left out. But sometimes, when the Vasus, Ādityas and so on are praised along with them, it seems that the Viśve-devas are not all the deities."

Lower Deities — the Ṛbhus (Adhama devategaḷu — Ṛbhugaḷu)

"In the Ṛgveda, besides the superior deities already discussed, there are some imaginary persons who have not obtained a natural and complete deity-hood. Among them the most important are the Ṛbhus. There are eleven sūktas praising them, and their name occurs more than a hundred times. They are a group of three deities. Their individual names are Ṛbhu or sometimes Ṛbhukṣan (leader of the Ṛbhus), Vāja and Vibhvan. At many places all three names are said together; sometimes Ṛbhu alone is said, or in the plural Ṛbhavaḥ. Whichever of the three names is used in the plural, it is understood as the triad of deities. Sometimes the plural forms of three words, or the plural forms of two words, are used unnecessarily (4-?-?; 4-?-?). In one place (4-?-?) there is the usage 'vājo vibhvā ṛbhavaḥ'. In some places the Viśve-devas appear to be indicated by these words ('all the Ṛbhus' (2-?-?), 'Ṛbhu accompanied by the Ṛbhus, Vibhvan accompanied by the Vibhus' (2-?-?); they are invoked). Among the Ṛbhus, the elder, the younger and the middle-aged have also made their differences clear, in accordance with age (4-?-?)."

"The sons of Sudhanvan, that is, 'the good archer', are said to be called Saudhanvanas; twelve passages call the Ṛbhus so. All three together are called sons of Indra (4-?-?). In the same mantra they are also called 'children of strength'…"

original p. 659

"[(śavaso napātaḥ)]. This epithet, apart from once for Mitra and Varuṇa, is used for them in all the other places (five times). In (3-?-?) they are called sons of Manu. Their fathers too are stated in many places. In one sūkta Agni is called their brother (1-?-?, ?)."

"They have been invoked again and again to come to the sacrificial hall and drink Soma (4-?-?; 4-?-?; 2-?-?; 4-?-?, ?; 4-?-?). Since their dwellings are in the upper world, an invitation is made to them to come to this lower world, where the Soma juice is (4-?-?). In this context they are generally with Indra (3-?-? to ?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?); sometimes with the Maruts (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 4-?-?), once with the Ādityas, Savitṛ, the mountains and the rivers (4-?-?). In other matters too they have very great nearness to Indra. They are like Indra (4-?-?), and Ṛbhu is like a new Indra (1-?-?). Joined with Indra, they become helpers of men in the work of conquering enemies (4-?-?) and are prayed to help Indra in conquering enemies (2-?-?). The Ṛbhus were the first to create the forms of Indra's horses; by this skill they gained Indra's friendship (3-?-?; 4-?-?, ?). In the sūktas that praise them, they are not praised with any deity other than Indra; only in one mantra (4-?-?) the name of Indra is not mentioned. How close the relation between Indra and them is, is shown by the fact that the word ṛbhukṣā ('leader of the Ṛbhus') is applied to Indra too; and the same word is used two or three times of the Maruts. In the sūktas addressed to the Viśve-devas they are joined with some other deities (mainly with Tvaṣṭṛ)."

"The description of the body of the Ṛbhus or their weapons and such materials is very small. In form they are like Sūrya (1-?-?). They have a chariot drawn by horses (1-?-?). Their chariot flows, and their horses are strong; they bear iron helmets and charming necklaces (4-?-?). Ṛbhu too is one with horses (like the Aśvins, 4-?-?). The extraordinary skill and the dexterity of the Ṛbhus (4-?-?, ?, etc.) cannot be imitated (3-?-?). It is said again and again that they obtained deity-hood by their skill. By their wondrous deeds they obtained deity-hood (3-?-?). By their skilful works they obtained deity-hood and immortality, and like eagles dwelt in heaven (4-?-?). The men of the sphere of the air, by their own power, climbed to heaven (1-?-?). By their intelligent works, by the path of immortality, they joined the deities (4-?-?), and, immortal like them, gained their friendship (4-?-?, ?,"

original p. 660

"4-?-?, 4-?-?). They were mortals at first, the sons of Manu, and afterwards, desiring deity-hood, obtained it (3-?-?; 1-?-?). In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (Ai. Brā. 3-?-?) it is said that the Ṛbhus, who had been men, by the greatness of their penance attained the right to drink Soma like the deities. By their work the deities were greatly pleased; hence Vāja became a craftsman for the deities, Ṛbhukṣan for Indra, and Vibhvan for Varuṇa (4-?-?). Coming near to the deities and showing their skill, they obtained the sacrifice, or a share in the sacrifice, through it (1-?-?, ?; 1-?-?, ?). For that reason the third or evening pressing belongs to them. They obtained it by their skilful work (1-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?). Hence they are sometimes invoked plainly as deities (4-?-?, ?; 4-?-?)."

"As one prays to the great deities, they too are prayed to grant prosperity and lordship (4-?-?; 4-?-?), cows, horses and heroic sons (4-?-?), and strength, nourishment, offspring and skill (1-?-?). The Ṛbhus show favour to the one who prepares Soma (1-?-?; 4-?-?). He who has obtained their help becomes unconquerable in battle (4-?-?). Ṛbhu and Vāja are prayed to be helpers in battle and to gain victory (1-?-?)."

"In describing the skilful works done by them, the root takṣ, generally used of Tvaṣṭṛ, is used. What they have achieved is five great deeds. In general, in every sūkta praising the Ṛbhus there is a reference to these works. They built a chariot without horses, without reins, with three wheels, which could travel in the space in between (4-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?; 4-?-?; 4-?-?). The Ṛbhus built a chariot of circular shape for the Aśvinī deities (the Aśvins) (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 10-?-?). In the mantra 4-?-?, each of their works is stated in one word each. Here it is said that they made the Aśvins. This too may be applied to the building of the chariot of those deities."

"For the sake of Indra they created two tawny horses (haris); these horses carry him swiftly in the air (4-?-?; etc.). Though it is said that they wished to create a horse, or that they created two horses one after another, what is meant is the work stated above (1-?-?, ?)."

"A cow that gives immortality (1-?-?), is a stimulant, and has all forms (4-?-?), was created by them (1-?-?; 4-?-?). The Ṛbhus made this cow out of a skin (1-?-?) or brought it out of a skin (1-?-?; etc.). They themselves…"

original p. 661

"…protected it and made its flesh grow (4-?-?). Indra yoked to the chariot the two tawny horses created by the Ṛbhus; the Aśvins built the chariot, and Bṛhaspati brought out the cow of all forms (1-?-?). From this sentence it can be said that the cow was made by the Ṛbhus for Bṛhaspati. Another ordinary work is also said; it probably relates to the earlier creation of cows; that is, they reunited a mother and her calf, who had become separated (1-?-?; 1-?-?)."

"They made their father and mother, who had become very weak, like worm-eaten posts, youthful again (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 4-?-?). They made the two aged ones (father and mother) young again (1-?-?, ?). In 4-?-?, summarizing the works they achieved, it is said that they gave a form to their parents. Here too rejuvenation must be what is intended. That they gave youth to their aged parents, and made them move about again, is praised by all the deities (4-?-?). In the first mantra of the same sūkta (4-?) it is said that making Heaven and Earth grow shows that they possess divine power (probably this is the work of rejuvenation of the parents)."

"The greatest praise is of their skill itself, and that is their best quality. In this part, they made from one wondrous bowl made by Tvaṣṭṛ four equal bowls (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 4-?-?, ?; 4-?-?). This bowl is a means by which the deities (1-?-?; 4-?-?) or the 'Asura' (1-?-?) drink. If the deities, with Agni's help, make this one bowl into four for the Ṛbhus, said the deities, 'we too shall give you worship' (1-?-?, ?). Tvaṣṭṛ praised this effort of the Ṛbhus to turn one bowl into two, three or four, and when four bowls were made, he accepted them (4-?-?, ?). In another sentence it is contradicted (1-?-?). As soon as he saw the four bowls, Tvaṣṭṛ hid himself among the wives and wished to kill the Ṛbhus, who had defiled the bowls from which the deities drink; but in the preceding mantra the Ṛbhus themselves say that they did not wish to defile it. In order to gain fame among the deities, the Ṛbhus ruled the wide bowls as one rules the earth (1-?-?) — thus is the description. It is said that they made the bowls or gave them forms (1-?-?; 3-?-?; 4-?-?)."

"They established the prayer-sentences (10-?-?) and the sacrifice (3-?-?). When it is said that they created the two worlds (4-?-?) or became supports of the sky (10-?-?), their skill is again suggested."

original p. 662

Ṛbhus, end "Another story connects them with Savitṛ. Tired out by the wind, they moved swiftly round the sky (4-?-?; compare 1-?-?). After a long journey they arrived at the house of Savitṛ named Agohya. Then Savitṛ granted them immortality (1-?-?, ?). Afterwards, accepting his hospitality and being satisfied, they slept there for twelve days; then they made the best fields; they made water flow there; fields grew crops in barren land, and water flowed into all the low places (4-?-?). While asleep, by their own power, they made grass grow in all the high places and water stand in the low places (1-?-?). Waking from sleep they asked Agohya (Savitṛ): 'Who woke us?' and looked round for a year (1-?-?)."

"The word Ṛbhu seems to be derived from the root rabh ('to grasp'; compare 3-?-?); for this reason the sense 'one suited to the time', 'skilful', is given to it. This word ṛbhu is used many times in this very sense as an epithet of Indra, Agni and the Ādityas. Vāja means 'able', and Vibhvan 'one of famous name'. Therefore the words Ṛbhu and the rest are meaningful names which also indicate their skill."

"It is clear that these were not deities at first. But what their nature was before they became deities is not clear. Even when called Saudhanvana, it is not known who they are. Sudhanvan is used only twice in the Ṛgveda, applied to Rudra and the Maruts. As said in many places, Heaven and Earth may have been their parents. Since they were in the house of Savitṛ and were capable of rejuvenation, they may have had the power of making the earth fruitful. Many scholars hold that these three are the deities of the three seasons, that their sleeping for twelve days corresponds to the twelve days during which the seasons stand still at the time of the Makara Saṅkrānti; that the bowl is the moon, and that its being made four is the four phases of the moon. In short, they may be said to be persons of the earth or of the sphere of the air, and their skill may be said to have given rise to the stories of many bold deeds about them — but if one takes the Ṛgveda alone as the basis, no definite opinion is possible."

Apsaras Women (Apsara strīyaru)

"There is no great basis in the Ṛgveda concerning the Apsarases. This name occurs only five times. There is no basis for any part of nature in them. In the very high region of the sky, an Apsaras (the Gandharva mentioned in the previous mantra) smiles gently at her beloved…"

original p. 663

"…(10-?-?). From this very Apsaras, Vasiṣṭha was born (7-?-?); the Vasiṣṭhas sit near the Apsaras women (7-?-?). The Apsarases of the ocean flow towards the Soma juice (9-?-?). Here, the waters that are mixed with the Soma juice must be called Apsarases. A scholar with a beautiful lock of hair can move in the path of the Apsaras women and Gandharvas (10-?-?). The water-deity (apyā yoṣā), the wife of the Gandharva who is in the water, must also be an Apsaras (10-?-?)."

"The matter of these Apsarases is understood more fully in the Atharvaveda. Their dwelling is in the water; coming up for a moment, they go away again (Av. 4-?-?); they are prayed to depart from the neighbourhood of men to the bank of a river or a pond (Av. 4-?-?). It is said that they are connected with the female deities who accompany the Gandharva named Viśvāvasu, and with clouds, lightning and stars (Av. 2-?-?). It is plainly said that the Apsarases are the wives of Gandharvas (Av. 2-?-?); this relation of Gandharvas and Apsarases is stated in the other Saṃhitās as well, in the Sūtras (Vāj. Saṃ. 30-?; Av. 8-?-?; etc.). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?) it is said that the Apsarases took the form of a kind of bird that lives in the water (compare 9-?-?). In the Purāṇas, the Apsaras women come step by step to the neighbourhood of rivers and lakes; the coming to the river Gaṅgā is very common; and it is said that they live in Varuṇa's palace. Even by the formation of the word, it means 'those who move in water'."

"From the above points it is clear that the Apsarases are female companions of the Gandharvas, water-deities in the world of the deities. But in other Vedas, the earth, and in it the trees, are their playgrounds. They live in the Nyagrodha and Aśvattha trees, and the sound of their lute and cymbals is heard from those trees (Av. 4-?-?). In other places (Tai. Saṃ. 3-?-?-?) trees such as Nyagrodha, Aśvattha, Udumbara and Plakṣa are the dwelling-places of Gandharvas and Apsarases. The Gandharvas and Apsarases that live in those trees are prayed to be favourable to the marriage-processions that pass there (Av. 14-?-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?) it is said that the Apsarases are absorbed in dance, song and instrumental music. In the Purāṇas it is said that these two groups live on real and historical mountains. According to the Atharvaveda, the Apsarases are fond of gambling, and give gamblers good luck (Av. 2-?-?; etc.). But they also bring disaster: it is feared that they cause derangement of the mind. To avoid this, a spell and vidyā are used (Av. 2-?-?; etc.)"

original p. 664

"…they are women of unequalled beauty (compare Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?). The love of Apsaras women was not confined to Gandharvas: sometimes men too have been given happiness (compare 10-?-?). The story of such love between a man and an Apsaras woman is told in the Veda. Only the names of some other Apsaras women are mentioned. In the Atharvaveda and in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Vāj. Saṃ. 15-?-? to ?), three persons — Ugrajit, Ugraṃpaśyā and Rāṣṭrabhṛt — Urvaśī, Menakā and others are mentioned. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Śakuntalā (Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?) and Urvaśī (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?) are plainly indicated."

"In the Ṛgveda it is only Urvaśī who is introduced. In one mantra it is said that Vasiṣṭha was born of Urvaśī, and in the mantra before it that he was born of an Apsaras; from this it may be guessed that Urvaśī is that Apsaras (7-?-?, ?). In one place (5-?-?) Urvaśī is also praised along with the rivers. Apart from these two places, in the tenth maṇḍala this name occurs in only one sūkta. Here there is a conversation between her and Purūravas, the son of Iḷā (10-?-?, ?). There she appears in the form of water. She covers the whole of the sphere of the air and moves in the sky (this too is related to a Gandharva, in 10-?-?). She is said to have lived four years among men (10-?-?) and is asked to return. This request is rejected. But Purūravas is consoled that if his children offer oblations to the deities he will be happy in heaven (10-?-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?) a complete story is composed taking some mantras of this Ṛgveda sūkta. The story there is as follows. Urvaśī chooses as husband Purūravas, the son of Iḷā, on a condition: he must not appear naked before her. When night comes, the Gandharvas make a strange sound. Purūravas, who is sleeping, gets up from the bed naked. At the same time lightning flashes. By its light Urvaśī sees him and, as agreed, vanishes. Purūravas wanders searching for her. At last, in a lotus lake, he sees Urvaśī playing in bird-form with other Apsarases. Urvaśī shows herself to him in her real form. After he has begged much, she promises to be with him for only one night after a year. At the appointed time Purūravas comes to that place. On the third day the Gandharvas, by performing a peculiar fire-kindling, grant that he become one of them. Apart from this sūkta 10-?, this word Purūravas occurs in another place (1-?-?). For Purūravas, who walks the good path, Agni makes a refuge in the sky. In this context Purūravas may be an epithet. Some scholars consider Purūravas and Urvaśī to be the sun and the dawn."

Gandharvas (Gandharvaru)

original p. 665

"As said before, in connection with the Apsarases, Gandharva or Gandharvas denote a person or a class of persons. Among the twenty-odd places where it occurs in the Ṛgveda, it is in the plural three times. In the Atharvaveda, of the thirty-two, it is in the plural quite often. Looking at this, it seems that at first there was one, and then, step by step, they grew in number. In the other Vedas, like the deities, the Fathers and the Asuras, the Gandharvas too are one group (Av. 11-?-?; Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?). In the Yajurveda their number is 27, and in the Atharvaveda about 6333 (Av. 11-?-?). There is no basis in the Ṛgveda for determining their characteristics and nature from the beginning. In this context, the most important point is in which maṇḍalas these words occur: in two or seven maṇḍalas it is only once each; in the eighth, twice, it is said as opposed to Indra. Or it may be that this word was thought to be an epithet. Sometimes it is used together with the word Viśvāvasu (9-?-?; 10-?-?, ?; Av. 2-?-?; Vāj. Saṃ. 2-?). In one context Viśvāvasu is used to indicate the Gandharva (10-?-?, ?; compare 10-?-?, ?). In other Saṃhitās, Brāhmaṇas and Purāṇas, Viśvāvasu is the name of a Gandharva."

"According to the Ṛgveda, the Gandharva dwells in the very high region of the sphere of the air, or of the sky. He rules the sky (10-?-?). He is in the unfathomable regions of the atmosphere (8-?-?), a deity by nature, standing erect in the atmosphere (10-?-?). It is on him that the Apsaras smiles gently (10-?-?). His dwelling is in heaven too (Av. 2-?-?). The virtuous dwell with the Gandharvas (Av. 4-?-?). In some sentences it is said that the Gandharva has some connection with the light of heaven. He is the messenger of Varuṇa, with golden wings, is joined with Sūrya (10-?-?), with the bird Sūrya (10-?-?), with the horse of Sūrya (1-?-?) and with Soma, who is like Sūrya (9-?-?). Besides this, a relation to the twenty-seven stars in the path of the moon (Vāj. Saṃ. 18-?), especially to the Rohiṇī star (Av. 13-?-?), is imagined. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Vāj. Saṃ. 18-?) the Gandharva is counted as a deity along with Agni, Sūrya, the moon and Vāyu. In the Purāṇas, 'the city of the Gandharva' (gandharvanagara) is a name for the mirage."

"The name of the Gandharva is mentioned especially with Soma in the ninth maṇḍala. He protects the place of Soma and the lineage of the deities (9-?-?; compare 1-?-?). He stands in the sky, watching all the states of the Soma juice (9-?-?). With Parjanya and the daughter of Sūrya the Gandharvas increase the Soma juice (9-?-?). It is from the mouth of the Gandharva that the deities drink Soma (Av. 2-?-?). For the deities…"

original p. 666

Gandharvas, continued "…[For the deities] it is said that the Gandharvas were guarding the Soma juice, and gave an opportunity for it to be stolen, and that, as a punishment for this, Soma-drinking was forbidden to the Gandharvas (Mai. Saṃ. 3-?-?). It is also said that the Gandharvas became acquainted with crops through this Soma juice (Av. 4-?-?). The Gandharva who was appointed to guard Soma, removing Indra's displeasure, is described as being driven by him in the sphere of the air (8-?-?). And on the same account it is also said that the hymns praise Indra, in order to defeat him (8-?-?). In another place (Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?-?) it is stated that, to escape from the Gandharva Viśvāvasu, Soma should come in the form of an eagle. It is said that the Soma juice was stolen by the Gandharva Viśvāvasu; that, giving Vāgdevatā (the goddess of speech) as the price to the Gandharvas who were lovers of women, Soma was obtained from the Gandharvas (Ai. Brā. 1-?; Tai. Saṃ. 6-?-?-?; Mai. Saṃ. 3-?-?). Kṛśānu, who shoots an arrow at the eagle carrying Soma away, must also be a Gandharva. In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (Tai. Ā. 1-?-?) Kṛśānu is plainly said to be a Gandharva."

"There is a relation between the Gandharvas and water. The Gandharva who is in the water, and the Apsaras women who are of water-form, are said to be the progenitors of Yama and Yamī (10-?-?). The Soma juice that is purified in the water is called 'the Gandharva of the water' (9-?-?). The Gandharvas who are joined with the Apsarases live in the water (Av. 2-?-?; 4-?-?)."

"The union of the Gandharvas and Apsarases is a sign of marriage. Therefore a relation of Gandharvas with marriage and its ceremonies is imagined. An unmarried maiden belongs to the Gandharva, Soma and Agni (10-?-?). In the first days of marriage Viśvāvasu is the rival of the bridegroom (10-?-?). The love of Gandharvas for women is well known in the other Vedas (Mai. Saṃ. 3-?-?). Those who desire offspring praise the Gandharvas and Apsarases, the deities who preside over fertility (Paṃ. Brā. 19-?-?)."

"There is no basis anywhere in the Ṛgveda for the Gandharvas' having become famous in the Purāṇas as the singers of the deities (compare 10-?-?; 10-?-?)."

"With regard to their body and so on, only one or two places have a statement. The wind itself is their hair (3-?-?) and they have weapons that flow (10-?-?). In this matter the Atharvaveda is clearer (especially Av. 4-?-?; 8-?-?). There it is said that they are hairy, that they have bodies like half-animals, and that they cause calamity to men in many ways. Elsewhere they are described as beautiful (Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?). In the Ṛgveda the Gandharvas wear garments of fine smell (10-?-?); and in the Atharvaveda it is said that fragrance from the earth joins the Gandharvas (Av. 12-?-?)."

"From this it may be said that the word Gandharva has come from gandha ('smell'). Even if this derivation is right, nothing is known of the nature or characteristics of the Gandharva. From the descriptions found above, the Gandharva too is a brilliant divine person. Along with his companion, the Apsaras…"

original p. 667

"…it may be said at most that he is a dweller in the water. Various scholars have expressed various views: that they are bodiless persons joined with the wind; that they are the rainbow; that the moon, Soma, the rising sun, or the deity presiding over clouds, and so on."

Protective Deities (Rakṣaka devategaḷu)

Vāstoṣpati. "The name Vāstoṣpati has occurred seven times in the Ṛgveda. In one sūkta of three Ṛks (7-54) this deity is praised. Here entry into a favourable house, removal of disease, auspicious blessings on men and animals, the prosperity of cows, horses and the like, and constant protection are prayed for. In the sūkta that follows (7-55-1) Vāstoṣpati is described as one who drives away disease and as one of all forms. In one place (7-54-2) the name Indu is used for Vāstoṣpati. In a sūkta of the Viśve-devas, together with Tvaṣṭṛ, or as if Tvaṣṭṛ, who is the carpenter of the deities, and this one are the same, he is praised (4-?-?). In another (10-?-?) it is said that Vāstoṣpati is Indra himself, like a firm pillar. In the tenth maṇḍala (10-?-?) it is said that he is the guardian of rules, and that Brahmā and the deities gave him form. As said above, though Vāstoṣpati is equated with many deities in many places, no deity can be said with certainty to be called by this name, as Agni is called gṛhapati. In the Gṛhyasūtras (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?; Sāṃ. Gṛ. Sū. 3-?; Pā. Gṛ. Sū. 3-?-?) it is ordained that Vāstoṣpati be satisfied at the time of entering a new house. If this rule of the Sūtras and the matters in the sūkta addressed to this deity are studied, it may be said that this deity is a presiding deity of the house or a protecting deity. Like the deities presiding over trees or mountains, this deity may also be a single person."

Kṣetrasya pati. "The deity Kṣetrasya pati ('lord of the field') too belongs to the class of Vāstoṣpati. This deity is the protector of the land. In the first three mantras of the sūkta 4-57, sweetness and the like of cows, horses, heaven and earth, trees and water are expected from him. In a sūkta of the Viśve-devas (2-?-?) he is prayed to be prosperity-giving along with Savitṛ, the goddesses of dawn and Parjanya. In 10-?-? the worshippers hope that they may be in his grace. It is said that this deity should be worshipped, or homa should be made to this deity, when beginning to till the land (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?; Sāṃ. Gṛ. Sū. 4-?-?). In a sūkta praising deities of agriculture (4-57-6) a good crop is prayed for from the deity Sītā ('furrow'). In the Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra (Pā. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?) this very Sītā is said to be the wife of Indra, and that Sāvitrī is her name on the basis of her father's name (Tai. Brā. 2-?-?). In the same Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra a deity called Urvarā ('tilled land, fit for agriculture') is mentioned."

(Imaginary) Historical Seers and Persons of Divine Descent (Kālpanika — aitihāsika ṛtvijaru mattu devāṃśapuruṣaru)

original p. 668

Manu. "As the word Manu, manus or manuṣya is used also in the general sense of 'human beings, mankind', it is difficult to know when they mean human beings and when they mean Manu. In the second sense, Manu in the singular is used about thirty times, and in the plural about eight times. Manu is called father five times, and in two of them, still more clearly, 'our father' (3-?-?; etc.). Those who perform sacrifices have the name 'Manu's people' (viśaḥ, 4-?-?; etc.). Agni dwells in the lineage of Manu (1-?-?). Manu is the one who began the sacrifices. Having kindled Agni, he gave the first offering to the deities together with the seven seers (10-?-?). It is the very sacrifice practised by Manu that all now practise. The present sacrifice is compared to the sacrifice that Manu made for the deities (1-?-?). By the adverb manuṣvat ('like Manu'), sacrificial rites are compared at every step. Like Manus, the worshippers complete the sacrifice by Agni (1-?-?). Like Manus, they kindle Agni (5-?-? etc.). Agni, kindled by Manu, they praise as Manu did (2-?-?). Like Manus they offer Soma-juice (4-?-?). As was done before for Manu, they pray to Soma to flow for them (9-?-?). Manu established Agni so that it might be the light for all the people (1-?-?). The ancient sacrificers, the Aṅgirases and Yayātis (1-?-?), together with Bhṛgu and the Aṅgirases (8-?-?), with Atharvan and Dadhyañc (1-?-?), and with Dadhyañc, the Aṅgirases, Atri and Kaṇva (1-?-?), Manu too is joined (1-?-?). The deities, Mātariśvan (1-?-?), Mātariśvan and the deities (1-?-?) or Kāvya Uśanā (8-?-?) gave Agni to Manu or appointed him as the sacrificing priest of Manu. In four contexts, Manu must mean 'man'."

"Indra drank Soma in the company of Manu, son of Vivasvat (Vāl. 4-?), or Manu Sāṃvaraṇi (Vāl. 3-?). To gain the strength needed to fight Vṛtra, Indra drank the Soma juice belonging to Manus, to the extent of three lakes (5-?-?). A bird brought Soma-juice to Manu (4-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Manu is described as the nourisher of righteous acts."

"Manu is thought of as the son of Vivasvān; he has the name Vaivasvata Manu (Vāl. 4-?; 2-?; compare). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 8-?-?), the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā."

original p. 669

"13-?-?-?) and the Purāṇas, the name Vaivasvata has become fixed for Manu. Among the children of Vivasvān, Yama is also one; and he is the first among them. That is, Manu and Yama are the progenitors of mankind. But as Manu is the first among the living, Yama was the first of the dead, and became the king of the world of the dead. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is said that Vaivasvata Manu is the king of men, and Yama the king of the dead (Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?, ?). In the Nirukta (Nir. 12-?) Manu is interpreted as the son of the Āditya named Vivasvān and of Savarṇā (here perhaps Saraṇyū stands in its place) (compare 10-?-?), and he is pointed out as one of the deities of the heaven-world (Nir. 7-?; 12-?)."

"A story is told in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa that at the time of the Flood, when all other beings were drowned, Manu alone was saved by a fish (an incarnation of Viṣṇu) in a boat (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-? to ?). Manu then became the cause of the human race through his daughter Iḍā (Iḷā), who was born of oblations. This story of the Flood is relevant in the Atharvaveda too (Av. 19-?-?)."

The Bhṛgus (Bhṛgugaḷu)

"Bhṛgu occurs twenty-one times in the Ṛgveda. Besides this, Bhṛguvat has been used twice. Bhṛgu in the singular has occurred only once.
