Therefore the Bhṛgus may be said to denote one group of mythical persons. The sūktas addressed to Agni alone mention them about twelve times; and generally in contexts describing how men obtained Agni. Mātariśvan gave Agni to Bhṛgu in the form of a treasure (1-?-?), or kindled for the Bhṛgus the Agni who had been hidden (3-?-?). Mātariśvan and the deities made Agni; the Bhṛgus, using their power and strength, produced Agni (10-?-?). The Bhṛgus saw Agni hidden in the water (10-?-?), and there, worshipping him, they (the sacrificer) established him in the houses of men (2-?-?; compare 2-?-?). They made Agni stand well in the forest (6-?-?) or placed him among men like a treasure (1-?-?). Agni was a thing given by the Bhṛgus (3-?-?). They churned him well and praised him with words of praise (1-?-?). They satisfied him with songs in the form of praise and made him shine well (10-?-?), and afterwards made him as if in forests (4-?-?). They called him to the navel of the earth (1-?-?). Atharvan laid down rites distinguished by homa and the like; the Bhṛgus displayed divine characteristics by their skill (10-?-?). Though their skill was seen already in the production of Agni, it too is thought of as an art…"

original p. 670

The Bhṛgus, continued "…[it too is thought of as] an art. As the Bhṛgus built a chariot, the worshippers compose a hymn of praise to Indra or to the Aśvins (4-?-?; 10-?-?)."

"The Bhṛgus must be very ancient. Among the sacrificers, together with the Aṅgirases and Atharvans, they also, including the Bhṛgus, call themselves their Fathers, who love Soma-juice (10-?-?); and, like the Bhṛgus, the Aṅgirases and Manu, they praise Agni (8-?-?). They beg Indra to favour their prayer as he favoured the prayer of the Yatis and the Bhṛgus (8-?-?), or to help them as he helped the Yatis, the Bhṛgus and Prasanvara (8-?-?). With Druhyus and Turvaśa too the Bhṛgus are said to be enemies of Sudās (7-?-?). In these three sentences (7-?-?; 8-?-?; 7-?-?) the Bhṛgus appear to indicate a small tribe. Thirty-three deities, the Aśvins, the Maruts, the deity of the watery Abhūṇi (?), the Aśvins, Uṣas and Sūrya: with these, the Bhṛgus too are invited to drink Soma (8-?-?). They are likened to Sūrya and are said to be of all-fulfilling desires. In (8-?-?; 9-?-?) the worshippers pray, 'as the Bhṛgus drove away the Rākṣasa, let [us] drive away the niggardly'. Who the Rākṣasas that the Bhṛgus drove away are, and what story this relates to, is not known."

"Like the seers connected with the Ṛgveda, such as Vasiṣṭha, the Bhṛgus are not people belonging to the group of seers now in use. As the Aṅgirases have Aṅgiras and the Vasiṣṭhas have Vasiṣṭha as leaders, Bhṛgu too must have been the leader of a group of seers named Bhṛgu."

"That Agni came down from heaven and was given to man is a matter connected with Mātariśvan and the Bhṛgus. If Mātariśvan is the one who brings Agni from heaven, the work of bringing it to the beginning and practice of rites such as sacrifices on earth belongs to the Bhṛgus."

"In other Vedas Bhṛgu is the representative of a gotra (Av. 5-?-?; Ai. Brā. 3-?-?). Born of the seed of Prajāpati, he is accepted by Varuṇa as his son; hence he gets the name Vāruṇi (Ai. Brā. 3-?-?; Paṃ. Brā. 18-?-?); it is also plainly said that he is the son of Varuṇa (10-?-?)."

"The word Bhṛgu is derived from the root bhrāj ('to shine'). Some hold that Bhṛgu is a name of Agni, and others that this name refers to the form of Agni's spark."

original p. 671

Atharvan

"Atharvan occurs fourteen times, three of them in the plural. In the Atharvaveda too it appears many times. Generally Atharvan is an ancient priest or seer. He churned Agni (6-?-?), and as Atharvan churned Agni, the priests churn Agni (6-?-?). The Agni produced by Atharvan became the messenger of Vivasvān (10-?-?). It was Atharvan who first brought the sacrifice (ṛta) into practice by means of oblations (10-?-?). By means of oblations Atharvan spread out the paths (of Sūrya); afterwards Sūrya was born (1-?-?). Together with Manu and Dadhyañc, Atharvan brought dharma (faith) into practice (1-?-?). Indra is a helper to Atharvan, Trita, Dadhyañc and Mātariśvan (10-?-?). There is a prayer that Agni, who destroys wicked Piśācas, should burn them with his divine flames as Atharvan burns the ignorant (10-?-?). Still more characteristics of Atharvan are stated in the Atharvaveda. Atharvan brought a vessel of Soma juice for Indra (Av. 18-?-?). A wonderful cow was given to him by Varuṇa (Av. 5-?-?; 2-?-?). Atharvan is a companion of the deities, their kinsman and a dweller in heaven (Av. 4-?-?; etc.). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa Atharvan is an ancient teacher (Śat. Brā. 14-?-?-?; 14-?-?-?)."

"In the plural, the Atharvans, the Aṅgirases, the Navagvas and the Bhṛgus are all counted as Fathers (10-?-?). They dwell in heaven and have the name of deities (Av. 11-?-?). By the power of a wonderful root they destroy Piśācas (Av. 4-?-?)."

"In some sentences of the Ṛgveda, Atharvan appears to mean generally a priest or purohita. In 10-?-?, the word Atharvan is an epithet of Bṛhaddiva, who composes praise-sentences. The seer pours oblation on Atharvan (8-?-?): here it appears that the word Atharvan is used for Agni. The Atharvans make the Soma juice sweet (9-?-?), or the Atharvans obtain a hundred cows from a giver (6-?-?); in these contexts it is used in the sense of priests. Agni has the name Atharyu (athar-yu), 'one distinguished by flame'; from this word athar ('flame') a group of priests called Atharvan (priests) may have become established."

Dadhyañc

"The name of Dadhyañc, son of Atharvan, occurs nine times (6-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?). Except once, all the rest are in the first, ninth and tenth maṇḍalas only."

original p. 672

"He is a seer who kindled Agni (6-?-?), and is counted among Atharvan, the Aṅgirases, Manu and other ancient seers (1-?-?; 1-?-?)."

"The Aśvins gave a horse's head to Dadhyañc, the son of Atharvan; afterwards he taught them the Madhu-vidyā (1-?-?). Dadhyañc, who had a horse's head, told the Aśvins where honey was (1-?-?). The Aśvins covered Dadhyañc's heart; afterwards the horse's head spoke to them (1-?-?). Indra too is related to this story. Searching for the horse's head hidden in the mountains, and finding it in Śaryaṇāvat, he killed Vṛtra with the bones of Dadhyañc (1-?-?, ?). Besides rescuing for Trita the cows that were in the hands of the serpent, he gave the cow-pens to Dadhyañc and Mātariśvan (10-?-?). The cow-pens that Dadhyañc opened by the power of Soma juice must be these. Apart from these eight places, the name Dadhyañc occurs in one place only, in the sixth maṇḍala (6-?-?); there Dadhyañc is the son of Atharvan: like his father he too is engaged in the work of bringing fire from the lower fire-stick. Beyond this, in general, the secret place of Soma, and the freeing of cows by Indra — his relation to these is greater. As his name speaks of a horse's head, it can be said that he has a relation to the horse called Dadhikrā. If the derivation of the word is taken (dadhi + añc), the sense could be 'one facing the curds', that is, one who has respect for curds. Some think that Dadhyañc and Soma are both one. But the grounds for reaching this conclusion are not enough. Dadhyañc must be the fire in the form of lightning; the speed is to be understood from the horse's head, the sound as the neighing, and the lightning from the bones. If one looks at its relation with the Soma juice, its relation to Soma and the eagle is suggested; by the name, the lightning-fire's flash when the fierce wind blows is suggested. In the Purāṇas it takes another form, as Dadhīca; and it is said that Indra made the vajra-weapon from his bones and killed Vṛtra."

The Aṅgirases (Aṅgirasaru)

"In all, it occurs about 60 times, thirty-odd of them in the plural. There are thirty-odd forms derived from this word. The sūkta 10-62 praises this group entirely."

"The Aṅgirases are sons of the sky (3-?-?; 10-?-?; 4-?-?). They are the seers who were sons of the deities (10-?-?). Among them one Aṅgiras is imagined as the first man and the rest as his sons (10-?-?). In the mantras they are called Fathers (10-?-?), our Fathers (10-?-?) or our ancient Fathers (10-?-?). The Atharvans and the Bhṛgus along with them, the Aṅgirases are counted as Fathers (10-?-?); especially Yama…"

original p. 673

"and the Aṅgirases are counted as Fathers (10-?-? to ?). In places equality with groups of deities is also stated. With the Ādityas, Vasus and Maruts (2-?-?; 8-?-?), and in some contexts with the Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus and Atharvan (Av. 11-?-?), and in some places they have been offered Soma juice (8-?-?) and praised like deities (3-?-?; 10-?-?). They are those who hold the place of Brahmā in sacrifices (2-?-?). They found Agni hidden in the forests (3-?-?) and thought out the first rule connected with the sacrifice (10-?-?). By sacrifice they gained immortality and Indra's friendship (10-?-?)."

"There is a very close relation between Indra and them. It is to them that Indra showed the cows (8-?-?). It was for them that he opened the doors of the cow-pens (1-?-?; 1-?-?); rolling Vala away, he drove the cows out (8-?-?); accompanied by them Indra dug out Vala (2-?-?) and drove the cows out (6-?-?). In the idea that they are his helpers, Indra is called 'the most Aṅgiras' in two places (1-?-?; 1-?-?). In 8-?-? it is said that the Soma that gives enthusiasm to Indra opens the doors of the cow-pens for the Aṅgirases. In the matter of releasing the cows, the singing of the Aṅgirases is peculiar. Praised by them, Indra dug out Vala (2-?-?), split the doors of the cow-pens (4-?-?), killed Vala and opened the doors of his fort (6-?-?); or, driving away the gloom, he spread out the earth and set the lower regions of the sky (1-?-?). The singing of the Maruts, who sing in diverse ways, is compared to the singing of the Aṅgirases (10-?-?), and from the statement that they call the deities to the sacrifice by their songs (1-?-?) one can guess the distinction of their singing. Also the sentences of praise uttered by ordinary priests are compared to the praise of the Aṅgirases (1-?-?, ?; etc.). In the history of cows, as it comes up, the part of the Aṅgirases appears greater than that of Indra. Taking Indra along, the Aṅgirases made the cow-pens and horse-pens (10-?-?). Later the Aṅgirases themselves did this work, in which Indra has no share at all; this may be called the first step. By the power of the rites they performed, they drove out the cows, rolled Vala away and killed him (10-?-?), made the sun rise in the sky and spread out the earth (10-?-?). By the power of the sacrifices they performed, they broke the rock and rejoiced with the cows (4-?-?). Singing, they found the cows (1-?-?). By their songs they broke the rock and found light (1-?-?). In the story where Saramā went in search of the cows seized by the Asura named Paṇi, the Aṅgirases also have a part (10-?-?, ?); in Saramā's finding the cows, Indra and the Aṅgi-…"

original p. 674

Aṅgirases, end "…[Indra and the Aṅgi-]rases helped Saramā (1-?-?; compare 1-?-?). It is also said that the Aṅgirases themselves discovered the cows and horses belonging to the Paṇi (1-?-?). Bṛhaspati too has a part in the work of freeing the cows belonging to the Paṇis (10-?-?, ?, ?); when, breaking the mountain, he took the cows, he too has the epithet Aṅgiras (6-?-?), and when he grants cows as Bhaga would grant (10-?-?), the same epithet."

"When, joined with Indra, he drove out the cows and made the water flow, Bṛhaspati is called Aṅgiras himself (2-?-?). Leaving aside this one context, all the other singular usages are of Agni. Agni is the first seer, Aṅgiras (1-?-?), the ancient Aṅgiras (10-?-?), or the most ancient among the Aṅgirases (1-?-?), and the one of greatest brilliance (6-?-?). Agni is many times called the leader of the Aṅgirases (1-?-?; etc.). But the word Aṅgirastama ('the most Aṅgiras', i.e. the foremost of the Aṅgirases) is used, once or twice, also of Indra, Uṣas and Soma. Sometimes the word is used of persons such as Agni without any relation: of the ancient Aṅgirases among the Fathers, one (1-?-?), or in the usage 'Aṅgirasvat' (1-?-?) the singular sense, according to the context, is evident; but the usage itself has no connection. In 'O Agni, O Aṅgiras, as you were prayed to by Manu and the Aṅgirases, come near us, granting our prayer' (1-?-?), both Agni and the Fathers are intended by that word."

"In the Anukramaṇī, the Aṅgirases belong to a lineage of purohitas; they are the seers of the mantras of the ninth maṇḍala. In 'Atharva-Aṅgirasaḥ' too they are intended. The Atharvaveda itself has the name Atharvāṅgirasa (Av. 10-?-?). The same idea is in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?; etc.)."

"This group were slightly superior to men; they moved between the deities and men, or they may be called the messengers of Agni, the messenger of the deities. They may be said to be the flames of Agni embodied."

Virūpas

"The name Virūpa, connected with the Aṅgirases, has occurred three times in the plural. The Aṅgirases and the Virūpas are sons of the sky-deity (divas putrāḥ, 3-?-?). The Virūpas are seers, sons of Aṅgiras, born of Agni, of the sky (10-?-?, ?). 'One who praises Agni' is Virūpa in the singular in one place (8-?-?). In 1-?-? it is used in the singular sense, like medhāvat, atrivat, aṅgirasvat, as virūpavat ('like Virūpa'). In 10-?-? the Aṅgirases, the Vairūpas (sons of Virūpa) and Yama are praised together. The meaning of Virūpa is 'one with changing forms';"

original p. 675

"generally this word is used together with the word Aṅgirasaḥ; therefore it may be considered an epithet of Aṅgiras or of the Aṅgirases."

Navagvas

"Including six occurrences along with the Aṅgirases, this word occurs fourteen times in all. They are our ancient Fathers (6-?-?); or the Aṅgirases, Atharvans, Bhṛgus and Navagvas are our Fathers (10-?-?). In the matter of Indra, Saramā and the cows connected with the Paṇis, and in the history of these cows, the Navagvas too are included (1-?-?, ?; 5-?-?; 10-?-?). Making the Navagvas his friends, Indra found the cows (2-?-?). Preparing the Soma juice, they praise Indra with songs and break the doors of the cow-pens (5-?-?). With the stones that purify Soma they sang for ten months (5-?-?, ?). In the plural, it occurs twice; in one of them it is an epithet of the rays of Agni (6-?-?). In the singular it occurs thrice, as an epithet of Aṅgiras (4-?-?; 10-?-?) or of Dadhyañc (9-?-?). The meaning of that word is 'going in a group of nine'. Probably it may indicate nine ancient seers."

Daśagvas

"It occurs seven times — three times in the singular, twice only separately in the plural of seven — generally together with the Navagvas. They were the first to perform sacrifice (3-?-?). Indra found the cows, accompanied by the Navagvas, and saw Sūrya in the company of the Daśagvas (3-?-?). Joined with the Navagvas and Daśagvas, Indra split the mountain and Vala (1-?-?). The Navagvas and Daśagvas praised Indra and broke open the cow-pens (5-?-?). Uṣas shone upon the Navagva Aṅgiras and the Daśagva of seven mouths (4-?-?). The Daśagva accompanied by the Navagva is called 'the most Aṅgiras' (10-?-?). It is said that Indra helped the Daśagva when he was in trouble (8-?-?). Though the Navagvas and Daśagvas differ in number, they may be said to be of one kind."

The Seven Seers (Saptarṣigaḷu)

"This class of seers, famous as the Saptarṣis, appears in the Ṛgveda in only four places: our Fathers, seven seers (4-?-?); those of divine nature (10-?-?); those connected with the deities (10-?-?). This number may be suggested by the seven priests mentioned in 3-?-?; those seven would be the Saptarṣis. In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa each of these seven has a name (Śat. Brā. 14-?-?-?; Bṛhadā. Upa. 2-?-?). In the same Brāhmaṇa (3-?-?; Ṛk. Ve. 8-?-?) it is said that those seven persons were at first called bears (ṛkṣa), and that they are the seven stars of the Saptarṣi-maṇḍala. The word ṛkṣa has two meanings, 'star' (1-?-?) and 'bear' (5-?-?), and in both contexts the number is the same; so this idea may have arisen."

original p. 676

"…[In the Brāhmaṇa it is said that] they were formerly bears. The seven vipras and the Navagvas praised Indra (6-?-?; compare 3-?-?; 4-?-?): there the seven vipras must be the Saptarṣis. 'The seven hotṛs, together with Manu, gave the first oblation to the deities' (10-?-?): here too the same idea must be meant."

Atri

"One of the ancient seers who is most often mentioned in the Ṛgveda. In the singular it occurs sixty times, and in the plural thrice, in the sense of those of the Atri gotra. The seer belonging to the five peoples (1-?-?); one of the original men of the human group such as Manu (1-?-?)."

"Agni helped Atri (5-?-?) and other ancient seers (1-?-?; 10-?-?). Indra too, hearing Atri's prayer, together with the Aṅgirases, opened the cow-pen for Atri (1-?-?). But Atri is mainly presented as dependent on the Aśvins, and the story about Atri is related to the Aśvins. They freed Atri from darkness (6-?-?; 8-?-?), destroyed the magic nets of a wicked Rākṣasa (1-?-?), and lifted Atri, along with his companions (1-?-?; 1-?-?), out of a pit (5-?-?). Atri fell into a large fire-pit, and the Aśvins lifted him; but they give him revivifying drink (1-?-?; 1-?-?). Or they made the very fire-pit into which he fell pleasant to him, and made his dwelling-house favourable to him (10-?-?; 8-?-?); they covered him so that fire would not burn him (8-?-?); they saved Atri, who was being burned by the heat of the pit (10-?-?), giving him coolness and removing the heat (1-?-?; 8-?-?), and favoured him as the cooling water of cold would (1-?-?). They again made the aged Atri young (10-?-?)."

"Atri found Sūrya, who had been hidden by Svarbhānu, and set him again in the sky (5-?-?, ?). In the mantra that follows it is said that Atris are those who accomplished this great deed. In the Atharvaveda too the matter of finding this Sūrya and setting him in the sky is raised (Av. 13-?-?, ?, ?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Atri is the purohita who removes darkness (Śat. Brā. 4-?-?-?), one born of the goddess of speech (1-?-?-?), and also said to be the goddess of speech himself (14-?-?-?)."

original p. 677

"The whole of the fifth maṇḍala is seen by the seer Atri, or the mantras are seen by the Atris. In the usage of the word Atri in singular or plural, a quarter of the usages are in this very maṇḍala. By the plural word Atrayaḥ, the seers of that gotra are meant."

"It may be derived from the root ad ('to eat'). The word atrin ('devourer') too is formed from this root and is used in the Ṛgveda as an epithet of Rākṣasas and so on. Probably in this sense Atri is an epithet of Agni (3-?-?). Along with the word Atri, the word Saptavadhri has occurred about four times. Saptavadhri is dependent on the Aśvins; the Aśvins are prayed to release him from bondage (5-?-?, ?), and Saptavadhri made the flame of Agni green by his praise (8-?-?). The Aśvins did what was good for the burning womb-region by means of Atri-Saptavadhri (10-?-?). Probably Atri and Saptavadhri are two names of one person."

Kaṇva and others (Kaṇva modalādavaru)

Kaṇva. "This name occurs about sixty-odd times. He too is an ancient seer and the Kaṇvas are his descendants. There are about equal numbers of singular and plural usages. Kaṇva is the son of Nṛṣad (10-?-?); therefore he has the name Nārṣada (1-?-?; Av. 4-?-?). Kaṇva's name is also in the list of the primal men of the world, such as Manu and the Aṅgirases (1-?-?). Agni was given to Kaṇva and others by the deities. Agni kindled by them did not favour them (1-?-?, ?, ?). Agni helped Kaṇva, Atri, Trasadasyu and others in battle (10-?-?), and he is the leader and friend of Kaṇva and the rest (10-?-?). Indra favoured Kaṇva, Trasadasyu and others with gold and cows (Vāl. 1-?; 3-?); and the Maruts showed favour in wealth to Kaṇva, who was joined with Turuśva and the Yadus (8-?-?). The Aśvins helped Kaṇva many times (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?). When Kaṇva was blind, the Aśvins healed him (8-?-?) and gave him sight (1-?-?)."

"Most of the eighth maṇḍala has the Kaṇvas as seers; the names of the seers in the mantras are Kaṇva. But the story of 'the blind Kaṇva' has not been raised there. Some say that the blind Kaṇva is the sun of the night, or Agni who is hidden, or Soma."

Medhyātithi (Medhātithi). "Of the lineage of Kaṇva, and also called Kāṇva (8-?-?). The name has occurred nine times. Further, in the lists of the ancients, along with Kaṇva and the others…"

original p. 678

Medhātithi, end "…[the name] is used (1-?-?, ?, ?). By its meaning it denotes 'one having a guest connected with sacrifice' (i.e. Agni). Priyamedhā occurs five or six times along with Kaṇva and others (8-?-?). His descendants are called Priyamedhas."

Kutsa

"This warrior is known in the histories connected with Indra. His name occurs about sixty times. Only once, in the plural, it is used in the sense of singers who sing for Indra (2-?-?). Because he is the son of Arjuna, he also has the name Ārjuneya (1-?-?). One son of his who obtained Indra's help in a fight with a Dasyu is mentioned (10-?-?). Kutsa is young and brilliant (1-?-?). It was he who, when cast into a pit, prayed for Indra's help (1-?-?). Kutsa and Indra travel in one chariot (4-?-?; 5-?-?); Indra carries Kutsa in the wind (5-?-?; 8-?-?), or makes him his charioteer (2-?-?; 6-?-?). Kutsa is just like Indra (4-?-?); the pair of deities Indra and Kutsa are prayed to come in a chariot (5-?-?)."

"Indra and Kutsa unite in the defeat of the enemy Śuṣṇa. For Kutsa's sake Indra struck Śuṣṇa (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 4-?-?; 6-?-?); he helped Kutsa, who was Śuṣṇa's opponent (1-?-?); he subdued Śuṣṇa for Kutsa (2-?-?); or, joined with Kutsa and other deities, he utterly overcame Śuṣṇa (5-?-?). Taking Kutsa's side, he is prayed to fight Śuṣṇa (6-?-?; 1-?-?), or to carry out the killing of Śuṣṇa for Kutsa. Indra fights on behalf of Kutsa against the deities (4-?-?, to ?) or against a Gandharva (8-?-?). The result of fighting Śuṣṇa was the pulling of the sun's chariot (1-?-?; 6-?-?). For Kutsa, who was oppressed by enemies, Indra seized the wheel of Sūrya's chariot (4-?-?) and gave it to him to use (5-?-?). It appears said that Indra secured the sun for men's happiness, and made the sun move (1-?-?; compare 10-?-?). Having conquered Sūrya, Indra made a broad path for the travel of Kutsa, who was the charioteer (6-?-?). Joined with Kutsa, Indra is prayed to destroy the wicked and make the wheel of Sūrya roll (4-?-?). Not only Śuṣṇa, but other enemies too (Tugra, Sphiḍibha and Vetasu) were made subject to Kutsa by Indra (10-?-?)."

"Kutsa, who was helped by Indra and was his favourite (1-?-?), is sometimes seen as Indra's enemy. Kutsa, Āyu and the warriors of Atithigva…"

original p. 679

"Indra rolled in the dust (2-?-?); he oppressed Āyu, Kutsa and Atithigva (Vāl. 5-?), and gave these three into the hands of the young king Tūrvayāṇa (1-?-?), or yoked the three for that king and made them roll on the ground (6-?-?). In the Nirukta (Nir. 3-?) Kutsa is one of the names of the vajra-weapon."

Kāvya Uśanā

"The name of the seer Uśanā occurs eleven times. Twice he is called Kavi and five times Kāvya. Soma, who speaks the words of wisdom, is likened to Uśanas (9-?-?); and by reason of the instruction, Soma himself is called Uśanā (9-?-?). Kāvya Uśanā set Agni in the place of the hotṛ in the sacrifice (8-?-?). It was he who drove the cows this way (towards the earth) (1-?-?). He is a dependant of Indra (6-?-?); Indra rose with satisfaction in his company (1-?-?); and Indra himself says that Kutsa, Uśanā and the rest are the same as he (4-?-?). Joined with Kutsa, Uśanā also took part in the uprooting of Śuṣṇa by Indra (5-?-?). Also in the making of the vajra-weapon used for the killing of Vṛtra, Uśanā had a hand (1-?-?; 5-?-?; compare 1-?-?)."

"Many more ancient seers are mentioned. Gotama, Viśvāmitra, Vāmadeva, Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha and others are some of them. These, or their descendants, are the seers of the mantras of the second, third, fourth, sixth and seventh maṇḍalas respectively. Agastya too is one of the seers mentioned many times in the Ṛgveda. Among well-known ancient warriors are Sudāsa, Purukutsa and his son Trasadasyu, and Divodāsa Atithigva, and some others."

"The seers mentioned above have been depicted as having had such importance in sacrifices, as being the original men of the human race, as having done superhuman deeds, and as having shared in the works of the deities as equals, and so on. But it is not so easy to say that they truly reflect various parts of nature, or that the deities themselves have come down to earth in other forms and are moving about in this shape."

Animals and Lifeless Things (Prāṇigaḷu mattu nirjīva vastugaḷu)

"In the Vedic histories the animals too have a fitting, important place. Looking at these histories, the difference between men and animals is not much made clear. The deities too have the forms of various animals. The best deities themselves sometimes take the forms of animals. Besides, persons of superhuman nature in the form of useful animals such as the cow…"

original p. 680

"…are held to be of the middle class, and those who have the forms of fierce animals are lower than them, or of the Rākṣasa nature. Moreover, just as the four-footed animals useful to man live around him, the belief is that there are animals of the world of the deities also near the deities. Last of all, in sacrifices, some animals were used as representatives of the deities, who were considered as having that kind of form. This worship of representatives has little use now; for the deities are of great glory, dwellers in heaven, and by their power they come invisibly into the sacrificial hall and accept their shares of oblations: such is the lofty idea, and there is a fear that this would be lost."

The Horse Dadhikrā

"Apart from the horses that draw the chariots of the deities, some horses are mentioned individually. Among such special horses the chief is Dadhikrā. This horse is mentioned in four sūktas (4-38, 39, 40; 7-44). Among them the word Dadhikrā occurs twelve times, and Dadhikrāvan ten times. In other Vedas there is hardly any mention of it. That Dadhikrā is the name of a horse is proved by the very fact that the Nirukta (Nir. 1-?) includes it among the names of the horse. It is very swift (4-?-?, ?; 4-?-?); it is the first horse in the line of many chariots (7-?-?); it destroys chariots, and runs with the speed of the wind (4-?-?). All people praise its speed (4-?-?, ?). It gallops along the turns of the roads also (4-?-?). It has wings as well; it is like a bird, and its wings are compared to the wings of a bird or of a hawk (4-?-?, ?). It is compared to a hawk that flies down from above and called śyena (4-?-?, ?). In 4-?-?, with epithets applicable to Agni — the swan that lives in light, the vasu in the sky, the hotṛ seated on the altar, the guest seated happily in the house — this horse is described."

"Dadhikra too is a hero who strikes the Dasyus and becomes victorious (4-?-?, ?, ?, ?). When he fights, facing thousands of men, the enemies fear him; he plunders in the wars; and the various peoples call him in wars (4-?-?, ?, ?). Bearing a garland, raising dust, it shakes off from its shoulders (4-?-?, ?). It belongs to all the peoples; by his own power he covers the five peoples as Sūrya covers the heroes by his lustre (4-?-?, ?, ?). Mitra and Varuṇa gave this victorious horse to the Pūrus (7-?-?; compare 4-?-?, ?); for the sake of the favour of man they gave the horse named Dadhikrā."

original p. 681

"At the time of sunrise, when Agni is kindled, they praise the horse Dadhikrāvan (7-?-?). He is invoked along with the goddesses of dawn (4-?-?; 4-?-?); the goddesses of dawn are prayed to be, like Dadhikrāva, turned towards the sacrifice (7-?-?). Regularly, he is praised, many times, with the goddesses of dawn, sometimes with Agni and the Aśvins, with Sūrya and other deities (3-?-?, ?; 7-?-? to ?; 10-?-?); but the first invocation is to Dadhikrāvan (7-?-?)."

"From the derivation of the word, nothing is known of the nature and characteristics of this horse. It may be that the latter part of the word (krā) is derived from the root 'to scatter': that is, one who scatters the curds, the frost seen at the time of sunrise. In the opinion of some, it may be the orb of the rising sun. Dadhikrā has a special relation with the goddess Uṣas; and Sūrya also is often called a horse or a bird, and is described in a certain place as having the nature of a warrior. From these too it may be said that Dadhikrā is the orb of the sun. According to some, Dadhikrā is a special form of Agni. And some say that this is not a deity but an excellent horse (uttamāśva)."

"In the two names Dadhyañc and Dadhikrā there is a similarity, and since Dadhyañc has a horse's head, there may be some similarity of nature between them too."

Tārkṣya. "This name, which is related to Dadhikrā, occurs in only two places (1-?-?; 10-?-?). One sūkta of three Ṛks praises this (10-178). The excellent horse urged on by the deities, destroying chariots, swift and running towards the battlefield, was given by Indra (it is said that, with the very words applied to Dadhikrā, he covers the five peoples, 4-?-?). Its name is also Ariṣṭanemi (1-?-?). But in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā Ariṣṭanemi, like Tārkṣya and Garuḍa, is an independent name (Vāj. Saṃ. 25-?). In the Nirukta (Nir. 1-?) Tārkṣya too is one of the names of the horse. In other Vedas the idea is that Tārkṣya is a bird; in the Purāṇas it is one of the many names of Garuḍa. It may probably be the name of the horse-formed Sūrya. There may be some relation between Trasadasyu, or a person named Tṛkṣi, and this (8-?-?). On that basis some say that a horse called Tṛkṣi is this very Tārkṣya."

Paidva. "The horse given by the Aśvins to Pedu is also one of these imaginary horses (1-?-?; 2-?-?); hence it has the name Paidva (1-?-?; 9-?-?). The aim of this gift — giving an excellent horse in return for Pedu's useless horse (1-?-?) — is that it is worthy of praise (1-?-?; 10-?-?; 4-?-?);"

original p. 682

Paidva, end "…[it is worthy of praise] like Bhaga (10-?-?), and is praised by men (1-?-?). It is likened to Indra (1-?-?) and has the name 'killer of the serpent' (ahihan) (1-?-?; 1-?-?; 1-?-?; compare 8-?-?); generally this is a word suited to Indra. In wars it is victorious and desirous of heaven (1-?-?). This too may indicate only Sūrya."

Etaśa. "In the sense 'swift', this word is used some times, and more often to denote a horse. In the plural the same word denotes the horses of Sūrya (2-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?). About twelve times it occurs as a proper name, used as relating to Sūrya; in those contexts it applies especially to the wheel of Sūrya's chariot. The horse named Savitṛ that marked out the limits of the regions of the earth (Etaśaḥ, 5-?-?). The swift Etaśa, a deity (the horse), draws Sūrya (2-?-?). Tied to the nose of the chariot, Etaśa makes the wheel of Sūrya's chariot move (2-?-?); he drove the wheel of Sūrya's chariot (1-?-?; 5-?-?); Indra stops the horse of Sūrya (8-?-?; compare 8-?-?). Indra helped Etaśa, who took part in the race with Sūrya (1-?-?). Carrying away the lost wheel of Sūrya's chariot and fixing it to the chariot, and being in front in the race, it may be guessed that Sūrya gave Etaśa a place at the front of his chariot. What the real meaning of this race is, is not said. But it may be definitely said that Etaśa means the horse of Sūrya."

The horse as the emblem of Sūrya and Agni. "That the horse is the emblem of Sūrya is clear from some sentences. The goddess Uṣas comes driving a white horse (2-?-?); the sacrificial horse was made by the deities from Sūrya (1-?-?). In one special Soma sacrifice, the horse is the symbol of Sūrya."

"Agni, who is swift and brilliant, is many times spoken of as a horse. In rites, the horse is a reflection of Agni. They bring a horse and make it stand at the place where Agni is churned. When carrying Agni to the eastern quarter, they do so by following the footprint of a horse walking in front. Addressing the horse they say: 'Your birthplace is heaven; your navel is in the sphere of the air; your house is on earth' (Vāj. Saṃ. 11-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is said that the horse is lightning, born in the water or in the clouds (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?; 2-?-?-?)."

The Bull (Vṛṣabha)

"The sign of a bull is more often used of Indra. Less often it is used of Agni, the sky-deity and others in an imperfect way. In the Atharvaveda a bull is called Indra (Av. 9-?-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is said that the bull is a special form of Indra (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?). In one of the Vedic rites, the bull is the representative of Rudra. In the history of 'Mudgala and Mudgalānī' the bull has played a part (10-?-?)."

The Cow (Gō)

original p. 683

"In accordance with the greater use of the cow in the world, it holds an important place in Vedic histories too. The rays of the time of dawn are cows, and it is conceived that they draw the chariot of the goddess Uṣas. A rain-cloud too is a cow; it has a calf (a spark). This cloud-formed cow has become established under the name Pṛśni; she is the mother of the Maruts (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-?). Her milk (6-?-?) and her udder are mentioned at every step: 'the many-coloured cows that yield what is wanted in the heaven-world where the best dwell' must be these very clouds (Av. 4-?-?). Afterwards, in the Purāṇas, this is the root of the famous Kāmadhenu. It is also customary to imagine the goddess Iḷā (Iḍā), in the form of the homa of milk and butter, as a cow. Aditi is also sometimes thought of as a cow. It is also said that the deities are born of the cow (gojātāḥ). But the Veda deals with the cow mostly in the history of Indra's freeing of the cows that were in the mountain region."

"The earthly cow too has obtained holiness. She is also called Aditi, Devī and the like, and it is said that she must not be killed (8-?-?, ?; Vāj. Saṃ. 8-?, ?). Because the word aghnyā ('not to be killed') is used sixteen times of the cow, it is evident how holy she was thought to be. That the cow is a holy animal and should be worshipped is established in the Atharvaveda (Av. 13-?-?). One who eats beef is born again, famed as wicked on earth (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?); but beef may be cooked for a guest (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?)."

The goat (Ajaḥ). "It draws Pūṣan's chariot. It is seen also as a deity named Aja Ekapād ('the one-footed goat'). In other Vedas many times a relation between the goat and Agni is stated; sometimes Agni is called a goat."

The ass (Gardabha). "It is the draught animal of the Aśvins in particular."

The dog (Śvā). "Two spotted dogs, called Sārameya, belong to Yama. From this name (Sārameya) these two dogs may be said to be descendants of Saramā, who worked as Indra's messenger. That Saramā is a bitch has no basis in the Ṛgveda; but there is a basis for it in other Vedas, and in the Nirukta (Nir. 11-?) Saramā is explained as the bitch of the deities."

original p. 684

The boar (Varāha). "Rudra, the Maruts and Vṛtra are figuratively called Varāha. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā and the Brāhmaṇas, the form taken by the creator in raising the earth out of the midst of the water is this. Later, this became famous as an incarnation of Viṣṇu."

The tortoise (Kūrma). "In other Vedas the tortoise is given a half-divine character, because 'it breaks all the water' (Vāj. Saṃ. 13-?); or it appears, under the name Kaśyapa, at the side of Prajāpati or as Prajāpati himself; in this form it is also called Svayambhū (Av. 19-?-?). In the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa it is said that Viśvakarman had promised to give the earth to this very Kaśyapa (Ai. Brā. 8-?-?). In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is said that Prajāpati, taking the form of a tortoise, created all beings (Śat. Brā. 7-?-?-?; 2-?-?-?). This form became famous in the Purāṇas as the Kūrma incarnation of Viṣṇu. In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Tai. Saṃ. 5-?-?-?) it is said that the puroḍāśa cake is transformed into a tortoise."

The monkey (Vānaraḥ). "In 10-?-? there is a reference to an ape who was dear to Indra; the enraged Indrāṇī, angered by his gifts, drives him away; at last he gets back his first place."

The frogs (Keppe). "The frogs awakened by the rain (7-?) are said to give cows and long life, and there is a belief that mantras and knowledge come to them."

Birds (Pakṣi). "In the Vedic histories birds too have a part. Soma is compared to a bird, and is called a bird. Agni in particular is compared to birds or called a bird. Sūrya too has the name bird; in two contexts he has the name Garutmān. In the Purāṇas, Garuḍa as the vehicle of Viṣṇu must have this very basis. The chief work of the bird in the Veda is, in the form of an eagle, bringing Soma-juice for Indra. In the manner of the Kāṭhaka Upaniṣad, Indra himself, in the form of an eagle, takes the Soma or nectar."

"Omen-birds and other animals are sent by some deities. The owl and the pigeon are Yama's messengers. In the Sūtra books the owl is a messenger of evil deities, and the fierce bird stained with blood, and the pigeons that are wild, are Yama's messengers. In the Ṛgveda there is a prayer to an omen-bird that it may indicate only good omens (2-?-?)."

Fierce animals. "These are seen as Rākṣasas or as possessing the characteristics of Rākṣasas. In the Ṛgveda, to indicate Rākṣasas, the word mṛga ('beast') is also used (1-?-?; 5-?-?; 5-?-?). A Rākṣasa named Ūrṇavābha (of the kind of the spider) is mentioned three times (2-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?); and another is Uraṇa, that is, a ram (2-?-?)."

original p. 685

The serpent (Ahi, sarpa). "The word ahi is most often used to indicate Rākṣasas in this way. It is generally another name of Vṛtra; as a serpent coils round creatures, he too encircles men; hence the name may have come. Indra, who killed Vṛtra, also kills Ahi (8-?-?; 4-?-?). That Ahi and Vṛtra are one person is clear from the mantras 1-32-1 to 14. In those sentences, in the places where the word Vṛtra should have been said, Ahi is used; likewise, in place of the word Ahi, Vṛtra is said. The Ahi born in the first part of 1-32-3, 4 is no other than Vṛtra; in many other sentences the two words stand in the two halves of a verse. It may be said that Vṛtra is Ahi-formed. Even if only Ahi is spoken of, the results of Indra's victory are the release of the waters and the gaining of cows, as when Vṛtra is slain. When it is said that Ahi has covered the water, the same root vṛ ('to cover') is used. Likewise the serpent swallows the water (root gras; 4-?-?; 10-?-?). Cloud, thunder and the like are the weapons of Ahi (1-?-?). He too is brilliant; the Maruts have the epithet ahibhānavaḥ ('shining like serpents') (1-?-?). Agni too has been given this word; he is described as a serpent hissing like wind blown from a bellows (1-?-?). Soma is prayed to hand over the enemy to the serpent (2-?-?). In the plural, ahayaḥ, the race of Rākṣasas is meant (9-?-?; 10-?-?); among them Ahi was the first born (1-?-?). By the name Ahi Budhnya, this serpent has also been counted as a deity."

"In other Vedas, serpents too are counted, like the Gandharvas, as semi-divine. They live in heaven, earth and the sky (Vāj. Saṃ. 13-?; Tai. Brā. 3-?-?). In the Atharvaveda they are mentioned in many places. In one place a whole sūkta is devoted to the praise of serpent-deities (Av. 11-?). In the Sūtras, oblations are laid down separately for the deities of earth, sky and heaven (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?; Pā. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?). Along with the deities, crops and Rākṣasas, serpents too are worshipped (Sāṃ. Gṛ. Sū. 4-?-?; 4-?-?; Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?); protection from them is also sought (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 4-?-?). As the serpent is a fierce animal, it is believed to be of the Rākṣasa nature and to be satisfied only by oblations. Oblations are made to ants too (Kau. Sū. 1-?)."

Material Things Imagined as Deities (Devategaḷendu bhāvisalpaṭṭa bhautika vastugaḷu)

"Besides the natural phenomena and powers connected with heaven and the sphere of the air, earthly things too are conceived as deities; this is established in the Ṛgveda. Things that come within this class of deities are generally only those that are very useful to man. Such worship is called sarvadevatārādhana ('worship of all the deities'), or Viśve-devas, the deities themselves…"

original p. 686

Material things, continued "…[the deities themselves…] one should not think of this as the doctrine of 'all (viśva)'. Here each thing has its own place. It may be called merely worship of things."

"The rivers, being of the form of deities, have been discussed already."

Mountains. "Mountains possess divine life. They are praised about twenty times in the plural and four times in the singular. In this way mountains alone are nowhere praised; generally they are praised together with water, rivers, plants, trees, heaven and earth (2-?-?; etc.), or with Savitṛ, Indra and other deities (6-?-?; etc.), as those who are endowed with manliness, firm and well satisfied (3-?-?). In Indrā-parvatā it seems that a position equal to Indra's is intended (1-?-?; 1-?-?). The two travel in one big chariot; they are called together to come to the sacrifice (3-?-?). Here the mountain is a mountain-deity and Indra's companion."

Herbs (Oṣadhi). "The herbs too have obtained divinity. The whole of the sūkta 10-97 is devoted to praising the power of these to cure diseases. They are described as mothers, as deities, and the like. All the crops are subject to the Soma plant, and Soma is available to all. A crop that is useful as a medicine is praised as a goddess born in the earth-goddess (Av. 6-?-?). So that they should not stand in the way of offspring, an animal is also offered as a sacrifice to these herbs (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?)."

Trees (Vanaspati). "Trees (in the plural, 2-?-?; 10-?-?, or in the singular, 1-?-?; Vāl. 6-?) are conceived as deities together with water and mountains. At marriage ceremonies, the worship of big trees (the Aśvattha and others) is prescribed."

The Forest (Araṇyānī). "In the sūkta 10-146 the forest-deity (the presiding deity of the forest) is described under the name Araṇyānī. She is the mother of the wild beasts; though there is no agriculture, there is no lack of food. The various sounds heard in the forest are described in various ways. But the part played by these crops and forest-deities is not important, not only in the Vedas but in sacrifices and rites. Only in Buddhist books is a very close kinship between them and men established."

Implements (Upakaraṇagaḷu)

"Another group of things that come within personification and the ascription of divinity are the implements of sacrifice. The chief of these is the sacrificial post (yūpastambha). It has the names vanaspati and svaru as well. Both are praised in 3-?-? as being of the form of deities. They are purified and adorned by the priests. The posts set up by the priests go, like the deities and other deities, near the deities. In the ten and eleven mantras of the Āprī-sūktas it is said that the sacrificial post, purified three times with ghee, and placed at Agni's side, is prayed to send the oblations to the deities…"

original p. 687

"…(the same sūkta, 3-?-?; 10-?-?). The barhis (sacred grass) too is said to be a deity. The doors of the sacrificial hall have often been called deities (Devīr dvāraḥ)."

"The stones used for pressing Soma-juice (grāvāṇaḥ, adrayaḥ) are conceived as deities in three sūktas (10-?-?, ?, ?). They have no destruction, and no old age; and they are greater than heaven. At the time of pressing Soma they are like horses or bulls, and the sound produced by them reaches heaven. They are prayed to ward off Rākṣasas and harm, and to grant lordship and progeny. In 1-?-?, ? the kalabatta (pestle), kuṭṭaṇi (mortar) and the like, sounding loudly, are prayed to press the Soma juice."

"In the Atharvaveda it is said that the remnant of the homa (the left-over, ucchiṣṭa) has great divine power (Av. 11-?); likewise the sacrificial ladles sruk, sruva and the rest, used in sacrifice, have power."

"There are some praise-sentences too for the agricultural implements, the plough (śuna, sīra), (4-?-? to ?), and for them the puroḍāśa is prescribed (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?-?)."

"Weapons too have the form of deities. The whole sūkta 6-75 is devoted to the praise of implements of war — the bow, arrows, the quiver and so on. The arrow too is divine; it is prayed to protect and to strike the enemies. The drum too is dealt with in the same way, and it is prayed to drive away the evil, the enemies and the Rākṣasas. A whole sūkta of the Atharvaveda praises it (Av. 5-?)."

Emblems — Images (Lāñchanagaḷu — Pratimegaḷu)

"In other Vedas, a little of the practice of speaking of ordinary things as representatives of the deities is seen. 'Who will buy this Indra of mine for ten cows? After defeating his enemies, he may be returned' (4-?-?; compare 8-?-?): in a statement like this, a certain image of Indra must have been the thing for sale. References to images are found more in the Brāhmaṇas and Sūtras."

"In some rites the wheel is used as the representative of Sūrya (indicating form and motion). In the Vājapeya sacrifice, at the time of the installation of the fires, they use it in this way. In the Purāṇas, the wheel is a weapon of Viṣṇu."

"After sunset, when sprinkling water, they place in the place of the sun a piece of burning charcoal or a burning torch (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?); but when there is a sign of the sun…"

original p. 688

"…it also serves the same purpose (Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?). When building the fire-pit, in place of the sun they use a gold plate with a hole in it (Śat. Brā. 7-?-?-?)."

"Worship of the male organ seems to have been current; the word śiśnadevāḥ occurs in two places. But it may be said that this worship was opposed to the Vedic view. Indra is prayed not to let the śiśnadevas come near the sacrifice (7-?-?); it is also said that Indra killed the śiśnadevas when he was obtaining the wealth of a fort with a hundred doors (10-?-?). In the Purāṇas, as an indication of Śiva's being the creator, worship of the śiśna or liṅga came into use."

Evil Deities and Piśācas (Pāpadevategaḷu mattu Piśācigaḷu)

Asuras. "Certain persons who are opposed to the auspicious deities and are violent are called by many names. In all the Vedas, asura is a Rākṣasa of the heaven-world, always an enemy of the deities; they fight with them constantly in historical wars; and sometimes they become strangely enemies of men too (Av. 8-?-?; Kau. Sū. ?-?-?; ?-?). But in the Ṛgveda this word has this meaning in a strange way. In the plural, in the sense of Rākṣasas, it is used only four times. A prayer to Indra: 'Drive away the Asuras who have no faith in the deities' (8-?-?). The remaining three usages are in the tenth maṇḍala itself: 'the deities struck the Asura' (10-?-?); Agni promises, 'I shall find and catch a means to uproot the Asuras' (10-?-?); it is said that the deities placed their trust in the Asuras, who were hard to conquer (10-?-?). In the singular, three times it refers to one Rākṣasa. Bṛhaspati is prayed to guard the warriors of the Asura as a rock that looks after (2-?-?). Indra destroyed the forts of the Asura named Pipru (10-?-?); Indra and Viṣṇu defeated the hundred thousand warriors of the Asura Varcin (7-?-?). Even in the epithet asurahā ('killer of Asuras'), applied to Indra (6-?-?), Agni (2-?-?) and Sūrya (10-?-?), asura means a Rākṣasa. This war of the deities and Asuras, beginning at first with one deity, Indra, and one Asura, Vṛtra, seems gradually to have grown into a constant war between the two parties — the deities as one group and the Rākṣasas as the other. The same idea is expressed in the Brāhmaṇas. In these wars there is a peculiarity: in the beginning the Asuras have the upper hand, and in the end the deities win by trick. The most important example is the Viṣṇu who, in the Trivikrama incarnation, takes three steps and makes the Asuras give back their kingdom, covering the earth."

"In the Brāhmaṇas a relation is imagined between Asuras and darkness (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?-?). The day belongs to the deities, and the night to the Rākṣasas (Tai. Saṃ. 1-?-?-?). But the Asuras too were born of Prajāpati, and at the beginning were equal to the deities, like them…"

original p. 689

"…It may be for this reason that some harmful persons are indicated by the word deva (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?; Av. 3-?-?)."

"In the Atharvaveda and thereafter, asura means Rākṣasas only; but in the Ṛgveda it is mainly the deities themselves who are meant by this word. It may be that the meaning 'Rākṣasa' became fixed in the word that was first used mostly of the deities. There seems to be a peculiar meaning in the word asura. It is generally used of Varuṇa or Mitra and Varuṇa, and their māyā power is their distinction. But māyā may also mean a power of deceit or harm. The evil meanings that the word asura has (10-?-?; 10-?-?) may also have given room for the decision that it is unfit for the deities. In one sūkta (10-?) the word seems to be used in both senses. It must have grown less as the sense 'deity'. Moreover, they were very mighty. For those who are opposed to the suras, a separate name was also needed, which is another reason. Therefore the name came to be fixed for the Rākṣasas, as those who are not the suras (deities — as seen in the Upaniṣad)."

Paṇis. "The Paṇis in the sphere of the air are mainly enemies of Indra (6-?-?; 6-?-?), of his friends, of Soma, Agni, Bṛhaspati and the Aṅgirases. In all the places where the name of these Rākṣasas occurs, their cows are mentioned, plainly (10-?-?; 6-?-?), or under the name paṇīnāṃ nidhi ('treasure of the Paṇis') or their wealth (3-?-?; 8-?-?). It is said that the deities discovered the ghee hidden in the cows by a Paṇi (4-?-?). Indra overcame them in strength (2-?-?), but they did not obtain the strength of Mitra and Varuṇa (1-?-?); even so they are very strong among the lower beings."

"It occurs sixteen times in the plural and four times in the singular. Indra, or Agni-Soma, took the cows from a Paṇi (10-?-?; 1-?-?); and the deity Soma is prayed to strike down the wolf-formed Paṇi and make him lie dead (6-?-?)."

"The word paṇi has been used many more times in the singular; but not as indicating a Rākṣasa — in the sense of 'miser'. Even then, it is used to indicate stinginess in the matter of giving gifts and making homa in sacrifices. By saying that they let no one obtain heavenly wealth and the like, the idea may have come that the Paṇis are Rākṣasas."

Dāsa or Dasyu. "By the word dāsa, or the word dasyu that is equal to it, the Rākṣasas of the sphere of the air are also meant. These were probably men at first, and…"

original p. 690

Dāsa/Dasyu, continued "…some of the undesirable qualities seen in them may have brought them into the class of Rākṣasas. Some of the names of Rākṣasas of certain clans seem to have historical prominence."

"The singular (2-?-?; etc.) and plural (1-?-?) forms indicate Rākṣasas destroyed by Indra; many times these words are used together with the word Vṛtra (6-?-?; etc.). For this very reason Indra has the names dasyuhā ('killer of Dasyus', 1-?-?; etc.) and, for this act, dasyuhatyā ('killing of Dasyus', 1-?-?, ?; etc.). To protect those who sought his shelter, Indra put thirty thousand Dasyus into a long sleep (4-?-?); he bound a thousand Dasyus (2-?-?); or, with Dadhyañc and Mātariśvan, he took the cow-pens from the Dasyus (10-?-?). Where help from Indra is sought against enemies in the form of Āryas and Dasyus (10-?-?; etc.), or where it is said that he makes a division among the Ārya Dasyus (1-?-?; 10-?-?), the ordinary enemies on the earth must be intended. When it is said that Indra fights the Dasyus for the Āryas (6-?-?; 6-?-?), the same meaning applies. In this way, as the Āryas in wars took the Dāsas or Dasyus as prisoners, the word dāsa seems to have been used two or three times in the sense of 'slave', which is now current (2-?-?; Vāl. 8-?). Those thrown down by Indra, having climbed to heaven (8-?-?; compare 2-?-?), or those burnt and thrown down in heaven (1-?-?), or those destroyed as soon as they were born (1-?-?; 8-?-? to ?), or those on whom Indra helps the deities in war (10-?-?), the Dasyus were Rākṣasas. Overpowering the mist and the clouds, Indra attacks the Dasyus (10-?-?), kills the Dasyus, and obtains the sun and the waters (1-?-?); and in contexts like 'the deities and the Dasyus are enemies of each other' (3-?-?) the same sense. One Dāsa, the lord of the waters (the deity presiding over the waters), must also be a Rākṣasa (1-?-?; 5-?-?; 8-?-?); defeating him, Indra makes those water-deities wives of the best deity (10-?-?). Like the cities of Vṛtra, the seven forts of the 'Dāsa' who is thought of as autumnal (6-?-?; compare 2-?-?) also belong to the sphere of the air."

"It is fitting to say 'Piśācas' for both Dāsas and Dasyus. As generic terms, these words are used of each Piśāca who is mentioned in battles with Indra. Namuci (3-?-? to ?; etc.), Śambara (3-?-?; etc.), Śuṣṇa (2-?-?; etc.), sometimes Pipru (8-?-?; 10-?-?), Cumuri and Dhuni (2-?-?; 2-?-?), Varcin (4-?-?; 6-?-?), Navavāstva (10-?-?, ?), once Śvāpṛ (?), and a serpent named Ahi (2-?-?)."

original p. 691

Vṛtra

"Of the Rākṣasas of the sphere of the air, the most important is Vṛtra. No other Rākṣasa is mentioned so many times. He is Indra's principal enemy; and for the killing of him Indra was born or grew (8-?-?; 10-?). Vṛtrahā is Indra's personal epithet. In two places the meaning of this word is explained. 'To kill Vṛtra, O killer of Vṛtra, slay Vṛtra' (8-?-?) and 'O Indra, killer of Vṛtra, slay the Vṛtra' (8-?-?). This deed of Indra's is indicated by the words vṛtrahatyā (killing of Vṛtra) and sometimes vṛtratūryā (conquering Vṛtra)."

"It is known beforehand that Vṛtra had the form of a serpent. For this reason he has no hands and feet (1-?-?; 3-?-?). His head, which is cut off by Indra (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 8-?-?), and the trunk that is struck by the vajra (1-?-?), are mentioned many times. He hisses or snorts (8-?-?; 3-?-?, 1-?-?, 1-?-?, and 6-?-?). Thunder, lightning, frost and the like (1-?-?) are under his control."

"Vṛtra's mother has the name Dānu, and she is compared to a cow (1-?-?). The same word (dānu) in the neuter gender indicates a stream, and in the feminine, heavenly water. These two words may be the same. The same word in the masculine is used of Vṛtra. Probably it is because he is the son of Dānu that the name came (2-?-?; 4-?-?). The same name is applied to Ūrṇavābha (2-?-?) and to the seven Rākṣasas killed by Indra (10-?-?). From the word dānu (meaning 'son of Dānu') the word dānava is formed, and it indicates a Rākṣasa who fought with Indra (generally Vṛtra himself). Indra drove away all the deceitful arts of the Dānava (2-?-?); he struck and destroyed the hissing Dānava (5-?-?), and afterwards released the waters (5-?-?)."

"Vṛtra has a hidden dwelling; released by Indra, the waters escape past Ahi and come out of that dwelling-house (1-?-?). Vṛtra lies on the water (1-?-?, 2-?-?), or in the lower part of the sphere of the air, covered by water (1-?-?). When Indra made the water flow, Vṛtra was lying in a high place (1-?-?), or from many high regions Indra pushes him down (8-?-?). When Vṛtra was killed, Indra pierced his ninety-nine forts (2-?-?; 8-?-?; 10-?-?)."

"There is no doubt that the word Vṛtra is formed from the root vṛ ('to cover, to encircle'). Apovaṃvāṃsam (3-?-?; etc.; 'one who covers the water') or…"

original p. 692

"vṛṣṭi (1-?-?), or nadīvṛt (1-?-?; 8-?-?; 6-?-?; 6-?-?) — such usages confirm the derivation given above. Vṛtraṃ avyanot (3-?-?). In usages such as avāvṛṇot (1-?-?; 1-?-?) there appears to be a pun on this word. Vṛtra has encircled the rivers (paridhiḥ, 3-?-?)."

"By the word Vṛtrahā not only the killing of the Rākṣasa Vṛtra but also the killing of the Vṛtras is meant. In the plural, and in the neuter, as vṛtrāṇi (bhūrīṇi vṛtrā, 2-?-?), it is used to indicate various Piśācas (2-?-?; 10-?-?). The result of Indra's fight with these Piśācas is also the release of water (2-?-?), or the freeing of the rivers (8-?-?); these too were covered by Piśācas (8-?-?). As soon as he was born, Indra was created by the deities to strike these (3-?-?) and to destroy them (3-?-?); as, with the bones of Dadhyañc, he destroyed the ninety-nine forts of Vṛtra, he also destroyed the Vṛtras (1-?-?)."

"By this plural word Vṛtra the enemies on earth too are indicated. There are two kinds of Vṛtras, Āryas and Dāsas (6-?-?; 6-?-?). In many sentences, the enemies of men are also intended, as the enemies of the deities. In such contexts, Vṛtra does not mean merely an enemy or ill-wisher; the qualities of the Rākṣasa Vṛtra are also in view. This word in the neuter gender must at first have had the general sense of 'obstacle' or 'obstruction', and afterwards the sense 'Piśāca' came."

"In the Brāhmaṇas, Vṛtra is the moon; and on the new-moon day, Indra, in the form of the sun, swallows him."

Vala

"It has occurred about twenty-four times. Indra or his companions, especially the Aṅgirases, are those who destroy him; it is in connection with the freeing of the cows by them that he is mentioned. When the Paṇi had seized the cows, Indra destroyed Vala, who was the guardian of those cows (10-?-?; compare 6-?-?). When Bṛhaspati took them and was going away, Vala grieves for them (10-?-?; compare 10-?-?). Indra forcibly took his forts (6-?-?); Indra cut the creepers (1-?-?); and Indra broke the unbroken high ground (the peak, sānu) (6-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā, Indra, opening the hole of Vala, threw out the best creature in it; the remaining creatures followed it (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?). It appears that the word is used many times in the sense of a covering, a hole, a cave, which is not applicable to any person. In two…"

original p. 693

"…contexts (1-?-?; 4-?-?; 8-?-?) it is used together with phalaga as a refuge for water; in the Nirukta (Nir. 1-?) vala too is one of the names of cloud. Indra drove all the cows out and opened the door of Vala (2-?-?); or he opened the hole of Vala that was filled with cows (1-?-?). In the Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa it is said that the cave of the Asuras (vala) was broken by a stone (Paṃ. Brā. 14-?-?). In some sentences this word may indicate the person Vala or a cave and the like (1-?-?; 2-?-?; 3-?-?). In Valaṃruja ('breaker of Vala'), the epithet of Indra along with Vṛtrakhāda, the Rākṣasa Vala must be intended (3-?-?; compare 3-?-?, ?). The change of person into 'cave' is clear in 3-?-?. In the name 'Vala himself is the cow-pen; Indra strikes him', this Vala opens the door of the pen. By not using, for the killing of Vala, the roots han, bhid, dṛ or ruj, the personification is incomplete. Valabhit ('splitter of Vala') is an epithet of Indra; it is seen especially in the Purāṇas. Here Indra kills both Vala and Vṛtra, who are brothers (Vala-Vṛtra-hā)."

Arbuda. "It occurs seven times; always as an enemy of Indra. He is deceitful; Indra drove his cows out (8-?-?). Indra threw him down (2-?-?, 3-?-?; compare 8-?-?), crushed him with his foot (1-?-?), or cut off his head (10-?-?). Two or three times he is mentioned along with Vṛtra (Ahi), and is by nature of his race."

Viśvarūpa. "Son of Tvaṣṭṛ, with three heads; Indra and Trita killed him and brought his cows under their control (10-?-?, ?). In two or three other sentences too he is indicated only by the word Tvāṣṭra ('belonging to Tvaṣṭṛ'). Tvāṣṭra was rich in cows, horses and so on (10-?-?); Indra seized him and handed him to Trita (2-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?), Viśvarūpa, though connected with the Asuras, is the purohita of the deities. In the Mahābhārata, the notion is that the three-headed Tvāṣṭra and Vṛtra are one and the same."

Svarbhānu. "He too is a Rākṣasa by nature. He has occurred four times in one sūkta (5-40). He covers Sūrya with darkness. Defeating his deceits, Indra fought; and Atri placed Sūrya's eye again in the sphere of the air. His story is told in many places in the Brāhmaṇas. In the Purāṇas, Rāhu is in the place of Svarbhānu. The meaning of this word is 'one who obstructs the light of the sun'."

Uraṇa. "This one, with ninety-nine arms, was killed by Indra (2-?-?)."

The Dāsas — Dasyus

Śuṣṇa. "His name occurs about forty times. He is Kutsa's chief enemy. Together with Kutsa, or for Kutsa's sake, Indra uproots Śuṣṇa (4-?-?,…"

original p. 694

Śuṣṇa, continued "…(4-?-?, etc.). He has horns (1-?-?) and hoofs (6-?-?, ?), that is, there are hoofs made of horn (compare 10-?-?); so Śuṣṇa too may be said to be a serpent. He hisses (śvasanaḥ, 1-?-?). Six times the epithet aśuṣa ('swallower') is used of Agni only. He has strong forts (1-?-?) or a fort (4-?-?), and these are moving forts (8-?-?). Indra destroys Śuṣṇa's forts and sets the waters free (1-?-?); having struck Śuṣṇa, he creates the water-store (Vāj. Saṃ. 3-?) or, uprooting Śuṣṇa's family, he lets heavenly water (svarvatīḥ) flow (8-?-?). Four times Śuṣṇa has the epithet kuyava ('one who causes bad grain'). The word kuyava is found twice, probably used in place of Śuṣṇa (1-?-?, 1-?-?). The result of the fight of Indra and Śuṣṇa may be not only the release of water, but the gaining of cows or of the sun (8-?-?). While fighting with Indra, Śuṣṇa moves about in darkness. He is called a son of frost and a Dānava (5-?-?). Śuṣṇa is a Dānava who holds nectar within himself (Kāṭhaka)."

"From the sentences above, Śuṣṇa may be said to be a cause of drought. The root of the word Śuṣṇa, śuṣ, means 'to dry up' or 'to reduce'. This too supports the idea of a cause of drought."

Śambara. "This name occurs about twenty-odd times. It is associated with other Piśācas: Śambara is mentioned especially along with Śuṣṇa, Pipru (1-?-?, 1-?-?, 2-?-?, 6-?-?) and Varcin; when fighting Ahi and Śambara, the Maruts help Indra (3-?-?); when he split Śambara, Indra shook the very sky (1-?-?). Searching for Śambara, who lived on a mountain (2-?-?), he rolled him down from the mountain (1-?-?, 6-?-?). Indra rolled down from the big mountain the Dāsa named Śambara, son of Kulitara (4-?-?). Considering himself a minor deity, he struck Śambara and made him fall from a high place (2-?-?). Ninety-nine (1-?-?; generally ninety-nine, 2-?-?, etc.) or a hundred (2-?-?, etc.) forts are under him. Once, in the neuter ending, this word means 'the forts of Śambara'. Bṛhaspati pierced these and entered the mountain region that was joined with treasures (2-?-?). Atithigva (1-?-?), generally Divodāsa (2-?-?, etc.): sometimes both (1-?-?; 4-?-?); Indra destroys Śambara for them. Śambara and Divodāsa may be two names of one person."

Pipru. "An enemy of Ṛjiśvan, who is dependent on Indra (Vāl. 1-?). This Ṛjiśvan makes Indra drink pressed Soma and obtains help against Pipru in battle (3-?-?; 10-?-?)…"

original p. 695

"…Indra, joined with Ṛjiśvan (1-?-?, ?; 10-?-?) or in his cause (4-?-?; 6-?-?), subdued Pipru. Many forts are under Pipru, who is accompanied by the deceits of Ahi; Indra splits them (1-?-?; 6-?-?). Indra killed the Dāsa Pipru and some others and drove the waters out (8-?-?). When the sun, in the middle of the sky, drove his chariot, the Ārya saw a warrior equal to Pipru; Indra, joined with Ṛjiśvan, destroyed the strong forts of the deceitful Asura Pipru (10-?-?). Indra gave Pipru, in the form of a forest animal, to Ṛjiśvan; he subdued fifty thousand black-skinned people and split forts (4-?-?). With Ṛjiśvan, Indra destroyed the family of the dark-coloured ones (1-?-?). Since he has the epithets Asura and Dāsa, some hold that he may also have been an enemy of men."

Namuci. "Apart from the nine times it occurs in the Ṛgveda, this name is seen in the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. He has the epithet Asura ('one of Asura nature') (10-?-?; Śat. Brā. 12-?-?-?), and in the other Vedas he is called an Asura. He is called a Dāsa in three or four sentences (5-?-?, ?, etc.) and māyin ('one of deceitful power') in one place (1-?-?). When Namuci is mentioned, Indra's companion is a protégé named Namī Sāpya (1-?-?, 6-?-?). Like many other Piśācas, Namuci too is killed by Indra (2-?-?, 2-?-?), or struck and killed (1-?-?). Killing Vṛtra and Namuci, Indra destroyed a hundred forts (2-?-?). He splits Vṛtra's head, but twists and crushes the head of Namuci (5-?-?; 6-?-?). Indra twists Namuci's head (5-?-?) or has cut it with the foam of water (8-?-?). In the Brāhmaṇas it is also said that he cut the head. Indra sat at the side of Namuci and drank liquor; then, with the help of the Aśvins, Sarasvatī healed him (10-?-?, ?)."

"According to Pāṇini (6-?-?), Namuci means 'one who does not (na) release (muc)'; that is, he may be called a Piśāca who obstructs the waters."

Dhuni and Cumuri. "Generally the two names come together; once Cumuri alone has come. Once they are used in the dual (6-?-?), from which it is known how close the relation between them is. Indra put both of them to sleep (2-?-?; 6-?-?; 2-?-?); the same happened to Cumuri alone (6-?-?). Along with Śambara, Pipru, Śuṣṇa and others he destroyed these too, and destroyed their forts (6-?-?). For Dabhīti, who prepared Soma juice for himself (6-?-?), these two were destroyed by Indra, or made to sleep…"

original p. 696

"…(10-?-?); and Dabhīti received from the deities a reward suited to his devotion (2-?-?). For Dabhīti, Indra made thirty thousand Dasyus sleep (4-?-?); for him he bound the Dasyus without a rope (2-?-?)."

"Dhuni means 'one who roars'."

Varcin and others. "He is mentioned four times together with Śambara. He too is an Asura (7-?-?), but Śambara and he are called 'Dāsa' (6-?-?). Indra, breaking Śambara's forts, destroyed one hundred thousand warriors of Varcin (3-?-?; 4-?-?). Varcin means 'one who shines'."

"Along with Vala, Śuṣṇa, Namuci and others, some more Piśācas are named, and they too were destroyed by Indra. Among them are Vṛśīka, Rudhikra (2-?-?, ?), Anarśani, Spabinda (8-?-?) and Ilībiśa (1-?-?)."

Rākṣasas (Rakṣasaḥ)

"The Piśācas or ghosts (bhūta) of the earth are haters of men. The generic name for them is rakṣaḥ ('Rākṣasa'). It occurs more than fifty times in the singular and plural; generally it comes in the form of a prayer to destroy the Rākṣasa with some deity, or praise that the deity killed the Rākṣasa. They are described in the sūktas 7-104 and 10-87; there the words rakṣaḥ, yātu, yātudhāna and the like indicate them. The word rakṣaḥ is a name for all evil deities and Piśācas; so it may be understood as a generic word, and yātu as a sub-generic word."

"These Piśācas or ghosts have the forms of dogs, wild beasts, owls and other birds (7-?-? to ?). Being in the form of birds, they fly about at night (7-?-?). Taking the form of brother, husband or lover, they approach women and wish to destroy their children (10-?-?). In the form of dogs or monkeys they wait to fall on pregnant women (Av. 4-?-?); therefore women with child and children are afraid of them (Av. 8-?-?). At marriage times they run round the bride; to peck out their eyes, little arrows are shot in the sky (Hā. Gṛ. Sū. ?). The description of their forms and the rest is in the Atharvaveda. They especially take the form of men. They have heads, eyes, hearts and other limbs; but there is always some deformity: three heads, two mouths, four eyes, five feet, no fingers, feet turned backward or horns on the hands, and so on (Av. 8-?-?;"

original p. 697

"Hi. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?). Blue, yellow or hairy Piśācas are also mentioned (Av. 19-?-?, ?). Among them there are males and females, families and kings (Av. 5-?-?; Hi. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?); they too are mortal (Av. 6-?-?; etc.)."

"The Yātudhānas eat the flesh of men and horses, and drink the milk of cows (10-?-?, ?). To satisfy their desire for blood and flesh the Rākṣasas attack men; this attack is generally by entering them. Agni is prayed to prevent Rākṣasas from entering the worshippers (8-?-?). A Piśācī in the form of a disease flits here and there and enters men (Av. 2-?-?). These ghosts and spirits enter us generally through our mouth when we eat or drink (Av. 3-?-? to ?); sometimes by other doors (Av. 8-?-?). The obstacle is only entering; having entered, they cut the man's flesh, eat it and cause disease (Av. 5-?-?, ?). They cause madness and destroy the faculty of speech (Av. 6-?-?; Hi. Gṛ. Sū. 1-?-?). They attack the dwelling-houses of men (Kau. Sū. 1-?-?). Some ghosts, at evening time, move round the houses crying and howling like jackals, or wander in the forests, or laugh loudly, or drink from skulls (Av. 8-?-?, ?, ?; Hi. Gṛ. Sū. 2-?-?)."

"Their time of movement is night or evening (2-?-?). In the east they have no play; there the rising sun drives them away (Tai. Saṃ. 2-?-?-?). It is believed that a burning torch is the form of a ghost (Kau. Sū. 1-?-?). The new-moon day and the dark half are favourable times for the movement of ghosts, as they are for the dead (Av. 1-?-?; 4-?-?)."

"There is nothing that they will not do to harm sacrifices. In sacrifices meant for the deities they cause loss and defects; and the Yātus pour the prepared oblations out (2-?-?, ?). In seeing the hymn they cannot stand (10-?-?). Agni is prayed to burn up Rākṣasas and the like so that the sacrifice may not suffer a curse (1-?-?). There is a mantra that makes ineffective the sacrifice of an enemy through the deceit of Yātudhānas and Rākṣasa-groups (Av. 2-?-?). At the time of giving rice-water to the dead (the annodaka), they appear in the form of the dead and block it (Av. 18-?-?; compare Vāj. Saṃ. 2-?). It is common in the Purāṇas that these Rākṣasa groups (behaving like Rākṣasas) trouble yogis."

"Both Agni, who produces the sacrificial fire, and the sacrificer hate those who move the skulls and who cause trouble. Agni alone is prayed to burn, drive away or destroy them (10-?-?, etc.). By this work Agni and some other deities have received the name rakṣohā ('destroyer of Rākṣasas')."

original p. 698

Rākṣasas / Piśācas, continued "These ghosts are not only harmful by nature; they sometimes do harm when urged by others. The words rakṣoyujaḥ ('those who impel Rākṣasas') (2-?-?) and the ghosts and Yātus of mantra-wizards are found here (2-?-?; 8-?-?). One who has come under the attack of a ghost sent by an enemy may drive them away by making an offering in the Yaviṣṭha fire (Tai. Saṃ. 3-?-?-?); and the prayer to the ghosts themselves is, 'swallow the one who sent you' (Av. 2-?-?)."

"In the sense of ghosts, the word rakṣaḥ is used both in the masculine and the feminine. In the neuter it also has the meaning 'harm'. From the root rakṣ ('to protect') the word rakṣaḥ may be formed — in the sense that they are to be protected against (rakṣitavya) as one who does harm; but this use is very unusual. Or it may come from the usual root rakṣ ('to guard'). In this context rakṣaḥ means 'what is to be avoided'."

Piśācas. "The third kind of ghosts are the Piśācas. In the Ṛgveda only in one place (1-?-?) the word occurs, ending in the singular, as piśācī. Indra is prayed to destroy the golden-yellow-crowned and water-formed Piśācī and to strike and destroy every ghost. The Asuras, Rākṣasas and Piśācas are, in order, enemies of the deities, of men and of the Fathers. Piśācas in particular must have been connected with the dead ones (preta). The dead ones have the name kravyāda ('eaters of raw flesh or a dead body') (Av. 3-?-?; etc.); this is a word equal to piśāca. Agni is prayed to get back the flesh of the sick man eaten by the Piśācas (Av. 5-?-?). For that reason they are a kind of flesh-eating Piśācas. Piśācas flow in the water (Av. 4-?-?; 4-?-?) or haunt the houses and villages of men (Av. 4-?-?)."

"The feminine word arāti ('miserliness') and the masculine and feminine words druh ('one who causes harm, trouble') are each counted as one kind of Piśāca."

"Kimīdin is a group of ghosts (2-?-?; 10-?-?)."

"There are many Piśācas connected with our everyday life. From their names alone the trouble they cause can be understood. They have no relation to nature. Generally it is believed that those who are hostile to us, being dead, come in these forms and give us trouble. They have less relation to persons; certain powers that cause disease, childlessness, sin and the like to men are moving about in the air and cause trouble. The chief use of the mantra-science is to turn these back towards those who are not ours."

"Some Piśācas who move on the earth are not harmful; they even help us. They help in getting back the lost, and they grant a long life to the bride…"

original p. 699

"…Arbuda is the chief of a group of Piśācas, who cause fear to enemies and help us in wars (Av. 3-?-?; 3-?-?; 11-?-?)."

Eschatology (Antimagati śāstra) — The Doctrine of the Last Journey

Funeral rites (Āntyakriye). "In the Vedas there are very few sentences relating to death. The ones that do occur incidentally are only to pray that death may come to enemies and that one's own life may be long. Thought about the other world arises only at the time of the funeral. Burning and burying of dead bodies are both customary. In 10-?-? the burning rite, and in another (10-?-? to ?) the burial, are mentioned. 'The house of earth' too is said in one place (7-?-?). Fathers burnt in the fire and those not burnt are both seen (10-?-?; Av. 18-?-?). Burning is the right way for the dead to go to the upper world. In the books describing rites, it is laid down that only the ashes and bones of the burnt, and of children and ascetics, are to be buried (compare Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 4-?)."

"With the funeral, the history of the next-world life is connected. Agni takes the dead body to another world, to the neighbourhood of the Fathers and the deities (10-?-? to ?; 10-?-?). He places the mortal in the most excellent immortality (1-?-?). Ancient seers, those born at first, have gone to the very high place of Sūrya, to the highest heaven, or to the world of the virtuous, through Agni, the bird of the world of the deities, and men go there (Vāj. Saṃ. 18-?, ?); Agni, the lord of the household, leads the dead to the world of the virtuous (Av. 6-?-?). Agni first burns the body of the dead and then places him in the world of the ṛtvijas (Av. 18-?-?). The Agni that burns the dead (kravyāda) is different from the Agni that carries oblations to the deities (10-?-?). It is prayed that Agni should burn the goat, his share, and protect the body (10-?-?). The dead body is placed on the skin of a black goat, and in the sacrifice a cow or a goat is sacrificed. In the matter of the body, Agni and Soma are prayed to heal at the time of burning the cows (the wounds) that may have been made by any bird, beast, ant or serpent (10-?-?)."

"It is believed that the soul of the dead goes to heaven with the smoke (Āś. Gṛ. Sū. 4-?-?). It is a very long way; there Pūṣan is the protector and Savitṛ the one who shows the way (10-?-?). The sacrificed goat goes ahead to the Fathers and makes known the coming of the dead soul. On the way, the dead is made to cross the black dog, and then he must cross the third inner stage of heaven, the place of the Fathers (compare Av. 8-?-?, ?; 9-?-?)."

"So that it may be useful to the life in the other world, ornaments and clothes are offered to the dead person's soul; this practice is current still (Av. 14-?-?). His wife and…"

original p. 700

"…weapons too are indicated as burnt along with the corpse (10-?-?, ?). A rope was tied round the corpse. The aim of this is that the soul of the dead should not know the way to come back (Av. 8-?-?; 10-?-?; and 18-?-?)."

The soul (Ātman). "Agni or funeral pyres consume only the body; they cannot destroy the personality of the dead. Even in the state of unconsciousness, the life can be separated from the body, and it is believed that life remains even after the body is destroyed. The whole of sūkta 10-58 calls back the life of one bound like a captive. In the Ṛgveda there seems to be no basis for the belief that the soul takes another body; but in the Brāhmaṇas it is said that one who has not performed sacrifices in the prescribed manner, dying, is born again and is subject to death again (Śat. Brā. 10-?-?-?). Prāṇa, ātman, asu (the power of the body, 1-?-?; 1-?-?), manas (the support for thought and feelings, located in the heart; 8-?-?) — all of these indicate the soul. Many sentences, especially in the Atharvaveda, say: if there is asu or manas, there is life; otherwise death. Asunīti or asunīta is the name of the path along which the souls of the dead are taken from this world to the upper world (10-?-?; 10-?-?). The words asu or manas are not used in the mantras of the funeral; they use the words father, mother and so on. For this reason the 'soul' is not a thing without form; it too has a personality. Only after men have given up the body is immortality attained (Śat. Brā. 10-?-?-?); as heaven and the other worlds are material, the body too has an important place. In the existence of other worlds the body too has a share (10-?-?; Av. 11-?-?). A body free of any fault (Av. 6-?-?) is not an ordinary earthly body; it is a body purified by the power of Agni (compare 10-?-?), what the present Vedāntins would call the 'subtle body'. If, after burning, the bones that remain to be collected are destroyed, it is said that this is a harsh punishment (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?; 14-?-?-?); from this it can be understood how important the place of the corpse is. In 10-?-?, ? it is said that the eyes of the dead go to Sūrya and the breath to the wind. But it is not clear that, after Agni takes the dead to the other world, each limb goes to a separate place. This may have been said following the description of the Virāṭ-Puruṣa. In the same sentence (10-?-?; 10-?-? to ?) it is said that the life of the dead enters the water or the crops; probably this is the beginning of the 'entering another body' idea."

"Proceeding along the path followed by the Fathers (10-?-?), the life of the dead goes to the world of eternal light (9-?-?); then, in a chariot of a splendour equal to the deities (Av. 11-?-?) or on wings (4-?-?), killing ghosts…"

original p. 701

"…it goes on the wings which Agni uses (Vāj. Saṃ. 18-?). Pushed upward by the Maruts, serving the beneficent Vāyu and filled with the waters of the rain, the soul regains its old form (Av. 18-?-? to ?), and, distinguished by splendour, goes with Yama to the highest heaven, where the Fathers pass time with delight (10-?-?, ?; 10-?-?, ?). It is said that, in order to reach heaven in this way, one must return home (astam, 10-?-?). Yama, recognizing him as his own (Av. 18-?-?), gives him also a place of rest (10-?-?)."

"According to the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, the dead leave this world and go along a path between two dogs; the dogs burn the wicked souls and let only the best pass ahead. Thus the best souls that go ahead continue, taking the path to the neighbourhood of the Fathers or the path that goes near Sūrya (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?; etc.). In the Upaniṣads, two paths are told to those who have obtained the knowledge of Brahman: one (for those of complete knowledge) goes to the world of Brahman, the second is the path of heaven. When the fruits of their meritorious acts are exhausted, they come back from this heaven and are again born on earth. Those who have no knowledge of the Self go to the world of evil deities or ghosts, or are born again on earth as wicked."

Heaven (Svarga). "The place where the Fathers and Yama dwell is in the middle of the sky, standing on eternal light (10-?-?), in the highest heaven (10-?-?), in the third heaven, in the deepest regions of the sky (9-?-? to ?).
