In the Atharvaveda too it is the same: the very high (Av. 11-?-?) and the world of lustre (4-?-?), the back of the sky (Av. 18-?-?), the third sky (Av. 8-?-?, ?; 18-?-?) and the third heaven (Av. 18-?-?) are described as the worlds of the Fathers and the place of Yama. In the Maitrāyaṇī Saṃhitā (Mai. Saṃ. 1-?-?; 2-?-?) the world of the Fathers is the third world. The world of the Fathers is the very highest part of the sphere of the sun (9-?-?). The Fathers have gone with Sūrya or protect Sūrya (10-?-?; 10-?-?), or have joined the rays of Sūrya (10-?-?; compare Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?), and Sūrya shines for them (3-?-?). There is a relation between them and the foot of Viṣṇu (10-?-?), and it is said that the righteous rejoice at the third step of Viṣṇu in that beloved dwelling (1-?-?). As Viṣṇu placed his three steps in the place where the deities rejoice, so the virtuous go to the place where oblations are offered, and Sūrya also goes there, carrying Uṣas in his lap."

"The lights of the virtuous who go to heaven are the stars (Tai. Saṃ. 5-?-?-?; Śat. Brā. 6-?-?-?), and the seven ancient seers were raised to the group of stars (Tai. Ā. 1-?-?-?)."

original p. 702

Heaven, continued "In the Ṛgveda a tree is mentioned. Near it Yama drinks, seated with the deities (10-?-?). In the Atharvaveda (Av. 5-?-?) it is said that this is a tree of Atri."

"Life in the other world is dealt with especially in the ninth and tenth maṇḍalas, and generally in the first. To those who perform severe penance, the fruit of their penance is heaven; and the same fruit goes to those who die in battle (10-?-? to ?). But more than all these, heaven is the fruit for those who generously give the substances of homa (10-?-?; 1-?-?; 10-?-?). The fruits obtained from sacrifices and such acts are described much more in the Atharvaveda."

"The dead experience in heaven a very delightful life (10-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?, ?); there all desired objects are fulfilled (9-?-?, ?); among the deities (10-?-?), and especially in the presence of Yama and Varuṇa, there is this kind of life (10-?-?). There is no talk of old age (10-?-?). Distinguished by beautiful bodies, they are dear to the deities and are wished for by them (10-?-?; 10-?-?; 10-?-?). There they see father, mother, children and others (Av. 6-?-?), and meet again with wife, children and the rest (Av. 12-?-?). In that life there is not the least trace of defects; likewise there is no bodily suffering (10-?-?; Av. 6-?-?). All the diseased remain on the earth; lameness, a crooked belly or a hump and such defects are not there (Av. 3-?-?). In that world they are joined with a complete body, say the Atharvaveda and the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa."

"The dead are happy in heaven and rejoice (modante, mādayante: 10-?-?; 10-?-?, etc.). The happiness of life in heaven is given in great detail in 9-113, 114. There the light is constant; the waters flow quickly; there is no obstacle to the flow (compare Tai. Brā. 3-?-?-?). There too is food in the form of svadhā (what is offered to the Fathers), and satisfaction; there is contentment, joy and the gaining of desired objects. The happiness spoken of there as joy and contentment, without being plain, is later explained as sensual pleasure (compare Tai. Brā. 2-?-?-?; Śat. Brā. 10-?-?-?). In the Atharvaveda it is said that sensual pleasure is obtained there as one wishes (Av. 4-?-?). A hundred times more happiness than the greatest felt on earth is experienced there (Śat. Brā. 14-?-?-?, ?). In that world of the virtuous, the sound of the flute and of song is heard (10-?-?); streams of Soma juice, ghee, honey and milk flow for those who live there (Av. 4-?-?, ?; Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?). Cows, clean, of various colours and giving desired things, are always ready (kāmadughāḥ, Av. 4-?-?). There, no distinction of poor and rich, great and small exists (Av. 3-?-?)."

original p. 703

"This heavenly happiness described in the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas is said in the Upaniṣads to be not eternal and not the best; to those alone who know the truth of immortality are attained the unity with Brahman and the eternal bliss that arises from it. For that reason, the idea is that those who have done good deeds, after death, pass time in the heaven-world, desirous of pleasure, like (Somapāri) Soma-drinkers."

"Heaven is more glorious than this world and full of sensual pleasure. It is the world of those who do good deeds (10-?-?); here those who know the rites pass the time in joy. They enjoy the fruits of the homas they performed and the gifts they gave; and among these, the more they gave to priests and others, the greater the happiness (10-?-?). Those who have performed sacrificial rites in the prescribed way gain, not only the worlds of Āditya and Agni, but also union with the worlds of Vāyu, Indra, Varuṇa, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati and Brahmā (Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?; 10-?-?-?; 11-?-?-?, ?; Tai. Brā. 3-?-?-?). It is said that a certain seer, by the power of his knowledge, took the form of a golden swan, went to heaven and attained union with Sūrya (Tai. Brā. 3-?-?-?). In the Taittirīya Saṃhitā the view is that, by performing certain acts, man may attain heaven in this very physical body (Tai. Brā. 6-?-?-?)."

"Those who practise the Veda in the prescribed manner become free from the fear of birth and death and attain equality with Brahmā (Śat. Brā. 10-?-?-?). By the result of learning some secret matter, man is born again (Śat. Brā. 1-?-?-?). In these the beginning of the ideas of the fruits of sin and of transmigration may be seen. These are fully expounded in the Upaniṣads such as Chāndogya, Bṛhadāraṇyaka and Kaṭha, and in the Sūtras. The Kaṭhopaniṣad tells the story of Naciketas; in it the main part is the dialogue of Naciketas and Yama. Those who are not fit for heaven and release, again and again subject to death, are caught in the wheel of worldly existence, and are born on earth, if not as embodied beings, as inert matter; one who has self-control of mind can attain the world of Viṣṇu; there is no hell for those who are unable to attain release: so Yama instructs Naciketas."

Hell (Naraka)

"Though, alongside the statement that the virtuous obtain heaven and the like in the other world, no punishments are laid down for the wicked, there must be a separate place for them. The Atharvaveda and the Kaṭhopaniṣad say plainly that such people experience the fruits of their sinful acts in hell. As opposed to the world of heaven there is the hell-world (the world below) where female Piśācas and others dwell (Av. 12-?-?; Av. 2-?-?; 5-?-?); the murderer experiences punishment in this world (Vāj. Saṃ. 30-?). In the lowest region, darkness (Av. 8-?-?;"

original p. 704

"etc.), darkness covered with gloom (Av. 5-?-?), pitch darkness (Av. 18-?-?, etc.) — this world is described thus. The sufferings of hell are described in Av. 5-?, and still more fully in Śat. Brā. 11-?. The same Brāhmaṇa says: everyone is born again after death; his deeds are weighed in a balance; the virtuous experience happiness and the wicked suffering according to their deeds (Śat. Brā. 11-?-?-?; 12-?-?-?). But there is no basis, even in the Ṛgveda, for denying that there is such a place for experiencing sorrow. 'This deep place has been created for the wicked, for those who speak untruth, and for the untruthful' (4-?-?). Indra and Soma are prayed to throw the wicked into the nether world, into bottomless darkness, so that not one of them may rise again (7-?-?); like the owl, the Rākṣasī who moves about unseen by anyone should fall in the darkness (7-?-?); the hater and the one who speaks harshly should fall below the three earths (7-?-?). These sentences only make known that there is a region below the earth covered with darkness. The pleasures of this earth are the main aim; the happiness and sorrows after death are not so much the main concern. In the Brāhmaṇas it is only said that those who did good deeds and those who did evil are born again in another world and experience the fruits of their deeds (Śat. Brā. 6-?-?-?; 10-?-?-?); the duration of this suffering or punishment is not stated. It is also a belief that those who do not understand rightly the rules of the sacrificial limbs and do not practise them go to another world, before the time fixed for them in the world of earth (Śat. Brā. 10-?-?-?)."

"There is, one may say, no basis in the Vedas for the belief that after death each one is judged as good or bad according to his deeds. The one or two sentences cited above are not clear. In the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (Tai. Ā. 6-?-?) it is only said that Yama separates those who go the right path from those who go the wrong path; it is not said that he has the highest authority to decide this."

The Fathers (Pitṛgaḷu)

"Among the dead, the virtuous live in the third heaven; to them the name Pitṛ ('Fathers') is given. They are the original forefathers who followed the ancient paths (10-?-?, ?). The dead, following the very path these seers made, go to their neighbourhood (10-?-?, ?, ?). They are related to the third step of Viṣṇu (10-?-?; compare 1-?-?). Two sūktas have the Fathers as deity (10-15; 10-54)."

"Among the Fathers there are groups: Navagvas, Virūpas, Aṅgirases, Atharvans, Bhṛgus and Vasiṣṭhas (10-?-? to ?; 10-?-?); of these the last four names are the names of the seers of the second and seventh maṇḍalas of the Atharvaveda and the Ṛgveda. Among these…"

original p. 705

"the Aṅgirases have a special relation to Yama too (10-?-?, ?). Among the Fathers there are divisions as avarāḥ (those of lower rank), parāḥ (those of higher rank) and madhyamāḥ (those of middle rank). Though they are not known by their descendants, Agni knows all of them (10-?-?, ?, ?). Together with the Uṣases, rivers, mountains, heaven and earth, Pūṣan and the Ṛbhus, their favour is also prayed for (6-?-?; 6-?-?; 2-?-?; 1-?-?). Prayers for their kindly look (10-?-?) are made to give their descendants wealth, progeny and long life (10-?-?, ?; Av. 18-?-?; 18-?-?). They pray to Vasiṣṭha to help their lineage (7-?-?; compare 10-?-?); and Turuṣya, Yadu and Ugradeva are praised as a party of three (1-?-?)."

"The Fathers too are immortal (Av. 6-?-?) and are called deities (10-?-?). With the Aṅgirases and some other groups, priesthood too is joined to deity-hood. The works of creation are also stated of some Fathers; it was they who made the sky studded with stars; day was made bright and night dark by them (10-?-?); they found the hidden light and gave birth to Uṣas (7-?-?; compare 10-?-?); and joined with Soma, they spread out earth and sky (8-?-?). As the Agni who carries oblations to the deities (havyavāha) and the Agni who burns corpses (kravyāda) are different (10-?-?), so the paths of the deities and of the Fathers are different (10-?-?; 10-?-?; compare 10-?-?). In the same way a distinction between the world of heaven and the world of the Fathers is stated: the door of the deity-world is in the north-east (Śat. Brā. 6-?-?-?) and the door of the Fathers' world in the south-east (Śat. Brā. 13-?-?-?). The Fathers and men are different classes, and their creation too is different (Tai. Brā. 3-?-?-?). The Fathers are dwellers on earth, in the sphere of the air and in heaven (Av. 18-?-?; Ṛk. Ve. 10-?-?)."

"The ancient Fathers once offered Soma oblation (10-?-?). They pass time happily with Yama (10-?-?; 10-?-?; Av. 18-?-?) and eat with the deities (2-?-?). Living like the deities, they sometimes obtain worship suited to the deities. They come in the same chariot as Indra and the deities (10-?-?). They too long for Soma juice (10-?-?, ?); seated on the darbha seat, with the dakṣiṇā in front, they drink the pressed pāṇīya (10-?-?, ?). They are eager to drink Soma juice prepared for them; they are invited to come with Yama, their father Vivasvān and Agni, and to accept what has been offered (10-?-? to ?; 10-?-?, ?). They are invited to come in thousands, to sit in order on the darbha seat…"

original p. 706

The Fathers, end "…[to sit in order on the darbha seat…] and to partake [of the offering] (10-?-?, ?). When the Fathers come to the sacrificial hall, some Piśācas too, in the form of their friends, may mix with them (Av. 18-?-?)."

"When food is offered to the deities they say 'svāhā', and when it is given to the Fathers 'svadhā' (10-?-?); in all rites this difference between the shares of the deities and of the Fathers must exist (Śat. Brā. 2-?-?-?). They too are worshipped. There is also the prayer that they should listen to the prayers of their followers, take their side, and forgive the mistakes that happen naturally (10-?-?, ?, ?; compare 3-?-?)."

Yama

"Among all the virtuous dead, Yama is the chief. Because the Vedas have not much to say about the other world, Yama is praised in only three sūktas (10-14, 10-?, 10-?). In another (10-10) there is a dialogue between Yama and his sister Yamī. The name of Yama occurs about fifty times, in general once in the first and eighth maṇḍalas, and most of all in the tenth."

"He is always engaged in play with the deities (2-?-?; 10-?-?). He is mentioned along with Varuṇa (10-?-?), Bṛhaspati (10-?-?; 10-?-?) and, especially, Agni, who leads the souls of the dead to other worlds. Agni is Yama's friend (10-?-?) and purohita (10-?-?). One deity and Yama (the two being indicated as one) together found Agni, who was hidden (10-?-?). Agni, Yama and Mātariśvan are three names of one (1-?-?). Yama is included in the list of Agni and other deities (10-?-?; 10-?-?)."

"From the sentences above it can be guessed that Yama too is a deity. He is not plainly called a deity; he is said to be king of the dead (Yamarājñaḥ, 10-?-?). After death, the soul sees the two, Yama and the deity Varuṇa (10-?-?). One whole sūkta (10-14) deals with the relation between Yama and the Fathers, and in it too there is special mention of the Aṅgirases. Yama comes with them to the sacrifice and is pleased (10-?-?, ?; 10-?-?). The matter of his horses, with golden eyes and with the lustre of dark clouds, is raised (Tai. Ā. 6-?-?; Āp. Śrau. Sū. 14-?-?). He is the one who gathers all the people (10-?-?); he provides a place of rest for the dead (10-?-?; Av. 18-?-?) and provides a separate dwelling-house for him (10-?-?)."

"Yama's dwelling is in a corner of the sky (9-?-?). Of the three heavens, two belong to Savitṛ and one to Yama (1-?-?; compare 1-?-?); the world of Yama is the third and the very highest. In the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā (Vāj. Saṃ. 18-?) it is said that Yama and Yamī live in heaven at this highest place. In this place of his — this is also the place of the deities — the sound of the flute and of song is heard around Yama (10-?-?)."

original p. 707

"For Yama, Soma-juice is prepared and ghee offered (10-?-?, ?); and he is prayed to come to the sacrificial hall and be seated on the seat (10-?-?)."

"Vivasvat is his father (10-?-?), and a woman named Saraṇyū is said to be his mother (10-?-?). He is many times called Vaivasvata (10-?-?; etc.). Since he has no superior, Yama alone is greater than Vivasvat (Av. 18-?-?; 18-?-?, ?; compare)."

"In the dialogue between Yama and Yamī, they both say that they are children of a Gandharva and a water-goddess (apyā yoṣā) (10-?-?). Yamī says that Yama alone is mortal (10-?-?). It is said that Yama gave up his body and desired death itself (10-?-?). Showing the path to the many who would come afterwards, he went to another world; here the ancient Fathers too have gone (10-?-?, ?). He is the first of all the dead mortals (Av. 18-?-?). 'Mortals' here must be men; but in some other contexts, by the word 'mortal', the deities too are indicated. Since he is the first and very ancient of the virtuous, it is natural that all of them should be known as his people. He has the epithets Viśpati ('lord of all settled ones'), and 'our father' (10-?-?). Through Yama, later, the family-name of all men, 'descendants of the Āditya Vivasvān', has come about (Tai. Saṃ. 6-?-?-?; Śat. Brā. 3-?-?-?; and compare Ṛg. 1-?-?). The 'horse that moves in the sky' given by Yama must be the place Yama gives to those who have become immortal (1-?-?; compare 1-?-?); so one may say that the relation of Yama and the sun is stated in the Ṛgveda too."

"Death itself is the path of Yama (1-?-?) and once (1-?-?; Mai. Saṃ. 2-?-?; Av. 6-?-? and 6-?-?) he is also called Death. The shackles used by Yama are equal to Varuṇa's noose (10-?-?). By such sentences and by the characteristics of his messengers, Yama can be shown to be terrible. In the Atharvaveda and other Vedic histories, since death and the sufferings after death are said to be caused by Yama, Yama is counted as the deity of death. But in the Purāṇas too, it is plainly said that hell alone is not Yama's kingdom. In other Saṃhitās also, Yama is one among the list of Antaka, Mṛtyu and Nirṛti (disease) (Vāj. Saṃ. 39-?; Av. 6-?-?; Mai. Saṃ. 2-?-?), and Death is his messenger (Av. 5-?-?; 18-?-?; etc.). Death is the lord of men, and Yama the lord of the dead…"

original p. 708

"(Av. 5-?-?, ?); Sleep (the deity presiding over sleep) is said to come from Yama's kingdom (Av. 6-?-?)."

"The word yama is also used in the sense of 'twin' (yama), generally in the masculine or feminine dual (yamau), and in some places in the sense 'rein' (yama) or 'guide' (mārgadarśaka). Yama and Yamī are conceived as twins (10-?-?). In other books, in describing Yama as a god of death, a harsh teacher and the like, the idea is that this word is derived from the root yam ('to restrain'); but for this there is hardly any basis in the Vedas."

"A bird — generally the owl or the pigeon — is Yama's messenger (10-?-?; compare 10-?-?). Here Yama himself is thought of as Death; therefore Yama and Death have one and the same messenger (8-?-?). A little more fully discussed is the matter of the two dogs who are Yama's appointed messengers (10-?-? to ?). They have four eyes and broad noses; their bodies are spotted and brown; they are the children of Saramā (Sārameya). They are guards who protect the path to Yama's world (10-?-?), or are seated on that path (Av. 18-?-?). To the dead man it is advised: 'Cross by these two dogs and go quickly and join the Fathers' (10-?-?). Yama is prayed to hand the dead over to the Fathers and to grant him well-being and health. Having been satisfied in their own life-form, they move like Yama's messengers among men. They too (the dogs) are prayed to be gracious to men so that they may enjoy the light of the sun for ever. They are watching which of men shall die and at what times, and their work must be to protect the blind on the path to Yama's world. There is basis for saying that these dogs do not harm the wicked on this path; this idea comes in the sentences of 7-?-? onward. To indicate Yama's messengers, words in both the plural and the dual are used in the Atharvaveda (Av. 8-?-?; 8-?-?; 5-?-?). Of the two dogs, one is Śabala and the other Śyāma (Av. 8-?-?). Some think the two dogs are Yama and Yamī themselves; some, the sun and moon. Some think that Yama is the representative of one part of nature — a special form of Agni, Sūrya, the evening time, or the setting sun; and that therefore there may be a deity of death —" Here the Pariśiṣṭa ends: the last line of the print breaks off in mid-sentence, with a small printer's ornament below and the printer's imprint:) "ಶ್ರೀ ಚಾಮುಂಡೇಶ್ವರೀ ಎಲೆಕ್ಟ್ರಿಕ್ ಪ್ರೆಸ್, ಕ್ಲಾಕ್ ಟವರ್ ಸ್ಕ್ವೇರ್, ಮೈಸೂರು, 1950" — Śrī Cāmuṇḍeśvarī Electric Press, Clock Tower Square, Mysore, 1950. Close of the Pariśiṣṭa and of Volume 5

Note on the translation of the Pariśiṣṭa (added at the user's request, 2026-10-06): the whole appendix (printed pp. 531–708) is now translated into English, page by page. It is a Kannada prose essay without Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya; the Sanskrit words and phrases in it are given in Devanagari + IAST + English; the bracketed Ṛgveda/Atharvaveda/Brāhmaṇa references (small Kannada digits) are reproduced as read at 150 dpi and are unverified — digits that could not be read are shown as "?" throughout, and passages where the print was crowded are rendered loosely. The statement in the header of this file that "the Pariśiṣṭa is not being translated" is therefore out of date, the file being append-only. The contents of the Pariśiṣṭa follow the list given in the header (deities of the heavenly region, of the atmosphere, of the earth; abstract-idea deities; female deities; paired deities; groups; the Ṛbhus; Apsarases; Gandharvas; protective deities; historical/imaginary seers and persons; animals; material things, implements and images; evil deities and Piśācas; and the eschatology: funeral rites, soul, heaven, hell, the Fathers, Yama).

74. p. 208 adds: the formation aśvayuḥ is made, in the sense of "one who wishes the horse for sacrificers", with the kyac from the Vedic rule; Yāska's other explanation takes the suffix u added to the kyac-ending stem in the sense "who has"; for example vasūyuḥ = "Indra, who has wealth"; so words like aśvayuḥ are also valid in the sense of possession — this is the sense.

The grammatical tail, p. 507, is characterized, not transcribed: asya — the word idam, the ending acute; ririce — ricir virecane, the perfect in the passive sense (chandasi luṅlaṅliṭaḥ), eś in place of ta, reduplication; pṛthivyāḥ — udāttayaṇo hal pūrvāt; svarāṭ — rāja dīptau, kvip, jaśtva; dame — damu upaśame, ghañ in the passive, the vṛddhi barred (Pā. 7-3-34 as read [?]); viśvagūrtaḥ — gṝ nigaraṇe / gūrī udyamane, kta, gūrta; amatraḥ — ama gatyādiṣu, atran (Uṇ. 3-[?]); vavakṣe — vah, leṭ, sip, śap → ślu, reduplication, hoḍhaḥ, ṣaḍhoḥ kaḥ si; raṇāya — the dative, kriyāgrahaṇaṃ kartavyam (the vārttika), or gatyarthakarmaṇi (Pā. 2-3-12 as read [?]).

30. pp. 508–509 — noted briefly

31. The grammatical tail, p. 510, characterized, not transcribed: śuṣantam — śuṣa śoṣaṇe, śa in place of śyan by vyatyaya, the accent of the vikaraṇa remains; vrāṇāḥ — vṛñ varaṇe, passive laṭ, śānac, the yak lost by bahulaṃ chandasi, yaṇ; avanīḥ — ava rakṣaṇe, the suffix ani in the instrumental sense (Uṇ. 3-[?] [?]), acute on the suffix; dāvane — āto manin kvanib vanipaś ca [as read, ?]: vanip, the a-elision not applied in the dative, by Vedic licence.

32. pp. 511–512 — noted briefly

33. Reading note: havirdātre — in the print the letters after havir-dā are crowded (dātravaśe-like); havirdātre is read, [?]. The grammatical tail, pp. 513–514, is characterized, not transcribed, below under the Vyākaraṇa notes.

34. p. 514 — noted briefly

35. Reading note: The Saṃhitā's tiraścēṣyan is read as tiraśceṣyan — tiraścā followed by iṣyan — as the Pada has tiraścā | iṣyan; the long ā of bharā and radā is the Saṃhitā lengthening of bhara, rada before a vowel/iti-less particle, noted in the grammar page.

36. The grammatical tail, p. 516 — characterized, not transcribed: bhara (the bha for ha, the Saṃhitā lengthening); tūtujānaḥ (tuja hiṃsāyām, kānac, the reduplicative vowel lengthened, the initial acute); kiyedhāḥ (explained under the sixth Rik); rada; tiraścā (tiryañc, kvin, the n lost, the elision of a in the instrumental, ścutva, the ending acute); iṣyan (iṣa gatau, śyan, nit); caradhyai (cara gatibhakṣaṇayoḥ, the infinitive adhyai).

37. pp. 517–518 — noted briefly

38. Reading note: in the print's Saṃhitā, line 2, iṣṇānaḥ is joined to the next word as yad iṣṇāna āyudhāni; the Pada has iṣṇānaḥ | āyudhāni.

39. The grammatical tail, p. 519, characterized, not transcribed: turasya — tura tvaraṇe, the suffix ka; navyaḥ — ṇu stutau, yat, āv for o; iṣṇānaḥ — iṣa ābhīkṣṇye, kryādi, the middle voice by vyatyaya, śānac; ṛghāyamāṇaḥ — explained in the passage Ṛg 1-101-4 [?]; nirināti — rī gatireṣaṇayoḥ, śnā, shortening; the absence of nighāta because of the relative yat (yadvṛttayogāt).

40. p. 520 — noted briefly

41. Reading note: the Saṃhitā has bhūmā, the Pada bhūma; the grammar page explains the Saṃhitā form with ā and the position of ca between dyāvā and bhūmā.

42. The grammatical tail, p. 521 foot, characterized, not transcribed: dyāvā ca bhūmā (divo dyāvā, ḍā for the dual, both members keeping their accents); januṣaḥ (janer usiḥ, an Uṇādi suffix); joguvānaḥ (guja avyakte śabde, yaṅluk, śānac, uvaṅ); oṇim (oṇṛ apanayane, the Uṇādi i); bhuvat (leṭ, aṭ, no guṇa); nodhāḥ (Yāska: "nodhā ṛṣir bhavati navanaṃ dadhātīti", Ni. 4-16 [?]; dhāñ, asun, nava → no).

43. pp. 522–523 — noted briefly

44. Reading note: the Saṃhitā prints dāyy eṣām as dāyyeṣām, i.e. dāyi eṣām with y before e; It is given as the Pada does.

45. Reading note: the Pada's word before āvat is printed susvim, with a plain s, while the Saṃhitā has suṣvim and the grammar page treats it as from ṣuñ abhiṣave: The Pada is given as printed with [?], not adjusted.

46. The grammatical tail, p. 524 foot, characterized, not transcribed: dāyi (the a-augment absent by bahulaṃ chandasy amāṅyoge 'pi); vavne (vanu yācane, the perfect, the penultimate lost by vyatyaya); paspṛdhānam (spardha saṃgharṣe, kānac, reduplication, the p remaining by śarpūrvāḥ khayaḥ, citaḥ); sauvaśvye (svaśva as a country-name that is also used of a kṣatriya, vā nāmadheyasya vṛddhasaṃjñā vaktavyā, ñyaṅ, no vṛddhi after v, initial acute by ñit); suṣvim (ṣuñ abhiṣave, kin, doubling by the perfect-like rule, yaṇ).

47. pp. 525–526 — noted briefly

48. The grammatical tail, p. 527 foot, characterized, not transcribed: eva — the Saṃhitā lengthening of the particle (evā); suvṛkti — loss of the accusative-plural ending; akran — kṛ, luṅ, the loss of cli (mantre ghasahvara…), ant, yaṇ, the aṭ augment; dhāḥ — dhā, luṅ in the sense of loṭ, loss of sic, no aṭ.
